Nature and mark are again not different: mark is the manifestation of nature and nature is the root of mark; to have the root but not manifest it is to have substance without function, and therefore the Buddha does not dwell in nirvāṇa. Why? Because living beings are clinging precisely to these marks, and if the Buddha did not manifest these marks he could not deliver them; therefore realizing the substance of the nature is originally for the sake of arising in practice. That the Small Vehicle is censured by the Buddha as a scorched sprout and a rotten seed, fallen into the pit of non-action, is for this reason. This section of text precisely unfolds this principle, so that one may know the reason why the Buddha has people dwell neither in the marks of dharmas nor in the marks of non-dharmas.

The Buddha teaches people to cultivate in order to deliver living beings; if one falls into the pit of non-action, how can one deliver? Therefore prajñā's essential point is not dwelling in either extreme: one must not dwell in existence and not dwell in emptiness before one can accord with the nature. Again, the nature is without marks and yet not without marks. Because it is without marks, one must not cling to existence and must not dwell in dharmas. Because it is not without marks, one must not cling to emptiness and must not dwell in non-dharmas. Precisely because the nature is without marks and yet not without marks, ordinary people cling to the one side of existence and cannot see the nature, and the Small Vehicle clings to the one side of nothingness and likewise cannot see the nature. The thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises say nothing but this principle, and the commentaries of the great masters unfold nothing but this principle.

Therefore the 'body-mark' here should not be spoken with regard to the Buddha's body, but must be spoken with regard to the body-mark of living beings themselves. From the Buddha above to all living beings below, all possess this mark. The Buddha realized the dharma-body, and so is called the Tathagata; and all living beings, in their joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure and the stirring of their minds, are fundamentally unawakened. Yet what can become a Buddha is precisely this mind of living beings. Hence this mind is the Tathagata; it is only obscured by ignorance, and so is named the Tathagata-garbha. The Buddha's asking this is to test Subhuti and the assembly, and even living beings of the future: how, after all, can the not dwelling in marks that I have spoken above allow one to see the nature in marks? If one answered that the Tathagata can be seen, one would be dwelling in the marks of dharmas, an ordinary person. If one answered that the Tathagata cannot be seen, one would be dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas, of the Small Vehicle.
(Chou) Second, the answer. Again two: (Yin) First, the double clarification; second, the explanation accomplished.
(Yin) First, the double clarification.
'No, World-Honored One. One cannot see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark.'

Readers of the Diamond Sutra have always read 'one cannot see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark' as one sentence. Miaoxu has recited and upheld this sutra for more than forty years, and some ten-odd years ago happened to realize that it should be read as two sentences, though he still dared not decide. Later, reading Master Nanyue's lecture on the Lotus Sutra — 'only a Buddha together with a Buddha can exhaust the real mark of all dharmas: what is called the suchlike mark of dharmas, the suchlike nature, the suchlike substance, the suchlike power, the suchlike action, the suchlike cause, the suchlike condition, the suchlike fruit, the suchlike reward, the suchlike beginning, end, and ultimate equality' — which has three ways of dividing the sentences, he then dared to decide on two sentences. But this sort of method can be used only with the sutras of the emptiness school and with the sutras translated by Master Kumarajiva.

The old explanations hold that the body-mark is of course empty: spoken from the dharma-body, the transformation body too is an illusory mark, and so it is said that the Tathagata cannot be seen. Yet the meaning is not exhausted; by such an explanation one would be dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas. One must know that the 'no' in 'No, World-Honored One' is a hesitant yes and no, and cannot be taken wholly as a negation. Since he answers 'cannot' and yet says 'can,' it is a double clarification. Moreover, if it were entirely a negation, why should the next line add the word 'see'? Subhuti's meaning is that one cannot take the mark as the nature and see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark; yet the mark is manifested from the nature, and so one can also see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark. Hence the following text again declares 'the body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata.'

Read as one sentence, it makes no sense in fact, in principle, or in wording. If one answered thus, that the Tathagata cannot be seen by means of the body-mark, then Subhuti would have awakened only to the point that marks are marks and the nature is the nature — still a Small Vehicle view, fallen into one-sided emptiness, not the supreme-meaning emptiness; how could he be called foremost in understanding emptiness? Moreover, in the preceding eight assemblies it was always Subhuti who was the interlocutor, and he had even spoken on the World-Honored One's behalf of the principle of clinging to neither extreme. How could he here, on the contrary, fail to understand? This does not accord with the facts. In the opening sequence of this sutra, the World-Honored One, in dressing and eating, displayed the great emptiness samādhi. The crowd did not know it, but Subhuti had already grasped its principle, and as soon as he opened his mouth he praised the World-Honored One as rare: 'the Tathagata is good at protecting and remembering the bodhisattvas, good at entrusting the bodhisattvas.' Plainly he saw the Tathagata manifesting the marks of an ordinary person, and saw that marks do not obstruct the nature. How could it be that after the World-Honored One's two rounds of instruction he still saw only one side, with nature and mark unreconciled? Then the word 'rare' in the preceding text would have no ground, and the two phrases 'the Tathagata is good at protecting and remembering' would be utterly meaningless. This does not accord with principle. Again, read in this way, it would be entirely a negation, and the one line 'No, World-Honored One' would suffice; why add 'see the Tathagata by means of the body-mark,' and why add the word 'see'? This does not accord with the wording.
(Yin) Second, the explanation accomplished.
'Why is this? The body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata is not the body-mark.'

That the body-mark as spoken of by the Tathagata is not the body-mark is the double illumination of both extremes. The nature is the substance of the mark, and the mark is the function of the nature. The mark cannot be fused without the nature, and the nature cannot be revealed without the mark. Apart from the mark there is no nature to speak of, and apart from the nature there is no mark to speak of. It is only a matter of whether one clings or not. One who clings to marks finds that the mark becomes an obstruction and he cannot see the nature; therefore the answer is 'cannot.' If one does not cling, then in the mark one can see the nature. A mark is like the surface of a thing and the nature like its interior: if the surface of a thing is clear as glass, one can see its interior. Hence the answer is that the Tathagata can be seen by means of the body-mark. For not clinging is not falling to either extreme, and one need not, like the Small Vehicle, annihilate form to reveal emptiness and annihilate marks to see the nature — which is the following text's 'one does not speak of the mark of annihilation.' The whole principle of prajñā lies herein, and one must contemplate and illuminate it and work at it carefully.

With regard to the mark, one speaks of the body-mark; with regard to the nature, one speaks of the very substance being empty, the nature being fundamentally without marks. With regard to the mark, one says that mark is mark and nature is nature, that the mark is false and the nature is real — hence 'cannot.' With regard to the nature, one says that the mark is originally empty in its very substance and that the nature can fuse the mark, so that the principle of the real is at once revealed; why then must one leave the false mark to see the real nature? Hence 'can see the Tathagata.' Only such an explanation accords with Subhuti's role as interlocutor in requesting the Dharma. The crowd, seeing the Buddha dress and eat and manifest the marks of an ordinary person, clung to the marks of an ordinary person and did not see the Tathagata. Subhuti saw the nature through the mark and, knowing the Buddha's not dwelling in marks, saw the Tathagata. Hence this is precisely the accomplished explanation of the double clarification.
(Zi) Second, unfolding the meaning and giving approval. Two parts: (Chou) First, clarifying that the nature is fundamentally not mark; second, clarifying that seeing the mark is seeing the nature.
(Chou) First, clarifying that the nature is fundamentally not mark.
The Buddha told Subhuti: 'All marks whatsoever are false.'

The compiler of the sutra placed 'the Buddha told Subhuti' here to show that the following principle is important. This line is the approval; what follows expands it further. The question and answer just now spoke only of the body-mark; in fact all marks whatsoever are false. That you said 'cannot' is very true, for the nature is fundamentally not mark. This word 'false' is broad in meaning: false means unreal. Knowing it to be unreal, one should turn the light back and shine within, and must not seek outward among marks, but return quickly to the nature. The nature is fundamentally real: how can one see the real by means of the unreal? Knowing this, the sickness of ordinary people can be avoided, and one does not fall into rebirth.
(Chou) Second, clarifying that seeing the mark is seeing the nature.
'If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.'

'All marks' means all marks, that is, all marks whatsoever. One need only understand thoroughly that all marks are false; then one does not pursue the false and knows there is the real. Hence, seeing all marks as non-marks, the mark cannot obstruct the nature, and one sees the Tathagata. Why annihilate marks? In the mark itself one can see the nature. That you answered 'one can see the Tathagata' is entirely right. The word 'see' also involves work: one must truly be able to see all marks as non-marks before it will do. If one merely speaks of the principle, one cannot see the Tathagata. As for the word 'then,' the circulating editions have always had 'namely'; here it follows the Tang manuscript, which has 'then.' 'Then' and 'namely' are interchangeable in general, but it can be understood as 'forthwith' and not as 'just so.'

All marks whatsoever, being false, should none of them be dwelt in. Therefore the preceding teaching of the marks of dharmas and the marks of non-dharmas already includes all marks; and the Buddha's teaching of not dwelling in marks is precisely to make one see the Tathagata. If one clings to the transformation body, one cannot see the dharma-body. Hence not dwelling in marks is precisely to make one see the nature. Again, not dwelling in marks is not clinging; not clinging, one is not turned by marks, and moreover marks are turned by oneself. Therefore one need only understand thoroughly that they are false; one need not annihilate them, nor may one annihilate them, for marks are originally manifested from the nature. The Buddha has people neither cling to worldly dharmas nor loathe them. Ordinary people cling to marks, dwelling in the marks of dharmas and giving rise to affliction; practitioners loathe worldly dharmas, again dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas and giving rise to affliction. One must know that the nature is fundamentally without marks and yet not without marks, and cannot be annihilated. In our work we must first contemplate and illuminate; after a long time we can dwell in illumination, and at the last can see through illumination. Cultivating according to the Buddha's teaching of clinging to neither extreme, practicing on and on until the work is ripe and deep beyond deep, only then is it prajñā-paramita, and only then does one truly see all marks as non-marks — which is the Heart Sutra's 'seeing through illumination that the five aggregates are all empty, and so passing beyond all suffering and distress.' The Heart Sutra's 'form' is this sutra's 'mark'; feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure and the stirring of the mind. Only when one has illuminated them all to be empty is it 'all marks as non-marks.' 'All empty' means the three emptinesses, not the mere emptiness of the Small Vehicle. Therefore it further says, 'form is not different from emptiness, emptiness is not different from form.' Since thus spoken, form and emptiness are still two separate pieces; therefore it further says, 'form is precisely emptiness, emptiness is precisely form.' This is emptiness and existence at the same time, and it accords with the four lines 'all marks whatsoever are false.' 'All marks whatsoever are false' accords with 'emptiness is precisely form,' for all provisional names are in their very substance empty. 'If one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata' accords with 'form is precisely emptiness': form being emptiness, it can be seen that emptiness is not outside form, and why annihilate form to reveal emptiness? Hence it says, 'then one sees the Tathagata.' To see the Tathagata is to see the nature. Not clinging to marks, one can pass beyond all suffering and distress.

Suffering and distress are measureless; to name the greatest: the fragmentary birth and death of ordinary people, and the transformation birth and death of the Small Vehicle. An ordinary person's body has long and short, his life has longevity and early death, and he flows through birth and death — this is called fragmentary birth and death. The Small Vehicle realizes that the nature is without marks; having attained the substance, it could manifest marks, but it fears suffering and will not enter the world to deliver living beings, and subtle arising and perishing stirs in its mind — the Buddha names this transformation birth and death. If one sees the Tathagata, one can pass beyond such suffering and distress. Passing beyond suffering and distress comes from seeing the Tathagata, and seeing the Tathagata comes from seeing through illumination; therefore in one's work the most essential thing is contemplation. If one dissolves this passage of scripture back into the self-nature, then when meeting any mark, the first step of the work is to contemplate that all marks whatsoever are false; and as for form, sound, fragrance, taste, touch, and dharmas, one contemplates all marks as non-marks.

Someone may doubt that amid the toil of the dust it is not easy to contemplate. Let us take Shanghai as an example. What we hear all day long is the sound of carts, the sound of people, and all sorts of clamorous sound. One must know that such sounds arise and perish without cease; and these living beings who come and go in crowds are all busy with food and clothing, not their own masters. Yet in fact these are not the sounds of carts, of people, or of clamor: they are the sounds of impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and no-self, empty in their very substance. Yet they are plainly sounds — and to contemplate thus is to cling neither to existence nor to emptiness; it is the sound of prajñā-paramita. Therefore whatever line of the scripture it may be, all can be contemplated. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, never apart from this, one's benefit is inexhaustible. Thus, in relying on the words to arouse contemplation and illumination, one must first go and read the sutra: this is the sutra turning me. As for contemplation, that is me turning the sutra. When the sutra turns me, the sutra shifts my ordinary feeling; when I turn the sutra, that is the more important work. This passage of scripture explains the reason why of the preceding text, and is the summary conclusion of subduing the mind, not dwelling, and the rest. Hence to contemplate according to this text is no different from contemplating the preceding text.

'All marks whatsoever are false; if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.' To see the Tathagata is to see the nature; seeing the nature is the reason why of not dwelling in marks. To see the nature by one part is to be a bodhisattva of the first ground, no longer retreating from the mind of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; to see it to the ultimate is to become a Buddha, which is the reason why of the preceding text's inconceivable merit. When one becomes a Buddha and sees the nature, the dharma-body is manifested, filling space throughout; this is the reason why of the preceding text's use of space as a simile. One must know that this sutra, from first to last, speaks throughout of non-dwelling. The preceding text's not dwelling in marks is the explanation of 'should not dwell.' Therefore, as soon as he opens his mouth, he first speaks of subduing the mind: 'all the various kinds of living beings, I shall cause them all to enter nirvāṇa without residue and be brought to deliverance' — this teaches us not to dwell. Delivering measureless living beings to Buddhahood points out to us the Dharma gate for arousing the mind; 'in truth not one being attains deliverance' then sweeps away even this dharma, and this points out to us not dwelling in the marks of dharmas. Afterward it says that a bodhisattva should not dwell, again teaching people not to dwell in the marks of dharmas; and 'practicing giving' teaches people not to dwell in the marks of non-dharmas. Though it then says 'should simply abide as taught,' the meaning is still to teach people to abide in non-dwelling. This is the ancient worthies' saying: only seek the stilling of delusion, and do not go further seeking the real. The real is the true mind, which is also suchness; 'should' means such and equal. Why such and equal? Because the substance of the nature is so of itself. Having this substance of the nature, one can manifest marks. Therefore one who has realized it must not retain this true mind; for once one seeks the real, that is the sixth and seventh consciousnesses, and it becomes delusion. The ancient worthies called this 'clinging to difference': clinging to difference is to divide the real and the false into two, which is not equality. Hence it is said, 'should abide as I have taught,' in order to subdue the deluded mind. Ordinary people are all deluded mind; only when the deluded mind is removed part by part does the true mind appear part by part. 'Only seek the stilling of delusion, and do not go further seeking the real' — this is the meaning.

'All marks whatsoever are false': as soon as one dwells, it is false. Therefore the preceding text, at its opening, speaks of subduing and not of dwelling. Why then does it again say, 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata'? This speaks of the benefit of non-dwelling. If one can see all marks as non-marks, one sees the true nature. This is the summary conclusion of the preceding text's not speaking of dwelling but of subduing, and of 'should simply abide as taught.' From this it can be known that the Diamond Sutra's writing moves like a heavenly steed across the sky, while its exposition of principle is as fine as a needle and as dense as thread, opening everywhere and concluding everywhere. In reading this passage, it is like a strange peak suddenly rising, seemingly unconnected with the preceding text; in fact it is the summary conclusion of the preceding. It is just like layered mountains and folded waters, wrapped layer upon layer, with the coming of the dragon and the going of its veins everywhere, and a concluding hollow everywhere. As for the wording, it speaks on one side and sweeps away on the other, which is precisely not dwelling in the marks of dharmas and not dwelling in the marks of non-dharmas — truly worthy to be called the prajñā of words. In reading and lecturing on this sutra, in the earlier text one must draw in the later text, and in the later text one should look back to the earlier. For example, 'all marks whatsoever are false' corresponds to the later four lines, 'if one seeks me by form, or seeks me by sound.' And 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata' is in constant communication with the later 'with regard to dharmas one does not speak of the mark of annihilation.'
The section 'further clarifying the why' has four essential meanings.

(1) The preceding text used only space to illustrate inconceivable merit, explaining the reason why one should give without dwelling in marks. Here it further clarifies that if one does not dwell in marks, one can see the Tathagata's substance of the nature — this is the reason why that merit is inconceivable as space.

(2) The preceding text spoke of not dwelling in marks, guarding against those who do not understand suspecting it to mean annihilating marks. Here it further clarifies that it is not grasping, and by no means annihilating the marks: this is the saying 'if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata.' This is the reason why of not dwelling in marks.

(3) The preceding text spoke of the causal practice, which should not dwell in marks, guarding against the doubt that not only do all living beings have the body-marks of the four elements and five aggregates of suffering fruit, but even the World-Honored One's ultimate fruit manifests the body-mark of sixteen or eight feet and thirty-two marks — how can one not dwell? (The ancients cited only the body-mark of the Tathagata's fruit-virtue; I hold that it can also apply to all living beings, which is more complete in meaning, since the following text plainly says 'all marks whatsoever.' And further on there is the question whether the Tathagata can be seen by the thirty-two marks, which refers specifically to the fruit-virtue.) Here it clarifies that none of them may be dwelt in. With regard to the fruit-virtue, to dwell is to be unable to see the Tathagata; with regard to the suffering fruit, to dwell is to be unable to see the inherently possessed Tathagata-garbha. This is the reason why of 'should simply abide as taught,' that is, of 'should not dwell in marks.'

(4) The Small Vehicle does not fuse nature and mark: it takes sound and form as the Buddha, while in its own cultivation it falls into clinging to non-action. Here it clarifies that in making offerings to the Buddha one must not cling to form-marks and so see the Tathagata, and that in one's own cultivation one should not be empty either, but only not cling to marks; then form is precisely emptiness and mark is precisely nature, with nature and mark perfectly fused and unobstructed and at ease. This is precisely the reason why the World-Honored One spoke the prajñā Dharma to cause them to turn from the small toward the great.

blocks.text: Genuine Faith Is Rare, Section Six

inline.s: (Xin) Second, the arising of faith. Four parts: (Ren) First, selecting and showing the faculties; second, clarifying the merit; third, concluding and revealing the middle way; fourth, questioning, explaining, proving, and accomplishing. (Ren) First, again two: (Gui) First, the question; second, the answer.
(Gui) First, the question.
Subhuti said to the Buddha: 'World-Honored One, are there living beings who, hearing such words and chapter-and-verse, give rise to true faith?'

Wherever this sutra places 'Subhuti said to the Buddha,' it is to treat the matter with gravity, because what is said is the most essential principle. 'Are there' means 'are there many?' 'Such' refers to the preceding section that directly showed. 'Words' means the Dharma spoken above. 'Chapter-and-verse' does not mean a single chapter or a single line: Master Kumarajiva followed the idiom of this land, for the explanations of the Chinese in expounding the classics were mostly called chapter-and-verse. These two words refer to the principle spoken above. 'True faith' is not an idle and vague faith; it is the ability to understand the true meaning of such words and chapter-and-verse. Subhuti's question here puts weight on true faith, that is, on showing us that with regard to such words and chapter-and-verse one must give rise to true faith before it will do. What the World-Honored One has spoken above is exceedingly deep; all living beings who hear it will of course give rise to faith. Yet are those who can give rise to true faith many or not? I fear they are not many. For the principle being so deep, to give rise to true faith is impossible without the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom, and such faculties are not often seen. After all, must they be of the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom, or need they not be?
(Gui) Second, the answer. Again two: (Zi) First, selecting the faculties capable of faith; second, showing the thickness of former roots.
(Zi) First, selecting the faculties capable of faith.

The Buddha told Subhuti: 'Do not speak thus. After the Tathagata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and toward these chapter-and-verse passages they can give rise to faith and take them as true.'

The compiler of the sutra placed 'the Buddha told Subhuti' here to show that what is said is important. The phrase 'do not speak thus' is the World-Honored One directly stopping Subhuti's mouth, so that he may not speak in this way. Not only can the present assembly give rise to true faith; even after the Tathagata's deliverance, down to the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and toward these chapter-and-verse passages they can give rise to faith. That they can give rise to faith is to take these chapter-and-verse passages as the true meaning. Only these two kinds of people, those who keep the precepts and those who cultivate merit, can give rise to faith toward these passages; others cannot. The word 'these' also refers to the words and chapter-and-verse. 'As true' means being able to understand the principle of this sutra. In working from this point, the ability to give rise to faith depends wholly on taking it as true. Many great men of letters in ages past read the Tripitaka more than once, yet when asked about their practice, there was none at all: this is the sickness of not taking it as true. To take it as true is the direct answer to Subhuti's question whether true faith arises.

Subhuti's question is, on the one hand, to make people give rise to true faith, and on the other, a concern that so profound a principle cannot be truly believed without great faculties; his intent is also sound. Why did the Buddha stop his mouth? This contains three essential meanings, as can be seen from the following text. (1) One must not slight living beings: in the last five hundred years there will still be such people, how much more so now. (2) One must not obstruct others' good thoughts and cause them to grow discouraged, as can be seen from the following text's 'planting all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas.' (3) There is no need for the sharpest faculties and keenest wisdom: only the two kinds of people who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can give rise to faith. The first two meanings arise from the third. For these two kinds of people, who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, are not seen to be of high wisdom; and those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit seek blessings, and with regard to the exceedingly profound Dharma gate originally have the mind to shrink back. Therefore the Buddha warned him not to speak thus.

The above is still spoken in shallow terms; there is a deeper meaning in it. The single phrase 'do not speak thus' is addressed precisely to those who propagate the Mahayana Dharma — not only to the people of that time, but also to those who would later propagate the Mahayana Dharma. Not only was Subhuti warned not to speak thus; we today likewise must not speak thus. The Buddha's true intent was to exert every effort to propagate the prajñā teaching. This sutra was requested by Subhuti; in the first eight assemblies he had already spoken on the Buddha's behalf, which shows that Subhuti was a man who propagated prajñā. Later the text repeatedly says that there are those who can receive, uphold, read, and recite it and explain it to others. The Buddha's hope that prajñā be propagated is evident here. Had he spoken thus, would that have been the intent of propagation? And yet to propagate prajñā is truly not easy. In our own country, for instance, since the Song dynasty the ancient worthies, seeing that the prajñā teaching is hard to practice, were mostly unwilling to expound it. They thought that beings' karma was deep and their obstacles heavy, that they clung to marks in every way and could not easily comprehend; and they feared that people hearing this teaching would instead fall into one-sided emptiness, or even arrive at a wicked grasping at emptiness, so that it was better not to expound it at all. The World-Honored One foresaw this long ago, and therefore laid down 'do not speak thus' as a precept. That expounding prajñā should instead bring on such ills as falling into one-sided emptiness is the fault of the expounder who does not propagate it well, not the fault of the hearers. One should know that prajñā is precisely the Buddha-seed. This sutra says: 'All Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.' If it is not expounded, the principle of prajñā can never be made clear — would that not be cutting off the Buddha-seed? Hence one cannot but exert every effort to propagate it; and this is why the later text has the words 'shoulder the Tathagata's anuttara-samyak-sambodhi.'

In recent times the great virtuous ones for the most part did not expound prajñā, but expounded the perfect fusion of the three truths, which is truly not easy to understand. The Buddha spoke of the three truths at the Lotus assembly, which came right after his exposition of prajñā. Therefore the Buddha forewarned him with 'do not speak thus,' requiring Subhuti to propagate this teaching. His meaning was: if you do not propagate it, how can people be brought to understand it and give rise to true faith? You worry only that beings find it hard to believe, and forget the great matter of propagating prajñā — how could that be acceptable? Nor is that all: if you do not propagate it, you obstruct others' good thoughts; hence you should propagate it with all your strength. Yet if one propagates it without care, that too will not do. The Buddha expounded prajñā only in his later years. When he first attained the Way he first spoke the Avatamsaka. For in this kalpa Śākyamuni is already the fourth Buddha, and since it was so long since the last Buddha, he could not but set forth the Buddha's realm completely. Yet then he turned back to expound the Agamas, to make people practice in their own persons. When people's faculties had gradually ripened, he expounded the Vaipulya, making clear the principle of the Mahayana and turning people from the small toward the great. Only after this did he expound prajñā. From this one can see that this teaching requires care. Since it must both be propagated and handled with care, he had to select those whose foundation lay in keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. The Buddha's meaning was: you fear that people will not easily give rise to true faith, and worry that those who do give rise to it are few; you need only propagate as I have said and work hard in practice, and then the hearers will not be misled. It depends only on the method of the one who propagates — why worry that the hearers will not give rise to true faith? The single phrase 'do not speak thus' is of the utmost importance; those who propagate the Buddha-Dharma to the ends of the future should all be like this.

'After the Tathagata's extinction' — 'extinction' means deliverance. Deliverance has two meanings. In its fundamental sense it refers to the mind that is neither born nor extinguished. As it is said, when birth-and-death is extinguished, quiescent extinction appears before one, and this is called nirvāṇa. Later the term was borrowed, so that whenever a Buddha or bodhisattva passes into quiescence it is also called entering extinction. 'After the extinction' means after all the Tathagata's marks of birth and death have been extinguished, which must refer to the extinction of the manifestation body. The Tathagata is the dharma-body — why then speak of extinction? There is a subtle and profound principle here. Because the Buddha wished us to understand it, he specifically said 'the Tathagata's extinction,' and this has three essential meanings:

(1) The reward body and the manifestation body are both marks; what is extinguished is the extinction of the reward and manifestation bodies. The World-Honored One's putting on his robe and eating his food, and the extinction of the ordinary-being marks that he manifested — this is the extinction of the manifestation body. The reward body too is manifested from the dharma-body; since there is manifestation, there is also extinction. That the text does not say the manifestation and reward bodies are extinguished is to show clearly that the Tathagata will never again manifest a manifestation or reward body, so that we may be alert. One should know that even the manifestation and reward bodies displayed by the Tathagata are still birth and death. As it is said, 'whatever has marks is false and delusive' — how much more so our stinking skin-bag! Moreover, as for our bodily form, we do not know why it is born, nor why it perishes; we are wholly dragged along by the power of karma and cannot be our own masters. The Buddha is not like this. Though the manifestation and reward bodies are birth and death, the Tathagata is his own master: when he wishes to be born, he is born; when he wishes to be extinguished, he is extinguished. We all possess the Tathagata-store; we should quickly return to our original face.

(2) To realize the original nature is called the Tathagata; yet the dharma-body is without marks — how can it be seen? What can be seen is a mark: what bodhisattvas see is only the reward body manifested from the dharma-body, and what ordinary beings see is the manifestation body manifested from the dharma-body. Yet if one can see that the manifestation and reward bodies are not marks, then one sees the Tathagata. Therefore, if one would see the nature, one must see it through non-mark, and must not fall into annihilation. Hence we are warned that to see the Tathagata is by no means easy, and that one must advance with courage and vigor in order to realize it. If we would see the Tathagata, we should seek him in the nature. When we speak of the nature, then I and the Tathagata, self and other, are not two; to comprehend something of one's own nature-essence is already an occasion for seeing the Tathagata.

(3) The Tathagata's reward and manifestation bodies do indeed enter extinction and are indeed marks. But they are not extinguished forever; they will still be manifested. One should know that the reward and manifestation bodies are still shadows of the dharma-body. When we know that the dharma-body is not extinguished, then the reward and manifestation bodies again have their occasions for manifestation. From ancient times there have been those who saw the sixteen-foot golden body; those who, advancing with courage and vigor, saw a Buddha-body a thousand feet tall, as the arhats did; and those who saw a great body like Mount Sumeru, which is the reward body seen by bodhisattvas. Again, when Master Zhiyi finished commenting on the Lotus Sutra, he personally saw the assembly on Vulture Peak, still seated and not yet dispersed — all these are proofs of it. Hence the first meaning: that the Tathagata will not again manifest a reward or manifestation body, so that we may be alert. The second meaning: to make people know that if they would see the Tathagata, they must work upon themselves. The third meaning: to say that the Tathagata is not extinguished, and that if only one works hard, one may still see him.

The phrase 'in the last five hundred years' has traditionally had three explanations. (1) Taking 'after' in the sense of after the Tathagata's extinction, it refers to the five hundred years following the Tathagata's extinction. (2) Taking the first five hundred years after the Tathagata's extinction as the former, the second five hundred as the middle, and the third five hundred as the latter. (3) It means the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Tathagata's extinction. For the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma each last a thousand years, and the Dharma-ending age ten thousand years, so this refers precisely to the first five hundred years of the final age. In the thousand years of the True Dharma after the Tathagata's extinction, during the first five hundred years liberation was firm; during the next five hundred, meditative concentration was firm. 'Liberation' means realizing prajñā-paramita and passing beyond all suffering and distress. 'Firm' means that beings' faculties were firm. In the next five hundred years the faculties were somewhat poorer, yet people could still abide in meditative concentration. This liberation and concentration are precisely concentration and wisdom, and so it is called the True Dharma. In the first five hundred years of the thousand years of the Semblance Dharma, though there were still those who attained liberation and concentration, they were already very few; people devoted themselves to discussing principle and did not value practice, and so it is called 'firm in much hearing.' One should know that reading sutras puts the weight on contemplation; to occupy oneself merely with much hearing is like counting another's treasure, with not a penny of one's own — it is also called 'talking of food without being filled.' The World-Honored One told Ānanda that many kalpas before, he had cultivated together with him, and that to this day he remained the Buddha's attendant; his failing lay precisely in attending only to much hearing. In the next five hundred years, though even those of much hearing were few, beings knew only to build temples and erect pagodas, and so it is called 'firm in pagodas and temples.' During this thousand years the forms of the Buddha-Dharma still remained, but its original intent was already lost; it was merely a semblance, and so it is called the Semblance Dharma. By the first five hundred years of the Dharma-ending age the Buddha-Dharma had declined further, and beings knew only strife — what the new vocabulary calls struggle. The early extinction of the Buddha-Dharma in India was because strife had already become widespread in the Semblance Dharma period. It was the same in our country: in the middle of the Tang dynasty, the Chan, Pure Land, and Consciousness-Only schools all raised sectarian disputes. Hence it is called 'firm in strife.' The 'last five hundred years' of this sutra refers precisely to this time. Now we are again five hundred years further on within the Dharma-ending age. Therefore the Buddha said that at such a time, if there are people who can read this sutra, they are truly rare indeed.
'Taking these as true' refers precisely to those who can keep the precepts and cultivate merit. This has four meanings.

(1) Prajñā is right wisdom; wisdom is born of concentration, and concentration is born of the precepts. Therefore, if one would give rise to the right wisdom of prajñā, one must work at the precepts; otherwise there is no way to give rise to concentration and wisdom. Only when an ordinary being can keep the precepts can he be free of outward defilement. If he does not keep the precepts, his mind is not pure, he cannot gather his mind to one point, he cannot contemplate, and how could he give rise to prajñā? If one seeks to give rise to wisdom without keeping the precepts, one may well fall into a wicked grasping at emptiness. Therefore merit and wisdom must both be cultivated, like the two wheels of a cart, neither of which may be lacking. Only thus can the cultivator become the One Worthy of Offerings. Moreover, the two must be equal, with neither taken lightly. Some say that wisdom alone suffices; they do not realize that to stress wisdom and slight merit is to lack great compassion, and that this is utterly impermissible. Hence the Buddhas teach people to bring forth the mind of great compassion. This sutra speaks of giving at its very opening, which is enough to show that one who cultivates wisdom cannot fail to cultivate merit. If one does not cultivate merit, one has no affinity with living beings. Not only is there no affinity: even the cultivator's excellent marks cannot be complete. For those who propagate the Buddha-Dharma, excellent marks are also of importance; hence the sutras everywhere speak of the excellent marks of Buddhas and bodhisattvas. That the marks of an arhat do not equal the Buddha's has its reason. It was said above that after realizing the essence one must manifest marks — this is all for the sake of living beings, for those who see excellent marks are easily moved to draw near. The prajñā teaching is what enables people to become Buddhas; keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is the foundation for becoming a Buddha.

(2) One should know that those who keep the precepts must have few desires and be content, with comparatively little greed. Only such people can practice prajñā without going wrong. For the practice of prajñā requires detachment from marks, and one whose greed is great can never be detached. One who cultivates merit must deeply believe in cause and effect: worldly people, wishing to obtain fame and profit, seek them according to worldly ways, while such a person seeks according to the Buddha-Dharma. Therefore one who deeply believes in cause and effect will never lean toward the mark of annihilation. To not dwell in marks, those who keep the precepts are the most suited; to not fall into the mark of annihilation, those who cultivate merit are the most suited. But when one whose greed is great hears of prajñā, he falls into many faults. Some distort 'not dwelling in marks,' thinking that doing evil does not matter; they talk wildly and loftily and stop at nothing, imagining all the while that they have deeply grasped the principle of prajñā; they may even kill living beings and commit sexual misconduct, and regard it all as not dwelling in marks. Therefore the Buddha does not accept such people; he must select those of few desires and contentment.

(3) The preceding text said that one who brings forth the mind to practice prajñā should practice giving, and giving is relinquishment. These two kinds of people are those who can relinquish: those who keep the precepts can relinquish the desires of the world, while those who cultivate merit relinquish their own wealth and spirit, giving others wealth, Dharma, and fearlessness — and this accords precisely with the principle of prajñā.

(4) In cultivating this teaching, one should first block up the gate of the mark of no-dharma. Keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is precisely blocking up the mark of no-dharma. One need only further contemplate the marks of dharmas over a long time, and if one does not grasp at the marks of dharmas, one may then succeed. Therefore the Buddha selected these two kinds of people; from this it is clear that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is nothing other than pointing directly at those who study the prajñā teaching. And it is also said to us: if we would study prajñā, we must do no evil and practice all good. Not doing evil is the precepts; practicing good is merit. Only by carrying these out in earnest and making the foundation firm will it do. These two kinds of people are cautious and meticulous and can let go of everything; otherwise they cannot enter prajñā. That they can give rise to faith is because faith is the gate of entry to the Way. Only by practicing thus can one enter the gate; otherwise mere talk cannot enter it.

Someone says that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is the root of practicing prajñā, and that one must first block up one-sided emptiness. That is so; yet there is still a doubt. The sutra plainly says 'take these as true' — but these two kinds of people are, after all, deficient in knowledge, so how can they understand the true essential meaning of this sutra? There is an important principle here. Why? Because they are blessed by the Buddha's empowerment. Such people are the faculties the Buddha has selected; if they can act according to the Buddha's words, keeping the precepts and cultivating merit, they will surely receive the Buddha's empowerment and so be able to take these as true. Students of the Buddha must, in walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, at every moment, seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. Whatever practice one undertakes, it is thus. Even when expounding the sutras one must set aside one's ordinary views and seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. To be free of this thought is to have not yet given rise to faith. Take Buddha-recitation: when reciting, one must cast aside all one's ordinary views, so that the mind holds nothing at all, and single-mindedly seek Amitābha's empowerment.

Yet someone else says: if so, one need only imitate the simple folk, so why does the Buddha also say that one must read and recite the Mahayana sutras? This has two meanings. (1) When one understands the sutras, one's practice becomes more excellent. When the principle is stored in the field of the eighth consciousness, then once it responds, the three insights and six spiritual powers can all arise at once. (2) If one can truly believe, one should learn from the firm faith of simple folk. But there is no help for it: the world has many middling people who will not consent to be counted simple, and so one must certainly make them understand the principle.

When the ancient worthies wrote books, their openings often contained words seeking the empowerment of the Three Jewels. When great bodhisattvas composed treatises, the prefaces to those treatises likewise said 'by the Buddha's awesome spiritual power.' This is true and not false; it is not dependence, nor is it superstition. Without such a thought, a self-view would remain, obstructing one's own spiritual nature, and how could a book or treatise be thorough? Therefore one must completely set aside self-view. In worldly teachings, Confucius constantly referred matters to Heaven, which also captures this meaning. Scholars after the Han did not understand it.
(Zi) Second, showing the thickness of former roots.

'Know that such a person has not planted good roots with one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas, but has already planted all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas.'

The previous section, from 'keeping the precepts and cultivating merit' down to 'take these as true,' is precisely what this section comments on. 'Such a person' refers to one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit; it says 'such a person' and not 'such people,' which shows that although keeping the precepts and cultivating merit are spoken of as two matters, they are in fact one, and neither may be lacking. From one Buddha to two Buddhas is already an extremely long time, who knows how many kalpas, let alone three, four, or five Buddhas. This shows that such a person planted good roots very long ago; and the World-Honored One says further that this is not all — he has planted all good roots at the places of thousands of ten millions of Buddhas. Moreover, above 'thousands of ten millions' the two words 'measureless' are added, so that the time is an inexpressibly, inexpressibly long one. Such a person has not cultivated only one good, but all goods; 'all goods' refers to the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices. This shows that such a person has cultivated prajñā for an extremely long time. 'Planted roots' answers precisely to keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. Such a person's planted roots are already extremely deep; they are roots formed of all goods combined, and are truly what one calls rare and commendable.

The World-Honored One knows all matters of the measureless past; this statement is true and not false. From the standpoint of us ordinary beings, such a person's keeping the precepts and cultivating merit already accords with the wondrous Way. Why? Above, as soon as the World-Honored One opened his mouth to Subhuti, he said that all classes of living beings should be led into remainderless nirvāṇa and delivered, and that though measureless, countless, boundless beings are thus delivered, in truth no being attains deliverance — this is bringing forth the great mind. First one should deliver beings, which is not to fall into emptiness; next, that in truth no being attains deliverance, which is not to dwell in marks. Then he spoke of the great practice: one should dwell nowhere; he first spoke of not dwelling in marks, then of practicing giving — for if one dwells and does not practice, that is to fall into emptiness. In these two passages the World-Honored One repeatedly warns that one must not fall into emptiness before one may bring forth the mind and cultivate. That such a person begins at once with keeping the precepts and cultivating merit — is this not a hidden accord with the World-Honored One's words about first not falling into emptiness? Again, in the introductory section, when the World-Honored One was about to expound prajñā he first manifested as an ordinary being: putting on his robe and taking his bowl is keeping the precepts, and making beings give rise to a sense of shame is cultivating merit. That such a person keeps the precepts and cultivates merit — is this not likewise a hidden accord with the World-Honored One's original intent? From this one can see that unless one had planted good roots since long ago, one could not thus secretly accord with the wondrous Way. Judging by the World-Honored One's tone, he seems to praise such a person to the utmost, but in fact he is encouraging us, so that those who hear these words and chapter-and-verse should at once put them into practice; hence his admonition to Subhuti, 'do not speak thus.' For if it were as Subhuti said, later people would certainly think prajñā hard to cultivate, and would increasingly push the sage realm far away. In truth it is not hard: one begins precisely at keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. This is the World-Honored One's great compassion and great pity. Subhuti surely knew that to bring forth the mind and cultivate, one must not fall into emptiness; he was only asking on behalf of living beings — which is also great compassion and great pity.

We afflicted living beings, now able to hear these words and chapter-and-verse, are likewise rare, and are likewise those who have planted all good roots at measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas. Were it not so, then this most profound and subtle prajñā could not be heard; and even if heard, it would be as if not heard. We are already in a further five hundred years, when strife is firmer still, yet we have been able to come here to read, recite, receive, and uphold. Surely we are those who do not wish to compete, who have few desires and are content, and who are qualified to keep the precepts. If so, we should not belittle ourselves. Those who already keep the precepts should work still harder, and seek to make them firmer. Those who do not should keep them as the Buddha taught, and all Buddhas will greatly rejoice. Let the good roots so planted sprout here. Since we have this qualification, and the World-Honored One's empowerment as well, how can we not exert ourselves?

'Taking these as true': having understood the true meaning, one can also cultivate. Among the six paramitas, whichever one it be, all return to the cultivation of merit. Giving does not necessarily require ruining oneself; one need only relinquish a little wealth according to one's means, so that others benefit — that is the giving of wealth. To speak the Dharma for others, or to give people sutras, is the giving of Dharma, and is no difficult matter. Again, when one urges others to study the Buddha's teaching, one must urge them to keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and seeing those who do not keep the precepts one must urge them all the more. And seeing those who already keep the precepts but do not yet know prajñā, one must urge them all the more to understand prajñā. The greatness of this merit is inconceivable. Why? Because it perpetuates and exalts the Buddha-seed. One must further urge people to practice the Pure Land quickly and seek rebirth in the West. One should know that prajñā and the Pure Land are related most profoundly. It was said above that students of prajñā must first not dwell in marks; only by not dwelling in marks can one raise contemplation from the prajñā of words, and when contemplation is deep one realizes the prajñā of true reality — which is the nature. In practice one begins with contemplation and at the end must realize true reality, and this is not at all easy. In the Sahā world, with all its evil enticements, how could one immediately realize true reality? Therefore great bodhisattvas, cultivating and making vows, practice for three asankhyeya kalpas, passing through who knows how many rounds of birth and death. Such a person's good roots are indeed thick; yet even with so long a time as thousands of ten millions of Buddhas and measureless kalpas, he has only been able to give rise to faith. This shows how heavy his karmic obstacles are, and that he must therefore make the vow to seek rebirth in the West. Again, the text above brought forth the great mind: all classes of living beings should be led into remainderless nirvāṇa and delivered. Such deliverance of beings extends upward to the Heaven of Neither Thought Nor No-Thought and downward to the hells. Even if we bring forth this great mind, how can we go and deliver them? This in fact makes us first contemplate the principle that conditioned arising is equal. If one would fulfill the vow, one must first realize the nature; and to realize the nature, one cannot but first seek rebirth in the West. Rebirth in the West is not for one's own sake: it is originally for the sake of delivering living beings, and only thus does it accord with Amitābha's original vow, for by fulfilling the great vow one can realize the nature. Hence the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows says: space is endless, worlds are endless, living beings are endless, my vow is endless. Is this not entirely the same as this sutra's vow to deliver living beings widely? From this one can see that the prajñā teaching and the Pure Land teaching are one and not two. Only with this great vow will Amitābha come to receive and guide one, and one's rebirth will not be for one's own sake. Only with the teaching of rebirth can the prajñā teaching be accomplished.

Such a person's keeping the precepts and cultivating merit is also extremely difficult; he has already drawn near many Buddhas and planted good roots. From this one can see that to accomplish the prajñā teaching one should draw near Amitābha, and only then can the prajñā of true reality appear before one. Chan Master Yongming said: one need only see Amitābha — why worry about not opening to awakening? Therefore students of prajñā must quickly practice the gate of Buddha-recitation; and those who practice the Pure Land must likewise quickly practice the prajñā teaching. If one does not understand this supreme meaning, then one who merely recites the Buddha's name will, I fear, be born only in the lowest grade. Therefore those who promote the Pure Land teaching must not stop at speaking of Buddha-recitation alone. One should know that the practice of the Pure Land is precisely for fulfilling the great vow, and that mere Buddha-recitation resulting in a low-grade birth cannot fulfill it. Chan Master Yongming's verse — 'Without Chan, with the Pure Land, ten thousand practice and ten thousand go; one need only see Amitābha — why worry about not opening to awakening?' — can only be used to encourage the dull, not those of sharp faculties. The world overlooks the phrase 'see Amitābha' and attends only to 'ten thousand practice and ten thousand go,' thinking that one need not practice contemplation according to the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations. This is a mistake. That sutra makes clear the supreme meaning, which is precisely prajñā; if one is born only in the lowest grade, one cannot see the Buddha.
(Ren) Second, clarifying his merit. Two parts: (Gui) First, directly clarifying the merit; second, explaining and revealing the reason.
(Gui) First, directly clarifying the merit.

'Hearing such words and chapter-and-verse, even to the point of giving rise to a single moment of pure faith. Subhuti, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees that these living beings attain such measureless merit.'

'Hearing such words and chapter-and-verse' designates the person who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit. This word 'hearing' answers to the word 'hearing' in the earlier phrase 'hearing such words and chapter-and-verse.' Only when one has heard such words and chapter-and-verse and takes them as true can one give rise to faith. The two words 'pure faith' refer precisely to true faith. What is meant by 'pure'? It is what the later text calls 'when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born.' When such a person works earnestly at contemplation, practicing thus for a long time without the least grasping, pure faith is at once born — and that is true reality. This 'pure' is not spoken in contrast to defilement; it is absolute purity. Since one clings to neither of the two extremes of emptiness and existence, it is true reality. 'Even to the point of' is a word of omission. In giving rise to pure faith there are those whose pure thoughts continue without interruption, and those of many thoughts. At the very least there is the single moment in which pure faith is born, when one can have neither many thoughts nor thought following upon thought without interruption. These two words 'even to' include many people of differing degrees of practice; the later text calls them 'these living beings,' and yet, whatever the depth of their practice, the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees them. 'A single moment' means the arising of a thought, the stirring of the mind. 'Born' is what Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, yet prajñā arises.' From this one can see that without the utmost effort it cannot be born. Moreover, a single moment of response is the root of uninterrupted pure thought, and uninterrupted pure thought comes from a single moment of response. That this single moment is pure, no one can know; only the Tathagata can know and see it, for the pure mind is without marks and cannot be seen by the fleshly eye or the heavenly eye. Yet this explanation is still not the fundamental meaning. One should know that this sentence is precisely a commentary on the arising of pure faith. The Tathagata is the dharma-body; when such a person has a single moment of response, he is mind-to-mind sealed with the Tathagata, and light illumines light. Therefore the Tathagata's 'fully knowing' is knowing within the nature, which is precisely awakening thoroughly to the Buddha-nature; and the Tathagata's 'fully seeing' is the illumination of the nature-light, which is precisely the first opening of the Buddha-eye. This attainment is extraordinary; hence the ancients said: one moment of response, one moment a Buddha — and being a Buddha, how could his merit be measured?

These two small sections are precisely a commentary on 'can give rise to faith' and 'take these as true.' From 'know that such a person' down to 'has already planted all good roots at the places of measureless thousands of ten million Buddhas' explains the cause of keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. From 'hearing such words and chapter-and-verse' down to 'attain such measureless merit' explains the fruit of keeping the precepts and cultivating merit. The World-Honored One praises such a person to the utmost precisely in order to encourage us to bring forth the supreme mind, make great vows, and undertake great practice, and so to attain measureless merit.

Again, from Subhuti's 'do not speak thus' down to 'attain such measureless merit' is precisely a commentary on the earlier section that directly showed, from 'should thus subdue his mind' down to 'then one sees the Tathagata.' The earlier text states the principle; here a concrete person is brought forward to confirm it. One should know that only those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can thus give rise to faith, thus give rise to pure faith, and thus attain measureless merit. The meaning of this sutra's text answers everywhere to itself, its veins running through in just this way.
(Gui) Second, explaining and revealing the reason. Two parts: (Zi) First, direct explanation; second, reverse demonstration.
(Zi) First, direct explanation.
'Why is this? These living beings no longer have the marks of self, person, being, and life span. They have no mark of dharma, and also no mark of no-dharma.'

This is a direct explanation of why faith is born and merit obtained. Why one can give rise to pure faith and why one can attain measureless merit: only by eliminating the discriminating mind can this be done. Once discrimination is eliminated, right faith appears of itself, which is what Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, only prajñā arises.' Though such a person has not yet brought prajñā fully before him, he has already given rise to pure faith and is mind-to-mind sealed with the Tathagata, light illumining light, and so attains measureless merit — and this is truly not easy. Because discriminating deluded thoughts are eliminated, he can no longer have the marks of self, person, being, and life span. The phrase 'these living beings' covers a great deal. The earlier 'one who gives rise to pure faith in a single moment' refers to those of the lowest degree; there are still those of many moments of response, with pure thought continuing without interruption, and so it says 'these living beings.' The word 'again' in 'no longer' deserves attention: it says that such a person's self-attachment is already empty and will never recur. The lines 'no mark of dharma' and the rest say that such a person has no dharma-attachment.

The four marks arise from grasping at the mark of self. The sutras give many meanings when speaking of the four marks; here I take those that fit this sutra, which have a narrow and a broad sense. In the narrow sense they refer to grasping at the five aggregates and the physical body. This is the mark of self. Ordinary beings all share this affliction of grasping: they cannot forget anything, not only in the present but also reckoning on the future — after death they may ascend to heaven, or to the heaven of Great Brahma. This is what is called the pudgala, and from it all kinds of deluded thoughts arise, which the Consciousness-Only school calls the universally imagined attachment. Future and present stand in opposition to each other; viewed from the side of that opposition, it is the mark of person. From this body arise growth and decline, suffering and joy, and all the rest, which is the mark of being. Reckoning further that the five aggregates and the physical body continue without the root of life being cut off is the mark of life span. All these are various reckonings and discriminations made upon one's own five aggregates. In the broad sense, one reckons 'I' in all kinds of discrimination. That which stands opposed to it is the person; more than one person is a being; and this reckoning continuing without interruption is the life span. As soon as grasping arises there is a grasper and a grasped: the grasper is the self, the grasped is the person; the various discriminations are the mark of being; and the grasper and grasped continuing without interruption is the mark of life span. One should know that the four marks are opened out from the view of self. Opened, they are four marks; combined, they are the mark of self. Why the World-Honored One opened them out and spoke of them thus has a wondrous meaning. The view of self is discrimination; grasping at self is the seventh consciousness; the arising of discrimination is the sixth consciousness. Prajñā is right wisdom; if the prajñā of true reality is to appear before one, one must transform the sixth and seventh consciousnesses. When the sixth and seventh are transformed, the fifth and eighth are transformed together; hence the World-Honored One repeatedly spoke of the four marks. When the four marks are empty, self-attachment is empty, which is also called the emptiness of person.

The mark of self is grasping that arises from the body; the mark of dharma is grasping that arises from dharmas. 'No mark of dharma' is the emptiness of dharma-attachment, also called the emptiness of dharmas. 'No dharma' means nothingness, which is emptiness. 'Also no mark of no-dharma' is the emptying of emptiness itself, also called repeated emptiness, also called total emptiness. Prajñā reveals the principle of the three emptinesses, and its main work is to dispel grasping. After the person and self are empty, to grasp at the emptiness of dharmas is still impermissible; therefore one must dispel it layer upon layer, until even emptiness must be emptied. The ancients called this 'exhausting emptiness to the very bottom,' which is vastly different from one-sided emptiness; hence it is called ultimate-meaning emptiness, also called supreme-meaning emptiness.

This explains that those in the previous section who have given rise to pure faith can reach the three emptinesses. The three emptinesses contain many principles, measureless in breadth and bottomless in depth — what Samantabhadra's vows call the ocean of most profound teaching. According to the three emptinesses, having no four marks is the emptiness of self; having no mark of dharma is the emptiness of dharmas; and having no mark of no-dharma is the emptiness of emptiness. In fact this is simply the elimination of the two attachments, to self and to dharmas: 'no mark of dharma' empties dharma-attachment, and 'no mark of no-dharma' likewise eliminates dharma-attachment, for no-dharma is fundamentally without dharma. Yet one must not grasp at it either; a single grasping becomes attachment to no-dharma. Therefore the emptying of dharma-attachment by 'no mark of dharma' is the first layer, and the emptying of even the attachment to 'no mark of no-dharma' is the second layer. Taken together, both are dharma-attachment. With the four marks spoken of above, they are set out as the two attachments to self and to dharmas in contrast. That such a person gives rise to pure faith means that the two attachments to self and dharmas are both dispelled. Yet the two attachments to self and dharmas that arise from discrimination are coarse attachment. There are still the innate attachments to self and dharmas, subtle attachments that come from the stirring of thought, called the dormant afflictions, also called the ignorance of the ground of dwelling. Such a person can only eliminate the discriminated attachments to self and dharmas; he cannot eliminate the innate attachments to self and dharmas.

There is another essential meaning. Spoken separately, they are the three emptinesses; spoken together, they are the emptying of the two attachments to self and to dharmas. Yet they may also be viewed from the two extremes of emptiness and existence: the mark of no-dharma is emptiness and belongs to the extreme of emptiness, while self and dharma may be spoken of together and belong to the extreme of existence. That such a person gives rise to pure faith means that he can also not cling to either extreme. The extreme of existence is called the conventional truth, the extreme of emptiness the true truth. Here again the two truths are contained. In other sutras the Buddha speaks of three truths, including the truth of supreme meaning; but prajñā, in dispelling grasping, speaks only of the two truths. One should know that negation and illumination occurring at once is precisely the Middle Way; and so in speaking of two truths the three truths are in fact contained. Dispelling the two extremes is double negation, and double negation is double illumination. Yet there must also be negation and illumination at once. Such a person has not yet reached this degree; he can only not cling to the two extremes, as one may see by savoring the text closely. All that the Buddha says is thorough from head to tail and from beginning to end; it must not be read carelessly. Even the above, giving rise to pure faith and attaining measureless merit, has its shallow and its deep aspects. In sum, such a person only eliminates coarse attachment, not subtle attachment. That is why the Buddha speaks ever more deeply, to make clear that such a person's elimination of attachment is still only the first step, and that further effort is needed. Yet such a person has reached no easy point: a single moment of response is already extraordinary. Those who work hard often have this kind of state, feeling the mind hollow and empty, clean and pure; sometimes it lasts half a month or half a year, and all of it is this same scene. One should know that such attainment is still far short, and that one must not be self-satisfied. Otherwise two faults arise: with regard to the sutra's meaning one takes the deep for the shallow, while with regard to oneself one takes the shallow for the deep — not realizing that one is still far, far away! In the case of the person indicated by this sutra, discriminating self-attachment is already eliminated, and though greed, anger, and delusion are not wholly gone they are already very thin; still further effort is required. When we work hard we can measure ourselves and see whether or not we accord with what the sutra says. Speaking of this, I recall an episode from antiquity. When Emperor Suzong and Emperor Daizong of the Tang, father and son, put down the rebellion of An Lushan, Emperor Daizong strove mightily to propagate the Buddha-Dharma, and the Tantric Tripitaka Master Bukong also came to China at that time. Buddhism flourished as never before. One day, when Emperor Daizong was discussing the Buddha-Dharma with the National Master, Yu Chaoyen was beside them and interjected, asking: since the Buddha says all living beings are Buddhas, how does ignorance arise? The National Master at once said: you are not fit to ask this question. Chaoyen was furious, but since the emperor was present he dared not speak, though his anger showed in his face. The National Master then said: ignorance arises from this. Here we can test ourselves. If someone comes to slander and revile me, can I keep from giving rise to anger? If I meet with forms, sounds, fragrances, tastes, touches, and dharmas, can I keep from giving rise to thoughts? If I meet with poverty, so that today there is not even rice to eat, can my mind keep from worry? One must act as though nothing were the matter before it will do. Otherwise one clings to the marks of self, person, being, and life span. Yet to be hollow and empty is of course very good; but it is not enough. One should go and practice giving. The six paramitas and the ten thousand practices must all be practiced. If one settles for being hollow and empty, one clings to the mark of no-dharma. If one has a mind to deliver beings, one clings to the mark of dharma. Hence one should know that for such a person to give rise to pure faith and eliminate the discriminating mind is truly not easy. That is why the Tathagata fully knows and fully sees him, and acknowledges that his understanding equals the Buddha's mind, that he has opened the Buddha-eye and attained such measureless merit.

This not only explains the previous section; it also answers back to the whole section that directly showed, for what was not explained above is here pointed out and awakened to. 'All classes of living beings' down to 'I will lead them all into nirvāṇa and deliver them' answers precisely to the mark of dharma. 'In truth no being attains deliverance' answers precisely to the mark of no-dharma. 'If a bodhisattva has the marks of self, person, being, and life span, he is not a bodhisattva' is precisely 'no longer has the marks of self, person, being, and life span.' 'A bodhisattva should practice giving while dwelling nowhere' is relinquishment, which breaks the self; it requires us first to empty the mark of self. 'Not dwelling in marks' is not dwelling in any kind of mark, which is no mark of dharma. Again, the simile of space in the four directions and above and below is no mark of no-dharma. 'If one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata' is the fusion of the two extremes. For to see only marks is to cling to existence, and to see only no-marks is to cling to emptiness; but to see marks as no marks is the fusion of the two extremes, which is no mark and yet no absence of marks, and one attains to see true reality — hence it says 'then one sees the Tathagata.' Because one sees the Tathagata, one attains such measureless merit, which is the inconceivable merit spoken of above. The Buddha's meaning is that such a person can understand the Dharma I have spoken above, keep the precepts and cultivate merit, give rise to pure faith, and take these as true, and will of course be without the four marks of self and so on, and attain such measureless merit. This too is to encourage us: if we would cultivate prajñā, we should begin thus, and must not fall into emptiness; we should first block up the side of no-dharma, plant our feet on solid ground, and practice in our own persons. To cling to neither the mark of dharma nor the mark of no-dharma is the essential secret of practice.
(Zi) Second, reverse demonstration.

'Why is this? If these living beings' minds grasp at marks, then they cling to self, person, being, and life span. If they grasp at the marks of dharmas, they cling to self, person, being, and life span. Why? If they grasp at the marks of no-dharma, they cling to self, person, being, and life span.'

The previous section is called the direct explanation because it explains from the positive side why faith is pure and why measureless merit is attained: because such a person has already seen the principle of the three emptinesses. To have no marks of self and so on is the emptiness of person (also called the emptiness of self-attachment); to have no mark of dharma is the emptiness of dharmas (also called the emptiness of dharma-attachment); to have no mark of no-dharma is the emptying of emptiness itself (also called total emptiness). These are the three emptinesses. From seeing the three emptinesses, one advances with vigor and one's pure thoughts continue without interruption, and one then realizes the pure dharma-body; hence it says 'attains such measureless merit.'

This section is called the reverse demonstration because it further shows from the negative side why the three emptinesses are indispensable, making clear that the slightest clinging to marks is the discriminating mind and is not the pure nature. Why? Because whatever has marks is false and delusive. Therefore to cling to marks is to pursue the false, and to pursue the false is to lose the true nature. Once the true nature is lost, one is still an ordinary being who gives rise to delusion, creates karma, and receives the suffering retribution of birth and death — how could one attain measureless merit?

From this one can see that the purpose of adding the reverse demonstration after the direct explanation is simply to make living beings quickly awaken: relying on this sutra's principle of non-dwelling, they should on the one hand diligently practice the six paramitas and on the other contemplate no-mark, giving rise to pure faith, in the hope of realizing the nature-essence of the three emptinesses and passing beyond the ordinary into the sage. Such is the general meaning of the necessity of the reverse demonstration.

Yet there is another meaning: it guards against doubts arising in the reader of the preceding text. What doubts? (1) The marks of self and so on arise from the view of the body. The body is the root of suffering, and one should not cling to its marks — this principle is easy to understand. But dharmas are not so: to deliver oneself and others there must be a dharma. Giving and the six paramitas — are there not plainly dharmas here? Having a dharma, there are the marks of that dharma. Now the text says 'no mark of dharma.' If a dharma is without marks, then the dharma too hovers between existence and nonexistence. How then can the mark of dharma be absent? (2) If there is a view of the body, one will inevitably discriminate between self and others; and once there is discrimination, one will inevitably create karma and receive retribution. Therefore one should not have the view of the body, and should not discriminate self and others. But a dharma is not a body — where in it are self and other? Even if one raises discrimination over a dharma, that is to discriminate self and other. As for the two words 'no-dharma,' they are no different from another name for emptiness. Since it is called empty, how can it have marks? Why then does the text put dharma and no-dharma on the same footing as the four marks of self and person that arise from the view of the body, and say that all alike are absent? It is in order to cut off all these doubts that the text must add a clear explanation from the negative side.

'These living beings' refers to the living beings mentioned above who have given rise to pure faith and seen the three emptinesses. The word 'mind' in 'if the mind grasps at marks' is important. One should know that the mind is fundamentally without marks; the word 'marks' need not refer exclusively to the physical body but points rather to all marks of objects. The mind is fundamentally without marks; if there is any kind of mark, then one has grasped at an object. And if one grasps at the marks of objects, has one not already lost one's own mind? This is precisely the appearance of turning from enlightenment and joining with dust, which is why one has become an ordinary being. Hence one should further know: when one grasps at the marks of objects, who is it that grasps? It is not another; it is I. From this one can see that if the mind grasps at marks, it becomes the mark of self.
