And the marks grasped exist because of the grasping 'I,' just as the mark of person arises from the mark of self; therefore the grasped object becomes the mark of person. The grasped marks pile up and multiply, becoming the mark of being. When those marks continue without interruption, they become the mark of life span. From this it follows that whatever mark one grasps at, there is a grasper and a grasped, multiplying without interruption. Hence it says, 'if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to self, person, being, and life span.' 'Then it is' means simply 'thereupon is': as soon as one grasps, one has clung. Therefore if one grasps at the marks of dharmas, one likewise clings to the four marks of self, person, being, and life span. How can one say that a dharma is unlike the body, and that there is no self in it? As soon as one grasps there is the discrimination of grasper and grasped; how can one say that discrimination over a dharma is not discrimination of self and other?

From this one can further see that what the previous section calls 'no mark of dharma' means simply not grasping at it; it does not mean that dharmas and marks are ultimately nonexistent. If they were ultimately nonexistent, that would be the mark of annihilation! As for no-dharma, it is of course another name for emptiness, and emptiness is originally without marks. Yet once one grasps at it, there is the grasping 'I' and the grasped 'person,' multiplying without interruption, and the four marks are plainly there. Hence it says, 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span.' I once saw an edition in which someone, I know not who, had deleted the three words 'why is this?' above 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma,' thinking that the text ran straight on and its meaning was clear, and that these three words only made the tone tortuous and the meaning unclear. In the Jiaqing period there was an edition which, though it did not dare delete them outright, noted beneath them that the annotations of certain commentators and all the correct texts agreed these were a superfluous line. Those 'certain commentators' were mostly men of the Ming and Qing. From this one can prove that the words and phrases of this sutra differ greatly from the ancient texts; though there are indeed errors of transcription, they have also not escaped arbitrary addition and deletion by the shallow-sighted — truly lamentable. Fortunately, recent editions of the sutra have had this passage restored by clear-eyed men; yet in remote places there are still editions that delete it, and these must on no account be followed.

For the use of these three words contains a subtle meaning and is of critical importance; they must on no account be omitted. Someone says that the three words 'why is this?' are meant to lift up the preceding meaning, so that one knows that if grasping at no-dharma still clings to the four marks, how much more does grasping at dharmas. This meaning is still shallow. For the passage 'if the mind grasps at marks, then it clings to...' has already explained the reason; why need it be lifted up again? What then is the meaning? It guards against those who do not get the point: though they hear that grasping at the marks of dharmas means clinging to the four marks of self, person, being, and life span, they still do not understand what counts as not grasping, their insight is not true, and they may mistakenly grasp at no-dharma while still thinking that they are not grasping at dharmas. Therefore the three words 'why is this?' are used as a warning question, making one think deeply about the reason and not misunderstand. It follows immediately: 'if one grasps at the marks of no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span.' Then one knows that to grasp at no-dharma is still to cling to marks, no different from grasping at dharmas. Does this mean that 'not grasping at dharmas' does not mean ultimately not grasping? If it is not non-grasping, and grasping clings to marks, then one can see that 'not grasping' means causing one not to cling to marks and to return to the nature. What is this meaning? It is to practice the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices widely, while in the mind nothing is going on, still and concentrated, unmoved by anything. This precisely is the true meaning of not grasping at the marks of dharmas. Acting thus, one clings neither to dharmas nor to no-dharma; this is not clinging to the two extremes and according with the Middle Way. Thus with this one sentence 'why is this?' the two lines below about grasping at the marks of no-dharma are nothing other than an annotation on the two lines above about grasping at the marks of dharmas. Such is the wonder of expounding the Dharma. If these three words were deleted, the tone would be flat and parallel, and this meaning could not emerge.

One should know that existence is emptiness, yet existence; emptiness is not an emptiness apart from existence. Hence the Heart Sutra says: form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. That is why this sutra everywhere speaks of not grasping, and yet everywhere speaks of not annihilating. Though the words 'not annihilating' are pointed out only at the very end, in fact everything said at the beginning contains the sense that one should not annihilate. For instance, delivering beings without the mark of delivery is by no means only the single line 'in truth no being attains deliverance'; and 'one should practice giving while dwelling nowhere' makes the meaning even clearer. As for 'if one sees all marks as no marks, then one sees the Tathagata,' this is a crystallized saying. 'All marks as no marks' makes clear not grasping; for if one grasps, one sees only marks and does not see the nature. Precisely because one does not grasp, seeing marks is seeing no marks, and one returns to the Tathagata-store nature; hence it says 'one sees the Tathagata.' In sum, marks are originally no fault; the fault lies in grasping. Therefore if one abandons marks and grasps at no-marks, or abandons no-marks and grasps at a nothingness that can negate, the grasping itself becomes a mark and obstructs the self-nature. From this one can know that if only one does not grasp, marks do no harm; but if one does grasp, even no-marks become an obstruction. Why need one annihilate marks in order to see the nature? For this reason he selected keeping the precepts and cultivating merit alone as the faculties capable of faith. For those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit are already not clinging to emptiness, and when prajñā perfumes them, once the understanding of wisdom opens they do not grasp at dharmas. Naturally they can neither cling to existence nor again cling to emptiness, and so easily accord with the Middle Way. Compared with those of wild wisdom, the distance is as heaven from earth. Hence the sutras and treatises say: better to cling to existence as to Mount Sumeru than to cling to emptiness as to a mustard seed. This makes clear that for one who clings to existence it is easy to work, while for one who clings to emptiness it is hard to apply a remedy. The word 'grasp' here stands in close contrast to the word 'relinquish' below. Here the text makes clear that one should not grasp at dharmas; it does not say that one may grasp at no-dharma. (This is spoken in terms of the sense.) Below it makes clear that dharmas should be relinquished; it does not say that no-dharma should not be relinquished. The meaning above and below is exactly the same, and both contain the sense that one cannot speak of emptiness apart from existence. In sum, neither extreme should be grasped, which is to say both should be relinquished. Therefore the text below concludes with 'therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at no-dharma,' still pointing back to the Middle Way.

The use of these three words 'why is this?' has yet another meaning. In the previous section, from 'no longer have the marks of self' down to 'also no mark of no-dharma,' the text runs straight on to make clear the three emptinesses, as already explained. In this section, the placing of 'why is this?' between 'if one grasps at dharmas' and 'if one grasps at no-dharma' serves specifically to make clear the principle of not clinging to the two extremes of emptiness and existence, and so to lead into the two lines below beginning 'therefore.' The two lines 'if the mind grasps at marks' and the next are a general statement: 'one should not grasp at marks' is meant to include the marks of the body as well. The marks of the body belong to the extreme of existence, the same as the marks of dharmas, while the marks of no-dharma belong to the extreme of emptiness. If they were not separated here, and the text ran straight on as before, this meaning would not emerge, and the two words 'therefore' below would have nothing to rest on and could not be connected. This shows the excellence of Kumarajiva's translation.
(Ren) Third, concluding and revealing the Middle Way. Two parts: (Gui) First, concluding by double detachment; second, citing the raft simile to reveal the meaning.
(Gui) First, concluding by double detachment.
'Therefore one should not grasp at dharmas, and should not grasp at no-dharma.'

The word 'therefore' takes up precisely the preceding text. For if one grasps at the marks of dharmas or no-dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life span; hence neither extreme should be grasped. It also answers to the earlier phrase 'no longer' and the rest. For not grasping means no marks, and only with no marks does pure faith arise, so that one is known and seen by the Tathagata and attains measureless merit. In sum, the Buddha's saying this shows precisely the method of practice: first cause one not to grasp at the two extremes, and gradually one can empty marks and purify the mind-ground. Thence faith, understanding, and practice follow, and even at the ultimate one does no more than not cling to the two extremes. For it is by the prajñā of contemplation that one realizes the prajñā of true reality; and true reality is no mark and yet no absence of marks — is this not not clinging to the two extremes? This is what is called the cause encompassing the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrating the source of the cause.
(Gui) Second, citing the raft simile to reveal the meaning.
'For this reason the Tathagata constantly says: you monks should know that the Dharma I teach is like a raft. The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma.'
The 'this' in 'for this reason' takes up precisely the two lines above about not grasping at dharmas, and also echoes from afar the lines from 'no mark of dharma' onward.

The raft simile is a teaching the Tathagata constantly gave. A boat or raft is meant for crossing over; once across, the raft is abandoned. This illustrates that the Buddha-Dharma is for crossing over birth and death: while birth and death are not yet crossed, one cannot be without the Dharma; but once the other shore is reached, the Dharma too is of no use. This shows that the Dharma must not be grasped. It was constantly taught to the disciples in the Agamas.

The line 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished' follows directly from the raft simile. It also refers at once to the earlier 'one should not grasp at dharmas,' and thereby leads into the following 'how much more so no-dharma.' 'How much more so no-dharma' makes clear that no-dharma should be relinquished still more; relinquishing is not grasping. Yet the sense of relinquishing is deeper: it is not merely not grasping. What was previously grasped must now also be relinquished. Ultimately, even the two words 'not grasping' should be relinquished.

The reason for citing the constantly taught raft simile is that on the one hand the present meaning is used to make clear the constant teaching, and on the other the constant teaching is borrowed to make clear the present meaning. That is to say: by the principle that neither dharma nor no-dharma should be grasped, the raft simile that the Tathagata constantly told the monks, though it speaks only of relinquishing the Dharma, must be understood as relinquishing no-dharma along with it. Why? 'The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma': that no-dharma should be relinquished still more needs no saying. This shows that there is no small and no great, that all dharmas are equal, and it is to use the present meaning to make clear the constant teaching. Further, to make clear that in the present meaning the two extremes are not grasped — though the words stand in parallel — one should know that no-dharma should all the more not be grasped, so that one does not cling to emptiness. This is to borrow the constant teaching to make clear the present meaning.

The meaning contained in this passage of the sutra is deep and subtle, and is not exhausted by what has been said above. One should know that between the present meaning and the constant teaching there is one point of sharpest conflict, which must be clearly understood. The constant teaching is that when the Dharma is no longer needed, one relinquishes it; but the present teaching, spoken for those who have just brought forth the great mind, is that one should relinquish the Dharma precisely when it is needed.

Because of this sharp conflict, the World-Honored One, guarding against people clinging to the constant teaching and doubting the present meaning, or clinging to the present meaning and doubting the constant teaching, absolutely had to cite it, so that students might thereby see clearly that though the two differ, they are in fact the same.

What is the doubt? The doubt is: if one relinquishes the Dharma precisely when it is needed, then when the Dharma is relinquished, is there not no Dharma? And without Dharma, how shall one deliver? Is this not contrary to the constant teaching? And yet the text also says one should not grasp at no-dharma. Is there, after all, a Dharma or no Dharma? Does one who is not yet delivered need the Dharma or not need the Dharma?

One should know that the meaning spoken here is that neither of the two extremes, existence and nonexistence, may be clung to; this is what is called the supreme meaning of the Middle Way. One should know that not clinging to the two extremes is precisely the double illumination of the two extremes. Not clinging to the two extremes indeed means there is no such thing as a dharma; yet the double illumination of the two extremes also means there is no such thing as no-dharma. Moreover, not clinging is itself double illumination. From this one can know that just when there is no such thing as existence, there is likewise no such thing as nonexistence; and just when there is no such thing as nonexistence, what harm is there in there being no such thing as existence? Think on this, think deeply: is there ultimately a Dharma or no Dharma? Or is existence itself nonexistence, and nonexistence itself existence? Knowing this, one knows that the present meaning and the constant teaching, though they differ, are in fact the same.

Nevertheless, did the Buddha cite the raft simile solely to resolve doubts about the difference between the constant teaching and the present meaning? No. His deep intent was in fact to guard against people clinging to the present meaning and doubting the present meaning. What is that doubt? Have you readers seen it? Consider the two lines 'therefore one should not grasp at dharmas'; though they conclude the preceding text, they are greatly different in depth from what precedes. The World-Honored One, fearing that people would not understand and so generate obstacles, therefore cited the constantly taught raft simile to make it clear. Otherwise, the two lines beginning 'therefore' have already concluded the matter, and there would have been no need to cite the raft simile again. As for all that was said above about not clinging to the two extremes, down to the passage asking whether there is ultimately a Dharma or no Dharma — this is precisely borrowing the constant teaching to make clear the present meaning, lest doubts arise and obstacles be generated over the depth of the present meaning. If so, we should first make clear wherein that depth lies.

Consider the first passage: from 'no longer have the marks of self' down to 'also no mark of no-dharma' — this speaks of no marks. The second passage, from 'if the mind grasps at marks' down to 'if one grasps at no-dharma' and so on, likewise speaks of not grasping at marks. As for the third passage, the two lines beginning 'therefore' say that dharmas and no-dharma alike are not grasped, and not merely that marks are not grasped. Here precisely lies the great difference from the first two passages, and it is precisely here that people are guarded against giving rise to doubt and generating obstacles.

Consider: the first passage speaks of no marks, in order to cut off the doubts that the marks of dharmas cannot be absent and that no-dharma is originally without marks. Therefore the second passage says that grasping means clinging to marks, so that one understands that the 'no' spoken of means causing people not to grasp, and does not mean no dharmas and no marks. Moreover, since grasping means having marks, the marks of no-dharma also should not be grasped. It further points out that not grasping at the marks of dharmas is bounded by not grasping at the marks of no-dharma, so that one may understand that it is not an absolute not grasping at dharmas, but rather that even while one takes up the six paramitas and other dharmas in practice, the mind has no marks of them. Only then will students not lean to one-sided emptiness or one-sided existence, and only then do they have the correct place to begin.

One should know that in the wondrous teaching of prajñā, one must be thoroughgoing from the very start. What is thoroughgoing? One must not leave even a shadow of dharma or no-dharma. For since they are named the mark of dharma and the mark of no-dharma, one can know that they are marks of dharma and marks of no-dharma. If one grasps at dharmas or at no-dharma, grasping means having marks — can that still be called not grasping at marks? Therefore what is said before and after is in principle wholly consistent, differing only in the shallowness and depth of the words and their order. Hence the third passage's two lines beginning 'therefore' must be spoken: one should thus thoroughly not grasp, and only that is not grasping at marks. Then, because the mind is pure, one can realize the fruit of the pure dharma-body.

Question: put this way, the Dharma is indeed to be relinquished. And the added line that one should not grasp at no-dharma I also understand: it serves as the boundary for not grasping at dharmas, so that one knows that though one does not grasp at dharmas, one must on no account grasp at no-dharma. But if this is so, then the method of practicing the six paramitas while the mind has no marks of them can no longer apply. Why? Because here the text does not say one should not grasp at the marks of dharmas, but plainly says one should not grasp at dharmas. Where then is one to set to work? Answer: it is precisely for this that the World-Honored One spoke the fourth line, revealing a most wondrous method.

Consider the two important lines in the fourth passage: 'The Dharma itself should be relinquished — how much more so no-dharma.' These two lines are nothing other than an annotation on the two lines beginning 'therefore.' They point directly and tell the student: I am not telling you merely not to grasp at dharmas, but to not grasp at no-dharma together with them. To stop at not grasping at dharmas would turn into having no Dharma, and without Dharma how could one practice and be delivered? If dharmas and no-dharma are both not grasped, this is the wondrous Dharma. Now, the reason the raft simile is cited is that the raft is itself the Dharma. Therefore on the one hand one is made to understand that the constant teaching of relinquishing the Dharma includes relinquishing no-dharma as well, so that one knows that to relinquish both together is the Dharma of the raft simile that the Tathagata constantly taught. Then what is now plainly said to be the not grasping of dharmas and no-dharma together — is this not precisely that Dharma? And on the other hand, one is made to understand that the constantly taught raft simile says that before crossing one cannot be without the Dharma, and once crossed one relinquishes it, so that one knows that since one has not yet crossed, how can one be without the Dharma? Then one will not mistakenly think that 'one should not grasp at dharmas' means having no Dharma. Moreover, since it plainly also says one should not grasp at no-dharma, this is all the more proof that not grasping at dharmas and no-dharma together is precisely the wondrous Dharma revealed to us. Hence the citing of the raft simile is precisely to reveal this.

Question: how is it that not grasping at either together is precisely the wondrous Dharma? This has confused people again — how is it the wondrous Dharma? One should know that in the supreme meaning, dharma and no-dharma are fundamentally unspeakable. There is no such thing as birth and death, no such thing as nirvāṇa, and still less any such thing as deliverance. Even 'not clinging to the two extremes' and 'the double illumination of the two extremes' become superfluous words. One must simply exterminate feeling and intellect and cut off the tangled vines. Just when one is exterminating and cutting off, the path of words is suddenly cut off and the sphere of mental activity is extinguished. Then, birth-and-death being extinguished, all space becomes an unmoving place of practice, and throughout space there is a net of pure radiance; and one comes face to face with the Buddhas of the ten directions. At this point, though it is said there is no such thing as deliverance, one has already, leaving no trace, been delivered in just this way. Then one suddenly realizes that even this one phrase 'no such thing as deliverance' is itself a wondrous Dharma that leads people to deliverance. May I ask: this work of exterminating and cutting off — even if one would not call it a Dharma, how can one avoid it? And is not the not grasping of both dharma and no-dharma precisely this exterminating and cutting off? The two sides press in tight, so that as soon as a thought stirs it clings either to this or to that, leaving the discriminating deluded mind no place to stand. It is like suppressing bandits by closing in from both sides, until they have no foothold and naturally submit. This is the method of the sharp knife cutting through tangled hemp; hence it is said: exterminate feeling and intellect, cut off the tangled vines. This is precisely what the bodhisattva Nagarjuna meant by 'all dharmas do not arise, yet prajñā arises.' The orthodox essence of prajñā is non-dwelling, and not grasping at the two extremes is the ironclad footing of non-dwelling. This itself is the supreme, most profound, wondrous Dharma — what the sutra calls the Dharma of anuttara-bodhi. Because one takes this as the cause of one's fundamental practice, one realizes the fruit of anuttara-bodhi. One should then suddenly understand that it is exactly the same as the raft simile: it is not that there is no Dharma by which to be delivered, and still less that one relinquishes the Dharma before crossing. Yet you doubt how deliverance is to come about, and whether at the time of deliverance there is a Dharma or no Dharma — is this not raving?

Question: why did the Buddha not explain that not grasping is itself the Dharma, but instead let people grasp it for themselves? Answer: this too has a deep purpose. (1) Not grasping is fundamentally not a dharma, and there is no way to name it; it is provisionally called the dharma of no-dharma. Giving, prajñā, and the rest are all provisional names; since there is no way to name them, they are tentatively called dharmas — are there really such things? This is so of all worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike. (2) It is precisely because living beings cling everywhere that he speaks of not grasping at the two extremes, in order to cure their disease. If one took this to be the wondrous Dharma, one would again be dwelling and clinging. This is the painstaking care behind his not explaining. Yet the World-Honored One still feared that students, as thoughts stirred, might unawares dwell and cling to this and give rise to discrimination, so that ignorance would still remain and would have to be dispelled further. That is why he also spoke the second round — that is, the latter half of the sutra — precisely for this matter. (3) Though he did not explain, he guarded against people wandering in perplexity with no way to proceed; therefore he cited the raft simile to let slip a little news, so that true cultivators might likewise grasp it for themselves. One should know that in all things, what one grasps for oneself is of use. Why? Because at the very moment one grasps it, one is already receiving its benefit; this is more beneficial than what comes from outside through seeing and hearing. That is why the ancient worthies, in expounding the Dharma, often did not pour it all out — they were guarding against blocking people's gate of awakening.

I have set it all out this time, which is hardly in keeping with the ancient precepts, and I am well aware of the fault. Yet there are also my own small reasons for having to speak. Because the Buddha-Dharma has long declined, most people fear to hear of prajñā, and most of those who talk of prajñā go astray. And since you are so earnestly seeking the Dharma, if I absolutely did not awaken you a little, I could not open people's true gate of awakening. Moreover, there is something I rely on that makes me unafraid: there is the latter half of the sutra, which very profoundly remedies this disease, so there is no need to fear that hearing it will make one dwell in it. (And by awakening people here first, when we come to the latter half there will already be a groundwork. Here one should urge that no one be absent from a single session, lest what comes before and after fail to connect.)

Speaking to this point, there is one more thing I cannot but offer. Whoever wishes to grasp the true meaning in the sutra has only to read it with utmost sincerity and reverence. Once reading has made it familiar, one should constantly contemplate a passage or two, or a line or two. Contemplation is reflection. Yet this reflection is wholly different in flavor from what is ordinarily called research. Ordinary research into a subject uses ordinary feelings to conjecture; this is not so. Though it does not depart from words either, one must on no account weigh and tap at the words; even if one does, nothing will come of it. One must sweep away all distracting thoughts, quiet the mind and still the thinking, and focus the whole mind upon it. Not weighing and tapping at the words is not grasping at no-dharma; focusing the whole spirit on this sutra is not grasping at dharmas. This is the cultivation of concentration. In time, when not a single thought arises, the light of the nature appears, and the true principle in the sutra naturally wells up. This is reflection-cultivation; only this is receiving and upholding, and only thus can one grasp it. Therefore the moment of grasping is the moment of receiving its benefit. In reading sutras one should read in this way, and then the two studies of concentration and wisdom are cultivated together. One should further repent deeply and seek the empowerment of the Three Jewels. Otherwise, I fear that if one's obstacles are heavy, one will not only fail to grasp it but will not even manage the contemplation well. (Below one must say that not grasping at the two extremes does not mean not practicing giving and the other paramitas.)

Question: if not grasping at the two extremes is the prajñā teaching, may one then omit giving and the other dharmas? That is a mistake: to omit giving and the rest is to grasp at no-dharma. One should know that prajñā is the mother of giving and the other five paramitas. When prajñā is born, the five paramitas are born the more along with it, and one practices them all the more wondrously. When one practices the five paramitas with the contemplative wisdom of prajñā, then all five are paramitas indeed.

Whenever one sets forth a dharma, there are four alternatives. One may say it exists, or say it does not exist (that is, it is empty), or say it both exists and does not exist, or say it neither exists nor does not exist. In the most profound prajñā, all four alternatives are dispelled. This is what is meant by 'free of the four alternatives, cut off from the hundred negations.' (The hundred negations are nothing beyond the four alternatives.) Because the self-nature is pure and unstained by the least dust, all alike should be negated. And these four passages are precisely the freedom from the four alternatives.

The first passage dispels existence by nonexistence. (To cling to existence makes one an ordinary being, so it must be dispelled by nonexistence.) The second passage speaks of both existence and nonexistence, in order to dispel one-sided nonexistence. (Practice, the dharmas of the six paramitas, preserves existence; the mind having no marks of them preserves nonexistence. One-sided nonexistence is guarded against lest one fall into annihilation.) The third passage speaks of neither existence nor nonexistence, in order to dispel both existence and nonexistence. For 'both existence and nonexistence' cannot avoid preserving the two extremes; hence, by saying that neither extreme should be grasped — that is, grasping at existence is wrong and grasping at nonexistence is wrong — the two extremes are no longer kept apart but fused. As for the fourth passage, 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished': the Dharma refers to the six paramitas and the like; 'how much more so no-dharma': no-dharma refers to the dharma of neither existence nor nonexistence. For by the principle that all dharmas do not arise yet prajñā arises, the so-called not grasping at the two extremes is carried through to the very end. Therefore, while actually delivering, one begins with both existence and nonexistence and proceeds to neither existence nor nonexistence. Once deliverance is attained, then not only is the dharma of both existence and nonexistence relinquished, but of course the dharma of neither existence nor nonexistence is relinquished together with it; only thus does one become the Tathagata in whom all dharmas are one suchness. This is surely what all Buddhas and Tathagatas constantly taught. Thus our World-Honored One, putting on his robe and eating his food, appeared the same as ordinary beings, and yet his voice and excellent marks were fully present. At this point birth and death and nirvāṇa are both not dwelt in. Does it exist? Does it not exist? Does it both exist and not exist? Does it neither exist nor not exist? All four alternatives are unspeakable.

The two lines 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma' are the most essential words. All that was said above is not grasping at the two extremes. Therefore these two lines are nothing other than the concluding words of the preceding text. The passage on the raft simile likewise makes clear that these two lines are the wondrous Dharma, the so-called Dharma of anuttara-bodhi. (This should be explained in detail.)

As said above, what is spoken is the supreme-meaning siddhanta, spoken as an expedient within the unspeakable. All that this sutra says is supreme-meaning siddhanta, and therefore the expounder too cannot but speak thus. Yet when the Buddha's perfect voice is uttered once, no meaning is not encompassed; however one speaks, it is acceptable. What has been said above is very lofty, but there is no harm in explaining it according to the siddhanta of individual adaptation. Individual adaptation means fitting the faculties. The sutra says: this sutra is spoken for those who have brought forth the Mahayana mind, and for those who have brought forth the supreme vehicle's mind. For such faculties it is therefore spoken suddenly and directly. For example: 'no four marks of self and person' is the dharma of the emptiness of self, spoken to deliver from self-attachment. Again: 'no mark of dharma,' 'one should not grasp at dharmas,' 'the Dharma itself should be relinquished' — this is the dharma of the emptiness of dharmas, spoken to deliver from dharma-attachment. Again: 'also no mark of no-dharma,' 'one should not grasp at no-dharma,' 'how much more so no-dharma' — this is the dharma of the emptiness of emptiness, spoken to deliver from the attachment to emptiness. There are very many such teachings; why doubt that without a Dharma one cannot be delivered? One should know that the text says there are no marks of self and person; it does not say there is no self and person. It says there is no mark of dharma and no mark of no-dharma; it does not say that dharmas and no-dharma are ultimately nonexistent. In sum, to say 'no,' to say 'not grasping,' to say 'relinquish,' is only to dispel grasping, not to abandon the dharma itself. Once the three graspings are dispelled, the three emptinesses shine together and the three obstacles are wholly dissolved. Then even birth and death and nirvāṇa are both not dwelt in; how much less could this shore fail to be crossed or the other shore fail to be reached? Let it be explained further according to the siddhanta of counteraction. Counteraction means prescribing the medicine to fit the disease, healing the illness. The sutra says: the disease of living beings lies in clinging everywhere. Therefore the Buddha speaks of emptiness to those who cling to existence, and of existence to those who cling to emptiness, all simply to cure living beings of the disease of one-sided clinging. As soon as there is one-sided clinging, one does not accord with the nature-essence; one turns from enlightenment and joins with dust, so that karmic obstacles multiply and suffering is endless. Hence counteraction is needed. Thus here the text says the Dharma should be relinquished, and then says no-dharma should be relinquished still more. (Relinquishing is not grasping, which is also no marks; this is spoken in terms of the sense, not strictly according to the words.) From this one knows that 'relinquishing the Dharma' means relinquishing the disease of clinging to existence. Again, since it says both that no-dharma should be relinquished and that the Dharma should be relinquished, one knows that 'relinquishing no-dharma' means relinquishing the disease of clinging to emptiness. When the disease is gone, existence becomes wondrous existence and emptiness is true emptiness. One should know that to speak of wondrous existence makes clear that it exists yet does not exist, and therefore wondrous existence is true emptiness. To speak of true emptiness makes clear that it is empty yet not empty, and therefore true emptiness is wondrous existence. From this one can see that the reason one is made from the very start not to grasp at the two extremes is precisely so that one may attain the double illumination of the two extremes. Double illumination is alert yet still, still yet alert — what is called stillness and illumination at once. 'At once' means still and yet constantly illuminating, illuminating and yet constantly still; this is the samādhi of still illumination and suchness, this is the Buddha's realm. At this stage one not only extinguishes the obstacle of afflictions but extinguishes the obstacle of the known as well; one not only crosses fragmentary birth and death but crosses transformation birth and death too. This is what is meant by 'lead them all into remainderless nirvāṇa and deliver them.' From this one can see that all said here is the utterly perfect and utterly sudden supreme wondrous Dharma that directly causes one to become a Buddha. Whatever practice one undertakes, if one can grasp the meaning here and act accordingly, one's attainment will surely be swift and high. Moreover, the method is direct and to the point; if one calls it difficult, it is in fact not difficult. All you good friends, the Buddha-Dharma is hard to hear and yet you have heard it; the Buddha's kindness is hard to repay and yet it must be repaid — it lies only in our taking it up directly.

blocks.text: Nothing Attained, Nothing Spoken, Part Seven

inline.s: (Ren) Fourth, question, explanation, and confirmation. Three parts: (Gui) First, asking by citing the Tathagata's fruition-virtue; second, explaining by the ungraspability of dharmas; third, confirming by citing the unconditioned of all.
(Gui) First, asking by citing the Tathagata's fruition-virtue.
'Subhuti, what do you think? Has the Tathagata attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi? Has the Tathagata spoken any Dharma?'

This passage on question, explanation, and confirmation is again an explanation of the reason for the two lines 'one should not grasp' — how it is that one does not grasp at the two extremes, and why one must not grasp at the two extremes — and it cites the ground of fruition to confirm the ground of practice, to make clear that cause and fruition must be consistent. Therefore the World-Honored One cited the ultimate fruition and asked Subhuti, and after the explanation he further cited all worthies and sages in confirmation. All worthies and sages, viewed from the ultimate fruition, are the cause; but viewed from the beginner who has just brought forth the mind, they are the fruition. (This is divided into three small passages.) The sentences of the sutra often say one thing while meaning another, their gaze darting in all directions and wholly adaptable. Thus in the question here, looking at the two interrogative particles, the words plainly contain 'nothing attained, nothing spoken.' Yet if one said nothing is attained or spoken, one would be grasping at no-dharma; and if one said something is attained or spoken, one would be grasping at dharmas. The raising of this question is therefore a test of whether the hearer of the Dharma can truly comprehend the true meaning of not grasping at the two extremes.

Wherever this sutra places the four words 'what do you think,' in a shallow sense it is a test of whether the hearer of the Dharma can understand what has been said above. In a deep sense it points out to us who read and recite that we must not misconstrue the Buddha's intent, and that we must deeply experience the words that follow; only that is right knowledge and right view, and otherwise we do not accord with the Buddha's intent. In his question the Buddha says 'Tathagata,' yet in Subhuti's answer there appear all worthies and sages; from this one can see that whether one becomes a worthy, a sage, or a Tathagata, one cannot do so without this teaching. The two lines about the Tathagata follow closely upon the two lines about not grasping at dharmas. At first glance the word 'attained' seems to imply attainment, and 'spoken some Dharma' seems to imply speaking. The Buddha's meaning is plainly to ask whether the Tathagata, with regard to the Dharma he spoke, has anything spoken in his mind. That Dharma refers precisely to anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. Why did the Tathagata speak the Dharma? Precisely so that all living beings might realize supreme bodhi and thereby become Tathagatas — so of course there is attainment. The two interrogative particles in the question are on the surface about dharmas, but inwardly they contain no-dharma as well; for he feared that the careless might misunderstand, and he wanted Subhuti to explain. This not only tests whether the hearers can understand the principle of not clinging to the two extremes, but also points out to us that in our practice we cannot but begin from not clinging to the two extremes.

The careless person at once doubts: did not the Buddha attain the fruition by becoming enlightened beneath the bodhi tree? And were not the forty-nine years of teaching Dharma? How then can we who have just brought forth the mind be told not to grasp at dharmas? Once Subhuti explains — 'the World-Honored One attained yet without attaining, spoke yet without speaking' — the doubt is resolved. Going a step further: the text does not say the World-Honored One attained anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, nor does it say 'Buddha,' but says 'Tathagata.' The Tathagata is the dharma-body, the virtue of the nature. The Buddha-nature is possessed by everyone; it is only that ordinary beings hide it within the shell of ignorance. Hence these two lines are spoken to make us realize the nature. In the nature, is there anything attained? Is there anything spoken?
(Gui) Second, explaining by the ungraspability of dharmas. Two parts: (Zi) First, clarifying that there is no fixed dharma; second, explaining the double negation.
(Zi) First, clarifying that there is no fixed dharma.
Subhuti said: 'As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; and there is no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak.'

This answer is utterly perfect and utterly wondrous. It seems that what is answered is not what was asked. The World-Honored One asked from the side of the one who attains and the one who speaks, while the Elder answered from the side of what is attained and what is spoken. The question is one side, the answer another, and this is most perfect and wondrous. His meaning is: you, venerable sir, ask whether the Tathagata has anything attained or spoken. I have not yet become a Buddha — how should I know? So I merely take the side of the Dharma that is spoken, and briefly explain it according to the meaning the Buddha has always taught. In this way he keeps his proper place: since I have not realized Buddhahood, of course I cannot know; but if I comprehend according to the principle the World-Honored One has taught, I should not go wrong. In saying this the Elder on the one hand considers his own position and on the other reveals it to us. The World-Honored One's speaking of these two lines is of the utmost importance, and we should follow the Elder's intent and go on to comprehend it.

In the Elder's answer he does not say 'Tathagata' but says 'Buddha,' which has a deep meaning. His meaning is that good men and good women who wish to realize supreme bodhi should act according to the Buddha who has already realized the fruition. 'There is no fixed dharma' means that dharmas have no fixity. Put simply, it means that dharmas cannot be clung to; and 'there is no fixed dharma' is thus a commentary on the ungraspability of dharmas.

Anuttara-samyak-sambodhi has not even a fixed dharma by which it can be named; thus the meaning of the answer to the earlier question about attainment and speaking is already clear. If dharmas have not even a fixed name, how much less is there attainment? And how much less still anything spoken? Why did the Buddha, to good men and good women who have brought forth the bodhi mind, not speak of supreme bodhi but say that they should practice giving? From this one can see that apart from all dharmas there is no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi; hence there is no fixed dharma. The speaking of dharmas is always expedient; hence there is also no fixed dharma that can be spoken.
(Zi) Second, explaining the double negation.
'Why is this? The Dharma spoken by the Tathagata is wholly ungraspable and unspeakable, neither dharma nor no-dharma.'

The double negation is 'neither dharma nor no-dharma,' which is double detachment, which is also double negation, meaning that both are negated. These few words of the Elder are utterly perfect and wondrous and admit of all kinds of explanation. The sentences of the sutras should be viewed from every side; the Buddha himself said that in expounding the Dharma through endless kalpas he could not exhaust it — how much more should we ordinary beings comprehend it from many sides? 'No fixed dharma, and no fixed dharma that can be spoken' is understood from the preceding anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Elder is saying: how is it that I understand there is no fixed dharma and no fixed dharma that can be spoken? Because the Dharma spoken by the Tathagata is supreme enlightenment, is ultimate enlightenment. Ultimate enlightenment is no-thought. Why? The sutra says that by detaching from subtle thoughts one illumines the mind-nature, and this is called ultimate enlightenment; from this one can see that ultimate enlightenment is no-thought. How can no-thought be grasped? Only when the mind stirs can there be grasping. Both the grasper and the grasped must be done away with, hence it says 'wholly ungraspable.' The World-Honored One, wishing to point out our practice, therefore struck at it from the side and spoke with effort. And the prajñā mind-nature is free of the mark of speech, with nothing whatever that speaks or is spoken; hence it says 'wholly unspeakable.' If we cling to the idea that there really is an anuttara-samyak-sambodhi to be realized, we are wrong; hence it says 'neither dharma.' But if we cling to the idea that there is no anuttara-samyak-sambodhi, that too is wrong; hence it says 'nor no-dharma.'

Again, the word 'dharma' in 'the Dharma spoken by the Tathagata' refers to all dharmas. For all dharmas are anuttara-samyak-sambodhi. The Dharma spoken by the Tathagata tells us not to grasp. Yet he plainly also speaks of many dharmas and tells us not to grasp at no-dharma. Therefore we who hear the Dharma should grasp neither dharmas nor no-dharma. From this one knows that the one who speaks the Dharma also speaks only because he cannot do otherwise, and speaks according to the faculties. Since dharmas have no fixity, it is clear that to grasp at dharmas is wrong. But since he plainly speaks dharmas, it is clear that to grasp at no-dharma is wrong too. The two phrases 'neither dharma' and 'nor no-dharma' are precisely a commentary on 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma.' Why should one not grasp at dharmas? Because they are neither dharmas. Why should one not grasp at no-dharma? Because they are nor no-dharma. 'Neither dharma nor no-dharma' may also be viewed in reverse: the Tathagata's speaking of neither dharma nor no-dharma is wholly ungraspable and unspeakable.

The Elder says that there is also no fixed dharma that the Tathagata can speak. He specifically brings up the two words 'Tathagata' because the Tathagata is the dharma-body. The dharma-body is without marks — how could there be anything spoken? It contains the sense that the manifestation body, having marks, can speak; hence it says 'no fixed dharma.' 'No fixed dharma' means that one can neither insist that there is a dharma that can be spoken nor insist that there is no dharma that can be spoken. The dharma-body is the nature, and the nature is the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, measureless and boundless. All living beings and all bodhisattvas, viewed from the nature, are one true dharma-realm. Therefore the World-Honored One's speaking of the Dharma flows freely out of the great ocean of perfect enlightenment. If we would realize the great ocean of perfect enlightenment, we should first detach from the mark of mental conditions — how then can there be grasping? And we should detach from the mark of speech — how then can there be speaking? To detach from the mark of speech is precisely for the path of words to be cut off; to detach from the mark of mental conditions is precisely for the sphere of mental activity to be extinguished. Since the sphere of mental activity is extinguished and the path of words is cut off, how can there be discrimination? Hence it says 'neither dharma nor no-dharma.'

It was said above that no-thought means precisely detaching from the discriminating mind. Hence it says one should not grasp at dharmas and should not grasp at no-dharma. The World-Honored One realized the dharma-body Tathagata. Though there is attainment, there is nothing attained; though there is speaking, there is nothing spoken. To attain double illumination, one must first attain double detachment. The two things the World-Honored One asked contain this meaning. Would one say the dharma-body still has something attained? Would one say the dharma-body still has something spoken? The reason the Tathagata is called the Tathagata is that he first detached from discrimination. You who cultivate on the ground of practice should likewise first detach from discrimination; how can you hold the view that there is something attained or something spoken?
(Gui) Third, confirming by citing the unconditioned of all.
'Why is this? All worthies and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma.'

'Why is this?' points out the reason why both extremes must be negated. All worthies and sages use this method of double negation; how can we ordinary beings not use it? The ten dwellings, ten practices, ten dedications, and the four preliminary practices are the worthies; from the first ground to equal enlightenment are the sages; the Tathagata is the utmost sage. Hence it says 'all.' The unconditioned is nirvāṇa. Nirvāṇa in full Sanskrit is parinirvāṇa, translated as quiescent extinction, or as neither arising nor perishing; Kumarajiva, following the old Chinese term, translated it as 'unconditioned.' The Tang Tripitaka Master Xuanzang did not approve of using the old term, because the old term and the original Sanskrit meaning are not entirely the same; hence all the terms he translated were newly coined, to prevent readers from misunderstanding. The unconditioned here means neither arising nor perishing, and is different from Laozi's unconditioned, which is purely following nature without contrivance. To use the new translation is of course appropriate. But Xuanzang also coined many new terms where misunderstanding would not arise, and we do not approve of that either.

The unconditioned refers to the pure mind of the self-nature, which is complete from the first and has no mark of contrivance. When the sutras say there is no cultivation and no realization, they refer to this. One need only extinguish the mind of birth and death, and this quiescent extinction appears before one. As for the method of practice, it is the above 'neither dharma nor no-dharma,' not grasping at the two extremes. One must not grasp at the two extremes and must wholly eliminate discriminating deluded thoughts before it will do. Therefore in becoming a worthy or a sage, all use this method. Worthies and sages differ greatly: viewed with respect to the Tathagata they are the ground of practice, while viewed with respect to ordinary beings they are the fruition. Moreover, each later one viewed with respect to the earlier ones is a fruition, and each earlier one viewed with respect to the later ones is a cause. Hence it says 'all.' Worthies and sages realize the fruit by this unconditioned, hence it says 'all by.' So too with the Tathagata. Whatever the Tathagata speaks, he relies on the unconditioned that he has himself realized, so it cannot be called 'neither dharma.' Yet worthies and sages differ, their positions shallow or deep; from this one knows that whatever the Tathagata speaks accords with the faculties and is expedient, not ultimate truth, so it cannot be called 'nor no-dharma.'

Whatever the World-Honored One spoke, there is no shallow that is not deep and no deep that is not shallow. Therefore he taught the beginner to work from 'one should not grasp at dharmas' and 'one should not grasp at no-dharma.' When the fruit is ripened, even at the deepest stage of practice, it is still this method. We should begin at the stirring of thought, first contemplating no-thought. If one can know it the moment a thought stirs and immediately look back, one can illuminate and abide, and the thought is then no more; yet this is impossible without long practice. Hence at the first stage one must observe, and observation cannot do without deep reflection. In deep reflection one observes: these many thoughts, where do they arise from? As soon as one observes, one sees that arising is no arising, that they are fundamentally false and deluded; and when they arise again, one observes again. Working thus repeatedly, one can illuminate and abide, and can be without thought. Master Datian judged this section to be about the arising of faith, which is deeply apt. For the sutra text says 'can give rise to faith and take these as true,' and 'a single moment gives rise to pure faith' — plainly speaking of faith. The Tathagata became the Tathagata by this method, and all worthies and sages were accomplished by this method; therefore we cannot but thus give rise to faith and take these as true.

blocks.text: According to the Dharma Is Born, Part Eight

inline.s: (Xin) Third, comparing superiority. Four parts: (Ren) First, the merit of giving is great. Two parts: (Gui) First, raising the matter and asking; second, answering and explaining the reason.
(Gui) First, raising the matter and asking.
'Subhuti, what do you think? If a person filled the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures and gave them away in giving, would the merit he obtains be great?'

'Comparing' means comparing and measuring; 'superiority' means surpassing excellence. That is, with regard to merit, wisdom is used to compare and measure. Someone says: this sutra teaches people not to dwell in marks, so why does it everywhere compare and measure by merit? This has four essential meanings:

First, it makes one understand that merit and wisdom should both be cultivated. To cultivate wisdom alone without merit will not do. Suppose one expounds the sutras and speaks the Dharma; this is originally to deliver living beings. But living beings happen not to like hearing what you say — this is because you lack merit. Therefore merit is very important. To cultivate both merit and wisdom is to make one complete in compassion and wisdom: wisdom is the wisdom, compassion is the merit. All Buddhas and Tathagatas take the mind of great compassion as their essence. Because great compassion arises toward living beings, the Mahayana Buddha-Dharma is established on the side of living beings. Reading the Chapter on Samantabhadra's Vows, one knows that Samantabhadra's vow was brought forth from great compassion. In one passage it says: 'Or again, if a person with deep faith receives, upholds, reads, and recites these great vows, or even writes out one four-line verse, he can quickly extinguish the five uninterrupted karmic offenses.' It also says he quickly accomplishes a wondrous form-body complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man. From this one knows that if living beings can fulfill Samantabhadra's merit, they can extinguish offenses and obtain merit. And to practice Samantabhadra's vows, one must first bring forth the mind of great compassion. Therefore compassion is merit. The merit spoken of in this sutra all arises from great compassion; it does not make people seek the blessed rewards of gods and humans.

Second, since merit is so important, one should bring forth the mind of great compassion. Yet without wisdom the bodhisattva path cannot be practiced; hence great wisdom is even more important. The ancients spoke of the two wheels of merit and wisdom. From this one can see that the Tathagata must have both wheels before he can carry on his teaching. Yet the strength of the two wheels is like the left and right hands, with the right side weighted more heavily. Merit is indeed essential, but wisdom is even more so. Therefore filling the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures and giving them away is not equal to receiving and upholding a four-line verse and speaking it for others.

Third, by means of this comparison of superiority the preceding text is drawn together. Though the Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is a continuous discourse, in the midst of it he always draws things together at each point. The places in this sutra where superiority is compared are the places where the words and chapter-and-verse are drawn together.

Fourth, this sutra compares superiority many times, and each time the superiority is increased, so that the more it compares the more superior it becomes. This is not because the later text is deeper than the earlier and the difference so great; it is spoken with respect to living beings, indicating that the more excellent one's practice, the more merit one obtains.

The word 'if' is a word of hypothesis; there need not really be such a matter or such a person. In the sutras, the giving that fills the three-thousand great thousandfold world with the seven treasures is what the Great Brahma Heaven King did in a former life, during the time of his causal practice. It was not in one life but through many lives of giving, accumulated until there was this much. The Buddha says 'if there were such a person,' from which one can know that at that time there was no such person.

The sutras say that the greatest mountain in the world is called Mount Sumeru, also called Sumeru-lou, translated as Wondrous Height. This mountain enters the sea for eighty thousand yojanas and rises above the sea for eighty thousand yojanas (one yojana is forty li in Chinese measure), and so is extremely high. It is not made of earth and stone but of the four treasures of gold, silver, vaidurya, and crystal; hence it is called wondrous. Surrounding this mountain is a great sea called the Fragrant Water Sea. Around it again there are seas and mountains, seven layers in all, called the seven fragrant seas and the seven golden mountains. Beyond these there is another great sea called the Salt Water Sea. Around its edge is a great mountain called the Great Iron Enclosing Mountain. Beyond that mountain there are four great continents. One of the four is the southern continent of Jambudvipa, where we dwell. That the world takes the four continents of the globe to be the four continents of the sutras is a mistake. These four great continents, also called the four-under-heaven, lie on the slopes of Mount Sumeru. Of the six heavens of desire, the one nearest the human realm is the Heaven of the Four Heavenly Kings, whose palace lies on the slope of Mount Sumeru. The Four Heavenly Kings govern the human realm and the ghost realm; to inspect the good and evil of the human world is their duty. Above them is the Heaven of the Thirty-Three, which is likewise not in empty space but on the summit of Mount Sumeru. The Jade Emperor of Daoism and the August Sovereign on High of Confucianism are this heaven; from the Four Heavenly Kings down through the six paths, all are under the rule of this heaven. Four heavens further up are in empty space. Above the desire realm, the form realm has eighteen heavens, divided among the first, second, third, and fourth dhyanas. To be born in these heavens requires not only merit but also the power of concentration. There is no longer sexual desire, yet there is still material substance; hence it is called the form realm. To attain birth in the first dhyana one need not practice the concentration of the Buddhist gate; even the concentration of non-Buddhists can bring one to this heaven, as with the Great Luotian Heaven of Daoism. That too is the first dhyana, and Buddhists who practice concentration without escaping the three realms are also lodged in this heaven; hence they are all called dhyana. The Great Brahma Heaven King of the first dhyana has authority above Shakra Devanam Indra. Shakra governs one four-under-heaven, while the Great Brahma King governs a three-thousand great thousandfold world. The Sahā world taught by Śākyamuni is as great as this. The world governed by each Buddha is likewise so, differing only as pure or defiled. Even the Land of Ultimate Bliss is this great; but its land is level and made of the seven treasures, in stark contrast to the unevenness here produced by the perilous and evil minds of beings. When living beings cultivate great merit, they are rewarded with an abundance of the seven treasures; when their merit is small, the seven treasures are hidden. These gold, silver, vaidurya, crystal, mother-of-pearl, red pearl, and carnelian are all things not made by present-day human craft. That this person gave away the seven treasures filling a three-thousand great thousandfold world to living beings is likewise beyond human power. 'Would it be' means 'could it be called.' The World-Honored One's question is extremely skillful. It tests not only Subhuti but us as well; for he feared that we might misunderstand the preceding teaching of not dwelling in marks, thinking that since one does not dwell in marks, what need is there of merit? One should know that this person's giving that fills a three-thousand great thousandfold world is itself the delivering of living beings. Therefore one may only not dwell in marks; one must not fail to practice giving. Otherwise it is not the mind of great compassion.
(Gui) Second, answering and explaining the reason.
Subhuti said: 'Very great, World-Honored One. Why? This merit is precisely not the nature of merit; therefore the Tathagata speaks of much merit.'

This answer is deep and meaningful. Subhuti understood the World-Honored One's intent, and so said 'very great.' Yet he also feared that people would not understand: earlier the text plainly said not to dwell in marks, and now it suddenly says 'very great' — is not this petty calculation and measuring a dwelling in marks? Under 'why is this?' he himself explains the reason for answering 'very great.' In this sutra there are many sentences of the form 'is named, precisely is not.' This is the first place where they appear, and so the meaning is stated in fuller detail. He specifically brings out the word 'nature,' so that people may understand that wherever 'precisely is not' is said hereafter, it refers to the nature. 'Therefore it is said' means 'is named,' so that people may understand that wherever 'is named' is said hereafter, it refers to marks. With regard to marks: a name is the mark of a name, and speech is the mark of speech. Whatever is great or small, long or short, high or low, far or near, inner or outer — all that stands in opposition is a mark. Marks change and move, and are false and deluded; the nature does not move, and is empty and still. Therefore with regard to the nature, nothing can be spoken. Subhuti's meaning is: if the marks of merit can be spoken of as much, then it is not the nature of merit; but if it is the nature of merit, empty and still, then even the two words 'merit and virtue' cannot be affixed to it, and how much could be said about its quantity? Wherever 'precisely is not' and 'is named' appear hereafter, they should be understood in this way. Here the two words 'the Tathagata' are specifically added, for the Tathagata is a name for the nature-essence. To say that merit is much is spoken with regard to marks. Why bring up the Tathagata? This contains an essential meaning. The nature is the inner, marks the outer; the nature is the root, marks the branches. Only when there is an inner is there an outer, and only when there is a root are there branches. The meaning is that only with the Tathagata's nature is there merit to speak of; if there were no nature, what merit could be spoken of? 'This merit is precisely not the nature of merit' says 'merit' on the surface but in fact points out that we must not cling to marks. 'Therefore the Tathagata speaks of much merit' means that only with this nature are there these marks, causing us to return from marks to the nature.
(Ren) Second, the superiority of faith in this sutra.
'If again there is a person who, within this sutra, receives and upholds even so little as a four-line verse, and speaks it for others, his merit surpasses that.'

This section is the Buddha's word, and should have 'the Buddha said' or 'Subhuti' before it, which is here omitted. The word 'again' in 'if again' means 'further.' Readers may misunderstand, thinking that to read and recite the Diamond Sutra brings merit surpassing that of the Great Brahma Heaven King. In fact one should attend to the two words 'receive and uphold.' Only if such a person can receive and uphold this sutra and can also give does he surpass that one. 'Receive' is to take in and accept; it means one who can truly comprehend the meaning of the sutra and receive its benefit, one step beyond 'understand.' 'Uphold' means to hold it fast to the breast and never for a moment let it go, one step beyond 'receive.' Since one who receives and upholds it will certainly read and recite it, only the two words 'receive and uphold' are used. 'Even so little as' is a word of omission: whether one receives and upholds the whole or a part, at the least four lines, and so the word 'and so on' is placed. The character 'ge' in 'verse' was originally pronounced 'jie,' and the ancient worthies changed it to the departing tone, just as with the character 'jie' in 'understand.' This is originally Indian poetry; because rhymed text is hard to translate, when it was translated it was sometimes rhymed and sometimes not, and so it was specially renamed 'verse recitation.' In the Indian original, every four lines make a stanza. This 'four-line verse' does not designate any particular four lines in the sutra; any four lines may be so called. The above is self-benefit. The following 'speaks it for others' is benefiting others. The word 'his' refers to the merit of upholding and speaking. 'Surpasses that' means it exceeds the former person's, for he only accomplished giving, and that the giving of wealth, which is the mark of merit. Such a person can both receive and uphold in order to cultivate wisdom, and practice the giving of Dharma in order to cultivate merit. Cultivating both merit and wisdom and being complete in compassion and wisdom is the nature of merit; therefore he surpasses that one.
(Ren) Third, explaining and accomplishing the sutra's power.
'Why is this? Subhuti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of anuttara-samyak-sambodhi of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.'

The Buddha said in the Great Prajñā Sutra that no matter what dharmas there are, all are gathered up within prajñā. Hence among all sutras prajñā is the most essential, and the Diamond Sutra is the most essential part of prajñā. Whatever is essential in the Great Prajñā Sutra is fully present in this sutra. It is clear, then, that reading this sutra is no different from reading the Great Prajñā Sutra; indeed it is no different from reading the whole Tripiṭaka of twelve divisions. What this one sutra teaches is precisely the Dharma of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Hence it says that all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. "All Buddhas" means those who realize it; "anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" means the Dharma that is realized. Seen in this light, the Dharma-gate of attaining Buddhahood lies in this sutra, and the attainment of Buddhahood likewise lies in this sutra. One who can receive and uphold this Dharma-gate of Buddhahood and give it away in giving has merit and virtue that cannot be exhausted though one spoke for a whole kalpa. How could the giving of the seven treasures of a trichiliocosm possibly compare? This is the first comparison in this sutra, and the story of the Great Brahma Heaven King is brought in as exactly the right measure. For that was the giving that makes one a Great Brahma Heaven King, while this is the giving that makes one a Buddha. What the Buddha governs is likewise a trichiliocosm. Comparing that with this is quite apt. Yet the Great Brahma Heaven King is still an ordinary being, whereas the Buddha is a sage and the teacher of gods and humans. How could they be compared? Moreover, the Great Brahma Heaven King cannot even escape the three great calamities.

There is a further essential point. This sutra everywhere teaches people not to dwell in marks; this is precisely to make people realize the nature. It is clear, then, that whatever this sutra teaches is the nature. "All come forth from this sutra" really means, without any difference, that this sutra comes forth from the essence of the nature; and because it comes forth from the essence of the nature, people are taught that they must not dwell in marks. The affliction of ordinary people is that they cling everywhere: if not to this, then to that. This sutra everywhere teaches people to see the nature. Yet in the sutra the word "nature" appears nowhere except in the phrase "the nature of merit and virtue is not merit and virtue." The intent is to make people grasp it well for themselves, so that they do not cling even to the word "nature." "All Buddhas come forth from this sutra" also points out to us who study the Buddhadharma that we must enter through this sutra.
This section, which concludes the comparison of merit and virtue and sets forth non-dwelling as the way to generate faith, is most fitting. For faith is the gate of entry to the path.
(Ren) 4. Concluding in freedom from marks.
["Subhūti, what are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma."]

In the early Qing dynasty someone added, after "are not Buddha and Dharma," the line "are called Buddha and Dharma." This is a great mistake. Not using "are called" and saying only "are not" carries deep meaning; how could one add it recklessly? That no such phrase is added here serves to annotate the preceding text. To add it would both violate the style and miss the meaning. Whenever the phrase "are called" is added, it is to open up the following text. Here "Buddha and Dharma" refer to "all Buddhas" above, and "Dharma" to "the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas" above. The Buddha's meaning is: all Buddhas and their supreme enlightenment Dharma as I have spoken of them above are spoken in terms of name and mark; they are not spoken in terms of the nature. This sutra plainly teaches people not to dwell in marks; thus even the two lines above about all Buddhas must not be clung to as marks. If one clings to them as marks, they are not the Buddhas' supreme enlightenment Dharma. Concluded in this way, the meanings of the preceding passages on giving while not dwelling in marks, on not grasping dharmas and not grasping non-dharmas, are all brought to perfection.

The section above on showing non-dwelling in order to generate faith, from its opening words, has one give the vast deliverance of beings to Buddhahood (entering nirvāṇa without residue is precisely attaining Buddhahood); this shows us that we should not dwell in the marks of self and others. It then says, "in truth there are no beings who attain deliverance," which means we should not dwell in the marks of dharmas. It further says, "dwelling in no dharma, practice giving and the other dharmas," which means we should not dwell in the marks of non-dharmas. And so the four words "not dwelling in marks" sum it all up. Not dwelling in marks is the true explanation of non-dwelling. The reason we should not dwell is to subdue the deluded mind. (The deluded mind is consciousness, that is, discrimination.) The deluded mind is nothing else: it means discriminating and clinging to marks. Yet in the question, dwelling comes first and subduing second; in the answer, subduing comes first and dwelling second. And when answering about dwelling, it says, "should dwell in non-dwelling," and again, "should dwell only as taught." But what was taught is precisely non-dwelling. Is this not to say that one should dwell in non-dwelling? This again plainly shows that one need only remove delusion, and should not go seeking further for the true. For when delusion is removed, the true appears of itself. Moreover, the nature of true thusness is thus, equal and impartial. If one were to dwell in the true, one would fall into clinging to difference. Clinging becomes delusion; what truth would remain? Difference is not equality; what thusness would remain? Therefore one should only use non-dwelling to subdue delusion; this itself is right dwelling. How could one seek a dwelling place elsewhere? When one part of delusion is removed, one part of the true appears; why seek the true separately? Hence it follows: "All marks are delusive." This clarifies the fault of dwelling in marks. If one dwells in marks, one follows delusion. This is why subduing is spoken of first. Again it says: "If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathāgata." This clarifies the benefit of not dwelling in marks. If one can avoid dwelling in the marks of dharmas and non-dharmas, one sees the true nature. This is why it speaks only of subduing and not of dwelling, since subduing is itself right dwelling. Such an exposition is plainly evident. That is why all the passages above are gathered into one small section and entitled "Clear Indication."

Such a clear indication is given in order to enable people to generate faith, and so it is followed by the small section on generating faith. Here precept-keeping and merit-cultivation alone are singled out as able to generate faith, and this carries especially profound meaning. To speak briefly, there are three points.

(1) Prajñā here means right wisdom, and wisdom is born of concentration, while concentration is perfected by precepts. Now if one wishes to open right wisdom, one must keep the precepts. Otherwise right wisdom does not arise, and instead one develops mad wisdom and walks into wrong paths, in the greatest danger. The two wheels of merit and wisdom cannot lack either one. Only when both wheels roll together does one become the honored twofold body. If wisdom is great and merit small, then great compassion is lacking, and one cannot gather and transform beings. Therefore, in cultivating prajñā-wisdom one cannot cultivate it apart from giving and the other pāramitās. Thus the sutra says at its beginning, "deliver all beings," and again, "dwelling in no dharma, practice giving." To cultivate wisdom apart from merit means having no karmic connection with beings, and the marks of excellence are also incomplete. Even if one wished to transform beings, they would not listen to one's teaching. This is something we must understand.

(2) Keeping the precepts, one has few desires and knows contentment. Cultivating merit, one must deeply believe in cause and effect. Now as one cultivates the prajñā of contemplation, if craving is great, how can one leave marks behind? If cause and effect are unclear, one easily falls into the mark of annihilation. The sutra says that those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit can generate faith. This plainly shows that we should keep the precepts and cultivate merit, and only then can we enter the gate of prajñā. For faith is the gate of entry to the path. Its warning is deep and urgent. This, again, we must understand. In short, one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit is already free of the mark of non-dharmas. Therefore, contemplating emptiness of self and emptiness of dharmas in accord with the sutra, one will by no means step onto a wrong path. If one thought truly corresponds, one immediately enters the principle of the three emptinesses: what is called having no marks of self and others, no marks of dharmas, and no marks of non-dharmas.

What is called "no" is not stubborn emptiness; it means not grasping marks. The two words "not grasping" are again the true explanation of not dwelling in marks. And if one wishes not to grasp marks, one should not grasp dharmas and should not grasp non-dharmas. To grasp dharmas is to form the mark of dharma, that is, to cling to existence. To grasp non-dharmas is to form the mark of non-dharma, that is, to cling to emptiness. Not clinging to either emptiness or existence is the middle path and the ultimate meaning; it is the Dharma of unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. It is like a raft: while crossing, one relies on it; once across, one should still let it go. Therefore, though one has already become a Buddha, though one teaches the Dharma and delivers beings as a Buddha does, one attains without possessing what one attains, and speaks without possessing what one speaks. One cannot fixate on there being dharmas, nor fixate on there being no dharmas. Hence it says, "There is no fixed dharma." These four words are again the true explanation of not grasping dharmas and not grasping non-dharmas. They show that because there is nothing fixed, one should not grasp. What is called not grasping means simply not clinging. In short, whatever the Buddha teaches is from the outset ungraspable and unutterable. One must enter it where mental activity ceases and the path of words is cut off. Therefore to grasp dharmas and teach dharmas, to grasp non-dharmas and teach non-dharmas, are both wrong. This is called the unconditioned. Nirvāṇa, whether one aspires to sagehood or to Buddhahood, is reached by none other than this. Understanding this true meaning is true faith. One thought corresponding brings immeasurable merit and virtue. For one thought corresponding is the root of continuous pure mindfulness.

How is the merit and virtue immeasurable? Again, a small section comparing and surpassing makes its reason clear. It is as said: all Buddhas and the supreme enlightenment of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra. This explains that all Buddhas and all Buddhadharmas are not outside the principle of non-dwelling taught in this sutra. If one truly believes this principle, then with one pure thought one can go straight to unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. Is the merit and virtue then not immeasurable? Yet one must not, on hearing these words, seek it in the words and text. One must rely on the principle made clear in the sutra and turn the light back upon one's own nature. The nature is empty and still; there is no word "Buddha" and no word "Dharma" in it. If one can contemplate thus for a long time and realize and enter the empty, still nature, then one has accomplished unsurpassed enlightenment; then one has become a Buddha. Yet though the Buddha has become a Buddha, he never thinks that there is the slightest dharma to be attained. To have not the slightest dharma to be attained is not to think that one has become a Buddha. Hence it says, "What are called Buddha and Dharma are not Buddha and Dharma." From beginning to end, one thread runs through it all: non-dwelling, and nothing more. The cause embraces the ocean of fruition, and the fruition penetrates to the source of the cause. Thus, thus.

The above is the gist of the first section, showing non-dwelling; it is already detailed and complete. Our World-Honored One, in great kindness and compassion, wishing people to open wide a perfect understanding, again presses the meaning of non-dwelling forward layer by layer and makes it clear, hoping that when the wisdom of understanding is opened, the root of faith will be accomplished and the work of cultivation will grow accordingly.

(Geng) Next, pressing forward and unfolding non-dwelling in order to open understanding. It divides into five: (Xin) 1. Extensively explaining by way of the fruition; 2. Explaining in detail by way of the cause; 3. Asking for the name and its upholding; 4. Accomplishing the wisdom of understanding; 5. Fully revealing the merit of the sutra.
