These various dharmas, whether manifest or unmanifest, originally have no self-essence; their essence is only mind — hence “neither form.” Yet they are merely what mind manifests; they are not in fact mind — hence “neither mind.” The “wisdom” in “neither wisdom” means the wisdom of nature. The essence of nature is equal and void and still; how could it have any dharmas? Hence “neither wisdom.” Are dharmas, then, consciousness? You should know they are merely what consciousness manifests; one cannot say dharmas are consciousness. Hence “neither consciousness.” “Neither existent nor nonexistent”: when causes and conditions gather, dharmas seem to arise, so they are not nonexistent; yet being produced by conditions they are illusory marks, so they are not existent. These three phrases together say that all dharmas are merely set against one another in mutual contrast, seeming to exist while in truth not existing, empty right where they are. This explains the meaning of the words above: “you should know that defiled dharmas and pure dharmas are all mutually dependent; no self-mark can be spoken of.”

You should know that prajñā too is only so named in contrast to those dharmas. Because all dharmas are produced by conditions and illusorily exist, originally without self-mark, how could any self-mark be spoken of? How can one cling to the mark of names? Hence “prajñā is not prajñā.” And because the Buddha has realized the true wisdom of suchness, though he speaks blazingly there is in truth no mark of words; hence “the Tathāgata has taught nothing.” Only for the sake of living beings does he provisionally use words to guide them, causing them to leave thought and realize nature. From this one knows that the sutra’s saying “prajñā is not prajñā,” causing one to leave the mark of names, and again “nothing is taught,” causing one to leave the mark of words — is their purport not to cause the assembly to leave thought and return to suchness? Then what is meant by receiving and upholding is that one should receive and uphold the vajra that cuts off deluded thought, as is now clear.

It was said above that clearly understanding that there is no fixed Dharma clears the source of the view of self; now it is said that breaking climbing deluded thought cuts off the stream of the view of self. Consider the last few sentences of the passage cited above from the treatise: “because thinking of all dharmas causes the mind to arise and perish and prevents entry into true wisdom.” True wisdom is the essence of nature. From this one sees that nature is originally without thought; to realize the essence of nature one must cut off thought. One also sees that the arising of a thought is the mind of birth and death, and that because there is a mind of birth and death the fruit of birth and death is summoned. If one does not cut off thought, how can one end birth and death? Yet all living beings, from beginningless time, have had thought follow thought in unbroken succession, never once free of thought. This is called beginningless ignorance. Ignorance is non-awakening. Because of non-awakening, thought arises. What is non-awakening? It is what is called not penetrating the one dharma-realm: not comprehending that the principle and phenomena of the ten dharma-realms are solely one suchness, one substance, equal. This is non-awakening. Since one does not awaken to equal, one-substance reality, one’s thoughts move. When thought moves, the seer and the seen arise accordingly, and so there are marks of self and other, of difference. From this, discrimination never ceases, grasping and calculating continue, all kinds of karma are created, all kinds of suffering are summoned. And again, pervading and permeating each other, fruit turns back into cause, and cause receives further fruit. Ever more deeply deluded, one sinks and does not return. Now, wishing to return to the root and go back to the source, one must solve the matter at the root and cut off thought. Hard, hard! Because it is hard, the World-Honored One taught all kinds of skillful means so that beings might accord with them and enter. As cited above, “one who can contemplate no-thought is entering Buddha-wisdom” — this too is one of the skillful means. This is the critical juncture of birth and death for us all, the most important and urgent matter; it is also what this sutra causes us to receive and uphold. I do not shrink from prolixity, and will speak further of the skillful means.

You should know that the three words “contemplate no-thought” are indeed a skillful means. But how is one to contemplate? One still needs a skillful means in order to give rise to contemplation. What is the skillful means for cultivating contemplation? The Awakening of Faith has spoken of it. The treatise says: “You should know that because all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, they are called suchness. Question: if such is the meaning, how can living beings accord with it and be able to enter? Answer: if one knows that all dharmas, though spoken of, have nothing that can speak and nothing that can be spoken; though thought of, have nothing that can think and nothing that can be thought — this is called according with it. If one is free from thought, it is called entering.” “Because all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, they are called suchness” — this makes suchness plain in terms of all dharmas. The meaning is that all dharmas have no substance; their substance is only pure nature. (Pure nature is another name for suchness.) Since all dharmas have as their substance only pure nature — what is called “all dharmas are one suchness” — it is called the one true dharma-realm. For though the mind has no dharmas, dharmas arise from the mind; hence the dharmas of the ten dharma-realms are never apart from the one true mind. “One suchness,” “one true” — this is why the original nature is called suchness. Making suchness plain in terms of all dharmas makes the meaning of one-suchness and one-true very easy to understand. Such is the skillfulness of this way of speaking. Because all dharmas are one suchness, they cannot be spoken; because the true mind is without thought, they cannot be thought. Hence “all dharmas cannot be spoken and cannot be thought, and are called suchness.” The “such meaning” in the question refers to “cannot be spoken, cannot be thought.” Because living beings all have speaking and thinking, the question is how they can accord with it and enter. “According” is the meaning of skillful means. The question means: since living beings speak and think, and one wishes them to be without speech and without thought — without a skillful means, how can they realize and enter? In the answer, speaking and thinking are raised together; yet one who can be without thought will of course be without speech. Let us make it clear through the meaning of thought, and the meaning of speech will be clear of itself.

You should know that the sentence “though thought of, there is nothing that can think and nothing that can be thought” precisely points out the skillful means for cultivating contemplation. Hence it continues at once: “this is called according with it.” Why is this sentence the skillful means for contemplating no-thought? You should know it contains two meanings.

First, in terms of the essence of nature. You should know that thought is the karmic consciousness, and in the essence of nature there is no such thing at all. This is what is meant by “from the very beginning, free from the marks of all dharma-differences, because there is no deluded thought.” This makes clear that though the karmic consciousness stirs in confusion, the purity of nature remains as it is — just as when all phenomena teem in empty space, space itself remains as it is. This is an essential point and must not go unknown. Knowing it, one knows that nature and thought are originally apart, and one will not mistake a thief for one’s son.

Next, in terms of thought itself. You should know that thought as a thing arises right here and perishes right here, never pausing for an instant. The trouble is that as the former thought perishes, the latter thought arises again, thought following thought in succession. Only one without the skill of stillness does not notice the succession and mistakes the before and after for a single thought. If the before and after were truly a single thought, the practitioner would have no way to proceed. It is precisely because arising and perishing never cease that it is said: do not fear the arising of thought, only fear the lateness of awareness. This makes clear that thought arises and perishes as it goes, with no substantial thing — like a flower in the sky, illusorily existent and truly nonexistent. This too is an essential point that must not go unknown. Knowing it, one knows that thought itself is empty right where it is, and one will not grasp the void as real.

With these two meanings clear, one may at any time and in any place, in accordance with these two meanings, contemplate closely and intently. When a thought arises, rouse one’s spirit and reproach oneself: “Nature is originally without thought — where has this just come from?” With such a shining, the thought subsides of itself. A beginner without power of concentration will find a second thought suddenly arising within an instant; then reproach and illuminate again in the same way. In time, thoughts will visibly diminish day by day; even when they arise, their force will gradually weaken.

Question: to rouse awareness and illumination — is this not again giving rise to a thought? Answer: it is giving rise to a thought. You should know that since thought first stirred at beginningless time, the accumulated habit is deep and firm; to force it back and break it is very, very hard. One can only follow its habit without applying force, and instead switch to another thought to interrupt the original thought and prevent the succession. It is precisely because arising and perishing never cease that one can get a hold on it. You should further know that although contemplation and illumination are also thoughts, they are thoughts that arise as function in accord with the essence; one can therefore follow this function into the essence. They are utterly different in flavor from the thoughts that arise from losing the original nature. For the arising of thought is the same, but the function of the arising thought is vastly different. Because one knows that nature is originally without thought and that thought too is originally empty, one gives rise to the function of contemplation in order to remove deluded thought. This function arises in accord with the essence of nature, and so is utterly different from what arises from losing nature. This is called according with it; this is called skillful means. Yet you should know that this thought of contemplation is also illusory, also produced by conditions and without nature; it is now used merely to remove other thoughts. If one grasps this thought as real, it becomes a disease again. Prajñā-pāramitā is precisely the remedy for the disease of grasping; hence prajñā too must not be grasped. “Prajñā is not prajñā” makes clear that it should not be grasped. Prajñā originally contains three meanings: the prajñā of words, the prajñā of contemplation, and the prajñā of true reality. Through words one gives rise to contemplation and realizes true reality. And none of these three prajñās should be clung to. As for words: if one merely clings to the words without cultivating contemplation and practice, one is entirely within the mark of names. As for contemplation: if the mind harbors the thought of a contemplating subject and a contemplated object, one has not yet left the mark of names. And even when one realizes the prajñā of true reality, in truth there is nothing realized and nothing attained. If there is realization and attainment, one has still not left the mark of names, and it is not true reality; nor is it called prajñā-pāramitā. Hence “prajñā is not prajñā” here runs from beginning to end.

Returning to the source has no second road, but the skillful means are many gates. The one practice of reciting the Buddha’s name is especially the skillful means within skillful means for cutting off thought. Causing other thoughts to cease by reciting the Buddha’s name is likewise switching to another thought. And recitation is more intimate than cultivating contemplation: contemplation may be called wisdom-thought, while recitation is pure thought. One exchanges a pure, clean thought to cure the defiled, turbid thoughts one has always had, and further causes one to think single-mindedly — again using a single, undivided thought to cure the scattered, disordered thoughts one has always had. Moreover, “Buddha” means awakened: when every thought is the Buddha, every thought is awakening, and to be awakened is to awaken to the fact that nature is originally without thought — hence it is more intimate. Therefore one need only be diligent and single-minded to reach reciting without reciting. You should know that the aim of recitation must be to arrive at reciting without reciting. To arrive at no-thought is to arrive at suchness; then without speaking of cutting, it is cut, and without seeking realization, it is realized. How great a skillful means this is! Hence it is called the skillful means within skillful means.

What I just said — “without seeking realization, it is realized” — refers at first to realizing only one portion, because at that time only coarse thoughts are absent; subtle thoughts are still many. The Awakening of Faith says: “If one is free from thought, it is called entering.” “Entering” is realizing and entering. And this phrase is deep beyond the bottom. You should know that from contemplation and practice one reaches resemblance, and only then arrives at partial realization. Partial realization means realizing portion by portion; at first one enters only one portion. From there one passes through forty-one stages and reaches wondrous enlightenment, becoming a Buddha; only then are thoughts completely exhausted. Only when they are exhausted does one completely realize and enter the nature of suchness. Yet in truth there is no way to name this; it is provisionally called “entering.” Why? Because though attained, in truth nothing is attained; though entered, in truth nothing is entered. Only thus is it truly leaving thought, truly entering. As for the work of reciting the Buddha’s name: even if one cannot yet reach reciting without reciting, if one’s practice and vows are true and earnest, then by the power of Amitābha’s compassionate vows one is also received and reborn, and is then the same as avaivartika, which means non-retrogression. That is the stage of the first dwelling. To reach this stage by other practices would require long kalpas; here one life suffices to accomplish it. That it is the skillful means within skillful means needs no saying! You should know that “the same as avaivartika” makes clear that one’s own standing has not yet reached it, and that one attains non-retrogression only by being received by the Buddha’s power. How fortunate we are to hear this method — how can we waste time and let it slip through our fingers! Yet “true and earnest practice and vows” requires that the mind be single-mindedly fixed on reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth; only then is it true and earnest. If one recites the Buddha’s name with one hand while giving rise to dusty, turbid thoughts with the other, one’s practice and vows are not true and earnest. Hence one who recites the Buddha’s name, even if cutting off thought is not easy to accomplish, must certainly accomplish the two sentences: one should not dwell in form while giving rise to the mind, and one should not dwell in sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas while giving rise to the mind. Otherwise one’s vows are not earnest and one’s practice is not true — how can one be received by the Buddha? Why? Because one’s dusty, turbid energy is heavy and utterly out of accord with the two words “pure and clean.” Then even the Buddha can do nothing.

In sum: deluded thoughts flying in confusion are the root of disease that living beings have had since beginningless time, and must never be forcibly suppressed. If forcibly suppressed, one’s vital energy is injured instead. For deluded thought is nothing other than the function of the original mind; it is only that it has been misused, and so has become a disease. One need only follow the Buddhadharma and switch it over, returning it to wisdom-thought or pure thought; in time it returns of itself to no-thought. Then it is the wisdom of equality and the wisdom of wondrous observation. When the sutra says “cut off,” you should know it means removing the disease, not removing the dharma. The word “cut” means cutting off the deluded so that it returns to the true. If one can return to the true, one suddenly awakens greatly, comprehending that all dharmas are one suchness and are originally the one true dharma-realm, originally without differences of self and other. Then ten thousand thoughts melt away. This is why one can only use the method of switching thoughts. From this one knows that calling the switching of thoughts a “skillful means” is still a provisional, expedient expression; in truth it is the fundamental method of rescue. Apart from it there is no other method. This principle must not go unknown.

Even speaking of cutting off the deluded and returning to the true, one must advance gradually. A beginner cannot be spoken to of this all at once. For living beings have been deluded about the true and chasing the deluded since beginningless time, drifting on and forgetting to return. It is like a prodigal son in the world who has long since wandered off and forgotten to come home: to draw him back one must guide him well and entice him, and only then is there hope. Otherwise one only adds trouble to the household. So it is here. One must read and recite the Mahāyāna scriptures much, to wake one from delusion and confusion; and must draw near to spiritual friends much, to open what is covered over and point out the road of practice. And in applying effort one must proceed from the shallow to the deep, and only then enter ever better states. Otherwise the mind is only further unsettled. This too must not go unknown.

Take this sutra itself: a thousand words and ten thousand phrases have been spoken above, and only here, as the first half nears its end, does it plainly cause one to leave thought. That one cannot overstep the stages and speak of this all at once is now quite clear. Yet you should also know that from the detailed talk onward, all the various gateways of contemplation and practice that were taught are in fact means of entering from the shallow to the deep, skillful means for leaving thought. For one’s practice must be cultivated to the point of no-thought before one can realize nature and attain the ultimate. Now, by this meaning, I will summarize what came before once more and point it out layer by layer, so that it may be blended and comprehended and one’s complete understanding opened.
What is called opening understanding is opening wisdom. Relying on the various sutras and treatises, the opening of understanding has three steps.

The first step is to cause the wisdom that knows objects to be empty to open. Because living beings do not know that all dust-objects are originally illusory and unreal, they grasp everywhere and the view of self springs up at random. So first one causes them to comprehend that the six dusts and other objects are only empty and without reality. If they know this, they can begin not to be deluded by them. Not being deluded is wisdom. Hence it is named the wisdom that knows objects to be empty.

The second step is to cause the wisdom of no-dust to open. “Dust” means the six dusts and other objects; “no” means that everything is only mind, and outside the mind there are no dharmas. One must penetrate this, and also gain the skillful means for sweeping away dust-objects; then gradually the heart comes to have not a speck of dust. If one can be without dust, the light of wisdom grows brighter. This is the wisdom of no-dust. When this wisdom is clear, even if thoughts arise they are extremely faint. Only then can one cut them. Cutting off thought also requires the wisdom of skillful means; it is named vajra wisdom. This is the third step.

Vajra means the ability to cut. Consider how, from the very opening, the Buddha caused one to arouse the vast mind and save all living beings, as if forgetting oneself: this is the very first skillful means. For all living beings, because they do not penetrate the one dharma-realm, unawares give rise to thought and so have ignorance; hence they draw the boundary between self and other most sharply and grasp it most tightly. Now the Buddha causes them to give up self and save others, to arouse the vast mind: this causes them to penetrate that the one true dharma-realm is originally without distinction of self and other, and so to dissolve the rigid, ingrained habit of discrimination. This works from the root of the very non-awakening from which thought originally arose. Hence it is called the very first skillful means. After he had spoken of not dwelling in form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas in giving, he explained it in terms of bodily marks: “all marks are delusive.” This causes one to observe that roots, body, environment, and realm are all dust-objects, all delusive marks, so as to open the wisdom that knows objects to be empty. You should know that the reason living beings discriminate self and other so unbreakably is simply that they are bound by objects and cannot let go; and the reason they cannot let go is simply that they mistake all kinds of objective marks for real. Now the Buddha wakes them: “all are delusive.” Truly this is cold water poured down the back, making one’s hair stand on end. This is the second skillful means.

What follows continues with observing the precepts and cultivating merit being able to generate faith, and taking this as real. This causes one to believe this true meaning and begin to practice; for observing the precepts and cultivating merit is the very first skillful means for beginning practice. If one can truly give rise to pure faith in a single thought, then one has already been able to understand and practice each of the things taught above. Why? Because without understanding and practice one cannot be in accord in a single thought. At this point one gains immeasurable merit. Why? Because being able to be in accord in a single thought means one has already gained the wisdom that knows objects to be empty, and the mind that dwells in marks and the view of self and other are thereby reduced. Then, going a step further, the Buddha tells one that if the mind grasps marks it is grasping self, person, being, and life-span, and that neither dharmas nor non-dharmas should be grasped. Grasping is giving rise to thought; to say that the mind should not grasp dharmas or non-dharmas already contains the meaning that one must not give rise to thoughts and intentions. He further tells one that dharmas are originally without fixity, and so cannot be grasped and cannot be spoken of, and that all worthies and sages are distinguished by the unconditioned Dharma. The unconditioned is the mind without arising and perishing; the mind of arising and perishing is thought. This is again to coax and entice one, saying: since you can truly believe, aspire to worthiness and sagehood, and be in accord in a single thought, you should further still the mind of arising and perishing. Below he speaks further of the greatness of the merit, to delight and move one. And when he has fully made it plain in terms of the fruit, he plainly points out the word “thought.” If one cannot form a thought when attaining the fruit, then one should not move a thought when cultivating the cause — this is clear. He concludes with “one should give rise to a pure mind.” What is giving rise to a pure mind? It is giving rise to the mind while dwelling nowhere amid dust-objects. This is a further step beyond what came before: from the wisdom that knows objects to be empty, the wisdom of no-dust is opened. Before, one only knew it; now one is caused to be without it — is that not a further advance? Yet opening the wisdom of no-dust is in truth the preparatory skillful means for finally opening vajra wisdom. As for practice, to cultivate from the wisdom that knows objects to be empty up to the wisdom of no-dust requires several kalpas. The former is the stage of contemplation and practice; the latter is the stage of resemblance. This wisdom is the pivot for turning from ordinary to sage. Without gaining the wisdom of no-dust, one cannot advance further to open vajra wisdom, and so cannot ascend to the stage of the first dwelling. Without ascending to the first dwelling, one cannot pass from the stage of resemblance into the stage of partial realization and become a sage. Hence the merit of gaining the wisdom of no-dust surpasses the former by immeasurable, boundless times. Why is the merit so great? Because you should know that such a person accomplishes the supreme, foremost, rarest Dharma. “Accomplishes” means accomplishes the wisdom of no-dust. If the mind can truly be without dust-objects, then even if thoughts arise they are fewer than before and their force is thinner. Only when practice has come this far can one attain to cutting off thought. Hence this section on requesting instruction about the name and about upholding next tells of the method for cutting off thought. The stages, shallow and deep, are strictly ordered. Such is the Buddha’s teaching. You should know that from the opening sentence, “one should thus subdue one’s mind,” down to the teaching that one should not dwell in form and so on while giving rise to the mind, all of it is subduing delusion. One must be able to subdue before one can cut. Here it plainly says, “receive and uphold with this name,” and the name is Vajra Prajñā. Hence all the meanings made plain here are opening one’s vajra wisdom.

Vajra means the ability to cut; leaving names and words means leaving thought. If vajra wisdom is not opened, how can thought be cut? You should know that one who ascends to the stage of the first dwelling must possess this wisdom. Without it, one cannot cut off ignorance. Ignorance is non-awakening; because of non-awakening, thought arises. Hence cutting off ignorance is cutting off thought. One must cut off one portion of ignorance to realize one portion of the dharmakāya and ascend to the first dwelling. From the first dwelling upward there is nothing but this wisdom growing step by step, so that ignorance is cut portion by portion, the dharmakāya realized portion by portion, and the stages rise portion by portion. Passing through forty stages, one reaches the final mind of the tenth ground; there this wisdom is harder and sharper still, and is named the vajra path, and one ascends to Equal Enlightenment (the forty-first stage). After ascending to Equal Enlightenment, one again uses this wisdom to cut off the last, most subtle portion of ignorance, and so ascends to Wondrous Enlightenment and becomes a Buddha. Usually the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment alone is taken as vajra wisdom; below Equal Enlightenment it is still called the wisdom of no-dust. In truth the name of this wisdom simply reveals its ability to cut. If one does not possess it, one cannot cut off one portion of ignorance, realize one portion of the dharmakāya, and ascend to the first dwelling. Hence all from the first dwelling upward in fact possess this wisdom; it is only that it increases in superiority stage by stage, until at Equal Enlightenment it is complete. Thus the wisdom of Equal Enlightenment alone bears this name. This principle must not go unknown. From what has been said above, one must reach a corresponding degree before one can cut off thought; and if thought is not cut off, one cannot realize the dharmakāya and turn from ordinary to sage. And before cutting off thought one must first cultivate all kinds of preparatory skillful means — this meaning is clear indeed.

From the detailed talk up to this point, this sutra has already summarized its meaning several times, and each summary makes plain one meaning. The reason for this is simply the wish that hearers blend and comprehend it and gain more benefit, and also to make clear that the meanings stored in the sutra are inexhaustible and can never be fully expounded. All the teaching given above is but a drop in the great ocean.

To summarize what has been made plain above concerning these two sections — leaving names and leaving words — so that it may be remembered: (1) One must first thoroughly understand that there is no fixed Dharma, to clear the source of deluded thought. This is wisdom. (2) One must further break the mind of climbing thought, to cut off the stream of deluded thought. This is the ability to cut. This is the reason for receiving and upholding with the name Vajra Prajñā Pāramitā. As for cultivating contemplation and reciting the Buddha’s name, these are skillful means for the ability to cut. These skillful means are still contained within the meaning of the two sections; they do not come from outside. “One who can contemplate no-thought is tending toward Buddha-wisdom.” Buddha-wisdom is that prajñā-pāramitā is not prajñā-pāramitā. The Buddha’s speaking of prajñā is to cause one to give rise to contemplation through words; receiving and upholding is to cause the assembly to do the work of contemplation; and leaving names and words is to cause them to leave thought. Is that not plainly causing them to contemplate no-thought? “Receive and uphold” carries the sense of holding it earnestly to the breast: that is, one should never forget the Buddha’s words and never contravene the Tathāgata, thought after thought. Never forgetting the Buddha’s words, thought after thought, is precisely single-minded recitation of the Buddha. Never contravening the Tathāgata, thought after thought, means not only reciting the response-body Buddha but also causing one to recite the dharmakāya, true-reality Buddha. Again, because of non-awakening, thought arises; causing one to understand thoroughly that there is no fixed Dharma is causing one to awaken. Hence it is called clearing the source, because non-awakening is the source from which thought arises. Next, causing one to break deluded thought is leaving thought; hence it is called cutting the stream, because the arising of thought comes forth from non-awakening. And after non-awakening and the arising of thought, there comes the division of seer and seen, forming marks of difference between self and other. Now the whole effort lies in remedying non-awakening and the arising of thought; that is, it works at the root of the view of self. Once the root is pulled out, the view of self is gone of itself. This is the reason why receiving and upholding cuts off the view of self.

Again, these two sections make plain the empty tathāgatagarbha. “Empty” has two meanings: (1) the essence of nature is originally empty; (2) one empties one’s deluded thoughts. Here “prajñā is not prajñā” and “the Tathāgata has taught nothing” speak of the essence of nature being originally empty; while leaving the mark of names and leaving the mark of words is emptying one’s deluded thoughts. Hence these two sections precisely make plain the meaning of the empty tathāgatagarbha. The two sections below make plain the non-empty tathāgatagarbha. “Empty” reveals essence; “non-empty” reveals function. The two sections below on not destroying provisional names are the means of revealing function, for roots, body, and world are all functions manifested by the virtue of nature; hence the meaning of the non-empty tathāgatagarbha.

(Chou) Next, revealing the non-destruction of provisional names. This has two parts: (Yin) first, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping objects; next, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping bodily marks. (Yin) first again has two parts: (Mao) first, question and answer; next, the direct revelation.
(Mao) First, question and answer.
“Subhūti, what do you think? Are all the atoms in a great trichiliocosm many?” Subhūti said: “Very many, World-Honored One.”

“Name” means a name. All dharmas have marks of difference; according to those differences names are established. Hence talk of names is talk in terms of marks. Marks are illusory existence, and so names are provisional names. “Illusory existence” makes clear that they are nonexistent yet exist, exist yet are nonexistent. “Not destroyed” means not annihilated. Marks are the function arising from essence — how can they be annihilated? Though not annihilated, marks are in truth not the essence, and so still should not be grasped. For essence does not change, while marks constantly change; essence is the root, marks are the branches. One should not abandon the root to chase the branches, or be deluded by marks and forget essence; hence one should not be attached. “Leaving” and “not attached” at first hearing seem the same, but on examination they differ. To have nothing to do with each other is called leaving; to manifest and function without being bound by it is called not attaching. The two sections above that say “leaving” make clear that the practitioner’s weight lies in realizing essence, and that essence and marks originally have nothing to do with each other. The two sections below that say “not attaching” further make clear that the practitioner should first realize essence, and clearly must also penetrate function and must not destroy marks. Yet although one penetrates function, one should in the end return to essence, and so again must not grasp marks. What is said here should not be taken as mere explanation of section headings. The wondrous purport of prajñā is already entirely contained herein. Just now the distinction was drawn between “leaving” and “not attaching,” whose intent is different. You should further know that though the intent differs, the purport is the same. What is the same? It is cutting off thought. Why? The two sections above on leaving names and words are about leaving the climbing mind — their meaning was already explained at length; leaving conceptual activity is the means of cutting off thought. These two sections on objects and body — that is, dependent and principal rewards — being in every case not to be grasped mean that grasping again gives rise to thought. Though not destroyed, yet not grasped: this too is the means of cutting off thought. There are many other essential meanings; I will explain them layer by layer as they come.

The prajñā-pāramitā of the section above is one of the six pāramitās, and so is a name within the Buddhadharma; yet it is also a name for the principle-and-wisdom inherent in nature. The essence of nature is void and still, and names and words are originally not established in it. Since the section above expounds on the basis of this principle-and-wisdom inherent in nature, it must dispense with all marks. Hence it says only “is not,” says “nothing can be spoken of,” and does not say “is called.” For returning to nature is not being marks, and nature originally has nothing to do with marks; hence it speaks of leaving. The two sections below, on objects and body — which are dependent and principal rewards, with illusory marks plainly there — expound on that basis, and so it is convenient to make plain the meaning of not destroying provisional names. Hence of atoms, worlds, and the thirty-two marks it says “is called.” Yet after all they are illusory marks, delusive and unreal, so it says “is not” and that one should not be attached.

This question likewise follows on the text above. One who grasps marks, hearing that nothing is taught, will say: if nothing is taught, how is the great trichiliocosm taught and transformed? And words are originally without marks, so one may allow that teaching is teaching nothing; but the greatness of a world — its marks are plainly there. How can one say a world is no world? To block this doubt the Buddha asked this question. The question is very subtle: he does not ask about the world, but asks whether all the atoms are many. The meaning is that a world is a gathering of many atoms, which manifests the illusory marks of a great trichiliocosm. One who clings to the marks of the great trichiliocosm as truly existent may thereby suddenly awaken. The answer is subtle too: the elder deeply understood the Buddha’s intent, and so answered “very many,” meaning that all there is in a world is nothing but many atoms. Then apart from the many atoms, is there a separate world? Grasping that there are only many atoms, one knows that the great trichiliocosm exists yet is nonexistent.
(Mao) Next, the direct revelation. This has two parts: (Chen) first, not grasping subtle marks; next, not grasping vast marks.
(Chen) First, not grasping subtle marks.
“Subhūti, the Tathāgata says that all atoms are not atoms; therefore they are called atoms.”

This meaning goes further than the question before. It says that not only is the world not the world, but atoms are not atoms. This makes clear that “atom” too is a provisional name. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “You observe the nature of earth: coarse, it is the great earth; fine, it is an atom, down to the nearest-to-void atom.” What is an atom? What is the nearest-to-void atom? As the Abhidharmakośa and the Nyāyānusāra state, the size of an atom is already the finest thing the eye can see. For seven atoms make one metal-atom, and seven metal-atoms make one water-atom. “Metal-atom” and “water-atom” mean that they can travel through the gaps of metals or the gaps of water — so one may imagine the fineness of an atom. Seven water-atoms make one hare’s-hair atom, said to be as fine as the tip of a hare’s hair; from this one may grasp how fine an atom is. Yet this extremely fine atom can still be analyzed into seven ultimate atoms, which the fleshly eye cannot see; only the divine eye and above can perceive them. This is already the limit of form-marks, and cannot be further analyzed. Yet if observed with the wisdom eye it can be analyzed further into the nearest-to-void atom; “nearest-to-void” means that it is adjacent to empty space. The phrase is like our present saying “equal to zero.” From this one knows that an atom too is a gathering of seven ultimate atoms and is not a real thing. Hence “atoms are not atoms.” This way of speaking is the Small Vehicle’s analysis-of-emptiness contemplation, which requires analyzing one by one before one knows they are empty. The Great Vehicle is otherwise: observing solely in terms of the essence of nature, one knows that no matter whether marks are great or small, all are produced by conditions, illusorily existent, and empty right where they are; what need is there to analyze before knowing? To contemplate thus is named the contemplation of the emptiness of essence. This sutra is spoken for those who have aroused the Great Vehicle and the supreme vehicle; hence it says “the Tathāgata says.” “Tathāgata” is a name for the virtue of nature; “the Tathāgata says” makes clear that the observation is made in reliance on the original emptiness of the essence of nature — the so-called contemplation of the emptiness of essence. For spoken in terms of nature, atoms are originally without real substance, yet are not without illusory marks. Being originally without real substance, it says “is not”; not being without illusory marks, it says “is called.”
(Chen) Next, not grasping vast marks.
“The Tathāgata says that the world is not the world; therefore it is called the world.”

Knowing that atoms are not atoms but merely provisional names, one understands without further words that the world is not the world but merely a provisional name. Such is the skillfulness of this way of speaking. Taking these two small sections together, the intent is that one who cultivates prajñā, whatever the object — a matter as fine as an atom or as great as a world — should neither destroy nor grasp it. If even what is as fine as an atom should not be destroyed, how much less what is greater; if even what is as great as a world should not be grasped, how much less what is finer.
(Yin) Next, revealing that one should uphold it while not grasping bodily marks.

“Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?” “No, World-Honored One. Why? What the Tathāgata calls the thirty-two marks are not marks; therefore they are called the thirty-two marks.”

This question likewise arises from the text above. One who does not grasp the intent, hearing that the world is not the world but a provisional name, will say: the Buddha, responding to each occasion, manifests various bodies precisely to teach and transform the living beings of the great trichiliocosm. If, as said above, the world exists yet is nonexistent and is nonexistent yet exists, then why does the Buddha manifest the response body of the thirty-two marks? Is the response body too existent yet nonexistent, nonexistent yet existent? To block this doubt the Buddha asked this question. You should know that the Tathāgata, having already realized nature, nonetheless manifests the body of the thirty-two marks because living beings each have this tathāgatagarbha as their substance, yet pitifully are deluded by marks and do not know it themselves. Hence from the essence of nature he manifests the marks of the response body to teach and transform the great trichiliocosm, opening this treasury for living beings, causing them all to turn the light back and shine within, not grasp any marks, and see the original nature for themselves. This nature of living beings is originally one substance with all Buddhas — what is called the one true dharma-realm. Hence if one can see the original nature for oneself, one sees the Tathāgata. If one grasps marks, what one sees is the marks of the response body, not the essence of the dharmakāya; how can that be called seeing the Tathāgata? Understanding how the Tathāgata should be seen, one knows that the thirty-two marks too are produced by the meeting of conditions and are empty right where they are. Empty right where they are, they exist yet are nonexistent; produced by the meeting of conditions, they are nonexistent yet existent. Existing yet nonexistent, it says “are not marks”; nonexistent yet existent, it says “are called the thirty-two marks.”

The wording of the question here has the same tone as “can the Tathāgata be seen by bodily marks?” in the first great section, but the meaning is not entirely the same. There the question was raised in terms of bodily marks, including both the Buddha and living beings; here the question is raised in terms of the thirty-two marks, and refers specifically to the Buddha.

The answer “no” is a living phrase, with the same meaning as the “no” in the earlier answer about whether the Tathāgata can be seen by bodily marks: it says one cannot see him by them, and also that one can see him by them. The current circulating editions add, after “no,” the sentence “the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks.” The ancient text lacks it, and rightly so. You should know that in the section above the text below says only that bodily marks are not bodily marks, and so says “cannot,” and also says that the Tathāgata is seen by bodily marks — making clear that the “no” above and the “bodily marks are not bodily marks” below are both living phrases with double meaning. And here the text below already says “are not marks” and “are called the thirty-two marks,” which is quite enough to show that the “no” carries a double meaning. What need is there to add yet another sentence, “the Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the thirty-two marks”? One should follow the ancient text.

It says “the Tathāgata says” to make clear that this is spoken in terms of nature. Spoken in terms of nature, they are not marks: this makes clear that the essence of nature is originally not marks. If one knows that the essence is not marks, how can the thirty-two marks see the Tathāgata? Now it says that spoken in terms of nature they are not marks, and are called the thirty-two marks: this makes clear that a name is the guest of the reality. Since the thirty-two marks are merely a name, one may understand that their essence is nature. If one knows this principle and can be unattached to marks, then through the marks one can realize the essence — why must one annihilate the marks to see nature? Knowing this, one also clearly understands that the thirty-two marks originally arise from nature and so should not be destroyed, while nature is originally not marks and so should not be grasped.
What a great trichiliocosm is has already been discussed at length. As for what the thirty-two marks are, their meaning must likewise not go unknown.
(1) The mark of level and even feet: the soles of the feet have no hollows but are entirely full and level.
(2) The mark of the thousand-spoked wheel: the pattern beneath the feet is round like a wheel, and within the wheel are a thousand spokes, signifying that all marks are complete.
(3) The mark of long, slender fingers: the fingers are straight and tapered, fine, round, and long.
(4) The mark of soft and supple hands and feet: both hands and feet are as soft as cotton.
(5) The mark of webbed hands and feet: the fingers and toes are as if joined by a net, linked and interlaced with one another, like the shape between the toes of geese and ducks.
(6) The mark of full and complete heels: the heel is fully rounded, without hollows.
(7) The mark of high and beautiful insteps: the instep is high, arched, and full.

(8) The mark of calves like those of the king of deer: the calves are even and full, unlike the calves of ordinary people, which suddenly thicken. (The Chinese character for “calf” is here given two fanqie readings, one as in “Shan,” one as in “chuan”; in antiquity the calf was also called fei, pronounced “fei.”)
(9) The mark of hands reaching past the knees: when both arms hang down, their length passes the knees.
(10) The mark of the horse’s concealed organ: the male organ is closely concealed and not exposed.
(11) The mark of the body’s height and breadth being equal: from head to foot, the height equals the span of the outstretched arms.
(12) The mark of blue hairs growing from the pores: from each pore grows a single blue hair, without disorder.
(13) The mark of the body hair curling upward: every hair on the body curls to the right with its tip pointing up.
(14) The mark of a golden body: the body’s color is like a gathering of purple-gold light.
(15) The mark of constant light extending one zhang: the body emits radiance, one zhang in each of the four directions.
(16) The mark of fine, smooth skin: the skin is delicate and lustrous, neither holding dust or water nor letting mosquitoes and gnats alight.

(17) The mark of seven places full and level: the soles of both feet, both palms, both shoulders (that is, the hollows of the shoulders), and the nape of the neck — these seven places are all full and level, without the least defect.
(18) The mark of full armpits. The hollows beneath the two armpits are filled out. (They are not concave.)
(19) The mark of a body like a lion. This means that the deportment is grave and majestic.
(20) The mark of a body upright and straight. The bodily form is well proportioned, without stooping or bending.

(21) The mark of rounded and full shoulders. This means that the whole form of the two shoulders is neither raised nor sloping, but round, thick, and full. It differs from the even fullness of the seven places above.
(22) The mark of forty teeth. All forty teeth are complete. (An ordinary person has at most thirty-six teeth.)
(23) The mark of teeth white, even, and closely set. All forty teeth are white and pure, even and regular, firm and closely set.
(24) The mark of the four teeth white and pure. The four great teeth are of the purest and brightest white.
(25) The mark of the jaws like a lion's. The two cheeks are full and prominent, like a lion's cheeks.
(26) The mark of obtaining the supreme flavor. There is saliva in the throat; whatever food is eaten, it all becomes a flavor beyond compare.
(27) The mark of the broad and long tongue. The tongue is broad and long, soft, red, and thin. Spread out, it is broad enough to cover the face, and long enough to reach the hairline.
(28) The mark of the Brahma voice, deep and far-reaching. Brahma means purity. The sound of the voice is pure: nearby one does not find it loud, yet in the distance it is also heard.
(29) The mark of the eyes deep blue in color. The color of the pupils is like deep blue, utterly pure and luminous, like refined gold.
(30) The mark of eyelashes like a bull king's. The eyelashes are distinct, sparse, and supremely fine, like those of a bull king.
(31) The mark of the white hair between the eyebrows. Between the two brows there is a hair, white and pure, soft and curling, turning to the right and emitting light.
(32) The mark of the fleshy topknot. On the crown of the head there is flesh that rises up like a topknot.

These thirty-two marks are also called the marks of a great man, also called the marks of a great being, and also called the marks adorned by a hundred merits, meaning that a hundred kinds of merit and virtue adorn a single mark. To perfect all thirty-two requires passing through a hundred great kalpas; hence it is said, "a hundred kalpas of cultivating the marks and excellences." Merit and virtue are precisely the conduct and vows of Samantabhadra. Therefore the Chapter on Conduct and Vows says: "This good man well obtains a human body. Perfecting all the merit and virtue of Samantabhadra, before long he will be like the bodhisattva Samantabhadra, and will quickly accomplish a wondrous form-body complete with the thirty-two marks of a great man." One should know that the marks and excellences are all accomplished by great compassion and great vows. Why cultivate these marks and excellences? Because all sentient beings without exception cling to marks. If they see the marks and excellences, they then give rise to a joyful mind and a reverent mind. Only then are they willing to hear the Dharma, and only then can they give rise to faith. Moreover, Brahma kings, Indra, and wheel-turning kings also possess these marks, and bodhisattvas too often have them; but because the excellences are not complete, they are not equal to a Buddha. As for "marks and excellences," this does not mean that the marks are extremely fine. Rather, the great marks are called marks, and the subtle marks are called excellences. And "great" and "subtle" do not refer to size either. The great marks are seen as soon as they meet the eye. The subtle marks require careful observation before their excellence is known. The subtle marks are precisely what adorns the great marks. Thus the Buddha has thirty-two marks and accordingly eighty excellences, also called the eighty minor marks that follow the form; "following the form" means that they follow the thirty-two marks of form. Bodhisattvas, though they too have excellences, do not come up to the Buddha's completeness. The eighty are: (1) an invisible crown of the head; (2) nostrils that do not show; (3) brows like the new moon; (4) earlobes that hang down; (5) a body firm and solid as Nārāyaṇa; (6) bones like linked hooks; (7) the body turning at once like an elephant king; (8) when walking, the feet leaving the ground four inches, yet with imprint patterns; (9) nails of the color of red copper, thin and glossy; (10) knee-bones firm and round; and so on up to (80) hands and feet all displaying marks of virtue. Fearing prolixity, I do not give them in full; see the Treatise on the Meaning of the Mahayana for details. As for the names of the thirty-two marks, they are stated according to the Treatise on the Great Perfection of Wisdom; other books may differ. The thirty-two marks and eighty excellences above are what the transformation body manifests. As for the Buddha's reward body, it has more than this number; for the body has eighty-four thousand, even immeasurable, marks and excellences.

These two sections, on the great chiliocosm and on the thirty-two marks, if viewed together, hold inexhaustible wondrous meaning. For on these two matters our World-Honored One says "not so" and "is called," which is most intimate and flavorful. If those who hear the Dharma can truly ponder them with wholehearted attention, they may become utterly clear and luminous regarding the essential purport of prajñā. To sum up, this can be divided into four sections to make its meaning clear: first, clarifying by way of sentient beings; second, clarifying by way of cause and effect; third, clarifying by way of emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present; fourth, clarifying by way of the ultimate definitive meaning.

First, clarifying by way of sentient beings. In other words, the reason the World-Honored One says "not so" and "is called" concerning these two matters, the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, is that he is giving intimate guidance on the side of sentient beings. How is this so? The world is the environment on which all sentient beings depend. Without a world, how could they settle body and establish life? And if the Tathagata did not manifest the marks of the thirty-two response bodies, from where would all sentient beings hear the Dharma? From where would they give rise to faith? Speaking thus, these two matters are, on the side of sentient beings, of the most vital concern, as can be known. Therefore, speaking in terms of nature, although fundamentally they are all provisional names for what is condition-arisen and illusory, still to call them provisional names is acceptable, while to call them "not so" is greatly unacceptable. Hence it is said "is called," making clear that although they are provisional names, they are truly so, and thus cannot be destroyed. Yet one should know that the world is ultimately a field of dust; if all sentient beings grasp and cling to these dust-marks, the mind is not pure. When the mind is impure, the land is impure; how then can they end birth and death and escape rebirth? Further, one should know that the Buddha's response body is a form manifested by the Tathagata of the dharma-body. That is, only one who has realized the dharma-body can manifest the response body. Why manifest a response body? Without manifesting these marks, sentient beings would have no way to hear the Dharma. And the Tathagata manifests the response body to speak the Dharma originally because he wishes all sentient beings to realize the dharma-body they inherently possess. If sentient beings grasp and cling to the marks of this response body, they will be unable to see the nature. Why? Because if they cannot reflect back upon their own nature, then even standing face to face before a Buddha of thirty-two marks, they still cannot see the Tathagata. Would this not greatly contradict the Buddha's original purpose in manifesting the thirty-two marks? Therefore in every case he says "not so," making clear that in terms of marks it is indeed so, but in terms of nature it is not so, and hence one should not cling. Such guidance is intimacy itself.

Second, clarifying by way of cause and effect. In other words, the World-Honored One's establishing this teaching on these two matters is intended to enable sentient beings to understand clearly the true meaning of cause and effect. How is this so? Whence comes this dusty, ordinary great chiliocosm? It is what sentient beings feel in common through their shared karma. Whence come these supremely wondrous thirty-two marks? They are what the World-Honored One accomplished through perfuming and cultivation over many kalpas. That being so, both of these are nothing but the law of cause and effect, as can be clearly known. Cause and effect means arising through the meeting of conditions. Because they are condition-arisen, they are illusory existents; because they are illusory existents, they are provisional names. Yet although they are provisional names, where there is a cause there must be an effect, which is never destroyed; hence it is said "is called." The words "is called" are used to make sentient beings deeply reverence cause and effect: though empty in nature, the marks exist, and not the slightest bit is off or can be escaped. If one knows that cause and effect are empty in nature, existing in marks, and inescapable, one should then cultivate the supreme pure cause that is neither marked nor unmarked, in order to realize the supreme wondrous fruit that is neither marked nor unmarked. What is meant by "neither marked nor unmarked"? It is to understand that dharmas arising from causes and conditions are precisely empty and precisely provisional, precisely provisional and precisely empty, and that one does not cling to either extreme, thereby according with the supreme meaning of the middle way. One should know that "neither marked nor unmarked" and "the supreme meaning of the middle way" are the true reality of the nature, which is so from the beginning. Therefore to cultivate and uphold in this way is precisely prajñā-pāramitā. That is why cultivating this supreme cause must win the supreme fruit. Hence concerning the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks he says in every case "not so." He says "not so" in every case so that sentient beings may neither destroy the marks of cause and effect nor fail to return and merge into the nature. This is to be free of clinging to both emptiness and existence, and to accord with the middle way.

Third, clarifying by way of emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present. This makes clear that the World-Honored One's establishing this teaching is so that, by hearing this Dharma, beings may understand clearly the reason why emptiness and existence are simultaneously and together present. How is this so? The single word "not" is spoken to keep one from clinging to existence. The single word "is" is spoken to keep one from clinging to emptiness. And to say both "not" and "is," speaking the two together, is to keep one from clinging to either extreme. Why may one cling to neither? Because inwardly this body and outwardly the world, the two rewards of dependent and proper, are none of them anything but what arises from the union of causes and conditions. At the time conditions meet and it arises, the names and marks of the two rewards, dependent and proper, plainly appear: how could one cling to emptiness? At the time conditions disperse and it ceases, where is this body, where is this world: how could one cling to existence? Nor is this all. As for the two rewards, dependent and proper, when the time of their condition-arising comes, since it is a union of causes and conditions, we call it arising. From this one can see that apart from causes and conditions there is no other real dharma. Therefore when the provisional name appears, that is precisely the time of non-existence. Hence it is said, "existence is precisely non-existence." And again, when it is the time of non-existence, that is precisely the time the provisional name appears. Hence it is said, "non-existent yet existing." Viewed together, is this not emptiness and existence being simultaneously and together present? Since they are simultaneously and together present, clinging to either emptiness or existence is wrong. Therefore the present joint statement of "not" and "is" is precisely to enable those who hear the Dharma to understand the meaning that emptiness and existence are together present and neither may be clung to. Moreover, the two rewards, dependent and proper, are matters of name and mark so evident that all beings see them in common. Since these are simultaneously empty and existent, the rest can be understood at a glance. And since they are the matters most intimately and vitally connected with sentient beings, and here emptiness and existence alike may not be clung to, the rest can be understood clearly. In the two sections above, which are free of names, words, and speech, only the side of existence was being dismissed. In these two sections, both sides, emptiness and existence, are dismissed; this is the utmost in cutting off deluded thoughts.

Fourth, clarifying by way of the ultimate meaning. This explains that the World-Honored One speaks these two sections in order to enable sentient beings to comprehend thoroughly the nature-body in which the path of words is cut off and the reach of the mind is extinguished. How is this so? Since the two rewards, dependent and proper, are both condition-arisen, one can know that they are merely marks of the coming together of causes and conditions. Therefore in the sutra they are called "is called." "Is called" makes clear that they are provisionally named as arising. Since they are provisionally named as arising, one can see that in truth they have never arisen. Therefore in the sutra he says of them "not so." "Not so" makes clear that they are fundamentally unborn. Since there is no such thing as arising, there is also no such thing as ceasing. That being so, all dharmas are fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing; but ordinary beings do not know this, and in their delusion take them to be truly arising and ceasing, and following upon that, deluded thoughts arise in confusion. Therefore the World-Honored One calls them pitiable.

One should further know that body, mind, and world are fundamentally without arising and ceasing; yet marks of arising and ceasing are seen, and names of arising and ceasing are established. There is no other reason: it is truly the empty illusion of deluded, pitiable ordinary beings, the false marks conjured by deluded thoughts, and the names and words forcibly established by deluded thoughts. When the sutra says "is called," it is exactly so. This is the ultimate definitive meaning of "is called." Therefore if one is apart from thought, then the names and words of body, mind, and world do not even remain: how much less the names of arising and ceasing, and how much less could arising and ceasing be spoken of. In this way all marks are extinguished and one enters the true reality-body. Why? The nature-body of true suchness has from the very beginning been equal and thus. It is neither existent nor non-existent, neither both existent and non-existent, nor neither existent nor non-existent. It extends even to being neither all dharmas nor not all dharmas. In sum, as soon as thought arises, it is not so; and even the "not so" of the arising of thought is also not so. This is what is meant by being apart from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations. When the sutra says "then it is not," it is exactly so. This is the ultimate definitive meaning of "then it is not."

This ultimate definitive meaning is present wherever the text above says "then it is not" or "is called." Yet it was not spoken of earlier, and is spoken only now, for there is deep purpose in this. The text below says "deeply understood the meaning and purport," from which one can know that by this point in the sutra the deep meaning should be made clear. Hence the matter was temporarily set aside above. This is what is meant by leading from the shallow into the deep, drawing people into what is wondrous. Further, this meaning is most conveniently stated with regard to body, mind, and world. And again, in this request for the name and the upholding, the sutra's meaning is precisely to make clear the cutting off of thought as a means of realizing the nature. If one wishes to cut off thought and realize the nature, one cannot do so without upholding the ultimate definitive meaning. Hence it is said that by this point in the sutra the deep meaning should be made clear. Knowing this, one knows that this meaning should only be brought out here. To move it earlier would be too soon; to move it later would be too late. In expounding the sutras and speaking the Dharma, one must let the text and meaning be without error. For meanings have shallow and deep, and the text has its proper sequence. If one does not speak when one should speak, and speaks when one should not, this is an error in the text. Even if the meaning is without error, it is still idle talk and carries fault. This is a point that anyone with the vow to propagate the Dharma must not fail to know.

Further, above, when he says "then it is not," he only says "then it is not"; when he says "is called," he only says "is called." But the meaning of the fourth layer is not so. When he says "is called," the intent of "then it is not" is included; and when he says "then it is not," the intent of "is called" is also included. This too is the ultimate definitive meaning. How could it be that only dismissing marks and speaking of the nature counts as the ultimate definitive meaning? One should know that if there were only negation and no illumination, only extinction and nothing preserved, then what was spoken would not be the ultimate definitive meaning. Within negation there is illumination; within extinction there is preservation: only this is the ultimate definitive meaning. For without negation and extinction one cannot see the nature; yet a rigid negation and a rigid extinction also cannot see the nature. Hearing this ultimate definitive meaning, one should ponder it with wholehearted attention. A difference of a hairsbreadth becomes an error of a thousand miles. This is of the utmost importance.

Now let these two sections on not destroying provisional names and the two sections above on returning and merging into the nature-body be viewed together: there is a further essential meaning that must urgently be made clear. One should know that the reason for first causing detachment by way of the names and words of prajñā, and then causing non-clinging by way of the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, is nothing else. It is because the nature-body is absolutely unconditioned. The moment one falls into names and language, there is the namer and the named, the speaker and the spoken. Since there is a subject and an object, they plainly become a pair of opposites. Where there is the slightest mark of opposition, it is no longer the absolute body. The Buddha speaks prajñā to enable people to see the nature. For prajñā-pāramitā originally arises from the principle-body of true suchness and right wisdom. Therefore by this he causes detachment from names and words, making clear the meaning that one who would realize the nature must dismiss marks. And further, because this body is absolutely unconditioned, it can merge and absorb all worldly and world-transcending dharmas. As the Awakening of Faith says, "Because the Tathagata-garbha is complete with immeasurable intrinsic merit and virtue" (this sentence makes clear the greatness of marks), "because it can produce all worldly and world-transcending causes and effects" (this sentence makes clear the greatness of function). From this one sees that marks and function cannot be apart from the body. That is, because the body is great, the marks and function it absorbs are also great. Now these two sections on not destroying provisional names, in speaking of the great chiliocosm and the thirty-two marks, precisely make clear the greatness of marks. For they are all manifested by the nature-body: the so-called immeasurable intrinsic merit and virtue. Further, the great chiliocosm is what sentient beings feel in common through their shared karma, and is the cause and effect of worldly dharmas. The thirty-two marks are what the Buddha accomplished through perfuming and cultivation over many kalpas, and are the cause and effect of world-transcending dharmas. From this one sees that these two also make clear, in passing, the greatness of function. Moreover, to bring up the great chiliocosm is to absorb all cause and effect of worldly dharmas; to bring up the Buddha's thirty-two marks is to absorb all cause and effect of world-transcending dharmas. Further, to speak of the world is to absorb all vast marks; to speak of atoms is to absorb all subtle marks. That being so, if one here makes clear non-clinging, then one should not cling to anything at all, as can be known. If one here makes clear non-destruction, then one should not destroy anything at all, as can also be understood. Why should one not cling to anything? Because marks and function should merge into the nature-body. Why should one not destroy anything? Because the body must be complete with marks and function.

Moreover, from the sequence of first speaking of returning and merging into the nature-body and afterwards speaking of not destroying provisional names, it is plainly shown to students that at the outset they should use the work of sweeping away in order to remove the stains of old habituations, so that this mind may gradually become pure and there is hope of seeing the nature. Even the marks of names and words must still be swept away; then one can know that not the slightest mark may remain in the mind. Why? Because the nature is fundamentally not marks. Yet if one uses only this work, one must guard against falling into one-sided emptiness. Therefore one should also be all-embracing. All-embracing means that nature and marks are perfectly fused, unobstructed and free. Hence the teaching that follows on not destroying provisional names. This is to make clear the meaning of perfect fusion without obstruction. For the reason he first speaks of "not" before speaking of "is called" is to make clear that illusory existence does not depart from true emptiness, and that marks, being not the nature, are not fused. Therefore although one does not destroy marks, one must also not cling to marks, and only then can there be perfect fusion without obstruction. Without obstruction means that marks do not obstruct the nature. Further, the reason he speaks both of "not" and then of "is called" is to make clear that true emptiness does not hinder illusory existence, and that the nature, being not marks, would not be revealed. Therefore although one does not cling to marks, one should also not destroy marks, and only then is there non-obstruction and perfect fusion. Perfect fusion means that the nature does not reject marks. Such is the meaning here, the most refined and essential meaning of these four sections. The essential purport of prajñā-pāramitā is thoroughly laid bare. This is precisely the reason why the Diamond Prajñā-pāramitā is to be upheld. If one does not understand this, then with regard to the sutra's meaning, even if one happens to speak a thing or two, it will never touch the vital spot. Then what is called understanding is not true understanding. Since it is not true understanding, how can one uphold it? Then what is called practice is in truth blind practice. In this way, though one studies Buddhism diligently and laboriously, one can never gain great benefit, and may even walk into a side path without knowing it. The opposite is to advance a thousand miles a day and gain inexhaustible benefit. Prajñā is the fundamental meaning within the Buddhadharma, and is also the ultimate definitive meaning. If a student of Buddhism is unclear about this fundamental and ultimate meaning, he is forever seeking among branches and leaves. Having not seen the Way, how can he speak of cultivating the Way? Hence he cannot gain benefit. The old theory that the three teachings share one source is nothing but drawing analogies and forcing connections among the branches and leaves of the Buddhadharma. As for the fundamental and ultimate meaning, there is no way to compare it at all. One should know that the Buddhadharma surpasses all else precisely in this. If one studies Buddhism without understanding this meaning, one remains outside the gate. Hence it is said above: "All Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra." This plainly shows that the Buddhadharma must be entered through this gate.

Confucians have often plagiarized the meaning of the Buddhadharma in order to discuss Confucianism, and then slandered the Buddhadharma besides. This is truly an offense. Yet what they plagiarized was only a half-understanding. Not only was it not the definitive meaning, it was not even the complete meaning. To slander on such a basis: how could that be right! The path by which they plagiarized was nothing other than the recorded sayings of the Chan school. In Chan practice, though the school takes prajñā as its foundation, because it does not rely on words, it does not develop its teaching on the basis of the scriptures. Moreover, what it says is uniformly lofty and undifferentiated, and it is here that it is easily plagiarized and forced into analogies. Yet that the fundamental and ultimate definitive meaning does not suffer being pulled about and thrown into confusion is also a fortunate consequence of this. Why? Confucians who restrain themselves and cultivate the person, who follow the rules and tread the proper path: are they not gentlemen? Yet their vision is short and shallow and their mental scope narrow; most of them, having gained a little, are smugly pleased, and knowing one point they deny the second. Hence since the Han dynasty, when the honor of Confucius was proclaimed, apart from the Han scholars' philological studies, which still benefited the Confucian books, others dragged in the sayings of apocryphal prophecy, or pulled in the doctrines of Huang-Lao, or plagiarized the leftover threads of the Chan school that resemble Confucian texts, forcing analogies and dressing them up in splendor. In truth they had not even dreamed of the genuine meaning of Confucianism. Yet the factional strife was noisily at its height. With men of such deep self-view, even if they heard the fundamental and ultimate definitive meaning of the Buddhadharma, their inability to grasp it may also be settled. Consider how the Cheng brothers and Zhu Xi each drew near to great Chan masters for many years, and what they gained was no more than this. That they turned instead to raising spears against one another is enough to prove that my words are not mistaken! That being so, if such men had heard the teaching of the ultimate definitive meaning, even if they had not come to blows, they would surely have treated it as they treated Confucian principles, pulling in branches and leaves, plausible but false, so that the true meaning was obscured instead. This is again the greatest fortune within misfortune.

Further, these four sections contain another essential meaning that also must not go unclarified. What is that meaning? It is that the first section is the master, and the remaining three sections explain the reason why. How is the first section the master? "Prajñā-pāramitā is precisely not prajñā-pāramitā" is the master. One should know that prajñā is the wisdom everyone inherently possesses; it is precisely the pure mind. This pure mind has no place where it abides and leaves no trace when it is used; fundamentally it cannot be held and cannot be grasped. This is what is meant by the mind-moon standing alone in its roundness, its light swallowing all phenomena. Why? Because it is absolutely pure. Does the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment not say: "Where there is illumination and where there is awareness, both are called obstructions." The Buddha speaks prajñā in order to enable people to rely on the words, give rise to contemplation, and realize true reality. But he feared that people would retain the wisdom of illumination and awareness, and those of lower capacity might even seek prajñā within names and words. Therefore, precisely when explaining the reason for upholding it, he does not shrink from saying it himself and overturning it himself, declaring: "Prajñā is precisely not prajñā." Spoken thus, it straightaway leaves not a single word's footprint in the mind of the one who upholds it, and not a trace of any mark can adhere. This is truly what is meant by a sharp blade cutting through tangled hemp. This itself is the Diamond Prajñā, utterly different from the prajñā of resemblance. (Where the principle of prajñā is not seen through, the treatises call it prajñā of resemblance, meaning that it seems so but is not.) All practitioners should uphold it in this way.

Above it is said, "by this name": one should use this Diamond name. Therefore this Diamond Prajñā, upheld to break delusion, leaves no delusion unexhausted; upheld to illumine principle, leaves no principle unrevealed. Thus it can be identical with all dharmas and apart from all marks; and further, apart from all marks, it practices all dharmas. If one can truly uphold it in this way, then with regard to worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike one ultimately reaches their root and branch, their end and boundary. It is for this that it is called pāramitā. This is the true meaning of the Buddha's saying that prajñā is precisely not prajñā. Fearing again that students might not comprehend, he further speaks the next three sections to make its meaning clear, so that they may understand it thoroughly.

The section asking whether there is any dharma spoken makes clear that prajñā is without words and without speech. The statement above that prajñā is not prajñā precisely reveals that it cannot be reached by words and speech. Therefore the question whether there is any dharma spoken tests one's insight. The answer that nothing is spoken stands precisely opposed, point to point, to the intent of the question. If one understands that although he speaks all day and speaks ardently, in truth there are no words and no speech, then one does not seek it within words and speech. One who upholds it thus is practicing prajñā-pāramitā.

The section on the three-thousand great chiliocosm makes clear that in prajñā, object and wisdom are one suchness. That prajñā is not prajñā precisely reveals that prajñā is not really one dharma, and that every dharma is prajñā, making clear that all dharmas are one suchness. Fearing that this might not be understood, he borrows atoms and worlds to raise a question. The answer "very many" speaks of marks in terms of marks. And the Tathagata's saying "not" and saying "provisional name" means that precisely marks are without marks. If one awakens to the fact that the subtle atoms and the vast worlds are condition-arisen, without own-nature, and in their very substance are not, and are all provisional names, then every atom and every land is nothing but prajñā. This is what is meant by turning the great Dharma wheel within a single atom and establishing a jewel-king land on the tip of a hair. This is what is meant by the whole ten directions being one's own light, and by mountains and rivers with the great earth fully revealing the Dharma-king's body. All these express the meaning that object and wisdom are one suchness. When object and wisdom are one suchness, then there is no subject and no object, and one is absolutely pure. One who upholds it thus is practicing prajñā-pāramitā.

The section on the thirty-two marks makes clear that prajñā is without wisdom and without attainment.
