One should further know that the two meanings, marks being precisely non-marks and non-marks being marks, originally include each other and are together present; hence after saying that marks are precisely non-marks it uses the two characters "therefore" to carry on and state it, both to make clear that it supplies the earlier meaning and to make clear that the two meanings are originally linked throughout.

(3) The Buddhist scriptures often say that the nature-body is empty and quiescent. Because this guards against people misunderstanding the emptiness of the nature-body as nothingness and its quiescence as dead quiescence, the nature-body is further named true reality. "True" means that it truly exists and is not nothingness. "Reality" means that it blazes forth and appears, and is not dead quiescence. Here the text precisely makes this meaning clear. The two characters "non-mark" speak of its emptiness and quiescence. Why? If all marks are non-marks, is this not empty and quiescent? Yet one fails to see that precisely because all marks are non-marks, therefore, in terms of the Tathagata's nature-body, it is spoken of as named true reality. To name it "true" reveals that it is wondrously still and all-holding, constant and unchanging; though empty, it is not nothing. To name it "reality" reveals that whatever comes it shows itself, the barbarian comes and it appears, the Chinese comes and it appears; though quiescent, it constantly illumines. This is the third reason why the nature is named true reality.

(4) The ancient worthies explained the meaning of true reality as "no marks and yet not without marks." This explanation is most wondrous and extremely concise and clear. "No marks and yet not without marks" should be explained under two meanings to be complete. First: the nature-body is fundamentally not marks, hence it is said to be without marks. Yet though it is not marks, all marks arise in dependence on the nature; hence it is further said to be not without marks. Second: though it can manifest all marks, it still has nothing to do with any mark; hence it is said to be without marks, which makes clear that it is precisely marks and yet apart from marks. The nature is indeed not marks, yet it does not itself give rise to a single thought saying "I am not marks"; hence it is said to be not without marks, which makes clear that it is precisely non-marks and yet apart from non-marks. The second meaning is deeper than the first; in sum, it makes clear that the nature-body is apart from thought. Without thought there is no such thing as marks or non-marks; hence when thought is apart, marks and non-marks are all apart. That being so, because the nature-body is without marks, though one names it "mark," it still has nothing to do with that. And because the nature-body is not without marks, to name it "mark" is no harm to it at all. Moreover, "mark" has two meanings. One means outer mark, that is, the sense of an object-mark. The other means mark-form, which is a term of analogy. To name the nature as mark certainly cannot be taken rigidly as an object-mark. Hence the phrase "true reality" is like saying "true mark-form." "No marks and yet not without marks" is precisely the true mark-form of the nature-body; hence it is named true reality. Explained thus, the meaning of "no marks and yet not without marks" is indeed complete. And explained thus, the explanation of true reality is also quite skillful. And this phrase, "no marks and yet not without marks," the ancient worthies originally grasped from the sutra text of this section. Hence as "no marks and yet not without marks" possesses the two meanings stated above, so the sutra text of this section also possesses these two meanings.

Speaking in terms of the first meaning: because the nature-body is fundamentally not marks, the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." Yet though it is not marks, all marks arise in dependence on the nature; hence the sutra text says, "therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality."

Speaking in terms of the second meaning: because marks and non-marks are all apart, the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." "Non" carries the sense of being apart. True reality is precisely non-mark: is this not marks and non-marks both apart? Marks and non-marks both apart: such is the true mark-form of the Tathagata-garbha, exactly so. Hence the sutra text states it further: because marks and non-marks are both apart, speaking in terms of the Tathagata's nature-body, it may be named the true mark-form. This is the fourth reason why the nature is named true reality.

The Buddha speaks of the original nature and applies various names to it; and of all dharmas too he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term. This meaning is most essential, and no one has ever spoken of it; now I will briefly explain it for you all.

One should know that the Buddha's speaking of the Dharma is originally to break the clinging of sentient beings. Because of partiality and selfishness they cling, and because of clinging they grow more partial and selfish. The reason sentient beings create karma and suffer, transmigrating without end and dying and being born without rest, lies entirely in this. And the reason the world has so much affliction, so much contention, even to the point of slaughter filling the cities and slaughter filling the fields, is in every case none other than this. The World-Honored One came forth to save the world and deliver it from suffering, and so he must first break this. One should know that the reason sentient beings are partial and selfish and form clingings is nothing else: their wisdom is short and shallow. Seeing only one side of every matter, they take all dharmas to be fixed, and what they themselves see as necessarily unchangeable. They do not know that they are partial, and do not know that they are clinging. Hence the Buddha gives them a needle at the crown of the head, saying, "There is no fixed dharma," to break the root of their disease of partial clinging. And in speaking any one dharma he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term, precisely to show that dharmas have nothing fixed. This word "dharma" is used in a broad sense, taking in worldly and world-transcending dharmas alike. If one takes it that only world-transcending dharmas are so, one contradicts the Buddha's intent.

One should further know that the essential reason a person studies Buddhism, and the essential reason a student of Buddhism cultivates contemplation, is nothing else. By contemplating the perfectly fused Buddhist principle, one can transform all one's former conceptions and dissolve the disease of partial clinging. Hence one who studies Buddhism without cultivating contemplation gains very little. Why? Because only by cultivating contemplation can one understand the principle. Because contemplation is deep, afterwards the understanding of principle is deep. Because contemplation is perfect, afterwards the understanding of principle is perfect. And conversely, when the understanding of principle is deep, contemplation grows deeper; when the understanding of principle is perfect, contemplation grows more perfect. Thus cultivating and practicing back and forth, wisdom increases in brightness back and forth. Already without knowing or perceiving it, the clinging mind gradually dissolves and deluded thoughts quietly cease. Hence the wondrous function of what is called dismissing clinging lies here; it is not a forced dismissal. And the wondrous function of what is called cutting off thought likewise lies here; it is not a forced cutting off.

That being so, where exactly is this "here"? One should know that the Buddha, in speaking the Dharma, never states a single sentence flatly, never states a single word flatly. And whenever he speaks one dharma he invariably uses every kind of expression and sets up every kind of term, for no other reason than to make those who hear the Dharma view it from every side, and only then understand the meaning and purport within it. This is precisely where the wondrous function lies. Why? Because by this means one has already broken the bad habit of looking always at one side and clinging partially. And what this sutra speaks is all the more perfect and all the more wondrous; it is truly the diamond sword of wisdom. Why? Because if one can truly pass from viewing every side to deep contemplation and perfect contemplation, there is no delusion it does not break. Moreover, since one must view from every side before understanding the meaning and purport, one naturally cannot but read the Great Vehicle widely, to broaden one's hearing and seeing. And one further cannot but quietly illumine with awareness, to grasp its refinement and subtlety. Concentration and wisdom are thereby present. If one can truly be thus, then not only does one gain freedom and benefit in every kind of practice; in all worldly dharmas one can advance and withdraw with ease. And the turning from ordinary to sage has already laid its foundation here. Why? Because concentration and wisdom increase daily and deluded thoughts decrease daily. This is the essential key to hearing the Dharma, the most wondrous secret for entering Buddhism; one should urgently fix one's eyes on it.

I myself respectfully take this intent as my foundation, and whenever I explain one meaning I invariably give various explanations, turning it over and around with care, never wearying of detail, for no other reason than the hope that those who hear may open their minds and hearts and gain more means of contemplation. For the original face fundamentally cannot be reached by words and speech, and sentient beings have long since forgotten it. If, amid what cannot be spoken, one does not set up many skillful means to speak of it, how can one cultivate contemplation? What precedes makes clear the great benefit of viewing from every side, of deep contemplation, and of perfect contemplation. If one does the opposite, the harm is also very great. Take, for example, the two words "faith" and "understanding." One often sees people who insist one-sidedly that it is enough simply to muster faith and recite the Buddha's name honestly, and who forbid the reading and reciting of all scriptures, shelving the treasures of the Great Vehicle still higher. If someone studies the teaching and delights in attending Dharma assemblies, they scold him as not honest. One should know that honest Buddha-recitation requires a certain level. If one has not understood the slightest bit of the meaning and purport of Buddha-recitation, how can one be honest? To insist too far in this way not only dulls students but also contradicts the Buddha's intent. For the Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations plainly says that one who seeks rebirth in the Pure Land should read and recite the Great Vehicle and understand the supreme meaning. At the very least one must hear the supreme meaning and not be alarmed at heart. Hence of those who study by such methods, either they cannot rouse themselves and give up halfway, or they walk into a side path without knowing it. This is the fault of not knowing that faith is born from understanding. One also sees people who never let a scroll out of their hands, broadly learned and widely informed, who read through the entire canon more than once, yet never once burn a stick of incense or make a single bow, and do not know to revere the Three Treasures. Of the layer of practice there is no need to speak. Even their rolling speech and surging writing are plausible yet false, harming the Dharma and harming others. This again is the fault of not knowing that understanding comes forth from faith. This was why I did not shrink from tedious words before.

It was said above that the World-Honored One in speaking the Dharma never states a single word flatly, and so forth. One should know that the Buddha does not do this on purpose; it is because his wisdom is perfect and all-pervading, and his words and utterances are naturally so. Not only the Buddha is so; bodhisattvas are so too, and great virtuous patriarchs are all so. Hence with regard to all sutras and treatises and all the words of the ancient worthies, even in the most trivial place, one must not read carelessly. Not to read carelessly means one should view each one from every side and understand it deeply. One should further know that the insight of Buddhas and bodhisattvas is far beyond what we ordinary beings can hope to see. Even if one can understand deeply, it is no more than seeing one part in ten million. Even if one can speak well, it is no more than speaking one part in ten million. Though one spoke for a whole kalpa, one could not speak it out. For example, the meaning of "one should know" in the section above has already been explained in three or four layers. Yet it still contains many meanings. Now I may as well speak of several more, to show that it cannot be spoken out.

(1) One should know that this sutra must be heard. Why? Because such a person's generation of true faith and accomplishment of merit and virtue comes from hearing this sutra. Moreover, that this sutra must be heard means, in other words, that prajñā must be studied.

(2) One should know that faith is most essential. Why? Because the birth of true reality comes from the purity of the mind of faith. From this one can know that the earlier words, that keeping the precepts and cultivating merit can, with regard to such words and chapter-and-verse, give rise to faith and take this as true, deserve to be pondered three times over. In plain terms: if one wishes to study prajñā, one should give rise to true faith. If one wishes to give rise to true faith, one should first keep the precepts and cultivate merit.

(3) One should know that to turn from ordinary to sage and not retreat from bodhi, one must be apart from marks and see the nature. The line about accomplishment makes clear that one ascends to the first abode and transcends the ordinary to enter the sage. To be called one who abides makes clear that on reaching this position the bodhi mind can no longer retreat. This is the accomplishment of faith. And the mind being pure makes clear being apart from marks. True reality being born makes clear seeing the nature. This is why it first says that one should know prajñā must be studied. Why? Because without studying prajñā one cannot be apart from marks and see the nature. This is why it next says that one should know one must first keep the precepts and cultivate merit. Why? Because without keeping the precepts and cultivating merit there is no true faith. And without true faith one cannot have a pure mind of faith. These are all things a student should urgently follow and practice. Without practicing thus one cannot accomplish; hence it says "one should know." "One should know" makes clear that this must not go unknown.

Further, to extend the point: from the meaning of the section expressing praise and rejoicing, if one does not bring forth the great mind and does not hear this sutra, then at the very best one can only open the wisdom-eye and become an arhat of the fourth fruit. From the meaning of the section making clear the accomplishment, if one does hear this sutra and the mind of faith is pure, then at the very least one can give birth to true reality and become a bodhisattva of the first abode. This too is something students should know. Speaking thus, one can see that the sutra's meaning is truly inexhaustible and truly cannot be spoken out. One can see that in hearing the Dharma one must view from every side. For example, when I explain true reality through various meanings, if a hearer takes it only as an explanation of why the original nature is named true reality, that is not my intent in explaining it over and over in detail. And if one understands only why the nature is named true reality, that too brings the hearer no great benefit. Why? True reality is the original face of the master within us all. Such a true face fundamentally can only be known through realization. That being so, how is it to be realized? Nothing else: one must only apply effort in reflecting back. Not only should one reflect back while hearing; one should further, in the still of night and at the break of dawn, and when meeting objects and following conditions, rely on the various meanings spoken here and contemplate them deeply. One may take up one meaning alone, or merge all the meanings together; either is acceptable. In the still of night and at the break of dawn, one contemplates within one's own mind; when meeting objects and following conditions, one contemplates upon all dharmas. If one can truly be thus, the benefit is boundless. One should know that the reason the Buddha sets up various names for the original nature is to make it easy for people to grasp the body through the name. And among the various names, the one name "true reality" makes it comparatively easy to understand not clinging to the two extremes and the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. This is also the reason the elder singled out this name to speak of. And the reason I in turn open up various meanings from this name and explain them is to make it easy for the hearer, when reflecting back and applying effort, to have more means of understanding, not merely to explain the meaning of the name. From this one can know the significance of opening up various meanings to explain it.

This section has a further essential meaning. For the elder's speaking here is indeed to explain what true reality is and why it is named true reality, and so forth; but it is in fact also to indicate the method of applying effort. How is this known? Since here it makes clear that marks and non-marks are both apart, it corresponds exactly to what the text below says, that being apart from all marks one is called a Buddha. The word "apart" involves great work; without work, how could one be apart? How could one be called a Buddha? Hence one knows that here the text contains the work of cultivation. One should know that to speak the one word "non" is to cut off the hundred negations. It is also to be apart from all four propositions. That is, existence is also apart, non-existence is also apart, both existence and non-existence are also apart, neither existence nor non-existence are also apart. From this one can know that when the ancient worthies explained true reality as "no marks and yet not without marks," this one word "no" is likewise the no that is absolutely unconditioned, not the no spoken in contrast to yes. For marks and non-marks are fundamentally terms of opposition. Where there is opposition, there is change. Where there is change, there is arising and ceasing. Where there is arising and ceasing, there is no firmness. But the nature-body is truly constant through all ages, ultimately firm. Being firm, it has no arising and ceasing. Without arising and ceasing, there is no change. Without change, there is no opposition. Without opposition, it is absolutely unconditioned. Absolutely unconditioned means that though marks and non-marks never depart from mind and nature, mind and nature nonetheless stand utterly beyond marks and non-marks. In plain terms: marks are existence, and non-marks are non-existence. To stand beyond these, is that not to stand beyond existence and non-existence? Then the saying "no marks and yet not without marks" is speaking of absolute nothingness and not of a nothingness spoken in contrast to something: this can be understood at a glance. That being so, how can one attain absolute nothingness? By being apart from all four propositions of existence and non-existence. Hence the sutra text says, "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark." To speak the one word "non" is to indicate the work of cultivation. It is to cause the student who wishes to see true reality to quiet the mind and understand on the ground that all is non. If one understands that true reality is precisely non-mark, one understands that if the mind holds the slightest shadow of marks or non-marks, it is not true reality. Hence the line "what is called true reality is precisely non-mark" is exceedingly sharp; it cannot be touched even lightly, for whoever touches it loses the life of wisdom. In plain terms, it causes the student to enter at the tip of a single hair.

Now, wishing you all to have a place to set your hands, I will further, in accordance with this principle, speak one skillful means. What is that means? One must contemplate with precision before a single thought has been stirred. If a thought arises and leans toward existence, one scolds it, saying "non." Or if it leans toward non-existence, one likewise scolds it, saying "non." And even thoughts of both existence and non-existence, and thoughts of neither existence nor non-existence, are all dismissed with the word "non" as the scolding. This is the most wondrous gate of contemplation. One should know that if a thought does not arise, well and good; but if it arises, it must cling to one of the four propositions. To negate them all here is the sharp blade and keen axe that is apart from thought. Is this not the most wondrous gate of contemplation? As for the six pāramitās and ten thousand practices of world-transcending dharmas, one should advance diligently in each according to the Dharma, yet never let the slightest knot form in the breast. Advancing diligently in each is non-destruction, which is "not without marks." And the mind being as though nothing were happening is non-clinging, which is "without marks." As for all worldly dharmas, when a matter comes one responds, and when the matter has passed one lets it rest. Though one responds, one can let it rest; though one lets it rest, one can respond. This is what is meant by being able to pick it up and put it down. Whether in worldly or world-transcending dharmas, wherever one leans even slightly, one dismisses it with the word "non." Pondering the meaning and purport of being apart from all four propositions over a long time and practicing thus, one can reach the point where the time of response is the time of rest, and the time of rest is the time of response. Naturally one does not cling to the two extremes and accords with the middle way, and marks and non-marks, existence and non-existence, all four propositions, are all apart. This again is the most wondrous gate of practice.

The sutra plainly says, "Therefore the Tathagata speaks of it as named true reality." This shows the student that the reason he negates and yet still speaks is merely to make clear that there is no need to destroy. One should know that though it is spoken, it is a provisional name; the Tathagata's nature-body must still be self-realized apart from names and words. And being apart from names and words is being apart from thought. And of the skillful means for being apart from thought, none surpasses contemplating before a single thought has been stirred. If a single thought arises, one negates everything and drives it out: is this not precisely indicating the work of cultivation? One should know that from the section above, "when the mind of faith is pure, true reality is born," to here, this is precisely the elder's deep understanding of the meaning and purport. Hence one who hears the sutra should understand it deeply thus.

The World-Honored One sets up various names for the original nature, and the elder further singles out the one name true reality to speak of, both to make it easy for students to recognize the original nature. Hence the meaning of true reality should be developed at length. The great treatise states four lines of verse on true reality, the most refined and detailed, and most worth knowing, so that one may constantly illumine with awareness. True reality is the original face of the nature. Precisely because the original nature is obscured do beings become sentient beings. Now if one wishes to turn from ordinary to sage, can one do so without truly and vividly recognizing it? The verse says: "All is real, all is unreal, and all is real and also unreal; all is unreal and not unreal: this is named the true reality of all dharmas." From this one can see the bodhisattva's skill in speaking the Dharma. He does not speak in terms of the word "mark" but in terms of the word "real": this is the first point. He does not speak in terms of the nature but in terms of all dharmas: this is the second point. One should know that to speak of "mark" is a provisional name, merely to enable people to understand the condition of the original nature. Hence not speaking in terms of marks points out that the word "mark" should not be taken rigidly. If it is taken rigidly, one has already clung to marks. That he speaks in terms of the word "real" also has deep intent. For people cling to marks because they mistakenly take them as real. If one knows that all dharmas are real and also unreal, unreal and yet real, then one knows that all dharma-marks are precisely non-marks, and non-marks are precisely marks. Is such speaking not skillful?

That he speaks in terms of all dharmas must be made clear under three meanings. (1) It lets one know that outside the mind there are no dharmas. The Buddha says that all dharmas are merely illusory marks without real substance. The substance is only the pure mind. Hence it is said that the ten thousand dharmas are mind only. It is also said that outside the mind there are no dharmas. Hence one can make clear true reality through all dharmas, because the true reality of all dharmas is the nature. To speak in terms of dharmas is no different from speaking in terms of the nature. (2) It makes it easy for people to understand. Sentient beings have long since forgotten the original nature, while all dharmas are known and seen in common by sentient beings. It is better to speak in terms of all dharmas, so that through all dharmas one may awaken to the mind-nature. (3) It makes clear the one true dharma-realm. The Awakening of Faith says: "Because they do not know the one dharma-realm, unawakened thought arises, and there is ignorance." Thus they become sentient beings. The one dharma-realm is the one true dharma-realm. The ten dharma-realms with their myriad teeming forms, and true suchness, are one. This is the meaning that all is of one substance. If one knows that the true condition of all dharmas is in every case the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, then from the ten directions' Buddhas above down to all sentient beings below, and mountains, rivers, and the great earth, sentient and insentient, all without exception take the pure mind as their substance, as can be clearly known. Because the true reality of the pure mind is fundamentally the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, this is called the one true dharma-realm, also called all dharmas being one suchness. One should know that all dharmas are manifested by the mind, and since the mind-nature is the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, all dharmas are without exception the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. This is the second point of his skill.

Nāgārjuna took Aśvaghoṣa as his teacher; hence the Awakening of Faith already makes clear true suchness through all dharmas. Truly the robe and bowl have been passed down. "All is real": all dharmas plainly stand before the eyes. These words break the clinging to nothingness. "All is unreal": all dharmas in their very substance are empty. These words break the clinging to existence. And further, to guard against people hearing this and clinging to "both existent and non-existent" or "neither existent nor non-existent," he speaks the next two lines. "And" carries the sense of joining: it means one must not look only at the first line, but must join it with the second and third lines and understand them together. The meaning is as if to say: what has just been said, that all dharmas are real and unreal, is not separate and unfused. One should know that it is precisely real and yet unreal, unreal and yet not unreal. Real and yet unreal is what is called existence and yet non-existence, form and yet emptiness. Unreal and yet not unreal is what is called non-existent and yet existing, emptiness and yet form. In this way all four propositions are dismissed, and such is the true condition of all dharmas. It is also such as the true condition of the nature-body. And he concludes: this is named the true reality of all dharmas.

He further makes clear that the dharma-nature fundamentally cannot be spoken. To speak of it as true reality is likewise a provisional name and one must not cling to it. People often hear that all four propositions are dismissed and that emptiness and existence are simultaneous, and cannot help doubting. They think that "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent" are no different in meaning from the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. Why? To speak of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence: does it not make clear that to say existent is acceptable and to say non-existent is acceptable? And does it not further make clear that to say only existent is wrong and to say only non-existent is wrong? That being so, why is it that to say "both existent and non-existent" or to say "neither existent nor non-existent" is called partial clinging and dismissed? To speak thus is an error, a great error! For such a person has not understood the meaning of the words "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent," nor has he understood the meaning of the words "the simultaneity of emptiness and existence." One should know that the two lines "both existent and non-existent" and "neither existent nor non-existent" carry on from the lines of existence and non-existence above them, and hence are called the four propositions.

The intent of one who says "both existent and non-existent" is this: he thinks that the first person says only existent and the second says only non-existent, each leaning to one side, and this is indeed a fault. I, however, am not like that. I say that all dharmas are both existent and non-existent. Since both extremes are affirmed, the fault of leaning to one extreme is removed. He fails to see that if one says existent one cannot say non-existent, and if one says non-existent one cannot say existent; yet to say "both existent and non-existent" contradicts one's own words. Moreover, he takes it that existent is also right and non-existent is also right. Since the words are ambiguous and take either side, and the meaning is separate and unfused, it should be dismissed.

The intent of one who says "neither existent nor non-existent" is this: he thinks that what the third person says is indeed faulty, and that I differ from him. I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. Since both extremes are alike dismissed, the fault of the third person's clinging to the two extremes is removed. He fails to see that "neither existent" is precisely non-existent, so why further say "nor non-existent"? And "nor non-existent" is precisely existent, so why further say "neither existent"? Is this not idle disputation? Moreover, he still takes it that existent is existent and non-existent is non-existent. His separateness and lack of fusion is likewise the same fault as the third person's. Hence it should be dismissed. Further, the insight of the third person, having said that existence and non-existence are both affirmed, still leans to the side of existence. And the insight of the fourth person, saying that existence and non-existence are both negated, still leans to the side of emptiness. Should these not be dismissed? (Both-affirmed resembles both-illumined, and both-negated resembles both-concealed. Yet in fact they are greatly different. For the words both-illumined and both-concealed make clear that one has attained the middle; whereas the doctrines of both-affirmed and both-negated know only the two extremes.) As for the meaning of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, it makes clear that when it is empty it is precisely when it is existent, and when it is existent one sees the time of emptiness. Emptiness and existence perfectly fused, since they are not two, are without extremes. When extremes are not even present, where could one cling? Compared with both existent and non-existent and neither existent nor non-existent, the difference in meaning is as heaven from an abyss: how can one say there is no difference!

There is a further point. If beings understood that emptiness and existence are simultaneous, they would see that emptiness and existence alike are beyond all speaking; and if they understood that emptiness and existence are not yet fit to be spoken of, what use would they have for discrimination? This is the subtle intent with which the Buddha spoke of emptiness and existence as simultaneous. For it serves both to remove the discriminating views and feelings of beings and to lead them to leave behind names and words and realize for themselves. Hence whether one speaks of existence or of non-existence, of both existence and non-existence, or of neither existence nor non-existence, all alike is relinquished. The above is spoken from the standpoint of the remedy. If one speaks thoroughly from the standpoint of the ultimate meaning, then when relinquishing is spoken of, all is relinquished; when non-relinquishing is spoken of, nothing is relinquished. One should know that whenever relinquishing is spoken of, it is because of grasping that there is relinquishing. If there is nothing grasped, there is nothing to relinquish. Therefore even the simultaneity of emptiness and existence must not be grasped, and grasping itself should be relinquished. How do we know this is so? Consider the Heart Sutra: it first says that form is emptiness and emptiness is form, making clear the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, so that people may awaken to it and enter the right wisdom of prajñā. Yet further on it says, "no wisdom and no attainment." This is precisely the instruction that even the simultaneity of emptiness and existence should not be grasped. This sutra says so plainly as well, as when it says that prajñā is not prajñā. The same holds in this very section: above it says that the true mark is then produced and merit accomplished, yet this section says the true mark is precisely non-mark and is named the true mark. It is again to guard against people grasping at the true mark that it speaks of "not" and says "is named," thereby relinquishing it. The true mark is precisely the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. One should know why the simultaneity of emptiness and existence must not be grasped. Because if there is the least grasping, one leans to the side of existence and it is no longer the simultaneity of emptiness and existence. Hence it should be relinquished. And if one hears these words of mine yet does not in the least comprehend and contemplate the meaning of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, then one leans to the side of emptiness, and it is again no longer the simultaneity of emptiness and existence; this too should be relinquished. One should comprehend it in this way. This is of the utmost importance.

In short, if the views and feelings of beings are emptied, one may speak of the simultaneity of emptiness and existence, and may as well speak of the four propositions; but if they are not emptied, then the four propositions certainly may not be spoken, and the simultaneity of emptiness and existence likewise cannot be granted. Pay attention, pay attention!

In the second meaning of the true mark spoken of above it is said that this section and the preceding text, "if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata," illuminate each other. From this the elder's deep understanding of the meaning may also be seen. Yet what the elder deeply understood does not stop here. One should know that the nature has many other names. Not citing others, he cites the one name "true mark" alone; this too illuminates the meaning of the teachings above that dharmas and non-dharmas alike should not be grasped, that non-dharmas are not non-dharmas, that what is spoken is not the name, and so on. All that the World-Honored One spoke above was to keep people from grasping at either of the two extremes of emptiness and existence and thus to make all perfectly fused. For to grasp at the two extremes is to be no longer nature but mark. If one grasps at the mark of dharma, that is grasping at self; if one grasps at the mark of non-dharma, that too is grasping at self. Now the elder, even with respect to the true mark in which emptiness and existence are simultaneous, likewise says it is not and is named. This is precisely aimed at what the World-Honored One spoke above, illuminating two meanings for him so that the hearer may comprehend. What are the two meanings? (1) The nature is from the first the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence (the word "simultaneous" means perfectly fused). If one grasps at the two extremes, one is no longer in accord with the nature. (2) Even the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence should not be grasped, for if there is the least grasping it is no longer the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, to say nothing of the two extremes, which still less should be grasped. This is the deep intent of citing the true mark alone, and this is precisely why the elder deeply understood the meaning.

Again, as was said above, the word "not" in this section carries the sense of "free from," and it speaks of the work of cultivation. It corresponds to the section below, that one who is free from all marks is then named a Buddha. One should know that these two sections, the one encouraging by way of the present and the one encouraging by way of the future, are nowhere out of correspondence. For what the two sections say was from the first meant to illuminate each other. This meaning will be spoken of below.

(Zi) Next, encouraging by way of the future. It divides into two: (Chou) 1. Rejoicing now and encouraging those who come after; 2. Explaining and revealing the reason. (Chou) 1. Again divides into two: (Yin) 1. Rejoicing for himself; 2. Extensive encouragement.
(Yin) 1. Rejoicing for himself.
["World-Honored One, that I now hear such a sutra, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it — this is not difficult."]

"That I now hear such a sutra, believe, understand, receive, and uphold it" — this single phrase explains precisely why it is that the wisdom-eye he had gained in former times had never before heard such a sutra. Why? If one knows that he now hears it and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, one knows that his not having heard it before was due to nothing else: there was a wisdom-eye he had gained, and that very wisdom-eye produced its own obstruction to this profound sutra. Even had he heard it, he could not have believed, understood, received, and upheld it; he would have heard as though he had not heard. Hence he says that the wisdom-eye he had gained had never heard it. These words explain precisely that the whole obstruction lay in the wisdom-eye. How could the wisdom-eye produce obstruction? It was entirely because there was something gained. Why so? To have something gained is the grasping at dharmas; it is shallow and short wisdom. How then could one accord with this supreme meaning of the three emptinesses? Moreover, to have something gained is to feel that one's own enlightenment already suffices; it is to have no breadth of compassionate vows. How then could one accord with this wondrous practice of giving oneself up for others, ferrying others yet with no mark of ferrying? This is why in former times he had never heard it. Now, however, he had glimpsed the World-Honored One's total non-dwelling and his eye of the Way opened; for the sake of the assembly he asked that this profound sutra be spoken, and his great mind was aroused. Hence he could hear it and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it.

To understand is to comprehend. To receive is to take in, which is also to comprehend. Thus understanding and receiving are close in meaning. Since it says understanding and then says receiving, the two words "receive and uphold" are spoken together; for speaking them together makes clear that one should advance in understanding and practice side by side. Again, the word "uphold" also carries the sense of holding without loss. So the phrase "believe, understand, receive, and uphold" makes clear that one can not only believe and understand but can advance in understanding and practice together without retreating. "Not difficult" means not very difficult; it does not mean absolutely not difficult. That it is not very difficult is precisely why he rejoices for himself. Had it been absolutely not difficult, he could not have said that in former times the wisdom-eye had never heard it, nor would he have shed tears and wept and praised it as rare.

Why is it not difficult? There are three meanings. (1) His person met the time of a Buddha. With instruction given to his face and whispers in his ear, benefit came easily. Moreover, by the Tathagata's clear receiving, merely to see and hear and rejoice brings the greatest of blessings and gives rise to the greatest of wisdom, without any instruction being needed. And to be born into such a great assembly, one's former roots of blessing and wisdom must surely be deep. With causes and conditions thus complete, whenever the Buddha spoke the Dharma, those who realized the fruit on the spot could not be numbered. But to be born before the Buddha or after him is one of the eight difficulties. The elder was himself one of the great disciples, so he says it is not difficult. This is the first reason he rejoices for himself. (2) He had already realized the fruit of sagehood. The Great Prajñāpāramitā says: "Prajñā is most profound; who can believe it? Answer: one who has accomplished right view, and the arhat whose outflows are exhausted, can believe it." Now the elder had already realized the fruit of arhatship, so it is not difficult. This is the second reason he rejoices for himself. (3) He could understand the meaning of emptiness. The whole prajñā corpus makes clear the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and among the ten great disciples the elder was foremost in understanding emptiness. His nature was the sharpest and he entered most easily. Hence in the first eight assemblies the elder was the one who received the teaching, and now it is again the elder who sets this most profound sutra in motion. So he says it is not difficult. This is the third reason he rejoices for himself.

Looking over the text below, all these meanings are present as well. Why? The elder's own words that it is not difficult serve precisely to reveal how utterly difficult it is for the final age, since those beings are born when no Buddha is met. And where he rejoices for himself is precisely where he redoubles his encouragement of those who come after. The sense is: I am fortunate enough now to meet the World-Honored One, I have realized arhatship and understand the meaning of emptiness, and so I can believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. But those beings of the final age, meeting no Buddha and finding it very hard to hear and very hard to believe, understand, receive, and uphold — if they nonetheless hear, and can nonetheless believe, understand, receive, and uphold, they are truly rare and precious, and their capacities must far surpass my own (for bodhisattva-nature far surpasses arhat-nature). What is there remarkable in me? Hence he says it is not difficult. In these few lines the wording and sense turn and return with earnest urgency; how wholeheartedly he strives to inspire those who come after!
(Yin) 2. Extensive encouragement.
["If in a future age, in the last five hundred years, there are beings who hear this sutra and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, such persons will be foremost and most rare."]

"A future age" speaks broadly of the time after the Buddha. "The last five hundred years" refers to the fifth five-hundred-year period after the Buddha's entry into stillness, that is, the very beginning of the Dharma-ending age. Now it is nearly three thousand years, already at the end of the sixth five-hundred-year period. Wherever the sutras speak of "the last five hundred years," it is not necessarily the fifth; the phrase simply makes clear that it is the Dharma-ending age. The Surangama Sutra says that at this time beings are firm and solid in contention, and entry upon the Way is very difficult. "Contention" means affirming oneself and denying others, striving for superiority and fighting to win. "Firm and solid" means that contention is unrelenting and unbreakable. Consider how in China since the Song dynasty (from the early Song to the present is nearly a thousand years; that time was precisely the beginning of the Dharma-ending age) those devoted to moral cultivation and learning carried on sectarian quarrels far exceeding those of the Han and Tang. Thus arose the tendency of Song learning to reject Han learning, and the habit of Confucians to slander Buddhism. Later the so-called Neo-Confucians began contending among themselves, as with the two factions of the Cheng-Zhu and Lu-Wang schools. In every case it was nothing but planting one's own banner and striking down others. Cause must have its effect: in the end they were themselves struck down by others, and so came the movement that overthrew old learning together with the new, in which even Confucius was dragged down. They did not realize that since the Han dynasty no scholar has even dreamt of Confucius's true meaning. And within the Buddhist gate itself, after the Song the same tendency took hold; the various schools and factions contended fiercely, each holding its own school alone to be right and all others wholly wrong. The further it went, the worse it became, until in recent times some have wished to overthrow the Awakening of Faith. This is truly lamentable. If even the Buddhist gate is like this, and those devoted to morals and learning are like this, what of the rest? Hence the word "struggle" has become a motto. They do not realize that the ancients spoke of "striving," of "exerting oneself," of "self-strengthening"; even in Buddhism one speaks of "courage" and "vigor." Such expressions all refer to one's own person and are beneficial without fault. Today's "struggle," though also a kind of self-strengthening, carries the intent of excluding others. This comes from the habitual tendency to contention growing ever deeper, and it is why the world's way grows ever more bitter.

Whence does contention arise? It arises from grasping. Grasping comes from discrimination, and discrimination from the view of self, and the Buddha Dharma is the specific remedy for this disease. Now the World-Honored One and the elder both encourage people specifically with regard to the Dharma-ending age. From this it can be known that to remedy people's minds today and turn back the world's fortune, there is no way but to promote the Buddha Dharma, for it is precisely the fitting remedy for the illness. Yet precisely because it fits the illness, it runs counter to human sentiment. For those who are firm in contention have deep obstacles and heavy karma; their inner causes are clearly incomplete. Add that the sages are distant in time and good teachers are few, so the outer conditions are likewise insufficient. With both cause and condition lacking, in the case of this profound sutra, not only is receiving and upholding difficult, not only is believing and understanding difficult; even to hear it is already very difficult. It is not that there is no opportunity at all to hear the Dharma; it is that people are unwilling to hear. If then there are those free of these three difficulties, they must have long planted good roots, or must have been sent by the Buddha. Therefore it says, "they will be foremost and most rare," making clear that such a person is either a bodhisattva's manifestation or one who possesses bodhisattva-nature.

"Will be" means "shall be," and carries within it the sense of accomplishment. Someone may object: a bodhisattva's manifestation aside, how could one who merely possesses bodhisattva-nature accomplish this? One should know that the sutra first says "hears," then says "believes, understands, receives, and upholds," making clear that the three wisdoms are complete in him. How could he not accomplish it? Hearing is the wisdom of hearing; believing and understanding is the wisdom of reflection; receiving and upholding is the wisdom of cultivation. For to dwell in the final age and yet hear this profound sutra is truly no easy matter; such a one must have prajñā seeds from former lives, one of whom it is said, "not merely before one Buddha, two Buddhas, three, four, or five Buddhas did he plant good roots." Only with such a surpassingly good cause can one meet so surpassingly good a condition. So hearing it, he can at once give rise to faith and open understanding. There are, now and then, those who though they hear it meet some other obstructing condition, so that their faith cannot at once be fully aroused and their understanding cannot open widely; but if only they follow the Buddha's command, keep the precepts and cultivate merit, they will surely come to believe, understand, receive, and uphold. For keeping the precepts cuts off defiling conditions; this is the foundation of self-benefit. Cultivating merit unfolds the virtues of the nature (since the nature inherently possesses immeasurable pure virtues); this too is the work of benefiting others. Thus turning the back on dust and uniting with enlightenment (cutting off defiling conditions is "turning the back on dust"; unfolding the virtues of the nature is "uniting with enlightenment"), benefiting both self and others, one will surely receive the welcoming of all Buddhas, and from this one can give rise to faith in this sutra and take it as real. "Take it as real" means to understand its true meaning. Believing and understanding, one will naturally receive and uphold it in accord with the Dharma. With the three wisdoms thus cultivated together, what fear is there that one will not accomplish it? Again, in the words "such a person will be foremost and most rare" there lies the sense that one must not cast oneself away. This is the elder's earnest encouragement. This sentence echoes the words above, "you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue," and the words below, "then he is named a Buddha," exactly corresponding to them.

(Chou) 2. Explaining and revealing the reason. In three parts: (Yin) 1. Directly revealing that he does not grasp at existence; 2. Bending back to reveal that he does not grasp at emptiness; 3. Concluding by revealing that he is named a Buddha.
(Yin) 1. Directly revealing that he does not grasp at existence.
["Why? Such a person has no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life."]

The text above says such a person is foremost and most rare. How does he come to be so? The three sections that follow explain precisely why. In the circulating editions the word "no" is added before each mark, but the Tang manuscript sutras run "no mark of self" straight through, so the three "no"s below may be omitted.

"Why?" puts a hypothetical question: why is such a person called foremost and most rare? The answer: because in such a person the four marks of self, person, being, and life are all absent. Being all absent, he does not grasp at existence. Judging by the surface of the text, it seems only to say that he is empty of the marks of self and person, and seems only to make clear that he does not grasp at existence. But looking at the bending-back revelation below, such a person is not only empty of self and person, but also empty of dharma-self; not only does he not grasp at existence, he does not grasp at emptiness either. Yet the section heading says only "does not grasp at existence" because it follows the surface of the text; the meaning of not grasping at emptiness cannot be known without the bending-back revelation of the next section.

One should know that this sutra is devoted to making clear the true mark. The true mark is absolute, with nothing outside it, and is from the first no mark at all. What is called the relinquishing of both self and dharma, and non-grasping at emptiness and existence, is this. "The relinquishing of both self and dharma" means that the four marks of self, person, and the rest are all thoroughly relinquished. "Non-grasping at emptiness and existence" means that marks such as those of self and dharma are not grasped, which is not grasping at existence, and is also called the emptiness of self and the emptiness of dharmas; and that non-dharma marks are also not grasped, which is not grasping at emptiness, and is also called the emptiness of emptiness. Together with the two emptinesses of self and dharma, these are called the three emptinesses. Beings of the final age must possess prajñā-nature and have relatively thin grasping at self and dharma before they can, in this turbid and evil world, hear this Dharma; only then can they rise above the common run and believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. And being able to believe, understand, receive, and uphold it, their grasping at the emptiness and existence of self and dharma is relinquished of itself. This is why such a person is precisely a foremost and most rare bodhisattva. Hence the words "will be" above contain the sense of accomplishment. For this reason.
(Yin) 2. Bending back to reveal that he does not grasp at emptiness.
["Why is this? The mark of self is precisely non-mark; the mark of person, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life are precisely non-mark."]

"Why is this?" asks of himself the reason for the word "no" in the text above. From "the mark of self" onward he answers and explains himself. The sense is that the "no" just spoken is not "no" as opposed to "yes"; it is absolute nothingness, the nothingness of all four propositions, that is, emptiness carried through to the very bottom. How is this shown? Because such a person has not seen self, person, being, and life as truly existent and then been able to be without them, still less has he annihilated self, person, being, and life and then been without them. He is able to see that the self is from conditions, illusorily existing, and that when its illusory mark appears it is precisely non-existent; hence he says the mark of self is precisely non-mark. This sentence makes clear that he does not take up emptiness apart from the mark of self. The mark of person, the mark of a being, and the mark of a life being precisely non-mark is likewise so. The Great Treatise says: "If there were a single hair-tip of what beings grasp that could exist, it could not be left behind; but since in what is grasped there is not so much as a hair's breadth of existence, it can be left behind." The sense is that all is illusory mark, and there is from the first not a hair-tip's worth that truly exists. It makes clear precisely that existence itself is emptiness, and that is why it can be left behind. It is like one with a film over the eye seeing flowers in space: where the flowers are is where space is. Why bother to destroy the flowers and take up space apart from them? When the film is cleared the flowers vanish of themselves, and this is likewise so.

Spoken of the nature: if one understands the one true dharma-realm, then there is from the first no difference, from the first constant and everlasting; how could there be marks of self, person, being, and life? Spoken of marks: if one understands that the five aggregates are from the first empty, then one knows that when the mark of self appears, that is precisely when it is empty; hence the mark of self is precisely non-mark. And the mark of person and all marks of beings are likewise nothing but the false union of the five aggregates, from the first empty; hence the mark of person and the mark of a being are likewise precisely non-mark. As for what is called the mark of a life, it is because its continuity is unbroken that this mark is formed. But in truth, since it is called continuity, one can see that it is thought after thought flowing on, arising and ceasing in a single instant; is not the mark of a life precisely non-mark? Such a person, believing, understanding, receiving, and upholding, is able to be thus, and so possesses the wisdom of the three emptinesses and is free of the four propositions as well. Why? If one cannot thoroughly penetrate that self, person, being, and life are from the first illusory marks, appearing though not existent, then even if one can be non-grasping, it is forced suppression, that is, a "no" set against "yes." The insight being still untrue, not only is the effort laborious, but the root and stem remain and it is utterly unreliable. And even if one could suppress without slackening, that too is grasping at dharmas. As the Surangama Sutra says: even if one inwardly guards the secluded and still, that too is a shadowy affair of the discriminating dust of dharmas. The fault lies in the one word "guard": where there is something guarded, there is something grasped. Why is this so? Because the insight is not thorough. Now this person has thoroughly seen that marks such as those of self and others are precisely non-mark; he can penetrate clearly that all marks, being existent, are precisely non-existent. Existing yet non-existent, he sees as though not seeing. Though the myriad forms are myriad and tangled, his breast is serene. Then without suppression they vanish of themselves; what use is guarding? Where there is nothing guarded, there is nothing grasped; this is freedom from the mark of dharma. Moreover it is not merely the emptiness of dharmas: the mark of self being precisely non-mark, one can see that he does not take up emptiness apart from marks; this is also freedom from the mark of non-dharma. Is this not emptiness of emptiness as well? The emptiness of self, the emptiness of dharmas, and the emptiness of emptiness: this is wisdom penetrating the three emptinesses. Hence the title of this section says "not grasping at emptiness." Such a person is truly of great capacity, for he can empty through to the very bottom and is not one who works away at it twig by twig and joint by joint.

It was said above that he is free of the four propositions as well; what does that mean? The section above has him not grasping at existence and this section has him not grasping at emptiness, which makes clear that he is free of both existence and non-existence. And it says that the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark. Since it says "precisely," one can see that such a person does not regard existence and non-existence as both existing and not existing, or as neither existing nor not existing, kept apart and unfused. Rather, he has seen that existence is precisely non-existence. Then his wisdom is already thorough, and emptiness and existence are simultaneous; is he not free of the four propositions? The self-nature pure mind is from the first free of the four propositions, neither mark nor non-mark, absolute and perfectly fused. This person now transcends the four propositions, is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty, perfectly fused without obstruction, and so has entered into the nature-substance of the true mark. Hence it says he will be a foremost and most rare bodhisattva. The next section precisely concludes and reveals this meaning.
(Yin) 3. Concluding by revealing that he is named a Buddha.
["Why? One who is free from all marks is then named a Buddha."]

"Why?" asks: since the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark, why is he called foremost and most rare? The two lines "free from all marks" explain the reason. "All marks" are precisely self, person, being, and life. Marks are not one only, hence "all." And it further says "all" because it is not merely that the four marks of self and the rest arise from the view of the body. The text above says: if one grasps at the mark of dharma, or grasps at the mark of non-dharma, one grasps at self, person, being, and life. It can be seen that whatever is grasped becomes the four marks; hence "all." Spoken in terms of the four propositions: one may grasp at existence, or grasp at non-existence, or grasp at both existence and non-existence, or grasp at neither existence nor non-existence. Where there is grasping, there is grasper and grasped; grasper and grasped are opposition, and opposition becomes the marks of self and other. Since the graspings are not one, they become the mark of a being; since the grasping mind does not cease, it becomes the mark of a life. Hence "all marks." The nature of the true mark is from the first free of both marks and non-marks. So if one can be free of all marks, one realizes the dharma-body; hence, "is then named a Buddha."

"All Buddhas" has two meanings. (1) The Buddhas of the ten directions and three times. (2) From the first abiding onward, up to but not including the ultimate fruition, they are called those who awaken in part, and also called Buddhas of partial realization, because they can realize the dharma-body in part. From the first abiding to the ultimate enlightenment is forty-two stages in all; hence "all Buddhas." Spoken in the first sense, it means that the Buddhas of the ten directions and three times all obtain the name Buddha by being free from all marks. This person has already cut off the four propositions and penetrated the three emptinesses; he is free from all marks. Though he has not at once reached the ultimate Buddha-stage, he is unquestionably a bodhisattva. Hence it says only "foremost and most rare," not "the supreme, foremost, and most rare." Spoken in the second sense, from the first-abiding bodhisattva of partial realization upward to the ultimate enlightenment, all must be free from all marks in order to realize the dharma-body. This person can be free from all marks; he has already realized the dharma-body. Though we do not know how deep or shallow his realization is, at the least he is a first-abiding bodhisattva and a Buddha of partial realization. He is also one whose faith is pure, so that the true mark is produced and he accomplishes the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue. Hence it says he will be foremost and most rare.

What is said here, that the mark of self is precisely non-mark and so forth, is the non-duality of emptiness and existence, the perfect fusion of nature and mark. It is also the confluence of all the meanings spoken by the World-Honored One above. Why? Because to be free from all marks is then to be named a Buddha, which corresponds from afar to what the section on generating faith says: if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata. So it is enough to prove that this person, able to be free from all marks, has already seen the Tathagata's nature-substance; is he not foremost and most rare? The insight the elder sets forth is truly mind-to-mind with the World-Honored One; this is what is meant by deeply understanding the meaning. Hence below the World-Honored One at once confirms it.

It was said above that these three sections encouraging by way of the future and the two sections above encouraging by way of the present illuminate each other in meaning. Consider how the earlier text speaks only of the one word "faith," while here it says "believe, understand, receive, and uphold." This is precisely to illuminate that the earlier text, though it spoke only of faith, already included the sense of understanding and receiving and upholding; for faith is the mother of the merit and virtue that are the source of the path. To speak the one word "faith" is to run through to the very end. That here it speaks of being without all marks again illuminates the reason why the earlier text says that when faith is pure the true mark is produced. And that mark is precisely non-mark, non-grasping at the two extremes, the perfect fusion of emptiness and existence, is precisely the true exposition of the true mark. That here it says he will be foremost and most rare, and is named a Buddha, is likewise the meaning of the earlier text's accomplishing the most supreme, foremost, rare merit and virtue. Here it says "free from," and above it said "not": the two precisely answer each other, for since marks and non-marks alike are not, one should be free of them. Above it says "produces the true mark," and again says "the Tathagata says it is named the true mark"; here it says "is then named a Buddha." The meaning too is one thread. For to manifest a portion of the Tathagata's true mark is to be a Buddha of partial realization; to manifest it in full is the ultimate Buddha. And that both before and after it says "named" again makes clear that what is called the true mark, and what is called all Buddhas, are both mere names and therefore neither may be grasped. Hence all must be "not" and all must be "free from." From this one sees that before and after there is only one meaning. So when speaking the earlier text one should include the later meaning, and when speaking the later text one should include the earlier meaning. One is spoken by way of the present and the other by way of the future, each making the other manifest; this again is the skill of Dharma-speaking. Such a pattern is met with constantly in the sutras.
(Ren) Next, the Tathagata's confirmation and unfolding. In three parts: (Gui) 1. Confirming; 2. Unfolding the meaning; 3. Concluding.
(Gui) 1. Confirming.
[The Buddha told Subhuti: "So it is, so it is. If again there are persons who hear this sutra and are neither startled, nor terrified, nor afraid, you should know that such persons are most rare."]
To confirm is to approve what the elder said; to unfold is, on the basis of what the elder said, further to make clear the meanings above that were not yet exhausted.

Wherever the line "the Buddha told Subhuti" is set down, it carries a note of solemnity. Because the text below mostly supplies what the earlier meaning had not yet brought out, the compiler of the sutra specially marks this line to draw attention to it. That "so it is, so it is" is said twice confirms that his words are entirely apt. If one distributes the sense, it means that the praise and rejoicing above and the extensive encouragement are both without error. The elder earlier said, "If again there are persons," without yet indicating any particular time; but because it stood opposite the next section's encouragement by way of the future, it was judged to be encouragement by way of the present. Now the World-Honored One likewise says only "if again there are persons," also without being able to specify a time; yet when the text below comes to its conclusion it returns to the future. From this it can be known that these words refer generally to the present and on to the future.

To be startled is to be suddenly amazed and bewildered; to be terrified is to be anxious and unsettled; to be afraid is to draw back and obstruct oneself. Vasubandhu's Treatise says: "Startled means fearing that this sutra is not the practice of the right path; terrified means being unable to cut off doubt; afraid means that because of being startled and terrified one is unwilling to study and practice it." Zhiyi's Commentary says: "At first hearing the sutra one is not startled; next, reflecting on its meaning, one is not terrified; afterward, practicing it, one is not afraid." Taking treatise and commentary together, not being startled is faith; for when first hearing the sutra, not fearing that it is not the right path and so being startled is to be able to believe. Not being terrified is understanding; for next reflecting on the meaning, to have no doubt at all and so give rise to terror is to be able to understand. Not being afraid is receiving and upholding; for not drawing back in fear and so being willing to study and practice is to be able to receive and uphold. That the wording is changed here holds a deep meaning. Truly, when ordinary beings who grasp at existence hear that all marks are false and delusory, and when the two vehicles, grasping at dharmas, hear that dharmas should not be grasped, and when those of a certain lean-to-emptiness sort hear that non-dharmas likewise should not be grasped, they are sure to be startled and terrified and to fear any talk of prajñā. Believing and understanding they have not yet, to say nothing of receiving and upholding. How then could they together ascend the road of awakening and not be blocked at the conjured city? Hence he points out one by one the reason why they cannot believe, understand, receive, and uphold, so that all who hear may know that dharmas are from the first without fixed nature and that the Buddha does not deceive people. Why be startled, terrified, doubtful, or afraid? Thus there may be hope that they will believe, understand, receive, and uphold. Hence the words below about the first paramita precisely make clear that dharmas have no fixed mark; and the words about the five discourses precisely make clear that the Buddha does not deceive people. It can be seen that the present words, "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid," are precisely the groundwork for what is said below. And the intent of speaking what is below is precisely to cut off the startlement, terror, doubt, and fear of beings. The sense of the words before and after closely answers each other.

To say "most" of what is rare is also the meaning of "foremost and most rare." Judging by the tone of "if again there are" and what follows, it is also confirming what the elder said. The words above, "so it is, so it is," have already confirmed and settled it. That he speaks these few further words has no other purpose than to set forth the root of the disease in those beings who cannot believe, understand, receive, and uphold, so as to encourage them.

(Gui) 2. Unfolding the meaning. In two parts: (Zi) 1. Unfolding the meaning that contemplation and practice are free from marks; 2. Unfolding the true meaning of Dharma-speaking. (Zi) 1. Again in two: (Chou) 1. Making it clear by way of prajñā; 2. Making it clear by way of the remaining paramitas.
(Chou) 1. Making it clear by way of prajñā.
["Why? Subhuti, what the Tathagata says is the first paramita is not the first paramita; therefore it is named the first paramita."]

The words "why?" govern the whole section on patience below. In "first paramita," the two words "first" refer to prajñā. "What the Tathagata says" shows that it is spoken by way of the nature. Spoken by way of the nature, it is therefore said to be first and not first. For the nature-substance is empty and still; how could there be such a mark as this first paramita? Hence it says "not." To say "not" makes clear that its nature is from the first no mark, and therefore one should not grasp at marks. And again, spoken by way of the nature, it says it is named the first paramita. For though the nature-substance has no mark, it is also not without marks. All marks arise in dependence on the nature; this first paramita too arises in dependence on the nature, and is not without the name and mark of "first"; hence it says "is named." To say "is named" makes clear that its mark is not apart from the nature, and that one should still return and merge it into the nature.

Spoken thus, this is the basic meaning of this section's text. It is called the basic meaning because wherever this sutra says "not" or "is named," it is illuminating this meaning. This is the fundamental meaning, which students may not fail to understand. Yet the meaning of this section is exceedingly profound and exceedingly important. Were one to speak only this basic meaning, it would not be the Buddha's intent. For everything from this section onward unfolds the meaning, and to unfold the meaning is to bring out, beyond the basic meaning, further meanings that are deduced and illuminated. What are they? Consider that he opens his mouth with "Why?" These three words come in continuation of the words above: "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid; you should know that such persons are most rare." It can be known that the three lines on the first paramita precisely explain why one is not startled, and so on, and why such a one is rare. If one spoke only the basic meaning and did not bring out clearly the reason within it, then the three words "why?" and the words above about not being startled and so on would have no place to rest. Above it says "you should know"; this is precisely what students should know and must not fail to understand deeply. Not only this. Above it does not say "believe, understand, receive, and uphold," but changes the wording to "neither startled nor terrified nor afraid," because beings of the final age have the disease of fearing any talk of prajñā and being unable to believe, understand, receive, and uphold. Here it does not say "prajñā-paramita" but changes the wording to "the first paramita," thereby using it to unfold and bring out the essential principle of prajñā, so that all beings may understand it clearly. Thus they may suddenly realize that prajñā need not be feared and cannot be feared, and only then can they be counted as people who study the Dharma of unsurpassed bodhi and only then have they hope of turning the ordinary into the sage. Why? Was it not said above that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment of all Buddhas come forth from this sutra? That is to say plainly that prajñā absolutely must be believed, understood, received, and upheld, and that one should enter by this gate. If one does not enter by this sutra's gate, one cuts oneself off from the Dharma of unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment, and cuts oneself off from all Buddhas as well. Why? Since all Buddhas and the unsurpassed Dharma all come forth from this sutra, one who wishes to study the unsurpassed Dharma and to turn the ordinary into the sage, if he does not enter by this sutra, does he not cut off his own road? How could it be something to be feared? Therefore if one speaks only the basic meaning, only the former layer of meaning, and does not bring out thoroughly such profound meaning, then the World-Honored One's profound intent in changing the wording would be buried. Above it says "you should know"; this is what students especially should know and absolutely must understand deeply. All the various reasons above are contained within these three lines of text; one may imagine how extraordinarily profound their meaning is, and how important their bearing is.

To explain them, one must skillfully devise expedients, so that the words are few and the meaning clear. One should know that the meaning of prajñā has lain hidden and obscure for a thousand ages. Now if one wishes to remove the disease of fearing it, one cannot but expose the cause of that fear. Sometimes one cannot avoid touching on the ancients, and cannot keep silent out of regard for the worthy. For if the hidden and obscure meaning is not thoroughly explained, the root of the disease of startlement, doubt, terror, and fear remains, and one still cannot believe or understand, and is unwilling to receive and uphold; would that not be to fail the Buddha's kindness? I deeply hope you will all quiet your minds and listen attentively. If this meaning is not thoroughly understood, it will likewise be to have failed the Buddha's kindness.

Since the principle is so profound and subtle, though I now wish for few words and clear meaning, a few sentences cannot possibly make it clear, nor can it be grasped in a single breath. I will first take the two words "first" and set forth a rough outline, so that the listeners may have a foundation in their minds; then step by step we will go deeper. This too is the sense of an expedient.

Prajñā-paramita is called the first paramita because prajñā is the mother of the paramitas. If prajñā is the mother, the paramitas are the children, and children cannot be apart from their mother. Hence one who practices the paramitas, if he lacks the practice of prajñā, cannot, as to cause, break delusion, and as to fruition, can hardly realize the dharma-body. One should know that the paramitas are all called paramitas precisely because prajñā is within them; without prajñā they cannot be called paramitas. Why? Because otherwise they cannot break delusion, cannot realize the dharma-body, and cannot reach the other shore. This is why prajñā has the name of the first paramita. From this one sees that since the paramitas cannot be apart from prajñā, prajñā likewise does not exist apart from the paramitas; this can be known. Hence the second line says, "is not the first paramita." This one word "not" makes clear that one must not grasp prajñā as having a separate mark. Yet though it is not separate, it is not without the name "first"; hence the third line says, "is named the first paramita." These two words "is named" make clear that while the paramitas apart from prajñā are not paramitas, prajñā is not without the mere name of leader. The above explains why prajñā is named first, and also explains why, spoken by way of "first," it is said to be "not" and "is named." This meaning must be firmly remembered; it is the ground for breaking people's startlement, doubt, terror, and fear. What follows will speak of it.

Above, the elder used the fact that the four marks of self and person are precisely non-mark to make clear that such a person's emptiness and existence are perfectly fused, and thereby to explain why he is foremost and most rare. The World-Honored One has already confirmed and approved it. But whenever the World-Honored One speaks a dharma, it is never for one affair alone, never for one person alone. So because of this person's rarity he perceived that the reason all beings have the mark of self is nothing else: they grasp at dharmas. Hence after confirming and approving, he further unfolds the meaning by way of the six paramitas and other dharmas, to instruct all beings who discriminate and grasp at dharmas. That he speaks of prajñā first is precisely because beings fear prajñā. Why do beings fear it? Because they discriminate and grasp at dharmas, and do not understand the true meaning of prajñā. This is why he unfolds it for them. For when beings suddenly hear that prajñā is the emptiness of the supreme meaning, they think it lofty and hard to practice, and so are startled. And not understanding why the emptiness of the supreme meaning is so, they are terrified. Feeling that instead of studying prajñā they had better study some other perfect sutra and perfect dharma that is safer, they are afraid. All this comes from not having penetrated the Buddha's principle, so that they mistakenly give rise to the grasping at dharmas through discrimination. This is truly to lose one's own good benefit, and is deeply pitiable. Hence the World-Honored One, explaining why such a person is most rare, says: why do I call such a person most rare?
