Because in this prajñā Dharma-gate beings are startled, doubtful, terrified, and afraid, and this person alone is not.

This dharma is indeed lofty, so why wonder that they are startled and afraid? Yet this dharma is most essential; how can one obstruct oneself? I will now further unfold for the great assembly the true meaning of prajñā, which among the paramitas is called first, so that they may understand it clearly. I speak of prajñā in order to lead beings to the other shore. Not to reach the other shore is to sink in the sea of suffering, and without prajñā one cannot reach the other shore. It can be seen that this dharma is exceedingly important, that one absolutely must not doubt, fear, and obstruct oneself, and that one must believe, understand, receive, and uphold it. What is the other shore? It is the true mark of all dharmas. One should know that the true mark is no mark. Hence prajñā, though called first, is not first. Why? Because "first" is from the first without mark. Since it is from the first without fixed mark, it is said to be "not." To say "not" is to make beings understand clearly that of the dharmas the Buddha speaks, there is not one dharma that can be apart from prajñā; so prajñā cannot vaunt itself as first apart from the paramitas. Again one should know that the true mark is also not without marks. Hence prajñā, though not first, is named first. Why? Because "first" is not without a mere name. Since it is not without the name and mark of a mere existence, it says "is named." To say "is named" is to make beings understand clearly that since every dharma is not apart from prajñā, every dharma may be named first; so prajñā's being called first is a mere name.

I have thus unfolded the essential meaning of prajñā, and all beings should be able to awaken to it through this. Wherever I say "not," it is certainly to make people empty marks; and then I say "is named," to show that it is not without the name and mark of a mere existence. So what is called emptying marks is to empty the disease of grasping at marks, and is not to destroy the marks. This can be clearly understood. Not destroying the marks is to empty even the emptiness that is one-sidedly grasped; this is what is called the emptiness of the supreme meaning. If one can penetrate this meaning, one knows that because marks are mere names they must not be grasped, not that there are no marks; and that because dharmas have no fixed nature they must not be grasped, not that there are no dharmas. Then though this dharma is empty, how could it be the same as a blank, stubborn emptiness? And though this dharma is lofty, it is not without a place to begin. What then is there to be startled at, terrified of, or afraid of? Now such a person can believe, understand, receive, and uphold, and so is neither startled nor terrified nor afraid. He has penetrated the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and is precisely what is called one whose mind is not startled or moved with respect to the supreme meaning. Is he not most rare? What has been said above not only explains why the earlier text says "neither startled" and so on up to "most rare," but also thoroughly explains the principle that all beings need not fear and must not fear, so that the meaning of this section is fully brought out.

Yet there remains an essential meaning that cannot but be spoken. What is it? It is what was said above to have lain hidden and obscure for a thousand ages. One should know that the disease of fearing prajñā is deep and long-standing. If one does not expose its causes one by one, how can one remove the thousand-year disease of preconceptions? All the more should one explain in detail that the meaning of prajñā is perfectly fused, in no way different from what is called the middle way and the supreme meaning, and has nothing whatever to be feared. Thus one may not lose one's own good benefit. Though this is said by way of extension, it is still the purport of this section's text; the intent is to break the grasping at dharmas through discrimination and so remove the root of the disease of fearing any talk of prajñā.

The sutras say that the two vehicles fear emptiness, which means they fear the emptiness of the supreme meaning of prajñā. It can be seen that this was already so in the Buddha's time, and not only in later ages. But in the Buddha's time only the two vehicles gave rise to fear; the Great Vehicle did not yet have this disease. Later, when Xuanzang crossed to the west and met the masters of the Yogacara school in that land, he set the emptiness of the nature school over against the existence of the mark school. (The emptiness of the supreme meaning is absolute emptiness; how could it be set over against existence?) Once this point was mistaken, it was said that the mark school alone is the definitive meaning; this is the so-called classification of the teachings into three periods. Thus even among the Mahayana people of India at that time, there were already those who could not deeply understand the meaning and who mistook prajñā for one-sided emptiness. As for those in our Sui and Tang dynasties who classified the teachings, they likewise never placed prajñā among the perfect teachings. They were not unaware that it is the emptiness of the supreme meaning, but in the end they thought that since it speaks exclusively of emptiness it is not as perfectly fused as the middle way and the supreme meaning. That the ancients judged it so was meant to exalt what they themselves followed, and they could not but deliberately show a bias. Yet the bias went too far, and they inevitably grasped at the mark of words. Later people, because it was so judged by the ancients, grasped all the more and were all the more overawed at the sight of it. Hence never has anyone been willing to study prajñā or willing to speak of prajñā. This is truly sad, truly lamentable.

The Chan school, though it takes prajñā as its guiding principle, takes only its sweeping-away flavor for its practice and does not speak of the teaching. So the meaning of prajñā has not been made clear for a thousand ages. In the Chen and Sui dynasties there was the Three Treatise school, but it took the treatises as its guiding principle, not the sutra. What the three treatises make clear is certainly prajñā, but since the masters of the three treatises devoted themselves to researching the words of the treatises, they could not avoid being out of touch with the meaning of the sutra. Why? Because they had not directly contemplated it. In plain terms, they still could not avoid grasping at the mark of the three treatises' words. Hence the masters of the three treatises expounded the meaning of the treatises most exquisitely, yet the purport of the sutra they could not touch at the itchy place. One should know that since prajñā is the mother of the paramitas, and this sutra plainly says that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment come forth from this sutra, then if the meaning of prajñā is not clear, even reading other perfectly fused sutras and treatises, one has not worked at the fundamental meaning, and how could one's insight be thorough? And if the insight is not thorough, how could it be perfect? Now the World-Honored One, taking the name of the first paramita, unfolds its meaning, so that one may know that the meaning of prajñā is empty yet not empty, not empty yet empty, and perfectly fused, thereby keeping beings from being startled, terrified, doubtful, and afraid, from losing the treasure of the Dharma through neglect, and from finding it hard to reach the other shore. It is as though he foresaw where the root of the disease of fear would lie in later people and set it before them in advance; truly great kindness and great compassion.

Above, whenever I have spoken of "is not" and "is named," I have mostly explained them by way of non-grasping at the two extremes, that is, by way of the perfectly fused middle way. This time I explain them also by way of the emptiness of the supreme meaning, that is, by way of sweeping away. To speak thus truly involves pains. What pains? To make one know that the middle way and sweeping away, though the words differ, are in meaning truly without difference. How is this shown? It is named the emptiness of the supreme meaning because it empties through to the very bottom. Emptying through to the very bottom means that existence too is emptied and emptiness too is emptied. In other words, existence is relinquished and emptiness is relinquished. Relinquishing existence is what is called not grasping at existence; relinquishing emptiness, is that not what is called not grasping at emptiness? Then between the sweeping-away emptiness of the supreme meaning and the perfectly fused middle way of non-grasping at the two extremes, pray what difference is there? From this one may know that what the classifiers of the teachings said cannot be held as a settled verdict; this can now be clearly understood. And those who fear any talk of prajñā may well turn about and repent. Moreover, from this it follows that all the sayings that some sutra is purely perfect and some sutra is not purely perfect likewise cannot be held as fixed marks. Why? Since every dharma is prajñā, every dharma is perfect. As is said, when a perfect person speaks the Dharma, no dharma is not perfect. Why insist on discriminating?

It was said above that sweeping away and the perfectly fused middle way are without the slightest difference. Those who mistakenly believe there is a difference have no other reason than that they stare fixedly at the middle way. I will now further unfold its meaning by way of the middle way, so that it may be thoroughly understood, and then the grasping of discrimination may perhaps not arise of itself.

Since all dharmas are mere names, the middle way too is a mere name. Being a mere name, it has no fixed mark and therefore must not be grasped; to grasp it is to fall into the four marks, and can that still be called the perfectly fused middle way? One should know that the one word "middle" comes into being through contrast with the two extremes. If one leaves the two extremes, the middle is nowhere to be found. Hence the middle has no fixed mark. And marks being without fixity, how can one stare fixedly at it? To stare fixedly is to fall into grasping at dharmas. One should further know that the reason the middle has no fixed mark is that the two extremes are likewise mere names, likewise arising through contrast, and likewise from the first without fixed mark. Since the two extremes must not be grasped, how could there be a middle to grasp? Hence one who truly understands the meaning of the middle finds no place that is not the middle: even emptiness and the mere name are both the middle.

Take emptiness as an illustration. Emptiness means not grasping at existence; and when emptiness itself is also emptied, that is not grasping at emptiness. So emptying through to the very bottom returns to the middle way, as was made clear above. For this reason prajñā and the Avatamsaka and Lotus sutras are in meaning without difference. Not only this: carrying the mere name through to the very bottom is likewise so. For example, to know that all dharmas are not without a mere name is not to grasp at emptiness; and to further know that the name is merely provisional, is that not not grasping at existence? Then it too is plainly the middle way. This is why the Mantra and Pure Land schools both enter the Way through the gate of existence and both are perfect and sudden great dharmas. Even of the mark school one may say that it is from the first the perfect meaning of the Great Vehicle. Not to speak of other matters, consider how it unfolds the principle of the three natures, the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected; how perfect and wondrous. Yet alas, those who study it do not contemplate and work at these places but devote themselves to analyzing trivial names and marks. The more they analyze, the more they discriminate, and so the more they grasp. Thus the great becomes small and the perfect becomes one-sided; they may be called poor students. Not knowing how to use it to remove ordinary feeling, they instead increase ordinary feeling through it. How could this be the original intent of the Buddha's speaking of dharma-marks? Those who cultivate the Mantra and Pure Land schools, if they do not understand the meaning that self and other are non-dual and mind and land are non-dual, likewise make the great small and the perfect one-sided. From this one may know that whatever the Buddha spoke is from the first perfect in every dharma, and that where people see it as not perfect, it is truly due to the one-sided views of beings and has nothing to do with the Dharma. Hence one who studies Buddhism must first open wide a perfect understanding, contemplating the principle that there is no place that is not the middle, and cultivating all dharmas thereby; then every dharma is perfect, every dharma is the middle way and the supreme meaning, every dharma is the first paramita, and every dharma realizes the true mark and reaches the other shore. This is what is called the perfect middle, which students absolutely must know.

The four words just spoken, "open wide a perfect understanding," deserve the closest attention. All my sayings that there is no place that is not the middle can only be a small aid to the hearer. One must constantly take this perfect meaning and, upon one's own mind and upon all dharmas, subtly and closely contemplate it and work at it with vigor, so as to remove the one-sided and grasping ordinary feeling; only then may one's own perfect understanding perhaps be opened. Otherwise what is called perfect understanding still belongs to someone else and is not one's own. Though one knows that no place is not the middle, with respect to all dharmas one will still meet obstruction at every turn and cannot be without a place that is not the middle. This point is of the utmost importance; do not neglect it by any means. Not only is this one meaning so; all the meanings spoken are so. In short, hearing, reflection, and cultivation cannot be lacking in any one.

One should further know that this sutra's speaking of "is not" and "is named" makes clear that nature and mark are neither one nor different: though perfectly fused, they are laid out in order, and though laid out in order, they are perfectly fused. ("Laid out in order" is the sense of "thus, thus," that is, one yet two. "Perfectly fused" is two yet one. The above showed that sweeping away is the middle way, making clear that it is the same in meaning as the Lotus Sutra; here it shows that it is the same in meaning as the Avatamsaka.) Why? Wherever it says "is not," it speaks by way of the nature; spoken by way of the nature, one should not grasp at marks, and so it says "not." That one should not grasp at marks and so says "not" makes clear that nature and mark are not one. Wherever it says "is named," it speaks by way of marks; spoken by way of marks, one should not destroy marks, and so it affirms them. That one should not destroy marks and so affirms them makes clear that nature and mark are not different. Why? The nature is substance and marks are function, utterly distinct, and so they are not one; this is what is called being laid out in order. Yet function is born from substance, and apart from substance there is no function; from this one may know that marks are the working of the nature. Understanding this principle and not grasping, one sees the nature in seeing marks, and so they are not different; this is what is called perfect fusion. Since nature and mark are thus neither one nor different, it is one yet two, two yet one. Being one yet two, one should neither destroy nor grasp them; for though they are not different, they are already not one, and so one must see the laid-out order within the perfect fusion and obtain the perfect fusion within the laid-out order. Being two yet one, though marks blaze forth, they still return and merge into the nature; for though they are not one they are truly not different, and so one should let the perfect fusion not obstruct the laid-out order, nor the laid-out order the perfect fusion. In thus unfolding it, I find it plainly no different in meaning from the Avatamsaka, and those who follow the Avatamsaka need not fear. And as was said above, sweeping away and the middle way are without difference; if one understands this meaning, those who follow the Lotus Sutra need not fear either.

In this sutra, passages such as "if one sees all marks as non-marks, then one sees the Tathagata," "one should produce a pure mind," "one should produce the mind without dwelling," as well as the two words "true mark," and "the mark of self is precisely non-mark" and so on here, can all be explained by this meaning. Even when the sutra opens and speaks of various kinds of beings and of nirvāṇa without residue, that too is perfect fusion within the laid-out order. And when it further says that in truth there is no being who is ferried into extinction, then the laid-out order is perfectly fused. Here I have merely taken "is not" and "is named" and unfolded them thus, so that those who follow the Avatamsaka need not look askance at it. If one insists that only "is not" and "is named" can make this meaning clear, that again is wrong. In short, grasp the essential and comprehend the whole, and there is no saying that will not do. From this one may awaken to the fact that dharmas have no fixed mark.

There is a further most essential meaning that must be spoken. Since the sweeping-away Dharma-gate and the perfect-fusion Dharma-gate are without the slightest difference, why was it said above that one must enter by this sutra? One should know that though these two Dharma-gates are without difference in principle, in practice they differ greatly in sharpness and dullness. The reason one should enter by this sutra is that all ordinary beings without exception are deeply diseased with one-sided grasping, and must sweep away with all one's might before one can be perfectly fused. Otherwise, with not a fraction of the ordinary feeling of one-sided grasping removed, how could one comprehend a perfectly fused sutra or treatise, and how could one benefit from it? At most one might learn a doctrine or two to assist in idle talk.

Consider how since the Tang dynasty, among the great masters outside the Chan school, those whose virtue and insight later generations most admire, when one examines where they gained their strength, were almost all without exception tempered in the Chan gate. This is precisely because the practice of the Chan gate takes as its guiding principle prajñā's emptiness of emptiness and sweeps away the one-sided grasping of students with all its might. Hence I have often said that after the Tang, Chinese Buddhism depended entirely on the Chan school. From this one may know the importance of the work of sweeping away, and that the meaning of prajñā's three emptinesses must be understood. But when sweeping away, one should deeply and perfectly contemplate the perfectly fused meaning of the sutra. Otherwise one will not know what is one-sided, what is grasping, and what should be swept away; one may even think one is sweeping away when in fact one is only increasing one-sided grasping. This is why the Chan gate, though it does not speak of doctrine, must have strict and clear-eyed teachers and companions who constantly wield the tongs and hammer on one's behalf. What is called wielding the tongs and hammer is sweeping away and sweeping away again; what is called the hundred-foot pole requiring one further step.

Now since one has not met strict and clear-eyed teachers and companions, one can only observe and illuminate oneself, closely and precisely comprehending the sutra's clarifications of non-grasping at the two extremes and the perfect fusion of nature and mark. Or it speaks of emptying through to the very bottom, and even, the more it speaks, the deeper it goes, as in the latter half: all dharmas are one suchness, everything is, no sage and no ordinary being, from the first no arising, and so on. The student should assess how much his own level can bear, and from the shallow to the deep take up one phrase or join several phrases and use them to contemplate his own mind. If his own habitual tendencies, and even the arising of a single thought, are the least bit out of accord with the sutra's intent, that is one-sided grasping; then he should at once strike and shout at himself and sweep it away. This is the most wondrous method of practice, truly the talk of my own experience, which I make bold to tell you all.

Other perfectly fused sutras and teachings, if one enjoys studying them, may be looked at as well, but one should take prajñā as the master. Why? The Avatamsaka, Lotus, and the like are expressive statements; an expressive statement uses language that displays perfect fusion in order to make clear the nature-substance. Hence their phrases and flavor all tend toward perfect fusion; even when they speak of the method of sweeping away, it is lodged within the perfect fusion. So only one who already has the work of sweeping away, that is, one whose grasping views are already thin, can thoroughly comprehend them. Otherwise one knows only that they speak of perfect fusion and does not know that they speak of sweeping away. Hence those who enter by them often study for many years while the disease of one-sided grasping remains. They may expound perfect fusion according to the doctrine, yet it has no bearing on their own portion. Moreover, with the grasping feeling unsubdued, what they say is no more than a surface show; sometimes it looks profound and subtle, but examined closely it is neither clear nor awake. Or they think that only such-and-such a sutra is so and others are not, and still they do not see that they can truly be perfectly fused. Prajñā, however, is a negating statement; a negating statement uses language that sweeps away one-sided grasping in order to make clear the nature-substance. Hence its phrases and flavor all tend toward sweeping away; even when it speaks of the principle of perfect fusion, that is lodged within the sweeping away. This is why people fear any talk of prajñā, and also why prajñā is not placed among the perfect teachings: because they look at only one side of the words. On this one point alone it can be proved that one who has not worked at prajñā, even though he studies other perfect sutras, still has an insight that is kept apart and not perfectly fused.

The above has spoken of how prajñā differs in its formulation from other perfect sutras, and of the subtle point on which the sharpness or dullness of those who study it depends. Now, to uphold the true Dharma and to let everyone obtain benefit, I have not shrunk from turning it over and over in full detail and laying it out thread by thread for you all. From this one may know the wonder of prajñā, and that one must study it first. Why? For every portion of grasping feeling that is swept away, nature and mark are perfectly fused by one portion; sweeping away carried to its utmost is perfect fusion carried to its utmost. Wisdom penetrating the three emptinesses is the perfectly fused middle way. How wondrous, how wondrous! This is enough to show that prajñā is not only the broad highway of studying Buddhism but its direct path. If one does not enter by this gate, does one not fail to know the way? This is why many study Buddhism and few attain freedom. All that I have said here is one word, one drop of blood, all gained through a thousand hardships; all is my heart and liver dug out and shown to others. And these sutra passages unfolding the meaning are one word, one pearl, utterly perfect and utterly round. You must truly and earnestly comprehend them and not neglect them.

I said just now that after the Tang dynasty Chinese Buddhism depended entirely on the Chan school. Do not misunderstand this as urging people not to recite the Buddha's name and to go practice Chan instead. For where I praise the Chan school, I am praising prajñā; I am urging people to study prajñā, not urging them to practice Chan. One should know that to practice Chan one must weigh the time and the capacity. Capacity is capacity and time is time; they are not one thing. What is called capacity means one's own faculties. So one should first ask whether one can take a blow and a shout. Whether one's faculties are sharp or dull matters less; unless one has the spirit of a death-defying band, there is no use speaking of it. Again, capacity also means opportunity. So one should further ask whether one has met a good teacher. Chan practice cannot be apart from a teacher, and the teacher must not only be clear but fierce, and must further have the means to kill and to give life. Lacking any of the three, he is not a good teacher. If both one's faculties and one's opportunity are complete, Chan practice is very good. If either is lacking, to speak of practicing Chan will bring no benefit and may bring harm. This too is my talk of experience. What is called time: in the Northern and Southern Dynasties, Northern Wei and Southern Liang both greatly promoted the Buddha Dharma, and lecture seats were at their height; yet they could not avoid grasping at the mark of words. Hence when Bodhidharma came east he set up no words and pointed directly at the mind, precisely to meet the disease of the time. Today most people do not understand the Buddha's principle, so one should broadly encourage the reading of sutras to cure their emptiness and shallowness. To set up no words is still not fitting today. So it is better to arouse the great compassionate vow, cultivate merit and keep the precepts, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, and draw near to the two great good teachers Śākyamuni and Amitābha. On the one hand, relying on what I have said above, use this sutra's principle to contemplate one's own mind and sweep away its ordinary feeling; on the other hand, earnestly hold the name, seeking to be reborn in the Pure Land together with all beings and to fulfill the bodhi vow. For practice in this present life there is nothing that surpasses this method. This is what I, unwise as I am, have earnestly practiced these near twenty years, and I respectfully offer it to all good teachers. Again, since I began lecturing I have spoken of many methods of practice. Do not insist on which is the best; choose the one you are good at and practice it. Or try each one in turn, and whichever you find effective is the one best suited to your capacity. This too is the key to practice, and I tell it to you all.

The great reason for fearing any talk of prajñā, spoken of above, is that people have neither understood the sutra's meaning nor been free of preconceived words, so that they grow the more terrified and the less willing to study. Yet there is another great reason which one must also know: the great number of those who talk wildly of prajñā. The disease of wild talk existed in ancient times and is still more virulent today. Such people, though they have studied Buddhism, have very heavy former karma and do not understand the Buddha Dharma. Suddenly, as if gone mad, they break the precepts utterly, show no respect for the Three Jewels, and give free rein to evil. They practice greed, anger, and delusion in earnest and take themselves to be practicing precepts, concentration, and wisdom, saying that this is prajñā's non-grasping at marks. Thereupon those who fear prajñā seize it as a pretext and warn one another not to dare to utter a single word of prajñā, until it is almost a matter of turning pale at the mention of a tiger. Alas, to give up eating because of a choking fit, what a perverse plan. One should know that since there is this grotesque wild talk, one should all the more arouse the mind to study it and to spread it, and only then can the true meaning of prajñā be fully made clear. When the true meaning is clear, whence would the grotesque wild talk arise? Not knowing to do this, but only shutting the door and stubbornly refusing, one's disease, though different in appearance from that of the wild talker, has the same root; for both mistakenly take prajñā for one-sided emptiness. Judged by cause and effect, the guilt of wild talk is indeed heavy, but except for the retinue of demons, people can know it and keep away from it. The fearer of talk, however, is taken by people as a standard and they do not even know he is mistaken, so that prajñā, which surpasses all dharmas and on which the life-breath of the Buddha Dharma depends, is left unheeded by anyone. I fear the evil fruit summoned by his evil cause of harming the Dharma and harming people may not be much lighter.

Our World-Honored One clearly knew the diseases of all beings, so the earlier words that one who keeps the precepts and cultivates merit can give rise to faith and take this as real were a sharp lancet for those who talk wildly; and these several sections now are again a sharp lancet for those who fear to talk. Looking at what was said before, it shuts the wild talkers outside the gate. Why? Faith is the gate of entry to the path. Since it is by keeping the precepts and cultivating merit that one enters the gate, the wild talker who breaks the precepts and commits offenses is decisively shut outside. Looking at what these several sections say, they again warn the fearer of talk that he can by no means turn the ordinary into the sage. Why? Only one who is neither startled nor terrified nor afraid is allowed to be rare, so the fearer of talk clearly remains an ordinary, foolish being. And above it says "take this as real," while here it unfolds the meaning; this is plainly to instruct that if one wishes to remove the diseases of wild talk and fearful talk, there is nothing but believing, understanding, receiving, and upholding, and earnestly seeking to understand the true meaning within the sutra. Again, the fearful have a constant saying: Do I not know that prajñā should be studied? Truly, beings of the final age have deep obstacles and heavy karma and cannot easily attain it; better not to speak of it and so avoid adding to one's offenses. This again is a mistake. Did the World-Honored One not plainly say: after the Tathagata's extinction, in the last five hundred years, there will be those who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, who can give rise to faith, take this as real, and even obtain immeasurable merit and virtue? So to call them rare in the final age is fine, but to conclude that there are absolutely none, and to warn one another and block the road, is not only to slight beings but plainly to disobey the Buddha's intent. The World-Honored One's admonition to the elder not to speak thus is no different from admonishing the fearer of talk not to speak thus. And in these several sections the Buddha and the elder both encourage and exhort later ages specifically; all of it foresees the excessive worries of the fearful and instructs them, and is truly intimate and savory.

Again, in citing the name of the first paramita here, and in saying "not" and "is named," there is a further meaning that must be made clear. The one name "prajñā" is easily misunderstood as referring to the single paramita of prajñā alone, whereas the name "first" was from the first established to show that it penetrates the other five paramitas. Explaining the meaning on this basis makes it hard to grasp and easy to understand. Moreover, to say that the first is not first makes still clearer the meaning that all the paramitas are one prajñā and that prajñā does not exist apart from the paramitas. As for saying "is named": since none of the paramitas is other than prajñā, how could the title "first" belong to prajñā alone? Since it is not its alone, then though it is so it is a mere name; this makes clear that one must not grasp it as existent. And because of prajñā's being first, every paramita becomes first; so though it is a mere name, it is very much so; this makes clear that one must not grasp it as non-existent. In sum, it makes clear only that prajñā and the paramitas cannot be apart from each other. Hence this section unfolds the meaning by way of prajñā and the next section again unfolds it by way of the other paramitas. Such is the skill of Dharma-speaking; such is the thoroughness with which the meaning is made clear.

As to the essential meanings in this section's text, let me now gather the most essential and reduce them to a few phrases for ease of memory. They are: the most essential meaning of this section is to cure the disease of those who fear prajñā. The disease has two forms: first, fearing emptiness; second, fearing loftiness. Now it is made clear that prajñā does not exist apart from the other five paramitas, and that the other paramitas are all gates of practice; it can be seen that though prajñā makes clear the meaning of emptiness, the meaning of emptiness cannot be apart from actual practice, and it is clear that prajñā is by no means one-sided emptiness. Why then fear it? It is further made clear that the other paramitas apart from prajñā are not paramitas; in plain terms, they cannot reach the other shore. It can be seen that prajñā is indeed lofty, yet it must be studied; and it is clear how important its bearing is. Why then fear it? This is the utmost of warning; keep it in mind and do not forget it.
(Chou) 2. Making it clear by way of the remaining paramitas. In two parts: (Yin) 1. Directly making it clear; 2. Citing proof.
(Yin) 1. Directly making it clear.
["Subhuti, what the Tathagata says is the paramita of patience is not the paramita of patience."]

The remaining paramitas are, apart from prajñā, the other five of giving, keeping the precepts, patience, vigor, and meditative concentration. Every dharma should be free from marks, and so no dharma can be apart from prajñā. That among the remaining five he singles out patience alone is because patience is the hardest to free from marks, and its inability to be apart from prajñā is the easier to comprehend. Hence he specially cites this paramita to unfold its meaning, thereby covering the others. So the section heading does not say "patience" but "the remaining paramitas," precisely because the Buddha's speaking of it was meant to let beings infer the three corners from one. Such a heading follows what the Buddha said, relying on the meaning and not on the words.

The above, making it clear by way of prajñā, unfolded from the front side the true meaning of freedom from marks. For people know only that prajñā speaks of emptiness and freedom from marks, and those who grasp at marks therefore give rise to fear. Now it is made clear that even the mark of prajñā should be relinquished, which is to relinquish emptiness as well. Moreover, prajñā is within the other five paramitas and cannot stand alone, and the other five paramitas are all dharmas of actual practice; so what is called freedom from marks is the relinquishing of the mark of dharma and the mark of non-dharma together. If one understands this meaning, one may boldly study prajñā; why fear it?

This making it clear by way of patience unfolds from the reverse side the true meaning that one cannot but be free from marks. Looking at what is said below: if one practices the dharma of patience and is not free from the mark of patience, one gives rise to hatred, and hatred is precisely the opposite of patience. This makes clear that one who practices the dharma of patience, if he does not study prajñā, does not know to be free from the mark of the dharma of patience; not being free from the mark of dharma, hatred arises; and once hatred arises, the merit of patience is destroyed and it becomes the mark of non-dharma. From this one may awaken to the fact that the reason one must be free from the mark of dharma is precisely to be free from the mark of non-dharma. How wondrous, how wondrous. If one understands this meaning, one will surely apply the mind to studying prajñā and cannot fear it. Unfolded thus, the essential meaning of prajñā is exposed to the very bottom, and one may clearly see that prajñā absolutely must be studied.

These several sections of sutra text unfolding the meaning have expounded the principle of prajñā and the principle that prajñā should be studied with the utmost subtlety, perfection, penetration, and fineness. You should earnestly quiet your minds and comprehend them; for every portion comprehended is a portion of benefit obtained. Moreover, these several sections are precisely the crystallization of all the meanings spoken above. If the meaning here can be clearly penetrated, then all the meanings above will shine clear in your breast one by one.

That this section follows immediately upon the last carries a further sense. The intent is to use patience's inability to be apart from prajñā to prove and complete the last section's meaning that prajñā does not exist apart from the other paramitas. For since all the remaining paramitas must have prajñā, it can be seen that prajñā is a dharma that goes along with the remaining paramitas and is not a dharma practiced separately. In short, prajñā is the mother of the paramitas, and the paramitas are the children of prajñā. If there were no children, the name mother could not stand; if there were no mother, the name children could not stand. Mother and children truly complete each other. So prajñā and the remaining paramitas must complete each other; how could they be apart? Prajñā is emptiness; the remaining paramitas are existence. To say now that prajñā and the other five paramitas cannot be apart is to make students comprehend that emptiness and existence are from the first simultaneous, and so cannot be apart.

Because emptiness and existence are simultaneous, one should not grasp at the two extremes but return and merge into the middle way. There is a further point. Speaking in terms of mother and children, they certainly should complete each other; yet the children are truly born from the mother, and without the mother there are no children. So within their mutual help, the mother should still be the master. The six paramitas are likewise: the other five paramitas without prajñā are not paramitas. So the other five paramitas truly arise from the first paramita, and within their mutual help prajñā is still the master. To take prajñā as master is to take emptiness as master. Taking emptiness as master, though one should not destroy existence, one still should not grasp at existence; and though one returns and merges into the middle way, one does not grasp at the middle either. This is why the Buddhas and bodhisattvas take the great emptiness-samādhi as ultimate, and take no wisdom and no attainment as the attainment of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment. For only thus can one follow forms through the six paths and manifest hundreds of thousands of millions of transformation bodies, while though all dharmas blaze forth, the one mind is limpid and from the first nothing is produced. This is what is called great freedom; this is what is called great benefit. It is on this alone that one can ferry all suffering and distress. This is the ultimate meaning of prajñā, and the latter half of the sutra precisely makes it clear. Taking this occasion to disclose a hint of it shows that prajñā is the meaning in the Buddha Dharma that runs from beginning to end: without studying it one cannot enter the gate, and without studying it one cannot reach the ultimate. Why then fear it?

And from this one may know that to speak exclusively of non-grasping at the two extremes and the perfectly fused middle way is still not the ultimate meaning of the Buddha Dharma. Why? Without emptiness upon emptiness, there is sure to be something grasped. Not grasping at the extremes, one is sure to grasp at the middle; where then is the perfect fusion? Moreover, in the great emptiness-samādhi even the two words "perfect fusion" are unattainable. One should know that only when it is unattainable is perfect fusion attained. Why? Not grasping at perfect fusion, one attains perfect fusion. With the slightest mark, it is neither round nor fused. Then since the meaning of prajñā is ultimate in this way, how could it be only the first gate of entry to the path? Why classify it as the initial teaching of the Great Vehicle? And prajñā runs through all the paramitas, and the paramitas apart from it are not paramitas; so it can be seen that if there is a single dharma apart from it, one cannot be complete. Thus the meaning of prajñā is the utmost of completeness and surpasses all Dharma-gates; this too can be known. Why then not allow it to be purely perfect, but classify it as separate and also perfect?

The above spoke of the six paramitas helping one another; there is a further essential meaning that must be known. Prajñā is principle, is wisdom, what is called the gate of contemplation. The paramitas are affairs, are objects, what is called the gate of practice. That after speaking of the first paramita he further speaks of the remaining paramitas is to make clear that principle and affairs have never been apart, that contemplation and practice should advance together, and that object and wisdom above all must be merged in pairs. So judging by the text it seems to start a separate topic, but examining the meaning it is truly one thread. The textual surface of this sutra is for the most part like this; what is called the text not joining but the meaning joining. To regard them as having nothing to do with each other would be a great mistake.

The circulating editions have the line "is named the paramita of patience." This was added by someone between the Ming and Qing, and appears in the Sun family edition of the Qianlong-Jiaqing period. Its note says: "The ancients did not have this line, but by principle it should be there." They did not realize that the words "not" here are precisely the groundwork for the text below, which makes clear that if patience is not free from marks the Dharma-gate of patience is utterly destroyed, thereby revealing that it absolutely cannot be apart from prajñā. If one suddenly adds a line "is named," blocking the way in between, how can the "why?" below be connected? So planting this one line slackens the whole flow of text before and after, and on the contrary buries the sutra's purport. And to say that by principle it should be there, one cannot understand what principle is meant; truly ignorant and reckless. One should know that what the Buddha spoke cannot be lightly added to or subtracted from by oneself; how great the audacity. Even if the transmission contains errors, one must have real evidence, and the evidence must further be such that the meaning is truly perfect and precise before one may correct it on that basis. How could one knowingly add what the ancient editions do not have? All who wish to print sutras for merit must know this principle. If such a person does this, not only is there no merit; his offense is very great, because he relies on his own private guesswork, presumes to alter what the Buddha said, and thereby harms the Dharma and harms people. This matter may serve as a blazing warning for a thousand ages, and so I do not shrink from speaking of it incisively.

The Sanskrit word kshanti means peaceful endurance, and is also called patience. "Peaceful endurance" is the general name and "patience" the particular name. "Patience" is accepting in accord, meaning to receive single-mindedly and rightly; "peaceful" is abiding peacefully, meaning that the mind is unmoved; "insult" is injury and insult, that is, the sense of maltreatment. Let us first speak the meaning of the general name, and the particular meaning will appear of itself.

Only when a person can endure does his mind abide peacefully and unmoved. If it is moved, it is not endurance. So the single word "endurance" already contains the sense of abiding peacefully and unmoved. One who studies the Way should, in every place and at every moment, have a mind that is peaceful and unmoved. Hence whatever affair he undertakes, whatever circumstance he meets, whatever dharma he practices, he should receive it single-mindedly and rightly. Spoken of the supramundane Dharma: whatever dharma one practices, if one can rightly receive and peacefully abide in it, that is named endurance. For example, practicing the contemplation that all dharmas are from the first non-arising and attaining the non-arising of deluded thoughts: the mind has rightly received this dharma and abides peacefully and unmoved in it, and so it is named the patience of the non-arising of dharmas. It is also called realizing non-arising, or awakening to non-arising. The word "realize" describes the accepting in accord; the word "awaken" describes the mind's being at peace with the principle. Spoken of the mundane Dharma it is likewise so. As it is said: wealth and honor cannot corrupt him, power and force cannot bend him, poverty and lowliness cannot move him. This is what the ancients called firm endurance. That power and force cannot bend him does not mean stubborn resistance; it means the body may be killed but the will cannot be taken from him. That the will cannot be taken is the mind's abiding peacefully and unmoved; this is precisely what is called patience. This, together with not being corrupted by wealth and honor and not being moved by poverty and lowliness, all shows the mind at peace in the right and unmoved by anything; hence it is called firm endurance. From this one may know that peaceful endurance is the name that covers all: whatever affair one undertakes, whatever circumstance one meets, whatever dharma one practices, one should rightly receive and peacefully abide. Patience, then, is one matter within peaceful endurance. Hence it is said that peaceful endurance is general and patience is particular. One should know that whenever patience is brought up, the intent is to use the particular to cover the whole, to use the particular to make clear the general. Why? The hardest thing in the world to endure is being insulted without cause. If even this must be endured, one may know the rest. In the sutras and treatises, sometimes the general name is used and sometimes the particular, quite without uniformity. Roughly, the translations of Xuanzang and Yijing both say peaceful endurance, while other translators mostly use patience. People often suspect they are two different dharmas, or debate their relative merit, but in truth though general and particular seem different, their use to make clear the meaning of rightly receiving and peacefully abiding is not different. There is no need to discriminate merit in such places. Taking this occasion to explain the two names in detail makes them easier to hold together.

The sutra text does not say "patience" but says "the paramita of patience," which shows that in patience one can practice prajñā. Why? Because without prajñā it is not called a paramita. And to be able to practice prajñā is to be able to illumine the nature and be free from marks; hence it says that what the Tathagata says is not the paramita of patience. Why one should be free from marks, the text below precisely explains.
(Yin) 2. Citing proof. In two parts: (Mao) 1. Citing an affair of the present kalpa; 2. Citing affairs of many lives.
(Mao) 1. Citing an affair of the present kalpa.

["Why? Subhuti, as when I was in the past cut limb from limb by King Kali. At that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. Why? When in former times my body was dismembered joint by joint, had I had the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, I should have given rise to hatred."]

"Why?" is his own hypothetical question as to why patience should be free from marks. The citation of the factual case is meant to prove that patience must be free from marks. The affair of King Kali belongs to the present kalpa, which is named the Bhadra kalpa, the Good Kalpa, because a thousand Buddhas appear in it and there are very many sages and worthies; hence the name.

The word "kalpa" has two meanings: (1) an extremely long period of time; (2) a calamity. Here it is the first meaning. What is called "the present kalpa" refers to a great kalpa. Every great kalpa divides into four middle kalpas, named formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness. The world's having formation, dwelling, decay, and emptiness is like beings' having birth, old age, sickness, and death. Every middle kalpa again divides into twenty small kalpas. In each small kalpa, at the time when beings' life-spans are at their shortest, most have only ten years. At that time beings are utterly evil and life is utterly bitter; hardly any of the things that sustain life are produced, and whatever is produced is a thing that destroys life. All this is brought about by evil karma. Hence the number of such beings is also extremely small. The sutras say that the population of Jambudvipa at that time was no more than ten thousand in all. In the extremity of suffering they think of good and gradually turn back, and their life-spans gradually increase. But the increase is very slow, because their turning back toward good is not a forward leap but a gradual tending toward the road of good. Roughly, a hundred years pass before one year is added. Increasing gradually in this way, by the time ordinary life-spans reach twenty years, more than a thousand years have already passed. Seeing that doing good brings good reward, more and more people do good. The things that sustain life gradually multiply, the population gradually increases, and every hundred years one year is added. Adding one year every hundred years until ordinary life-spans reach eighty-four thousand years, the increase has reached its utmost and happiness has reached its utmost. At the extremity of joy sorrow is again produced, because the good mind gradually diminishes. Then one year is subtracted every hundred years. Subtracting one year every hundred years until ten years are reached, the decrease has reached its utmost; then they again turn back toward good and increase, and so enter the second small kalpa. And its one increase and one decrease continue cycling in this way. Kalpa after kalpa it is thus: one year added every hundred years, from ten years up to eighty-four thousand years, and again one year subtracted every hundred years, down to ten years. Reckoned thus, the length of every small kalpa is sixteen million seven hundred ninety-eight thousand years. Eighty small kalpas make one great kalpa, so the length of one great kalpa is one billion three hundred forty-two million eight hundred forty thousand years. Yet at a glance, though it is said to be more than a billion years, in fact at the time of the kalpa of formation the world is not yet complete, and at the time of the kalpa of decay the world is already gradually decaying; even if there are beings in the world then, their suffering may be imagined. At the time of the kalpa of emptiness there is not yet this world, so how could there be beings? The sutras say that when the world meets the kalpa of decay, the Buddha by his spiritual power moves the beings of this world to other worlds. Only a single kalpa of dwelling is a complete world, and even from it one half of the kalpa of decrease must be removed. The time when life-spans increase and beings are happy and at ease is no more than the kalpa of increase within the kalpa of dwelling, one hundred sixty-seven million nine hundred eighty thousand years. Even if one has the long life of eighty-four thousand years, in the end one cannot escape the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death. Think carefully: what is there in this world to cling to? So taking this occasion to explain the state of this world in detail, it is best for the great assembly to awaken quickly.

Our World-Honored One was born in the ninth kalpa of decrease within the kalpa of dwelling, when ordinary life-spans were a hundred years down to seventy or eighty. Counting to the present, nearly three thousand years have passed. So the life-span today is seventy at the most, and forty or fifty is most common; this is what is constantly seen in the newspapers. Reckoned by the sutras' saying that one year is subtracted every hundred years, it is in fact not far from the facts, which is enough to prove that the Buddha's words are not false. Now and then there are those who pass a hundred years, but they are exceedingly few; there must be some special good cause for this, and it is an exception. Hereafter it will decrease still further and life will grow still more bitter. So one who lives at this juncture can only urge the great assembly to take refuge together in the Buddha Dharma. If there can be a great many people who keep the precepts and cultivate merit, the world will at once be at peace. One who plants good causes will surely obtain good fruit. Though this is the kalpa of decrease, it is not impossible to see an exceptional flourishing. The Buddha says that all is made by mind alone, and again that all dharmas are nothing but illusory marks. So whether life-spans are many or few, and whether the world's affairs are in order or in chaos, though there is a fixed number, in truth the fixed is not fixed; it lies in what people do. One should further urge all to arouse the great compassionate mind, recite the Buddha's name single-mindedly, seek rebirth in the Pure Land, and obtain a final settlement. Then for the world and beyond the world there is a way. To repay the Buddha's kindness is here, to save all suffering is here, to fulfill the bodhi vow is here; I wish to encourage you all together in this.

"Formerly" and "in the past" make clear that this was a matter of former lives. At that time the World-Honored One was manifesting the body of a bodhisattva and practicing the bodhisattva path. "Was cut" means "was subjected to." Kali is Sanskrit; in the sutras it is sometimes written Kalafu, sometimes Kalinga, sometimes Katri, all being this same person. Its translated meaning is "evil king," like what China calls a benighted ruler. Kali was at that time king of the city of Kusinagara in southern India. He was cruel by nature and delighted in doing poisonous and vicious things, and so gained this evil name. At that time the bodhisattva, for the sake of beings, was sitting in meditation in the mountains. One day the king led his consorts on an outing in the countryside, and being weary he rested a while. The women went to gather flowers and so came to the place of meditation. The bodhisattva, wishing to cut off their greed, spoke the Dharma for them. The king suddenly came looking for them with sword in hand and angrily demanded: Why do you use magic to lure my women? The bodhisattva said: I keep the pure precepts and have long been without a defiled mind. The king said: Have you attained the fruit of arhatship? He said: No. The king said: Have you attained the fruit of non-return? He said: No. The king said: You are young; since you have attained no fruit, you possess greed, so why look upon my women? He answered: Though I have not cut off the fetter of greed, my mind is truly without greed. The king said: Even sages who live on air and eat fruit still feel greed at the sight of form, how much more you in the prime of youth. He answered: To see form without greed does not come from living on air and eating fruit; it comes from fixing the mind on impermanence and impurity. The king said: To slight and slander another, how can one be called a precept-keeper? He answered: Where there is envy there is slander; where there is no envy there is no slander. The king said: What is called a precept? He said: Endurance is called the precept. (From this one may know that unless the mind peacefully abides in the precepts, it is not called precept-keeping.) The king then cut off his hands, feet, ears, and nose with his sword and said: Do you still endure? He answered: Even if the great king were to divide my remaining substance into atoms, I could still endure and would not give rise to a thought of hatred. The ministers all remonstrated, but the king's anger did not cease. Then the four heavenly kings rained down diamond sand. The king, seeing it, was terrified and knelt long in repentance. The bodhisattva made a vow: If I truly have no thought of hatred, let this body of mine be restored as before. Having made this vow, his body was at once restored. He further made a vow, saying: In a future life I will first ferry the great king. Therefore when I now became a Buddha I first ferried Kaundinya, for this king was Kaundinya in a former life. This affair is found in the Mahāparinirvāṇa Sutra and the Vibhasa, with differences in detail; I have gathered them and cited them together. What this sutra calls being cut limb from limb refers precisely to the sword cutting off ears, nose, hands, and feet.

It was said above that if one grasps at the mark of dharma, one grasps at self, person, being, and life. So the present words "no mark of self" and the rest make clear that he does not grasp at the mark of the dharma of patience. That it does not say "no mark of patience" but says "no mark of self" and the rest is because only without the marks of self and others can one not grasp at the mark of patience; this makes clear that discriminating self from others is the root of the disease of grasping at marks. Without the discrimination of self and others, the mind is peaceful and unmoved, and so one can let oneself be cut limb from limb and endure this extraordinary insult. Hence it says: At that time I had no mark of self, no mark of person, no mark of a being, no mark of a life. "At that time" means "at that moment," that is, when he was formerly cut limb from limb. One should know that to endure this extraordinary insult is what others see as so; the bodhisattva at that time was as though nothing had happened, and there was no such thing as insult or no insult, endurance or no endurance. This is what is called patience that is not patience. To see that patience is not patience is precisely the right wisdom of prajñā. Hence inwardly he did not see one who endures, and so had no mark of self; outwardly he did not see what is endured, and so had no mark of person. The bodhisattva sat in meditation, his original aim being to realize the Way in order to ferry beings. Now he let others cut him limb from limb, forgetting even this matter and putting life and death outside his concern; hence it says no mark of a being and no mark of a life. This is because the bodhisattva possessed the right wisdom of prajñā, and so penetrated the one true dharma-realm. In the one true dharma-realm how could there be any such marks of opposition as self and other, being and Buddha, birth and death? Hence the four marks are all absent. With the four marks all absent, the ten thousand thoughts are all still. What is called insult, and what is called endurance? Only after this could he endure this extraordinary insult. Knowing this, one knows that no gate of practice can be accomplished without reliance on prajñā. Knowing this, one knows that no cultivator, without reliance on prajñā, can be without obstruction, can attain freedom, can reach the other shore. Hence it says that all Buddhas and the Dharma of the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment all come forth from this sutra; hence it says that wherever it is taught as occasion arises, all gods and humans should make offering, and that wherever the sutra is, there is the Buddha, or a venerable disciple. Hence whoever hears and believes, understands, receives, and upholds it, and teaches it to others, even a four-line verse, all accomplish what is rare and obtain immeasurable merit and virtue. Even if people in the world cannot all accomplish it thus, if only the discrimination of self and other is somewhat lightened, then contention will surely lessen, and the world will at once be at peace, with all dwelling in security and joying in their work. Therefore prajñā is the true spirit of Buddhism and the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma. All beings should revere and honor it, read and recite it, receive and uphold it, and never for a moment be apart from it.

The second "why?" asks why one should be free from the four marks. "Joint by joint" means "segment by segment." "To dismember" is to break apart; "to cut" is to dissect; both mean to analyze and divide. To analyze segment by segment refers to the hands, feet, ears, and nose being cut off one by one. "I should have given rise to hatred" shows by contrast that he could not have endured. Consider that at that time, suffering this extraordinary insult without cause, had he not been entirely without the discrimination of self and others and with all ten thousand thoughts empty, how could he possibly not have given rise to hatred?

Someone may say: that at that time he vowed to be restored and was at once restored as before means he must have had spiritual powers, and so could endure the pain; how could an ordinary being do it? This view is utterly mistaken; it is a perverse view and must be refuted. One should know that even one who has attained spiritual powers and can bear pain, if a thought of hatred arises, will surely be unable to endure it. Why? Because spiritual powers have nothing to do with hatred. Even those who are full of greed, anger, and delusion, like evil demons, can obtain powers. This is why the Buddha Dharma does not value spiritual powers. Though the Buddhas and bodhisattvas sometimes manifest spiritual powers, it is to express the Dharma, or to convert stubborn and darkened beings when there is no other way, and only now and then. In practice one does not emphasize them.

Moreover, this sutra cites this story to make clear that the unsurpassed bodhi takes great kindness and great compassion as its root, and so one must be free from the marks of discriminating self and others, causing the mind to give rise to not a single thought and to abide peacefully and unmoved. Only then can one obtain equality between gratitude and enmity and accomplish the samādhi of great compassion. When this samādhi is accomplished, one can then, even meeting the greatest adverse circumstances and evil conditions, give rise to no hatred. With hatred utterly absent, one can then ferry all beings and fulfill the bodhi vow. Why? Because beings are stubborn and hard to ferry. Hence the bodhisattva's practice of patience has this as its aim. How could one who merely has spiritual powers even dream of it? Otherwise, consider what is said below: to give body and life as many as the sands of the Ganges three times a day. One can know that such a person has the greatest spiritual powers. Such a person fears no hardship and is exceedingly hard to match; yet he is not equal to one who hears this sutra and whose faith does not oppose it. Why? It makes clear precisely that if one does not believe, understand, receive, and uphold the prajñā Dharma-gate, the discriminating mind surely cannot be thoroughly relinquished. If the discriminating mind is not pure, one has not reached the one true dharma-realm or realized the empty and still nature-substance; then one can by no means accomplish the unconditioned great kindness and the great compassion of one substance. Even if one can give up immeasurable, boundless bodies and lives, it is still with outflows, and one may still retreat upon meeting conditions. Why? Because not having reached the one true and empty and still, one's ignorance is not yet cut off, and so one's root of faith is not yet accomplished. Therefore one who has spiritual powers, even if he can be patient, is fundamentally utterly different from a bodhisattva's ability to be patient; how could they be mentioned together? Hence below he further cites affairs of many lives to prove that patience is no easy matter; unless one has long studied prajñā and attained the great emptiness-samādhi, one may suddenly meet the greatest adverse circumstance and evil condition, and with the least stirring of hatred lose all one's former work. That is why one who upholds and teaches this sutra has merit surpassing that of one who gives up bodies and lives as many as the sands of the Ganges; the reason lies here. In sum, it makes clear that without practicing the prajñā Dharma-gate one cannot be free from all marks or accord with the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and in the end cannot accomplish the bodhisattva of great kindness and great compassion. To know thus is right knowledge; to see thus is right view.

As for vowing to be restored and being at once restored as before, there are three meanings, each deeper than the last. (1) Because of the Buddha's empowering. This is why a vow, once made, is fulfilled. (2) Because of great compassion. This is why he received the Buddha's empowering. Consider that after being cut limb from limb he vowed that in a future life, when he became a Buddha, he would first ferry the great king. One can see that the reason he had not a trace of hatred was that he had already attained the samādhi of great compassion. How is that samādhi attained? By being without a discriminating mind. (3) Because of purity of mind. This is why he was without a discriminating mind and attained the compassion-samādhi.

For in studying prajñā one contemplates the one true dharma-realm, neither mark nor non-mark, and one's work becomes deep and mellow and the one mind is pure. Because the mind is pure, the dharma-realm is pure. At this time the power of the compassionate vow is great and boundless, and whatever vow is made is at once accomplished. To call it the empowering of all Buddhas is all right; to call it what is manifested by mind alone is also all right. Why? Because one has already realized that mind, Buddha, and beings are three without difference. If one speaks of spiritual powers, this is precisely the great spiritual power of the Buddhist gate, what is called the power of the exhaustion of outflows. How could that which has outflows be mentioned in the same breath?

The former passage (that is, what follows the first "why?") makes clear that being free from marks is what enables one to accomplish the dharma one practices; that is, being free from the mark of dharma is precisely what accomplishes the mark of dharma. The latter passage (that is, what follows the second "why?") makes clear that not being free from marks is precisely what destroys the dharma one practices; that is, not being free from the mark of dharma makes it become the mark of non-dharma instead. The former passage makes it clear from the front; the latter reveals it from the reverse. Taking the front and the reverse together, is it not that being free from the mark of dharma is precisely being free from the mark of non-dharma? In simple terms, being free from marks is what keeps one from falling into emptiness, and not being free from marks is what makes one fall into emptiness. To unfold this meaning is precisely to deal a blow on the head to the fearful. For the fearful suspect nothing but that being free from marks must fall into emptiness; now they know it is precisely the opposite. Such a refutation is incomparably sharp. And with this, the meaning of prajñā's freedom from marks is unfolded to the point where nothing remains unrevealed. Yet had the World-Honored One not thus skillfully brought it out, who could have clearly understood? If this meaning is not clearly understood, then one's grasp of freedom from marks is never thorough, and in the end one cannot avoid moments of doubt. So one who, hearing this sutra, can be neither startled nor terrified nor afraid must have deeply understood this meaning; he is truly most rare.

From this one sees that though the text above says only "is not the paramita of patience," it already contains the sense of "is named the paramita of patience." So one can see that when the Buddha speaks the Dharma, he says it on this side while the meaning penetrates the other side, and every side is complete. One may further awaken to the fact that wherever "is not" and "is named" are raised together, though the words stand side by side, the meaning truly leans to the side of "is not." To make this meaning clear in other words: was it not said above that "is not" is spoken by way of the nature, and "is named" by way of marks? Yet the nature is the root and marks are the branches. Only with the root are there branches; because of emptiness, existence appears. So one knows that one should lean to the side of "is not." Hence being free from the mark of dharma is precisely being free from the mark of non-dharma. This is the meaning of what was said above, that the Buddha Dharma takes prajñā as master and takes emptiness as master. Why? Because the nature-substance is from the first empty and still. This is why the Buddhas and bodhisattvas take the great emptiness-samādhi as ultimate, and why with no wisdom and no attainment they attain the unsurpassed, perfectly enlightened enlightenment; and though they attain it, they still have no wisdom and no attainment. Why? Because with the least attainment, one has still not attained.

That the Buddha says one should have given rise to hatred is not only to unfold the meaning spoken above; there is a further essential meaning that must be made clear. One should know that hatred is the great taboo of a cultivator. The World-Honored One, wishing to warn those who arouse the bodhi mind, teaches that no matter at what time, in what circumstance, or in what practice, one must absolutely not give rise to hatred; and he uses patience here as the occasion to make it clear. That he speaks of it with reference to patience is because patience very easily gives rise to hatred, and once hatred arises the practice of patience is destroyed, and such matters and principles are easy for people to understand. Speaking by way of what is easy to understand, as an example, so that one may comprehend all, this is the Buddha's subtle intent. Do not misunderstand it to mean that only in patience may one not give rise to hatred while in other matters it does not matter.

Why is hatred the great taboo of cultivation? Because hatred is precisely in conflict with bodhi. Bodhi is enlightenment, equality, compassion. Hatred arises because things do not go as one wishes, which is grasping at self; where then is equality? The affairs of the world are all dream and illusion; why take seriously whether things go as one wishes or not? If one does not know this, where is enlightenment? That it contradicts compassion needs no saying. So once the mind of hatred arises, the seed of bodhi is utterly destroyed. A cultivator who forgets and loses bodhi will, if it is light, grow slack and let his practice decay, and if it is heavy, lose his mind of the Way entirely. Even if he does not retreat, to practice with a mind of hatred can never accomplish the right fruit. The Buddha says: to forget and lose the bodhi mind while cultivating all good is to be held by demons. Samantabhadra Bodhisattva says: among the faults of a bodhisattva none is greater than hatred; though the merit formerly accumulated be as many as a forest, if the fire of hatred arises it is all burned away at once. Both are found in the Avatamsaka Sutra. Should one not fear? Should one not fear? One should know that of the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, delusion is the root of the poison, and delusion is ignorance. From ignorance arise greed and anger. And of the two poisons of greed and anger, the poison of anger does the greater harm. Why? Because its nature is violent. If it does not break out, well and good; but when it breaks out, one will not even pause to consider that one is utterly reversing all one's former conduct. So the cultivator should strictly guard against it. The Buddha spoke this sutra to open the right wisdom of beings and cure delusion; he speaks of giving at the sutra's opening to cure greed; and hatred was not yet spoken of, so he specially supplies it here. Above he said that in practicing giving one should be without dwelling in dharmas; here he says that giving rise to hatred comes from having the four marks. Both make clear that unless one opens the right wisdom of prajñā to cure the delusion of grasping at marks, greed and anger cannot be removed. "Should have given rise to" means that it must inevitably follow. Once one grasps at marks, one is bound to give rise to hatred; once hatred arises, all one's practice is bound to be destroyed. Therefore a cultivator who does not study prajñā cannot but have a mind like space in every place and at every moment. This is the original intent of the Buddha's speaking of this section. How could it be so only for patience?

One should know that all affairs in the world are nothing but opposition. (Such as cause and effect, self and other, male and female, yin and yang, birth and death, order and chaos, and even defilement and purity, prosperity and decline, suffering and joy, and so on; there is not one affair outside opposition.) Because of opposition, discrimination and calculation very easily arise. Since the common eye takes all oppositions as real things, discrimination and calculation become unbreakable. This is why there is greed and hatred. If one can, within opposition, see the principle of waxing and waning, increase and decrease, and adjust and adapt it to govern all the affairs of the world, one cannot but concede that such a one is a sage of the world. Yet though he can make use of opposition, in the end he cannot leap outside the circle of opposition. The Buddha Dharma is not so. Since all is nothing but opposition, one sees through it here: all of it is nothing but arising through the mutual contrast of this and that. Since all are matters of mutual contrast, all are illusory and unreal, and existence is precisely non-existence. Yet it is not that there is no illusory manifestation, which is non-existent yet existing. So one transcends its surface and is not bound by it, and yet one still accords with what is within it and does not abolish its affairs. To transcend its surface is non-grasping; without this one cannot realize the absolute nature-substance: this is great wisdom. To accord with what is within it is non-destruction; without this one cannot save the beings of the round of rebirth: this is great compassion. All Mahayana sutras speak this principle, and prajñā speaks it in especial detail; the Diamond Prajñā speaks it in especial subtlety.

One who studies Buddhism and can see as far as this is said to have opened the eye of the Way. If the eye of the Way is opened, one should at once nourish one's mind of the Way. How to nourish it? One should make the mind like space, transcending the dust. To be like space is to not dwell in marks. The sutra says that giving without dwelling in marks has merit like space; its meaning is precisely to make one free from marks so that the mind becomes like space. One must have the emptiness of beings and the emptiness of dharmas, and then the mind is empty. The emptiness of beings does not mean that there is no self, person, or being, but that one does not grasp at their marks. The emptiness of dharmas does not mean that there are no dharmas; the dharmas one should practice one still practices one by one in accord with the Dharma, but one acts as though nothing were happening. Practicing giving, one forgets that it is giving; practicing patience, one forgets that it is patience; even practicing the six paramitas, one forgets that they are the six paramitas. "As though nothing were happening" and "forget" mean not grasping at the marks of the one who acts and the act. This is the double emptiness of self and dharma, and the emptiness of emptiness as well.

For a beginner this is certainly not easy to reach, but one must not shrink from the difficulty; one must constantly comprehend this meaning and make one's mind empty and hollow: this is the essential point. To transcend the dust is not to mingle with all the opposing affairs and principles of the dusty world, and constantly to keep in the mind an intent to break free, never letting it lapse: this is the essential point. One should know that only by not mingling can the mind gradually become empty. And at this point one should raise the one phrase, the great name of ten thousand virtues, and recite it single-mindedly, without discriminating who is reciting and who is the Buddha, only letting the recitation be the Buddha and there be no recitation outside the Buddha. This mind has already been made like space, so this thought that is the Buddha also fills space, and above it is in breath-to-breath communion with the Tathagatas of the ten directions and below with the beings of the dharma-realm. Thus one may call it having thoughts or call it having no thoughts; may call it the Buddha being the thought and the thought being the Buddha; may call it the Buddha and the beings being in this mind; may call it this mind being without difference and without mark from the Buddha and the beings. One should further read and recite the Diamond Prajñā Paramita much, to perfume and nourish it, so that the eye of the Way opens day by day and the mind of the Way grows firm day by day. This is the method of cultivating prajñā and the Pure Land together. This method accords with the one true dharma-realm, accords with the true mark, accords with non-grasping at emptiness and existence and the perfect fusion of nature and mark, accords with the emptiness of the supreme meaning, and also accords with the meaning that when the mind is pure the land is pure. Try it, and you should find it beneficial. For this is to follow the opposing dharma of cause and effect and yet cultivate the absolute, surpassingly wonderful cause, and so realize the absolute, surpassingly wonderful fruit.

In the sutra above there are many places that speak of being without the four marks of self and person, but all are spoken from the front side, that is, by way of the benefit gained. Where harm is spoken of from the reverse side, there is only what is said at the sutra's opening: if one has the mark of self, the mark of person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then one is not a bodhisattva. Yet that states what must be so. Now, saying that one should have given rise to hatred states why it must be so. Why? Because if hatred arises, it is not the bodhi mind, that is, not enlightenment, and one is still a deluded ordinary being wandering on the wrong road; hence it says he is not a bodhisattva. From this one may know that one who wishes to leave the wrong road and be born in the Pure Land, how can he fail to give attention to the double emptiness of self and dharma? For whether one grasps at the mark of self or at the mark of dharma, with the least discrimination and calculation one is dwelling in dust and giving rise to mind. If the mind is defiled by dust, how can it be pure? If the mind is not yet pure, the Pure Land is not born. Be careful not to say that the Pure Land Dharma-gate need not speak loftily of prajñā.

The Buddha's words are indeed perfectly wondrous and should be viewed from every side.
