The second half is devoted to clarifying this meaning. One should know that wherever there is grasping, one is bound and fettered by it and cannot be liberated. Ordinary people, through the clinging to a person-self (that is, grasping the physical body as self), are bound by birth and death and cannot escape the round of rebirth. The Two Vehicles, through the clinging to a dharma-self (though they do not grasp the physical body, they grasp the dharmas of the five aggregates, and their view of self is not yet forgotten; hence it is called a dharma-self), are confined by nirvāṇa, so that they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness. A bodhisattva, with great compassion and great wisdom, is fettered by nothing; hence without hindrance or obstruction, and at ease. This is what is called the way of non-dwelling. Therefore even a little clinging feeling should be washed utterly clean, and one should dwell in nothing at all.

(2) The clinging to a person-self and the clinging to a dharma-self, in brief, are called the clinging to self and the clinging to dharmas. It is commonly said that this sutra breaks the clinging to self in its first part and the clinging to dharmas in its latter part. This is rather loose. The first half says at the very outset: a bodhisattva should dwell in nothing with respect to dharmas; as well as no mark of self, no mark of dharma, and no mark of non-dharma; one should not grasp dharmas, one should not grasp non-dharmas; even dharmas should be relinquished, how much more non-dharmas — and so on, said again and again. How can one say it breaks only the clinging to a person-self? One should know that both the clinging to self and the clinging to dharmas are coarse and fine. The coarse is called the discriminated clinging to self and dharmas, for it arises from discrimination when facing objects and meeting conditions. The fine is called the innate clinging to self and dharmas; this does not wait upon discrimination — as soon as a thought arises it is there, born together with the thought. The first half of this sutra dispels the coarse clinging. For example: one should not dwell in the six dusts when giving; one should not bring forth a mind dwelling in the six dusts; one should have a mind of non-dwelling; one should bring forth a mind of non-dwelling; one should be free from all marks — and so on. All of these dispel the ailment of dwelling and clinging that arises from producing a discriminating mind upon objects and conditions. This is what is called the clinging to self and dharmas arising from discrimination; hence it is coarse. How is it dispelled? By freedom from marks. The second half dispels the fine clinging, that is, one should not dwell or cling even as thoughts arise and move. If a thought is retained, then the emotional thinking of the clinging to self and dharmas is not transformed, and this becomes the root of the ailment of grasping marks and clinging to objects. This is to dispel the clinging to self and dharmas that is born together with mental thoughts; hence it is fine. How is it dispelled? By freedom from thoughts.

(3) The first half’s enjoining freedom from marks is to dispel what is clung to; the second half’s enjoining freedom from thoughts is to dispel the clinging itself. Did it not say above? The illusory marks that are clung to arise from the false views that cling. Hence at first glance the purport of this sutra is shallow in front and deep behind. Yet one cannot view it so narrowly, because in dispelling what is clung to, it has already covertly dispelled the clinging as well. Why? Because without freedom from thoughts there is no way to be free from marks. Hence though the first half does not explicitly speak of freedom from thoughts, it has in fact awakened one to it in no small measure. For example: “Can one form such a thought?”, “I do not form this thought,” “one should bring forth a pure mind,” “one should bring forth a mind of non-dwelling,” “if the mind dwells, then it is not dwelling” — all of these enjoin freedom from thoughts. Even the words “one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks” — a person of sharp faculties can grasp that the mind thus brought forth should also not dwell. Why? Because it clearly says that if there is dwelling, it is not. It was said above that one whose faith is not contrary bears the Tathāgata’s burden and shall attain bodhi; such a person must already have grasped freedom from thoughts. Otherwise he could not be said to bear the burden and to attain. Hence the ancients judged that the second half was spoken for those of dull faculties — this was their meaning. They meant that those of sharp faculties have no need of its being said again. Because those of sharp faculties are few in the world, the second half had to be spoken, so that those of dull faculties might enter deeply. This was the ancients’ meaning. But because of these words one must not misunderstand and take the second half to be shallower than the first. Nevertheless, the work of freedom from thoughts is very deep and very fine. If one does not cut into it layer by layer, not only will ordinary people find it hard to advance; even those of sharp faculties who already know freedom from thoughts, if they do not polish it finely, how can their practice be thorough? It is like peeling a banana tree: without peeling and peeling again, how can one penetrate to its fundamental emptiness and return to nothing attained? One should know that in the second half, from the clarification of the five eyes onward, the more it speaks the finer it becomes. As for the section on realization, it is precisely the most direct and immediate work for entering at the tip of a single hair — what is called pointing directly upward. Without understanding this, one may be round and complete, but one is not yet sudden. To narrowly say that the second half was spoken solely for those of dull faculties does not fully accord with the sutra’s purport either. This principle must not go unknown.

(4) The first half says that only by being free from all marks does one bring forth the bodhi-mind, and only so is one a bodhisattva who benefits all beings. This empties the ailment of dwelling and clinging to self and dharmas. The second half then says: there is no dharma that brings forth bodhi, no dharma called a bodhisattva, and all dharmas are Buddha-Dharma, and so on. This empties the ailment of dwelling and clinging to the twofold emptiness of self and dharmas. Hence the first half is non-dwelling in the two extremes; the second half is non-dwelling in the two extremes and non-dwelling in that too. The first is that the mind brought forth should be free from marks; the second is that even the mark of bringing forth the mind is also relinquished. One should know that so long as the thought of being able to be free remains, self and dharmas are still plainly there, and one has already discriminated and grasped marks. Hence it also says that it is not that one does not attain bodhi by the perfection of marks; that the view of self is then no view of self; that the mark of dharma is then no mark of dharma. All of this is to sweep away subtle clinging feelings — dispelling and dispelling again, until both the clinging and that which clings are free, and even the freedom is free. Only then does one realize the original. What is called realization is nothing else: simply exhaust ordinary feelings, and the original essence shows itself — there is no separate realizing and realized. Not only must ordinary feelings not be present; even noble understanding should be absent. To retain a cultivating and cultivated, a realizing and realized, is noble understanding, which is the obstruction of the known, precisely obstructing the essence of enlightenment. Hence Maitreya Bodhisattva’s verses on the Diamond Sutra say: “Cultivating within the mind, retaining ‘I am a bodhisattva’ — this obstructs the mind and goes against the way of non-dwelling.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “All bodhisattvas and beings of the last age should keep far from all illusory, phantom, false, and vain realms.” The first half of this sutra is nothing beyond this meaning. The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment also says: “Because one firmly holds to the mind of keeping far away, the mind that is like an illusion is also kept far from; the keeping far away, being illusory, is also kept far from; the illusion of keeping far from the keeping far away is also kept far from; when one reaches having nothing to keep far from, all illusions are removed.” The second half of this sutra is nothing beyond this meaning.

(5) The first half clarifies that all is “not” (as when it says, “non-dharmas and not non-dharmas,” “if there is dwelling, then it is non-dwelling”), in order to reveal the singular truth of right prajñā wisdom. For this wisdom is by nature unstained by a single dust, whereas all marks are nothing but illusory. Hence one should not dwell in anything, and only then does right wisdom shine forth perfectly. The second half clarifies that all is “is” (as when it says, “all dharmas are the meaning of suchness,” “all dharmas are Buddha-Dharma,” “this dharma is equal, without high or low”), in order to clarify the one suchness of the essence of prajñā principle. For this essence is the source of all dharmas, and hence all dharmas are nothing but true suchness; therefore even bodhi should not be dwelt in, and only then is the essence of principle perfectly fused.

From this it is seen that the whole Diamond Sutra expounds nothing but the two words “true suchness.” It concludes at the end: “Do not grasp at marks; be unmoved in suchness.” The whole sutra’s purport is entirely contained therein. Further, the first half clarifies that all is “not,” causing one to contemplate the unchanging essence; what is called right wisdom is the wisdom of suchness, the wisdom that is the essence. The second half clarifies that all is “is,” causing one to contemplate the functioning that follows conditions; what is called the essence of principle — “principle” meaning pattern and order, spoken with respect to the functioning of the nature, and functioning is not apart from essence, hence “essence of principle.” This is utterly different from the Song Confucians’ talk of principle and vital force. They took the undifferentiated single source as principle and the flowing into ten thousand differences as vital force. Later Confucians who refuted the errors of their talk of principle did so in detail. Further: since the first half has all as “not,” although “is not” and “is named” are spoken of together, the meaning inclines to “is not” — this is what is meant by “though following conditions, unchanging.” Since the second half has all as “is,” although it finely dispels the clinging to dharmas, it says “with respect to dharmas, do not speak of the mark of annihilation” — this is what is meant by “though unchanging, following conditions.” Summing up these five explanations and viewing the whole sutra thereby, the whole sutra’s purport will be clear in mind and eye, and not merely easier to grasp on entering the text.

blocks.text: Ultimately Without Self, Part Seventeen

inline.s: (Ji) Second, clarifying non-dwelling with respect to the mind in order to reveal the essence of prajñā principle. Two parts: (Geng) First, deeply contemplating non-dwelling in order to advance in practice; second, exhausting non-dwelling in order to accomplish realization. (Geng) First, again three: (Xin) First, no dharma in bringing forth the mind; second, citing the fruit to clarify the cause; third, revealing the supreme and concluding with exhortation. (Xin) First, again four: (Ren) First, asking again; second, showing the teaching; third, questioning and explaining; fourth, concluding.
(Ren) First, asking again.
[Then Subhūti said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, when a good man or good woman brings forth the mind of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, how should he dwell? How should he subdue his mind?”]

This section looks like a fresh start, but in fact it follows closely on the preceding text. “Then” refers precisely to the moment when the Buddha had just finished saying that the sutra’s meaning and its retribution are both inconceivable. The Elder’s thought was: since one should be free from names and cut off from marks, yet good men and good women plainly each have the mark of bringing forth the mind, and there plainly is the name “anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.” For each knows for himself that he should bring forth the mind, and each knows for himself that anuttara-bodhi is the supreme dharma. Are not the names and marks of self and dharmas plainly there? It was said above that one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks; now, when one thinks of bringing forth the mind, one is at once dwelling in marks. How is it that this mind alone should dwell? If it should not dwell but should be subdued, does that not mean not bringing forth the mind? Then how should one subdue his mind? The meaning is that the two clingings to self and dharmas are already born together with the very moment of bringing forth the bodhi-mind. To subdue is not to bring forth the mind; to dwell is to cling to self and dharmas. This is precisely boring in at the tip of a single hair, instructing practitioners to apply effort at the very moment thoughts arise and move. The Elder, in great compassion, therefore asks again on behalf of all beings for the instruction of the fundamental skillful means.

Formerly it asked, “How should one abide?” — asking how the bodhi-mind should be settled, so that it does not scatter. Now it asks, “In what should one abide?” — asking how the bodhi-mind alone should dwell and cling. For if one does not dwell in this dharma, what is meant by bringing forth this mind? Dwelling is not permissible, subduing is not attainable — what then is one to do? This is because, having heard it said that one should dwell in nothing with respect to dharmas, and even that if there is dwelling it is not, one thinks that bodhi too is a dharma, and in what then should one abide? Moreover it was said above that one should bring forth the bodhi-mind free from all marks; “all marks” is very broad in scope, and the mark of bringing forth the bodhi-mind should be included in it. Why, then, having said one should be free from all marks, does it also say “bring forth the bodhi-mind”? If that too should be relinquished, why is it called bringing forth the bodhi-mind? People of dull faculties, hearing the Dharma, often cling to names and words and are stuck fast without transformation. The Elder’s question here is again asked in accommodation of all those present and to come who are stuck fast and untransformed, requesting instruction.
(Ren) Second, showing the teaching.

[The Buddha told Subhūti, “A good man or good woman who brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi should thus bring forth this mind: ‘I should deliver all beings into nirvāṇa; and when all beings have been delivered into nirvāṇa, not one being has in truth been delivered into nirvāṇa.’”]

This precisely shows and teaches the skillful means of being free from marks at the moment thoughts arise and move. Look at the wording of the question in the section above: it seems there is no way out; look at the answer in this section: it is exceedingly relaxed and perfectly wondrous. After “bodhi,” the Tang-dynasty manuscript of the sutra has no word “mind,” and one should follow it. Consider: to open with the words “one who brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” and immediately continue, “should thus bring forth this mind,” is precisely to sweep away the mark that this is bringing forth the bodhi-mind. Hence the original text does not use the word “mind,” to show the intent of effacing marks. Even in terms of the wording, it reads well without “mind.” For to bring forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is to bring forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment; what objection is there to doing without the word “mind”?

The two words “thus” refer to the three sentences that follow. The word “should” in “I should” precisely echoes the word “bring forth.” For manifesting what is originally possessed is called “coming forth”; revealing what is originally absent is called “arousing.” All beings are originally of one substance; to deliver all beings into nirvāṇa is merely to complete what is inherent in one’s own share of the nature — a bounden duty — what is so extraordinary about it? If one thinks, “I ought to arouse this mind,” then there is a sense of self-display, and one clings to marks. Hence it does not say “should arouse” but “should bring forth” — for this reason. For to speak the word “should” is to dispel clinging to bodhi, breaking the clinging to dharmas; to speak “should bring forth” is to dispel clinging to the arousing of the mind, breaking the clinging to self.

The word “should” runs through the three sentences that follow. Their meaning advances in stages, each deeper than the last. The first sentence says that delivering beings is a duty one ought to fulfill; beneath the words lies the sense: how could one be self-satisfied that this is bodhi? The second says one should deliver beings to the very last; “last” means “exhausted.” Beneath the words lies the sense: beings are endless, so how could this duty ever be exhausted? How then could one claim, “I can deliver”? The third advances a step further. It says one should know that though they are delivered to the very last, there is not — (a slight pause at “not”) — in truth one single being delivered into nirvāṇa. Why? Because the nature of beings is itself nirvāṇa; and moreover, though it is nirvāṇa, it too does not dwell. For if it dwelt, it would not be deliverance into nirvāṇa. How then could there be one being in truth delivered into nirvāṇa? How then could one claim to have delivered anything?

One who brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment must first awaken to the fact that delivering beings is a duty to be fulfilled, and that this duty can never in the end be exhausted; even if exhausted, it is the same as not exhausted. One should bring forth such a mind: no deliverer, nothing delivered, no discrimination, no such thing as bodhi, no such thing as deliverance, and no such thing as bringing forth the mind. Only thus can one accord with the pure mind of enlightenment.

The earlier answer said, “in truth there are no beings who attain deliverance into nirvāṇa,” laying stress on the word “attain”: though they attain deliverance into nirvāṇa, in truth nothing is attained. Here the stress is on the words “deliverance into nirvāṇa”: there is not even anything called deliverance into nirvāṇa, so how could there be any question of attaining or not attaining? Its meaning is evidently deeper than before. Again, the earlier answer also dispelled both the deliverer and the delivered; and although that dispelling of deliverer and delivered was also a dispelling of clinging to the bodhi-mind, its tone was veiled and inclusive. Now it says deeply, clearly, and explicitly: one should bring forth just such and such a mind — so that even the shadow of “this is bodhi,” “this is bringing forth the bodhi-mind,” “this is the deliverance of beings” is not permitted to exist in the least. Hence though the words resemble the earlier answer, the meaning is like a ten-thousand-fathom pool, clear to the very bottom.

There is something further one should know. Having heard what is said here, one should begin cultivation accordingly. It was said above: the one section on generating faith has already gathered up the whole sutra’s purport; thereafter comes a broader clarification and a deeper, more secret unfolding. We learners should take up the deep and secret, and only so can we reach the ultimate. Hence those who have heard the first half of the sutra must not fail to hear the second half as well. That this sutra is naturally divided into the four parts of faith, understanding, practice, and realization does not mean that faith and understanding contain no work of practice; it indicates that all the practice-work that has come before should be cultivated in accord with what is said here. This is why, earlier, when explaining “the mind of faith is pure,” I strove to bring out that though faith, understanding, practice, and realization have an order, one must not be confined to that order; though divided into four items, one must not be confined to four. All good teachers should take this meaning to heart.
(Ren) Third, questioning and explaining.
[“Why? If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.”]

After “Why?” the circulating editions have the three words “Subhūti”; the ancient text does not, and it may be omitted. “Why?” is his own inquiry as to why one should bring forth such a mind. What follows is spoken in reverse to explain the meaning. It means: if one does not bring forth such a mind, then there is dualistic discrimination. Since one has not escaped the marks of discriminating clinging to self and others, one is still an ordinary person — how could one be a bodhisattva? The “why is this?” below further explains the reason why he is then not a bodhisattva. It was said above that if one grasps the mark of dharma, one clings to self, person, being, and life. If one thinks oneself to be bringing forth the bodhi-mind, one grasps and clings to the bodhi-dharma, and the four marks are plainly there. Hence it says, “then he is not a bodhisattva.” Therefore one should bring forth such a mind.

The four marks of self, person, being, and life, though the same as before, have a very fine meaning here. For one has already become unattached to everything, and clings only to the exceedingly subtle discrimination of seeking above and transforming below. They must not be lumped together with the ordinary four marks. The World-Honored One says this to instruct practitioners that if subtle discrimination is not purified, the root of the ailment of self-mark is still there. Though called a bodhisattva, the name does not match the reality. How profound is the intent to warn and spur on!
(Ren) Fourth, concluding.
[“Why is this? Subhūti, there is in truth no dharma that brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

The ancient text likewise has no word “mind” after “bodhi.” This sentence precisely introduces what follows — that there is no dharma by which one attains bodhi — and the word “mind” especially should not be there. “Why is this?” links what precedes and gives rise to what follows, concluding the meaning of the two sections above. “There is in truth no dharma that brings forth anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” has two meanings and may be read in two ways:

(1) Pause after the word “dharma.” It means: for one who brings forth right enlightenment, there is in truth no dharma. For unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is precisely the meaning of ultimate purity. In the pure enlightenment not a single dust is stained. If the least bit remains — “this is bodhi” — then it is a dust of dharma, and not pure enlightenment. What is then brought forth is called bodhi but is in fact a discriminating mind. Hence only when there is in truth no dharma is one called one who brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.

(2) Pause after the word “no.” It means: that there should be a dharma that brings forth unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment — in truth there is no such fact or principle. For beings, through unenlightenment since beginningless time, give rise to grasping out of craving, and so come to wander in birth and death. Hence no dharma whatsoever should be grasped; to grasp is to be unenlightened. How could that be called bringing forth enlightenment? Hence there is in truth no such thing as taking a dharma to be the bringing forth of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment.
Once these two meanings are clear, the reason why the text above says “should thus bring forth this mind” and “if there are the four marks, then he is not a bodhisattva” becomes clear.

What has been clarified above is nothing other than this: one who brings forth bodhi should bring it forth without thinking himself to be bringing it forth. Such bringing forth without bringing forth is true bringing forth. And dwelling and subduing are contained therein. For how one should dwell and subdue depends entirely on how the mind is brought forth; there is no need to seek elsewhere, and hence no separate answer is given. One should know that “should thus bring forth this mind” is the meaning of dwelling without dwelling. “I should deliver all beings into nirvāṇa” and the two sentences following are the meaning of subduing the mind.

The first question was answered only with subduing and dwelling; the repeated question is answered only with bringing forth the mind — this is indeed to show the order of shallow and deep. (If one does not bring forth the mind, why ask about subduing and dwelling? Hence bringing forth the mind is the root, subduing and dwelling the branch. Hence the order of shallow and deep.) Yet the earlier answer on subduing and dwelling includes bringing forth the mind within it; and the present answer on bringing forth the mind includes subduing and dwelling within it. Moreover, if one knows how to subdue, one knows how to dwell. This again shows that the three matters are but one matter: the earlier one, spoken from the side of subduing, is originally a subduing that does not subdue; the present one, spoken from the side of bringing forth the mind, is again a bringing forth that does not bring forth. These are all subtle methods for breaking the self and dispelling clinging; one should wholeheartedly grasp them at just such points to be a good practitioner.

(Xin) Second, citing the fruit to clarify the cause. Two parts: (Ren) First, detailed clarification; second, concluding revelation. (Ren) First, again two: (Gui) First, clarifying the fruit; second, clarifying the cause. (Gui) First, again two: (Zi) First, clarifying attainment without attainment; second, clarifying that every dharma is suchness. (Zi) First, again three: (Chou) First, raising the question; second, answering and explaining; third, confirming.
(Chou) First, raising the question.
[“Subhūti, what do you think? When the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, was there any dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?”]

This cites a past event as proof. At that time he realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and ascended to the eighth ground. The circumstances of the event have already been explained in detail above. Looking upward to the ultimate fruit, the eighth ground is still a causal stage; looking downward to those who bring forth the mind, it is a fruition stage. This matter lies between cause and effect. The principle that cause and effect are one suchness is easy to understand, and hence it is cited as proof. The World-Honored One, to guard against those who heard the above and doubted, “If bringing forth the mind involves no dharma, how does one attain the fruit?”, cites the fruit to prove it. If one knows that attaining the fruit is attaining without attainment, then bringing forth the mind must be bringing forth without bringing forth — this is clear. The section heading “citing the fruit to clarify the cause” contains both cause and effect. For it cites the fruit-dharma of the Buddha-ground to clarify the causal mind of the eighth ground; that is, by means of the mind of one at the eighth-ground fruition, it clarifies the practice of one who is first bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment.
This matter is cited twice, before and after, with different intents. The differences of intent are three:

(1) The earlier question asked whether he attained anything with respect to dharmas; the answer was, “with respect to dharmas he in truth attained nothing.” Its meaning stresses the word “attain,” showing that though he attained, he did not dwell in the mark of attainment. This is consistent with the meaning above that the four fruits attain the mark of non-attainment, and serves to introduce what follows — that one who brings forth the mind should bring forth a pure mind and should not dwell in the marks of form, sound, and the six dusts. Here, however, the stress is on the word “dharma,” for by “no dharma attains bodhi” it proves the meaning above that no dharma brings forth bodhi.

(2) The word “dharma” in the earlier question refers to the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas. The word “dharma” here refers to anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. At that time he had just ascended to the eighth ground and had not yet attained the ultimate fruit-dharma. One should know that the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas is called a limb of bodhi; it is a partial realization of bodhi, not the ultimate realization of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. Hence the intent of the question here actually inclines toward the reverse and direct explanations that follow. The meaning is that because at that time, through realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, not one dharma arose, he received the prediction; hence it may be known that at that time his mind did not dwell in dharmas. Because at that time his mind did not dwell in dharmas, today he has perfectly realized the ultimate fruit-dharma and become the Tathāgata. This makes one clearly understand that as the cause, so the fruit, without the slightest deviation. Then that one who brings forth the mind should not dwell in the bodhi-dharma is utterly beyond doubt.

If one misunderstands this sentence to mean that at that time he had already attained unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment but did not dwell in the mark of dharma, then one is far off. Consider what follows — “if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” — which suffices to prove that the word “attain” in this sentence does not refer to that time; for at that time he had not yet become the Tathāgata. In sum: “attain” means “shall attain,” not “has already attained.”

(3) The earlier question, whether he attained anything with respect to dharmas, was likewise citing the fruit to clarify the cause. But since the word “dharma” there refers to the non-arising of dharmas, it contains only the one meaning of citing the eighth-ground fruit to clarify the causal bringing forth of the mind. The “dharma” here refers to unsurpassed bodhi, and hence it should be explained with a twofold cause and effect, and only then is the meaning complete.

“Was there any dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi?” is to be read as one sentence. “There is a dharma” means the mind has that dharma, that is, the sense of dwelling in a dharma. The intent of the question is as if to say: in the past, when the Tathāgata was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, did his mind retain the fruit-dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, seeking to realize it? It is like asking whether his mind retained the thought that he should attain unsurpassed bodhi. The sutra does not put it that way, but says “there is a dharma by which he attained” and so on, in order to match the earlier phrase “there is a dharma that brings forth,” so that the intent of dispelling subtle clinging to dharmas may be clear at a glance.

To speak of “a Tathāgata” already contains the sense that one should not dwell in dharmas. Tathāgata is a title of the virtue of the nature. When the enlightened nature is perfect and bright, how could there be a dust of dharma? It is so when one becomes a Buddha; then when formerly on the eighth ground, since he had received the prediction of becoming a Buddha, it may be known that his mind had no dust of dharma. It is so when one realizes a limb of bodhi; then one who is first bringing forth bodhi should learn just so, and from this too it may be known. Cause and effect, earlier and later, are one suchness. Hence it is said that the “citing the fruit to clarify the cause” here contains a twofold meaning.
(Chou) Second, answering and explaining.
[“No, World-Honored One. As I understand the meaning of what the Buddha has said, when the Buddha was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was no dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

“No” is a live phrase. It means neither no dharma nor a dharma. At that time he had just received the prediction that in the future he would become a Buddha. “Becoming a Buddha” is the name for being granted future realization of the fruit-dharma; hence it is not “no dharma.” Yet at that time it was precisely by realizing the patient acceptance of the non-arising, with not one dharma arising, that he received the prediction; hence it is not “a dharma” either. “Understanding the meaning of what has been said” refers precisely to the meaning stated above, that no dharma brings forth bodhi. It means: by grasping the meaning that no dharma brings forth bodhi, one knows that only with no dharma does one attain bodhi. Why? Because cause and effect are one suchness. The Elder had not yet become a Buddha, nor was he an eighth-ground bodhisattva; how could he know that state? He grasped it only from the meaning the Buddha had spoken. This precisely indicates the importance of the wisdom of understanding. That it says “Buddha” and not “Tathāgata” has a profound meaning. For the “understanding the meaning” above was the grasping, by the meaning of the time of first bringing forth the mind and cultivating the cause, of the mind of one who had realized the eighth-ground fruit. Now, citing “Buddha,” it is by the fruit of having today become a Buddha that he proves the cause of formerly being due to become a Buddha. Why? Because “Buddha” is the title of one who has realized the fruit-dharma and accomplished ultimate enlightenment. In citing the single word “Buddha,” it shows that this is spoken with respect to realized fruition, and that it is not ultimately “no dharma.” Yet by the meaning he had grasped — that only with no dharma does one attain — one may infer: comparing today’s fruit with former causes, it may be known that when he was with Dīpaṃkara Buddha he must not have had the least mental thought of a dharma by which he attained anuttara-bodhi. Pause briefly after “no.” “There is a dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” was originally the wording of the question. Now adding the word “no” shows that this is spoken with respect to cultivating the cause, and that it is not ultimately “a dharma.” In sum, it reveals that only when the mind has no dharma to seek with can it then be attained. If one dwells in a dharma and seeks to attain, one cannot attain. Hence one should not dwell in dharmas when bringing forth the mind — the meaning is plain.
(Chou) Third, confirming. Two parts: (Yin) First, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and approval; second, explanation by reverse and direct statements.
(Yin) First, the Tathāgata’s confirmation and approval.
[The Buddha said, “So it is, so it is. Subhūti, there is in truth no dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.”]

In saying “so it is” twice, he approves his statement that it is neither no dharma nor a dharma as not mistaken. Pause briefly after “in truth no.” “A dharma by which he attained anuttara-bodhi” is to be read continuously. “There is a dharma by which he attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” was originally the wording of the question. Now the two words “the Tathāgata” are added within it, because Tathāgata is a title of the virtue of the nature. When the enlightened nature is perfect and bright, it is called attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. If there were a dust of dharma, it would not be perfect and bright — how could it be called attaining unsurpassed bodhi? Hence “the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi” is like saying “he attained becoming the Tathāgata.” “There is a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained” and so on is like saying “there is a dharma by which he attained becoming the Tathāgata.” “In truth no” means that at that time, when with Dīpaṃkara Buddha, there was in truth not the least thought of a dharma by which he attained becoming the Tathāgata. That the sutra text does not say “attained becoming the Tathāgata” but must say “the Tathāgata attained anuttara-bodhi” is because it is precisely in the midst of breaking the clinging to dharmas, and so it brings in the unsurpassed bodhi-dharma in speaking. It shows that only because in the causal mind there was in truth no such fruit-dharma did he then attain becoming the Tathāgata. This precisely confirms that the Elder’s understanding is not mistaken. The Elder cited the fruit to clarify the cause, and so spoke of “Buddha.” The World-Honored One, on the other hand, speaks with respect to the virtue of the nature, showing that the enlightened nature is perfect and bright — how could it admit a dharma? Hence he speaks of “the Tathāgata.” His intent is to make one know that only one who attains yet in truth attains nothing is a Tathāgata in whom the virtue of the nature is perfectly manifest. This serves as the premise for what follows — that “Tathāgata” means the suchness of all dharmas.
(Yin) Second, explanation by reverse and direct statements. Two parts: (Mao) First, the reverse explanation; second, the direct explanation.
(Mao) First, the reverse explanation.

[“Subhūti, if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Dīpaṃkara Buddha would not have given me the prediction: ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”]

These two sections, on explanation by reverse and direct statements, are precisely where the eye was fixed when the question was raised. All that has gone before was based on the fruit-position of the Buddha-ground today to clarify the causal mind of the eighth ground in the past. Here, however, it is based on the fruition-practice of receiving the prediction in the past to clarify the causal mind of one first bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment today. Hence all that was said above serves as the groundwork for this place. For becoming a Buddha, becoming the Tathāgata, came about through the prediction in the past; and that prediction in the past came about through realizing the non-arising of dharmas. If all bodhisattvas who bring forth the beginner’s enlightenment know that if there is a dharma, no prediction is given, and only with no dharma is the prediction given, then when they receive, uphold, read, and recite this sutra, they must follow the teaching and, with respect to all dharmas, dwell in non-dwelling. Only thus is their faith not contrary and do they bear the Tathāgata’s burden; only thus can they generate merit, extinguish offenses, and shall attain bodhi. Is not the meaning as plain as if held up to view?

After “saṃbodhi,” the ancient text has no word “one who.” From the statement that no prediction was given, it can be known that this “if there were a dharma by which the Tathāgata attained” and so on refers to the time before the prediction had yet been given. It means: before he received the prediction at that time, had his mind dwelt in the dharma of unsurpassed bodhi, hoping to become the Tathāgata and attain unsurpassed bodhi, then he could not have realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas, and would not even have obtained the prediction — how much less could he have become the Tathāgata! The three sentences “In a future life ...” are Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s words of prediction. Lest one not understand what a prediction is, they are cited here to explain it. That it does not use the phrase “made this statement” shows that it is not Dīpaṃkara Buddha who is reported as saying this.
(Mao) Second, the direct explanation.

[“Because there is in truth no dharma by which one attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, therefore Dīpaṃkara Buddha gave me the prediction, saying, ‘In a future life you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni.’”]

Pause after “in truth no.” It means: because in truth there was no mind dwelling in and clinging to the bodhi-dharma in order to seek and attain it. “Therefore” shows that it was precisely because his causal mind had no dharma that he realized the non-arising; for this reason he received the prediction. The phrase “saying” shows that the three sentences “In a future life ...” here were personally uttered by Dīpaṃkara Buddha’s golden mouth, unlike the preceding section, where they were cited to explain the meaning of a prediction.

Some take the meaning of Śākyamuni — Śākya being the surname and Muni the name — to be “able-in-benevolence and still-silence.” Hence they say: being able in benevolence, he does not dwell in nirvāṇa; being still and silent, he does not dwell in birth and death. Because he does not dwell in dharmas, he was given this name in his prediction. This explanation is not unacceptable, but one need not insist on it. For the prediction lays stress on approving his future becoming a Buddha, and has nothing to do with the name. Moreover, every Buddha does not dwell in dharmas, every one receives a prediction from a previous Buddha, and every one has a name, yet their names are not necessarily all taken from the meaning of non-dwelling — how could one rigidly explain it by the name?

What follows is the gist of the section clarifying that every dharma is suchness. The preceding section on attaining without attainment cites the matter of realizing the fruit, in order to clarify that one should not dwell in bodhi; this section on every dharma being suchness states the principle of the realization of the fruit, in order to clarify that there is no bodhi to dwell in. It is precisely the explanation of the reason why one should not dwell. It is the utmost of freedom from marks, and also the original suchness of the nature of dharmas. For in the realization of the fruit, marks and no-marks are alike extinguished. This makes one know that in the practice of the cause, both marks and no-marks should be relinquished together.

The meaning of “every dharma is suchness” is subtle and refined. Let me now first trace its gist to its source and follow it to its end, explaining it in order; then the purport made clear in the sub-sections will have some thread to follow and will be easier to understand. One should know that the World-Honored One spoke this meaning of “every dharma is suchness” in order to enable hearers of the Dharma to understand thoroughly the ultimate, complete teaching. For only when understanding is deep is faith deep, and only when understanding is complete is practice complete; then realization and entry are not difficult. Why? Because as understanding gradually opens, clinging feelings and the view of self gradually dissolve. This is why the study of Buddhism lays stress on the wisdom of understanding. The wisdom of understanding is what is called the wisdom of contemplation. This is why hearing, thinking, and cultivating do not depart from the one wisdom. How then could the gist of “every dharma is suchness” fail to be clearly discerned?

What is called unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment is nothing else than the true-suchness nature, also named the intrinsically pure mind. Because it is the source of all dharmas, it is called unsurpassed; because it is commonly possessed by all beings, it is called perfect. It is only that beings are obstructed by false thoughts of discrimination and clinging, and do not themselves know that their nature is unsurpassed and perfect. If they know it and can dispel false thoughts and remove obstructions, then it is called right enlightenment. When one first can be enlightened, it is called bringing forth the beginner’s enlightenment-mind. When enlightenment reaches the ultimate, so that the virtue of the unsurpassed, perfect nature is wholly manifest, there is no way to name it, and it is named the attainment of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In truth the nature is inherently possessed — how could there be any such thing as attainment! This is why, though one attains, it must come down to nothing attained. And one who attains unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, because beings are of one substance with him and because of his original vow of compassion, takes the principle-essence he has personally realized and, with all kinds of words and phrases and all kinds of skillful means, with apt similes and indirect figures, causes all beings universally to be able to awaken to this, understand this, cultivate this, and realize this. There is no way to name it, and it is named the dharma of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. In truth it is the nature inherently possessed by beings — how could there be any such thing as a dharma! Once this principle is understood, one knows that one should not retain the notion of a dharma or the notion of attainment.

Since the intrinsic nature is called pure, it may be known that it is originally unstained by the finest dust. It is like the bright sun in a clear sky: a single fleck of cloud obscures it and it has no light. Hence if one wishes the light of the nature to shine everywhere, one must make it pure without a speck of dust. All beings originally do not know that their intrinsic nature is thus pure. The Buddha, having personally realized it, teaches that one should reflect thus and awaken thus of oneself. If one does not practice in accord with the teaching point by point, how can it be called bringing forth enlightenment? Why? Because if a single dharma remains, if a single attainment remains, it is still the old habit of discrimination and clinging, and one’s original nature remains obstructed. Hence not only should all dharmas not be dwelt in; even the bodhi-dharma should not be dwelt in — for this reason.

Why do beings have the ailment of discrimination and clinging? For no other reason than that they do not penetrate the one true dharma-realm, and only cognize the marks of all dharmas. Since they are marks, mark differs from mark. Because they are deluded about marks, they unknowingly and unwittingly discriminate and cling accordingly. They do not realize that whatever is called a mark is changing at every moment. Hence it is said: “Whatever has marks is illusory and false.” “Illusory and false” means that it is unreal, not true — not that it absolutely does not exist. But beings do not know it is unreal. Thought after thought they discriminate and cling upon illusory marks; hence it is called a false thought, meaning that they pursue illusory marks and give rise to thoughts. Or, though they know it is unreal, still thought after thought does not stop, so that illusory marks churn and disturb the mind; hence it is called a false thought, meaning that illusory marks arise following the thoughts. Thus the single term “false thought” contains these two meanings. The skillful means for counteracting it are likewise two.

(1) Freedom from marks, as stated in the first half of this sutra. One must thoroughly awaken to the fact that all the objective marks of the sense faculties, the body, and the material world are flowers in the sky and moons in the water. To be deluded, cling, and calculate only adds affliction. And one must keep the precepts and cultivate merit, cutting off defiling conditions and removing greed and anger. When contemplation and practice go on thus for a long time, emotional clinging gradually thins, and false thoughts likewise gradually diminish. Why? Because what are called false thoughts are nothing but the work of emotional clinging. Hence freedom from marks is the skillful means for freedom from thoughts — this is one method.

(2) Freedom from thoughts, as stated in the second half of this sutra. For because the habitual tendencies since beginningless time are deep, though one knows that marks are all illusory, one’s climbing and grasping does not cease. One must apply effort at the place where thoughts move, and turn the gaze back upon the source of the mind. All the keeping of precepts, cultivation of merit, the six pāramitās, and the ten thousand practices should be pursued with yet greater vigor, tempering the mind through encountering affairs. If one can strike the thought-process dead, then all discrimination and clinging are of themselves absent, and whether marks exist or not no longer matters. Why? Because if one can refrain from giving rise to thoughts, all marks depart of themselves without departing. Hence freedom from thoughts is the ultimate of freedom from marks — this is another method.

These two kinds of dharma can be practiced side by side without conflict. Freedom from marks is itself freedom from thought, and only freedom from thought makes freedom from marks possible; hence it is said that they do not conflict. Yet freedom from marks removes only the coarser layer of deluded thought, the kind that arises in pursuit of illusory marks; freedom from thought removes the subtler layer, the kind from which illusory marks arise along with thought. Hence both must be practiced together. Practicing them together does not mean being rigidly bound to freedom from marks first and freedom from thought afterward. It means that when one is free from marks one also cultivates freedom from thought, so that freedom from marks can become complete; and that when one is free from thought one also cultivates freedom from marks, so that freedom from thought gains further skillful means. They should be practiced simultaneously, side by side.

In short, because sentient beings are deluded by all marks of dharma, they never know to turn back and illumine their own nature. How should they know that their own nature is of one substance with sentient beings? How should they know that the five aggregates and six faculties within, and all dharmas such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth without, are all made by mind alone? Not knowing this, they do not know that the Buddha's teaching that one should not dwell in any dharma is meant to rid them of the fault of discrimination, attachment, and grasping at marks, and has nothing whatever to do with the dharmas themselves. Once the fault of grasping at marks is removed, then the five aggregates within and all dharmas such as mountains and rivers without are, as the Surangama Sutra says, all the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind, the pure and luminous essence of nature. Why? Because all dharmas have only marks and no nature of their own. It is not that they have no nature: the nature of all dharmas is the self-nature itself. Why? Because there is one true dharma-realm. How then could they be dismissed? Why should they be dismissed? This is the true meaning of every dharma being thus. Hence the Awakening of Faith says: "This essence of true suchness has nothing that can be dismissed, because all dharmas are wholly real. Nor is there anything that can be established, because all dharmas are wholly such." You should know that anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is simply another name for true suchness. To dwell in it is still to grasp at marks. Where there is something grasped, there is something established. Though you dismiss every mark of dharma, if you set up the mark of bodhi alone, then it is no longer the case that all dharmas are such. Why? Because where there is establishment there is rejection. The self-nature is the source of all dharmas, excluding nothing, lacking nothing. To establish one and reject the rest is not the whole nature. How could that be the unexcelled and perfectly equal, how could it be true enlightenment?

In the first half of this sutra, the dismissing of every mark of dharma in order to reveal bodhi serves only to remove the fault of grasping at all dharmas. Lest one should still grasp at bodhi itself, the second half opens its first chapter by dismissing that as well. Once this fault is dismissed, the virtue of the nature is completely manifested, and every dharma is thus. There is nothing to dismiss, and nothing to establish. This is the final goal of the practitioner. All the meanings taught since the sutra began also come to rest here. Therefore the section on every dharma being thus is a vital meaning in the whole sutra, and indeed a vital meaning in all Mahayana Buddhadharma. Everything said afterward is nothing but an unfolding and a confirmation of this meaning. Nor is there anything in the first half that does not incline toward this meaning and gather it in. Here the World-Honored One lays out his own personal realization completely, without holding anything back, and teaches it in full detail, so that sentient beings may awaken through it and enter through it.

Therefore, for every dharma to be thus, every emotional clinging must be utterly dismissed; only realization knows it, and it cannot be put into empty words. If one has not dismissed the fault of grasping in the slightest, and yet tells others that everything is thus, then every dharma becomes an obstruction; how could every dharma be thus? Such a one is simply a deluded person. To speak wildly of prajñā is an offense that leads to falling into the uninterrupted hell, because such a one misleads and confuses sentient beings, causing them to slander the Buddha and the Dharma and to belittle the Three Jewels. You should know that if one has truly realized every dharma being thus, one will certainly be able to act it out: compressing immeasurable kalpas into a single moment, extending a single moment into immeasurable kalpas, fitting Mount Sumeru into a mustard seed, transforming the sahā world into a Pure Land. Only at this stage, where all phenomena are without obstruction, may such words be spoken. All students should simply contemplate every dharma as thus, so as to dismiss utterly the clinging of self-view and pervasive discrimination, and thereby seek to enter realization. That is what is fitting. How could one give rise to great pride and lightly turn the words "all is thus" into a mere topic of talk? Consider the very end of this sutra, which is also the beginning of the circulation section: after speaking of thus, thus, and unmoved, it immediately continues, "Why? All conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow; like dew, and like lightning; they should be contemplated thus." This precisely shows that thus, thus, and unmoved must be entered through contemplating all dharmas as dreamlike and illusory. To contemplate them as dream, illusion, and the rest is to dismiss emotional clinging. These are the crucial points in the sutra, and they must not be neglected.

What does it mean that the meaning of the first half is gathered in here? Let me explain briefly, to open the gate of awakening. For example: "If you see all marks as no marks, then you see the Tathagata." Consider: if one sees that marks are precisely no marks, is that not every dharma being thus? Hence it says, "then you see the Tathagata." Whenever the sutra says that such-and-such is not such-and-such, it is pointing to this meaning. Again: "When the mind of faith is pure, the real mark is produced." You should know that it is because there is no discrimination or attachment that the mind afterward becomes pure; when the mind is pure, the real mark is produced. The real mark means no mark and no non-mark, and then every dharma is thus. Hence it says: one should produce a pure mind; one should produce the mind while not dwelling; one should produce the mind that does not dwell; one should, free from all marks, arouse the bodhi mind and practice the six paramitas; if the mind dwells, then it does not dwell rightly. Again: one should not grasp dharmas, and should not grasp non-dharmas. Not grasping dharmas is because all dharmas are thus and nothing can be established. Not grasping non-dharmas is because all dharmas are real and nothing can be dismissed. This is exactly what is meant by every dharma being thus. Because every dharma is thus, there is no fixed dharma called anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, nor is there any fixed dharma that the Tathagata can teach. Therefore dharma and non-dharma are both negated; both cannot be grasped and both cannot be spoken. That all sages and worthies differ only through the unconditioned dharma is because, since every dharma is thus, every dharma is real. (This is why the Lotus Sutra says, "This dharma abides in the station of dharma; the marks of the world are ever abiding.") Hence all dharmas are pure by nature and are in no way fabricated; therefore they are called unconditioned. All sages and worthies without exception cultivate and realize this. But because the depth of their practice differs, there are differences in becoming worthies and becoming sages. In truth, in the dharma of oneness, how could there ever have been any difference? Other points may be thought through by this standard.

In short, if one comprehends that every dharma is thus, and harmonizes with it, then there is no such thing as emptiness, no such thing as existence, and no such thing as the middle; and then emptiness is no obstacle, existence is no obstacle, and there is neither emptiness nor the provisional that is not the middle. Why? Once the fault of self-view and emotional clinging has been utterly dismissed, then to see marks is to see the nature; everything is the Way, and nothing is unacceptable. Hence the sutras such as the Most Victorious King and the Vimalakirti say: the five aggregates are the dharma-body; birth and death are nirvāṇa; affliction is bodhi. All of them reveal the meaning that every dharma is thus. If even a little discrimination and attachment remains unbroken, then wherever one turns one is blocked; nothing is the Way, and nothing is acceptable. Even if one clings to nothing else but still clings to one bodhi, that too is grasping at marks and discrimination, and one obstructs one's own substance of enlightenment. Then what is called the middle is not the middle, to say nothing of clinging to existence or inclining to emptiness. For all who arouse the mind to save themselves and others, hoping to illumine the nature and see the Buddha, the essential method lies wholly here. What is that method? According to the teaching of this sutra, it is freedom from marks and freedom from thought. You should know that since this sutra is the source from which all Buddhas and the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi Dharma of all Buddhas come forth, whatever it teaches is nothing but root meaning and ultimate meaning. The other thousand sutras and ten thousand treatises all manifest and support this meaning. Therefore I have now set out this vital meaning in full detail, thoroughly and completely, and all good teachers should ponder it well.

(Zi) Second, explaining that every dharma is thus. In four: (Chou) First, the Thus in respect of name; second, the Thus in respect of the fruit of virtue; third, the Thus in respect of all dharmas; fourth, the Thus in respect of the reward body.
(Chou) First, the Thus in respect of name.
"Why? Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas."

The line "Why?" is the Buddha's own posing of a question. He asks: of the text above, which says that only where there is no bodhi dharma can one be granted the prediction of Buddhahood, and only where there is no bodhi dharma can the Tathagata attain bodhi, what is the reason? After "Tathagata," he poses his own answer. It is as if he said: the Buddha is called Tathagata; do you also know the meaning of Tathagata? Its meaning is nothing else: it is precisely because he is free from the empty marks of all dharmas' differences and has realized the true nature of the oneness of all dharmas. You should know that the Buddha does not see the marks of difference among dharmas; this is what is meant by "thus." Nor does the Buddha see the mark of any single dharma being different; this is what is meant by "the suchness of all dharmas." Thus means the meaning of no difference, and also the meaning of no distinctness: it says that the nature of dharma has no divergence. That the nature of dharma has no divergence is because it is empty and still. Hence "the suchness of all dharmas" is the meaning that the nature of dharma is empty and still. One is named Tathagata because one has realized the nature that is empty and still. If one were to hold that there is an emptiness and stillness, that would already be divergence, and it would not be empty and still; how could one be called Tathagata? Hence it is said: Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. (Stress the word thus.) How then could one who arouses the unexcelled, perfectly equal enlightenment keep in mind the mark of having aroused that enlightenment, so that it is not empty and still?

Again, the sutra speaks of "all dharmas," which is not-one; and it further speaks of "thus," which is not-distinct. Not-one and not-distinct: such is the nature of dharma. The Buddha is called the Greatly Awakened One because he has ultimately awakened to this nature of dharma that is not-one and not-distinct. Hence it is said: Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. (Stress both all dharmas and thus.) You should know that because it is not-one, the dharma of bodhi should not be grasped; and because it is not-distinct, the dharma of bodhi should likewise not be grasped. (The first statement treats essence alone; the second treats essence together with mark and function.) Seen in this light, to assert firmly that all dharmas are all dharmas is wrong, for they are one thus even though they are many; (stress oneness-thus) and to assert firmly that all dharmas are not all dharmas is also wrong, for they are the oneness-thus of all dharmas. (Stress all dharmas.)

The crux of all this depends entirely on whether one clings or not. If one does not cling to existence, all dharmas do not obstruct the oneness-thus; if one does not cling to emptiness, the oneness-thus does not obstruct all dharmas. To cling to all dharmas is not thus; to cling to the Thus is not the suchness of all dharmas. Hence whatever the Tathagata teaches can neither be grasped nor spoken. It cannot be grasped because the nature of all dharmas is the one true suchness, without discrimination, and because it is the equality of differences. It cannot be spoken because the nature of true suchness is not apart from all dharmas and is known only through realization, and because within difference one sees equality. Therefore one who has awakened should be free from all marks and cultivate the six paramitas and myriad practices. Being free from all marks is because on the ground of ultimate reality one does not stain a single mote of dust; cultivating myriad practices is because within the gate of Buddha-work one does not abandon a single dharma. Because all dharmas are one thus, one should not abandon a single dharma; because it is the dharma of oneness-thus, one should not stain a single mote of dust. To awaken thus, to be free thus, to cultivate thus, is for dharma to accord and nature to accord, and so to attain accord in realization.

In short, to be blind to equality and grasp at difference is for the mind to turn along with dharmas, so that even non-dharmas become obstructions. To see equality within difference is for dharmas to turn along with the mind, so that no dharma is anything but true suchness. What the ancient worthies called greeting guests and seeing them off, carrying water and hauling firewood, walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, so that at every hour of the day, whatever dharma one picks up is it, is a fine picture of the man of no affairs enjoying himself. You should know that the world is originally without affairs; it is ordinary people who trouble themselves. In the midst of no emptiness and no existence, they grasp at marks of emptiness and existence. In the midst of no good and no evil, they think of good and think of evil. Deluded marks fly about in confusion; is this not troubling oneself? How free it is to pick something up and find it is it! The ancient worthies also said: before awakening, mountains are mountains and waters are waters. After awakening, mountains are not mountains and waters are not waters. When mountains are mountains and waters are waters, one sees only all dharmas. When mountains are not mountains and waters are not waters, one sees only the oneness-thus. And there is a song of awakening that says: the blue mountains are still the same blue mountains. It means that all dharmas remain as they were, yet in seeing the oneness-thus of all dharmas, though the blue mountains are the same as before, their whole aspect is brilliantly new.

"Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas" appears to explain only the word thus, but in fact the word come is explained within it as well. How is this so? There is coming and there is going: these are marks of difference, that is, the oneness of all dharmas. Since all dharmas are thus, coming is thus too. All sentient beings come but are not thus. The sages of the Two Vehicles are thus but do not come. Bodhisattvas at the provisional stages are thus but not yet wholly thus, and though they come, they cannot come everywhere. Only the Buddha, the Tathagata, having realized the oneness of nature, comes everywhere to the very limit of true suchness. True suchness has no limit, so his coming has no limit. True suchness is unmoved, so his coming is unmoved. Though he is named as coming, in truth he comes without a mark of coming, and comes without coming. You should know that he is named Tathagata to make clear that his coming has no mark of coming, hence "thus"; and to make clear that his thus has no mark of thus, hence "come." (The meaning of this passage is that when we speak in terms of the marks of coming and going, the two words all dharmas cover it; when we speak of coming without a mark of coming, the word thus covers it. It also makes clear the suchness of all dharmas: by means of all dharmas one dismisses the Thus, and by means of the Thus one dismisses all dharmas, revealing the virtue of nature in which negation and illumination are simultaneous. All that has been said above is this meaning. The words quoted from the ancient worthies are not idle talk. Look into this.)
(Chou) Second, the Thus in respect of the fruit of virtue. In two: (Yin) First, explaining that there is no dharma; second, explaining the oneness-thus.
(Yin) First, explaining that there is no dharma.
"If someone says that the Tathagata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, Subhuti, in truth there is no dharma by which the Buddha has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi."

"If someone" means "perhaps someone." Since the text above contains the words "the Tathagata has attained anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi," the Buddha fears that one who does not grasp the meaning, hearing that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas, may accordingly doubt: since the meaning of Tathagata is the oneness of all dharmas, then it is clear that there is no bodhi to be attained. Why then did he say above that the Tathagata attains anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi? To block this doubt, he sets up a hypothetical saying and again calls the elder and tells him: what this person says arises from suspecting that there is still a dharma. He does not realize that in truth there is no dharma. It is only to make clear that his enlightenment is already ultimate, and that there is no way to name it, so it is named the Buddha's attainment of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Implied in these words is that, spoken in terms of the virtue of nature, it truly is the oneness of all dharmas. Hence here he does not say Tathagata but says Buddha, precisely to make clear that the one who is called the attainer of bodhi is so called to show that he has already realized unexcelled, perfectly equal enlightenment, which is the fruit of the oneness of all dharmas. How could it mean that there is a bodhi dharma to be attained? What doubt is there? The text below further uses the meaning of neither real nor unreal to make clear that he is said to attain while in truth attaining nothing, and that although nothing is attained it may still be called attainment. Then it will be all the clearer.
(Yin) Second, explaining the oneness-thus.
"Subhuti, in the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained, therein there is neither the real nor the unreal."

"Therein" means within what is attained. The meaning is: even granting what that person says, that the Tathagata attains bodhi, he does not realize that what the Tathagata attains is nothing but neither real nor unreal. Neither real nor unreal is precisely the suchness of all dharmas. This meaning should be expounded at length so that it may be grasped.

(1) This resembles the words above, "The dharma that the Tathagata has attained, this dharma is neither real nor unreal," yet the meaning is very different. The passage above explains that the dharma is real. It says that the dharma the Tathagata has attained is the real mark. The real mark is no mark and no non-mark. No mark is no reality; no non-mark is no unreality. To speak ultimately, the real mark has neither mark nor non-mark, hence it is said to be neither real nor unreal, meaning that both reality and unreality are absent. This is the real dharma, and it confirms the statement above about the real.

Here the text explains that in truth there is no dharma. Since there is already no dharma, how much less is there anything attained? Granting the words of that person, we may say that the Tathagata attains; yet if we look into it, therein nothing whatever is attained. Why? Because in truth there is no dharma. It is only a provisional name for attainment, and is not real. Yet there is no harm in saying that the Tathagata attains. Why? Because what is attained is nothing but thus; attaining this is what makes one called Tathagata. It is not unreal. (This is directed at the explanation above.)

(2) Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi is another name for the awakened nature of true suchness. Since Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas, it is as much as to say that one is called Tathagata because one has realized the awakened nature of true suchness. This is enough to prove that what the Tathagata attains is nothing but the oneness-thus. Hence although it is named attainment, within that attainment there is nothing real, because the awakened nature is empty and still; and there is nothing unreal, because the awakened nature is perfectly manifest. Hence it is said: therein there is neither the real nor the unreal. In short, there is no such thing as an attainment that has an attainment; this is no reality. It is not that there is no such thing as an attainment that has no attainment; this is no unreality. This is exactly what the Madhyamaka-sastra means by: "Where there is no grasping subject or object, there is existence; where there is a grasping subject or object, there is not." It is also what the Buddha-nature Treatise says: "Because the adventitious dust is empty, it is apart from the dharma-realm. Because the supreme dharma is not empty, it follows the dharma-realm." The adventitious dust being empty, therefore no reality; the supreme dharma not being empty, therefore no unreality. You should know that the Buddha says this to make clear that one must not hear of attainment and suspect that there is a dharma, and must not hear that there is no dharma and suspect that there is ultimately no realization. (This explains the meaning in terms of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.)

(3) To speak of no reality is to make clear that it illumines while ever still. To speak of no unreality is to make clear that it is still while ever illumining. Neither real nor unreal is precisely double negation and double illumination, stillness and illumination simultaneous. Therein not a single dharma arises, because it is still. Yet not a single dharma fails to appear, because it illumines. Not a single dharma arises: in truth there is no dharma, hence no reality. Not a single dharma fails to appear: all dharmas are one thus, hence no unreality. This is what is meant by anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. That the Tathagata attains means that he attains this. (This explains the meaning in terms of stillness and illumination simultaneous.)

(4) Neither real nor unreal is the Awakening of Faith's meaning of "empty in accordance with reality" and "not empty in accordance with reality." In accordance with reality is true suchness, and because true suchness is the real essence of nature it is called in accordance with reality. It makes clear that all dharmas are one thus, and this is the real. The treatise explains the meaning of empty in accordance with reality: "What is called empty is that from the very beginning all defiled dharmas do not correspond. That is to say, it is free from the marks of difference of all dharmas, because there is no deluded mind or thought." This says that although the minds of all sentient beings contain deluded thoughts and all the defiled and impure marks of difference arising from subject and object in opposition, this essence of the nature in accordance with reality still remains ever constant and unchanging, because from the very beginning the one purity and the one defilement do not correspond. Not corresponding means being apart. How are they apart? Because from the very beginning the essence in accordance with reality is itself not deluded mind or thought. It also says: "You should know that the self-nature of true suchness is neither with marks nor without marks, and indeed neither one nor different, nor both. In sum, because there is deluded mind, moment by moment discriminating, none of it corresponds; therefore it is called empty. If one is apart from deluded mind, in truth there is nothing to be emptied." This says that what is called empty is the emptying of deluded thoughts and marks of difference. Hence it says neither with marks nor without marks, and indeed neither one nor different, nor both. The meaning is that one is free from marks. If one is utterly free from all the four propositions of opposition, such as existence, non-existence, oneness, and difference, then one is apart from deluded mind and thought. Once these are apart, the self-nature of true suchness appears. Hence it says: if one is apart from deluded mind, in truth there is nothing to be emptied. This makes clear that what is called empty does not mean the absence of the self-nature of true suchness. How then can deluded mind and thought be separated from and emptied? Because all the deluded mind of moment-by-moment discrimination does not by nature correspond with the self-nature of true suchness. This makes clear that the self-nature is itself empty, and so can be emptied. Yet once deluded thoughts and defiled marks are empty, true suchness appears. This further makes clear that it is empty yet not empty.

It explains the meaning of not empty in accordance with reality: "What is called not empty is that, since it has already revealed that the essence of dharma is empty and without delusion, it is the true mind, ever constant and unchanging, fulfilled in pure dharmas; therefore it is called not empty." This says that once the essence of dharma is empty of all deluded thoughts, it is the true mind, ever constant and unchanging, fulfilled in immeasurable pure dharmas of virtue; hence not empty. The essence of dharma means the true nature of the oneness-thus, which is called true suchness. True suchness is the essence of all dharmas, hence it is called the essence of dharma. The treatise also says: "Nor are there any marks to be grasped, because the realm beyond thought is only corresponded with through realization." This says that the true nature of the oneness of all dharmas, which is the essence of all dharmas, is in truth without dharma and should not be dwelt in, because it is a realm beyond thought, known only through realization. Hence it says that there are also no marks to be grasped, making clear that it is not empty yet empty.

Considering the meanings of the treatise as set out above: empty in accordance with reality is no reality; not empty in accordance with reality is no unreality. Empty yet not empty: no reality is likewise no unreality. Not empty yet empty: no unreality is likewise no reality. This is the true essence of all dharmas, thus and unmoved. Hence here the Buddha says that in the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained, therein there is neither the real nor the unreal. This is precisely explaining the passage above, that Tathagata means the suchness of all dharmas. Moreover, if one reads the treatise carefully, it plainly says that not empty comes from empty, and one may know that no unreality comes from no reality, and that the oneness of all dharmas comes from there being in truth no dharma. Using the treatise to prove the sutra, the meaning is perfectly clear. One may also see that the two passages quoted from the treatise are no different from a fusion of the main purport of this sutra. Hence one who would understand this sutra cannot but read the Awakening of Faith. (This explains the meaning by way of the Awakening of Faith.)

(5) No reality may be referred to all dharmas. All dharmas arise from conditions, hence no reality. No unreality may be referred to the Thus. True suchness is not empty, hence no unreality. The marks of all dharmas, though arisen from conditions, are without reality; the nature of all dharmas, however, is the same one true suchness and is without unreality. Hence it is said: therein there is neither the real nor the unreal, making clear that the anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi that the Tathagata has attained is in truth without dharma and without attainment, and is simply the realization of the suchness of all dharmas. (This explains the meaning by way of the suchness of all dharmas.)

(6) Neither real nor unreal is emptiness and existence as one thus, the virtue of nature as it inherently is. The Tathagata realizes this, and so teaches this section, causing sentient beings to awaken to it and cultivate it. You should know that these four words are perfectly equal and should not be seen as two separate halves, nor should they be rigidly divided into before and after. To view all dharmas as only real is to be an ordinary being; to view all dharmas as only unreal is to be of the Two Vehicles; and even to view all dharmas as unreal within the real and real within the unreal is still to be a bodhisattva at the provisional stages. Only the Buddha is not so: he views all dharmas as neither real nor unreal, as one whole. No reality is likewise no unreality; no unreality is likewise no reality. This is what is meant by the oneness of all dharmas, and it is also emptiness and existence simultaneous. One should awaken thus and cultivate thus. How does one cultivate? By producing a mind that dwells nowhere, and by being free from all marks while practicing giving and the six paramitas for the benefit of all sentient beings. One must make the time of being free from marks itself the time of benefiting, and the time of benefiting itself the time of being free from marks. This is to produce the non-dwelling mind; this is to arouse unexcelled bodhi. Then though it is called arousing, in truth there is no dharma of bodhi. In this way one may come to correspond with the awakened nature of neither real nor unreal, the oneness of all dharmas. Indeed, even such names and marks as neither real nor unreal and the oneness of all dharmas are themselves transcended. Only then is there no dharma, and only then can one correspond.
