Therefore, at the first step of entry, one must first cause them to contemplate deeply all conditioned dharmas—like a dream, like an illusion, like a bubble, like a shadow, like dew, like lightning—none of them true, all of them empty, so that in the end not one thing is obtained. What is obtained is only a taste of bitterness. And that bitterness is endless and beyond words. This is what is meant by “ten thousand things you cannot take with you; only karma follows the body.” If one can constantly contemplate thus and clearly understand the principle that all is empty, one may perhaps no longer be deceived, and may be able to turn the light around with all one’s heart. This is why, wishing to contemplate the true nature of the unconditioned, one should first contemplate the illusory marks of the conditioned. This first essential meaning must be understood.

(2) The light of the nature of all ordinary beings has long been covered over by ignorance. It is like a single bright sun wholly veiled by dark clouds, its light utterly dimmed, so that the sun cannot be seen. It is the same here. False thoughts stir in confusion without a moment’s pause. If one now wishes to contemplate, the contemplating and the contemplated are both ignorance and false consciousness. How could one see the original nature? This is the same principle as when the whole sky is black with clouds and the sunlight cannot be seen: look as one may, there is nothing but a dizzy, turbid appearance. Hence the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “With a mind of saṃsāra, producing a view of saṃsāra, one enters the Tathāgata’s great sea of quiescent extinction—and in the end one cannot arrive.”

“Saṃsāra” means arising and ceasing. “Quiescent” means soundless: it says that true suchness cannot be explained in words. “Extinct” means formless: it says that true suchness cannot be revealed by marks. Vertically exhausting the three periods and horizontally pervading the ten directions is called “great.” The essence complete in ten thousand virtues and the function embracing the ten thousand existents is called “sea.” The Tathāgata’s great sea of quiescent extinction means the originally unmoved nature of suchness. Pitiable are ordinary beings, who are wholly the mind of arising and ceasing. Even when they arouse the mind to contemplate, it is the view of arising and ceasing. Now, to use this mind and view of arising and ceasing to contemplate the perfect-enlightenment sea of nature that neither arises nor ceases is entirely to turn the back on it. Hence it says one cannot arrive. “Cannot arrive” means one is driving south while the cart heads north.

Then does one who cultivates perfect enlightenment, wishing to illuminate with awareness the unmoved nature of suchness, truly have no place to begin? Our World-Honored One in his great compassion now tells us: do not worry, there is a wonderful method. What is that method? One should contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas, and of itself there will be a place of entry. The sense of this is no different from saying: at first one need not forcibly still false thoughts—though one wished to still them, it could not be done.

One need only turn toward all conditioned dharmas, which involve making and duality, and observe their ceaseless change, like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning. This causes the mind to understand clearly that all dharmas are nothing but, when conditions meet, the presently existing illusory mark of arising; in truth, arising is precisely non-arising. From this one may know that though on the surface the myriad appearances stand in dense array, at bottom they are wholly nonexistent. Contemplating and illuminating with awareness thus at every time and in every place brings inconceivable merit and virtue.

What is meant by inconceivable merit and virtue? One should know that in contemplating the principle of the conditioning of all dharmas, if one comprehends that all dharmas are empty in their very substance, one can accord with and enter the empty mark of all dharmas. When marks are empty, the nature of itself appears. Why? With marks, all dharmas are vastly different; with marks empty, all dharmas are one suchness. All dharmas being one suchness is the light of the nature appearing. The light of the nature appearing is ignorance already illuminated. Though ignorance may not yet be suddenly cut off, and may not yet suddenly merge with unmoved suchness, yet the dark merging of wisdom and principle is truly founded on this. Why? Because false thoughts from this point daily grow thinner, and when facing objects and meeting conditions one is not easily turned by them. From this we may say: to contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas is no different from contemplating the empty mark of all dharmas; to contemplate the empty mark of all dharmas is no different from contemplating unmoved suchness. In other words, to contemplate the conditioned dharmas of arising and ceasing as like a dream, like an illusion, is imperceptibly to be led into the unconditioned dharma that neither arises nor ceases. How could such merit and virtue be conceived? This second essential meaning is what we should understand even more.

Taking these two essential meanings together, one can see that to contemplate thus is like using a crane: four ounces can lift a thousand catties, without the least effort. Lightly and deftly, one parts the clouds and mist and sees the blue sky. Truly a skillful means.

Since this unworthy one began to study the Buddha’s teaching, in the first twenty years, though I practiced various methods and did various contemplations, I made no progress at all. One day, on these four lines of verse, I seemed suddenly to awaken. I practiced contemplation accordingly. At first it was half near and half far, half clear and half dim, not forming any continuous stretch, and without much effect. Then I understood that one should apply the mind with utmost effort to observe in every circumstance and condition. Even in the smallest matter, whether at a time of great contentment or great discontent, one should seal it with the principle that all is like a dream, an illusion. Even in practicing the Buddhadharma, one should seal it with the same principle. Walking, standing, sitting, and lying down, one does not depart from this. After a long time, though my work at not grasping at marks and being unmoved in suchness is still shallow, from the time I began this contemplation my mind has gradually felt empty and hollow: toward all circumstances and marks I am gradually able to remain unmoved within. In reading sutras my eyes feel a little brighter; in reciting the Buddha’s name I also feel a little more solid. Now I ask you all to try it; you will surely find it useful. One should know that for an ordinary being of this dusty world, wishing to turn the light around, there is no place to begin apart from this. Treasure it, treasure it.
Now the meaning of the preceding section and of this section will be set forth together.

The unmoved suchness spoken above is the perfect manifestation of the substance of the nature. To speak of its ultimate extent, one must reach the Buddha-stage before it can be perfect. From the first abiding stage upward it is only partially manifested; hence it is called the enlightenment of partial realization. As for those in the stage of faith, they only obtain its semblance—what is called the enlightenment of resemblance. Hence some earlier teachers explained the first “thus” above as “similar.” Yet the meaning of the line “unmoved in suchness” runs from the first arousing of the mind through to the very end without break. Therefore it should not be rigidly explained as “similar.” It should be explained as true suchness, and only then can it perfectly embrace all. Whether appearing as resemblance, as partial realization, or even as perfect manifestation, all comes from not grasping at marks. Therefore the words “marks” and “not grasping” likewise contain a deep and vast meaning and run through to the very end.

As for “marks,” whether emptiness, existence, both, or neither, all are included. The general mark of them is the two attachments, to self and to dharmas. Toward all these marks, not attaching at all is what is meant by not grasping. And even non-grasping is itself not grasped. Then one is free of it and free again; reaching having nothing to be free of, all illusions are removed. Thereupon the substance of the unmoved nature of suchness is fully revealed.

Yet the method of beginning must be to illuminate with awareness at the place where no thought has yet moved—that is, to contemplate the originally unmoved nature of suchness. This is the meaning of the Śūraṅgama Sutra’s taking the neither-arising-nor-ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and also the meaning of cultivating cessation based on the originally still nature, and thereby attaining concentration, and cultivating observation based on the originally illuminating nature, and thereby attaining wisdom. If one does not know to begin from here, one is practicing in confusion, cultivating blindly and refining in the dark—like boiling sand to make rice, which can never succeed.

Though the beginner is wholly ignorance and cannot see it by contemplating, he must deeply understand this principle and diligently practice perfect illumination. As said before: when the preceding thought has ceased and the following thought has not yet arisen, just at such a moment the single mind is deeply still, perfectly clear and bright—this is what is meant by illumination. “Perfect” means neither exerting effort nor not exerting effort, neither sinking nor floating. This is the single thread of wisdom-light, the first preparatory means for knowing illusion and being at once free of it. On the other hand, one follows this verse and contemplates all dharmas as like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning—conditioned and therefore empty. This method is an even more preparatory means within preparatory means; it is what is called knowing illusion. The two are best cultivated together.

These two methods mutually complete each other. For illuminating with awareness the original nature is working at the root, while contemplating all dharmas is working at circumstances and conditions. Moreover, the former contemplation is mostly intended as cultivating concentration; the latter is mostly intended as cultivating wisdom. Concentration can indeed produce wisdom, yet unless wisdom is first opened, that concentration cannot be accomplished either. Therefore, in their mutual assistance, the contemplation of conditioning is especially important, since by contemplating conditioning one can be led into unmoved suchness. This meaning has already been set forth in detail above.

Consider the line “thus should one contemplate them”: it carries a strong sense that nothing else will do. How earnest it is! The word “contemplate” is crucial; it means one should apply the mind with the fullest intent to observe.

The Buddha spoke this sutra originally for ordinary beings who have aroused the great mind. These two lines and one verse precisely point out where ordinary beings of the great mind should begin their work. Therefore the two contemplations, before and after, must be practiced dense and unbroken, alternating with each other. Practiced long, one will surely find a place of attainment.

The two words “thus” certainly refer to what was said above—like a dream, like an illusion. One should know that “like a dream, like an illusion” precisely means that the marks of all dharmas are originally empty; it also precisely means that the nature of all dharmas is one suchness. One can see that the words “thus” truly contain the flavor of “one suchness in all.” Therefore, to contemplate the conditioning of all dharmas is to be able to accord with and enter unmoved suchness. One who practices this contemplation can go to the bottom with a single pole and see the original nature through. Hence it says, “thus should one contemplate them,” which is to say: to contemplate all dharmas as like a dream, like an illusion, is to contemplate the one suchness in all; therefore one should practice it. The instruction is earnest and repeated—how could one pass over it in neglect?

Conditioned dharmas are not only worldly dharmas; Buddhadharma too is included. Hence it says “all.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment says: “Birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of yesterday. No arising, no ceasing; no coming, no going. What is realized has no gain, no loss, no grasping, no rejecting. What realizes has no making, no stopping, no bearing, no extinction. Within this realization there is neither subject nor object. Ultimately there is no realization, and no one who realizes. The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.” In this passage all is viewed as a dream and thereby dissolved. This is precisely what is meant by the empty mark of all dharmas, that is, the meaning of not grasping at marks. It also instructs one to contemplate all things as dream-like and so empty them, thereby according with and entering unmoved suchness. Hence it concludes: “The nature of all dharmas is equal and indestructible.” Equality is suchness; indestructibility is unmovedness. Therefore this passage of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment may fittingly be cited as a footnote to the two lines and one verse of this sutra.

In sum, whether defiled dharmas or pure dharmas: once there is such a dharma, there is duality. Once duality is established, it is conditioned and has arising and ceasing. Therefore all are like a dream, like an illusion. Yet if one wishes to realize the unconditioned dharma beyond duality, one cannot but begin cultivation from the conditioned dharma of duality, because apart from this there is no place of entry.

Not only is contemplating conditioning a conditioned dharma; even illuminating with awareness of the original nature is a conditioned dharma. Why? Because illuminating awareness is contemplation, and once there is a contemplating subject and a contemplated object, duality is established. With duality there are marks, and one falls into the conditioned.

All that this sutra speaks of is the unconditioned dharma. And it plainly says: all sages and worthies differ by virtue of the unconditioned dharma. Yet now, in instructing on proclaiming and on receiving and upholding, it causes one to contemplate conditioned dharmas. This is the greatest pivot of the whole sutra’s purport, and also the crucial pivot for students of the Buddha’s teaching. One should know that “unconditioned” means making no fabrication. If one makes no fabrication, how can delusion be removed? How can the true be realized? How can the ordinary be transformed? How can sagehood be attained? Therefore the unconditioned dharma must be accomplished out of the conditioned dharma. Hence it says “should contemplate.” The word “contemplate” has force. But the first essential meaning to be understood is this: the unconditioned dharma is the goal, and the conditioned dharma is the path borrowed to reach it.

To recognize only the unconditioned and to despise the conditioned is to cut oneself off; to cling to the conditioned without knowing the unconditioned is to draw a line around oneself. The former is what is called clinging to the nature and abandoning cultivation; the latter is what is called clinging to phenomena and ignoring principle. This is the second essential meaning to be understood.

To cultivate conditioned dharmas without clinging is precisely the unconditioned; apart from this there is no separately existing unconditioned dharma. Hence what this sutra says in its opening chapter—that in reality no being is liberated—must be carried out by liberating all beings; and that one should not abide in dharmas must be carried out by practicing giving. All that is said afterward has the same purport. Now, to liberate beings and practice giving are conditioned dharmas; no liberation and non-abiding in dharmas are unconditioned dharmas. Practiced thus, one is involved in existence yet does not abide in existence; one contemplates emptiness yet does not abide in emptiness. Though all day one practices the six pāramitās and the ten thousand practices, and all day expounds the sutra and speaks the Dharma, in truth one is all day in nirvāṇa.

From this one may know: not grasping dharmas must be accomplished out of not grasping non-dharmas; “is not” must be accomplished out of “is named”; non-attachment must be accomplished out of non-annihilation; non-substantiality must be accomplished out of non-voidness; and even no-sage-and-no-ordinary is seen within sage and ordinary; the not-one and not-different is seen within one and different; the not-coming and not-going is seen within coming and going. This is what is called the one suchness of all dharmas and the equality of all dharmas. Even non-arising and non-ceasing is seen within arising and ceasing. This meaning is: though there is arising and ceasing, in truth there is no arising and ceasing; though there is no arising and ceasing, arising and ceasing is manifested. This is what is called not abiding in birth-and-death and not abiding in nirvāṇa. Thereupon the purport of non-abiding is ultimately perfected.

And its pivot lies precisely in contemplating the conditioning of dharmas, as like a dream, like an illusion, understanding that all are empty, and thereby being non-abiding. Therefore the most essential preparatory means for a student is to contemplate thus.

To contemplate thus is to neither abolish the conditioned nor obstruct the unconditioned. Naturally and of itself, concealing and illuminating are simultaneous, and one accords with and enters, in the midst of the middle, the perfect-enlightenment sea of nature that is unmoved suchness.

A whole most profound scripture is gathered back into what is utterly plain, utterly near at hand: into a four-line verse. All sentient beings, whether of sharp or dull faculties, can accord with it and enter. This is what is called the supreme, profound, and wonderful Dharma, hard to encounter in a hundred thousand million kalpas. This is what is called true meaning.

This has the same flavor as the introductory section’s account of putting on clothes and eating food. Both point out that the Way is not far from man: it lies precisely in the ordinary affairs of daily use. One must see through them and hold firm within the ordinary affairs of daily use. Becoming a Buddha or a bodhisattva lies right therein. All the vows and practices of self-liberation and liberating others, and even such matters as bowing to the Buddha and reciting sutras, should be regarded as ordinary daily affairs, from which one does not depart even in haste or adversity, and yet one does them as though doing nothing. Only then is one near the Way.

Therefore, having gained this four-line verse, one holds not only the whole sutra but all Buddhadharma in hand; and becoming a Buddha or a bodhisattva is in hand as well. It is said that all Buddhas and the Buddhas’ anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi all come forth from this sutra. Now one knows that the Buddhas and the Dharma all come forth from contemplating all conditioned dharmas as thus and thus—like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, or lightning.

We are fortunate to have received the Buddha’s grace and been given this wonderful method. There is nothing to do but single-mindedly follow this method, receive and uphold it thus, and proclaim it thus, so that all sentient beings may contemplate thus and all realize non-arising. Only thus can we in some small measure repay the kindness of our original teacher.

The essential purport has now been concluded. As for the similes of dream and illusion and the rest, their meaning is most refined, most subtle, most wonderful; and by practicing this contemplation one may realize the Way. Now they should be explained in detail.

There are very many similes for conditioned dharmas in the Buddhist sutras. Besides the similes of dream and illusion and the rest, there are the city of the gandharvas, the moon in water, the stake in the tree, the snake of rope, flowers in space, the horns of a hare, the hair of a tortoise, and so on. Their main purport is simply to reveal the principle that all dharmas are empty and to warn ordinary beings not to take them as real, so as to break their discrimination and attachment and lead them out of delusion. The Wei translation of the Diamond Sutra has nine similes. It says: “All conditioned dharmas are like a star, a cataract, a lamp, an illusion, dew, a bubble, a dream, lightning, a cloud; thus should one contemplate them.” The Qin translation reduces them to six. The number differs, but the principle is one.

Among the six similes, the dream is the general one; illusion, bubble, shadow, dew, and lightning are the particular ones. All of them serve to make clear that things are like a dream. One of good faculties, hearing the dream simile alone, can understand that dharmas produced from conditions are empty in their very substance. Fearing that some may not yet understand, the other five similes—illusion and the rest—are spoken. If the five are understood, one may suddenly realize that ten thousand things all return to one dream. What is called a dream is one of the dharmas produced from conditions. An old saying goes: what one thinks of by day takes form in dreams by night. What one thinks of is precisely the condition that produces the dream. There are also dreams that occur without any thinking of anything, such as what the world calls a message from the spirits. Then that message is also the condition for entering the dream. Hence it is a dharma produced from conditions.

Where there is a condition there must be a cause. What is the cause of dreaming? It is the consciousness—also called the false mind. Without this cause, the condition could not be met either. Hence it is said, “The perfected man has no dreams.” For a person of the Way, though the false mind is not yet cut off, he must already be able to suppress it, and so he dreams little. From this one may know that all is made by mind alone.

Pitiable are ordinary beings: in dreams they are of course the false mind, and even in what they call their waking state they are wholly the false mind as well. Therefore what they call waking is still a dream. Why? Because from beginningless time they have been deluded and have never awakened. Had they already awakened, they would certainly not merely know that the sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, gain and loss, poverty and success in dreams are false, while still taking the sorrow and joy, parting and meeting, gain and loss, poverty and success of so-called waking hours to be real. One should know that the mind in waking hours and the mind in dreams are both false and not real. Therefore the various circumstances of waking life—whether brought about by planning or arising beyond expectation—are wholly the same in principle as entering a dream either from thinking of something by day or from a spirit’s message; and their being empty in the twinkling of an eye, with nothing whatsoever obtained, is likewise in no way different. Is waking then not dreaming? Hence the warning: like a dream. Yet people cling to it in delusion, calculating and discriminating, attached and unwilling to let go. Truly this is a fool’s talk of dreams. Hence it is said that sentient beings have never awakened. To say “like a dream” now is precisely to call them to awaken quickly. Someone may say: the principle of “like a dream,” as applied to worldly dharmas, is indeed not wrong; but Chan Master Yongming Shou said, “Greatly perform the Buddha-work within a dream.” How can Buddhadharma also be contemplated as a dream? Here there are four essential meanings that must be known. Spoken with reference to ordinary beings, there are two:

(1) To contemplate Buddhadharma as a dream means not to attach. Buddhadharma lays its weight on breaking the self. If there is attachment, how can the self be broken? Therefore it should be thoroughly dispelled. Even Buddhadharma must not be attached to, how much less worldly dharmas.

(2) One who studies the Buddha’s teaching does so in order to realize the nature. If one does not realize the nature, one cannot transcend the ordinary and enter sagehood. The substance of the nature is empty and still, and so all the work of cultivation must return to nothing-attained before it accords with the empty and still nature. To contemplate Buddhadharma as a dream causes one to diligently practice the Buddha-work while returning to utter unattainability, so that subject and object may both be gone and wisdom and principle merge in the dark.
Spoken with reference to Buddhas and bodhisattvas, there are also two meanings:

(1) Buddhas and bodhisattvas are all people who have already awakened. That they greatly perform the Buddha-work, broadly liberating beings, and yet can do things as though doing nothing is because they see it all as a dream. Seeing nirvāṇa as a dream of yesterday, they do not abide in nirvāṇa but greatly perform the Buddha-work; seeing birth-and-death as a dream of yesterday, they do not abide in birth-and-death but constantly dwell in concentration.

(2) When a bodhisattva performs the Buddha-work, it is to awaken himself and awaken others. As for the Buddha-stage, where enlightenment is already ultimate, and yet the Buddha-work is still performed: because beings without end are still within the dream, and by the compassion of shared substance he does not consider himself ultimate, he therefore constantly practices the bodhisattva path, manifesting his body among beings who have not yet awakened from the great dream, and there performs the Buddha-work. Hence Yongming said, “Greatly perform the Buddha-work within a dream.”

Summing up these four meanings, one may know that the greatly enlightened see birth-and-death and nirvāṇa as fundamentally unattainable. Hence it is said: birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are like a dream of yesterday. The sense is that to abide in birth-and-death is of course to dream, and to abide in nirvāṇa is also to dream. Only when one abides nowhere at all is one greatly enlightened. Therefore, if one abides in the dharma one cultivates, in the dharma one speaks, or in the dharma one has attained, all of it is dreaming. Hence the main purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding. Therefore it says: one should practice giving without abiding anywhere; one should arouse the bodhi mind free of marks.

In sum: to contemplate all defiled and pure dharmas as a dream is intended to penetrate the truth that all conditioned dharmas are fundamentally unattainable. When the single mind is pure, what is there to attain? If there were anything attainable, it would not be pure. Therefore one should contemplate all conditioned dharmas as a dream.

Our World-Honored One taught the Dharma for forty-nine years, and yet said that no Dharma was spoken. He also said: as to anuttarā-samyak-saṃbodhi, I attained not even the least dharma. So it is with the enlightenment of the fruition stage; and those who cultivate on the causal ground must likewise be able to know that it is so. The Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “One should carefully examine whether the mind aroused on the causal ground and the enlightenment of the fruition stage are the same or different. If on the causal ground one takes the mind of arising and ceasing as the cause of cultivation, and yet seeks the neither-arising-nor-ceasing of the Buddha-vehicle, there is no such possibility.” To have something attainable is the mind of arising and ceasing; to contemplate it as a dream, utterly unattainable, is neither arising nor ceasing. One should know that a dream is precisely a conditioned dharma. If one knows that the dream is utterly unattainable and does not deludedly cling, the conditioned dharma becomes the unconditioned dharma.

The word “like” has flavor. For the unawakened, one should contemplate that what they call waking is still like a dream, and only then can one be liberated from all and keep far from inversion. For the awakened, one should contemplate that what they call enlightenment is likewise like a dream; what harm then in entering the land of Huaxu and sporting in samādhi?

In sum, the six similes are all carried through to the very end. They are not spoken for ordinary beings alone. If the followers of the Two Vehicles know that liberating beings is like a dream, utterly unattainable, they will not sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence. If a certain class of bodhisattvas knows that seeking above and transforming below is like a dream, utterly unattainable, they can accomplish Buddhahood. Therefore to practice the contemplation of dream is precisely the precious mirror that illumines and breaks the two attachments, to self and to dharmas, and the compassionate ship that carries one across into the great sea of quiescent extinction.

From what has been said above, one may know that all conditioned dharmas are fruits produced when mind is taken as the cause, affairs are relied on as the conditions, and cause and condition meet. Apart from cause and effect there is nothing at all. Yet what is named a fruit in turn becomes a cause; what is called a cause presently summons a fruit again. Even of cause and effect themselves, then, there is no fixed form whatever. Hence it is said that they are empty in their very substance. Take dreaming: it is not that the affairs and marks are not plainly there, yet their existence is no existence. Hence it is said that dharmas produced from cause and condition are precisely provisional and precisely empty. Therefore one simile of the dream is enough to penetrate all.

But because sentient beings have long been on the deluded path, though in ordinary times they cannot but know that worldly affairs are like a dream, yet the moment a favorable or unfavorable circumstance appears before them they still cling in delusion and cannot let go. They even say: past affairs are indeed like a dream, but when circumstances are present and one experiences them distinctly in one’s own person, can one call them unreal? Therefore the Buddha further tells them: though favorable and unfavorable circumstances are distinctly experienced in one’s own person, in truth they are all like an illusion. An illusion is the magic art spoken of in the Buddhist sutras; in the present age it is called a play. The sense is: have you seen a magician and his magic? He conjures forth all kinds of flying, swimming, moving, and growing things—are they not plainly like the real? Or again, like a stage play: when the actors put on their paint and mount the stage, the wicked and the upright, the worthy and the foolish, sorrow and joy, gain and loss, their expressions come vividly to life, and can make one’s face brighten and one’s tears fall. Do you take that as real too? Would you, because their sorrow and joy are without cause and seem to be experienced in your own person, insist that it is actual fact? One should know that living in the world is the same: all that one encounters is nothing but the transformation of false consciousness and karmic conditions.

The world is a theater! All sentient beings are the various roles in the theater. When the gongs and drums are loud and the clamor is at its height, one who has wisdom should warn himself: in the twinkling of an eye one steps down from the stage. To play this role here and now is only to be pulled along by the power of karma and to finish out a stretch of karmic affinity—how could one take it as real? Just as in an opera, once one has become an actor in the play, there must be a former cause for this present fruit to appear. Of course one cannot but sing and act with all one’s heart, lest the aim one holds be missed. Yet there is certainly no one who clings to the character played in the opera and takes it as himself. What is the actor’s aim? Fame and money. So too with being a person. To come in this life and be this person is only to fill for a while one role in this play. The actor can still avoid clinging to the character he plays and taking him as himself; how can we mistake the role we temporarily fill for ourselves? One should know that cause and effect are hard to escape and are to be feared. Since one temporarily fills this role, one naturally cannot but sing and act with all one’s heart, lest the aim be missed. But one must never take fame and profit alone as the aim; one must recognize clearly one’s own inherent family treasure as the aim. What is the family treasure? It is the three jewels of the self-nature.

One must clearly awaken to this: in playing out this false play, one must neither mistake cause and effect and drag down the self-nature, nor mistake the false play for the real and lose the self-nature. Therefore, just when the music is loud and clear and the whole audience is watching, one should awaken oneself and realize: this act of illusory play is not my original face. One should vow to return to one’s first garments. Only then, when the gongs and drums fall silent and the wind blows the clouds apart, will one not be vexed and grieved, at a loss what to do with one’s hands and feet. Hence it is said that one should contemplate as an illusion.

The World-Honored One in his great compassion still feared that beings, clinging in delusion, would not awaken, thinking that though all human affairs may indeed be like an illusion, yet when one considers one’s own body and life it is in the end hard to let go. For in their minds they can understand that worldly affairs are like an illusion, yet they still take the vast world and their precious physical body to be truly existent, and so cannot let go. Therefore the Buddha further tells them: like a bubble, like a shadow. “Like a bubble” is a simile for the world; “like a shadow” is a simile for the physical body. Why? What is called a bubble is formed when water is stirred by wind and dashed into foam; and the world is formed by all sentient beings, within the sea of nature, raising the wind of ignorance and creating this shared karma, which then congeals. Hence it is likened to a bubble. What is called a shadow appears when the sun, moon, or lamplight shines upon something; and the physical body is transformed and manifested from the light of the nature. Hence it is likened to a shadow. Since this world and this body are of the same conditioned production as bubble and shadow, one can see that body and world are likewise of the same falseness as bubble and shadow. How can one deludedly take them as real?

This meaning is stated most clearly in the Śūraṅgama Sutra. It says: “Acknowledging delusion within enlightenment, one makes of it a murky void. Within the murky void, one knits darkness into form. Form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body.” This passage says that the enlightened nature, perfect and bright, is great beyond any outside and small beyond any inside. Originally there is no such thing as empty space, a world, or a physical body; all come about because sentient beings’ enlightened nature is obstructed, so that what was originally perfect and bright becomes murky. What is murky is the dizzy, turbid appearance. Since one has already failed to awaken, one instead takes the murky as empty space. Hence “one makes of it a murky void.” This comes from acknowledging delusion within enlightenment. “Acknowledging delusion within enlightenment” means that one supposes oneself enlightened when in fact one is still deluded. Why? Because one takes the murky for empty space. Since empty space is murky, one further knots this darkness into form. Hence, “within the murky void, one knits darkness into form.” Form means the four great elements, earth, water, fire, and wind. It refers precisely to the world and to all the marks of material form, sentient and insentient. First one takes the murky as empty space, then one takes the darkness knotted together as the world, and further one takes what is mixed of form and false thought as one’s precious body. Hence, “form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body.” The word “acknowledging” in the first line runs straight through to the end. The two words “false thought” also run through the whole passage, above and below.

Why does one mistakenly acknowledge? Because there is false thought. False thought is another name for consciousness. Feeling, perception, and mental formation are mental factors of consciousness; therefore the words “false thought” here refer to the four aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness among the five aggregates. The “mark” in “the thought-mark becomes the body” is the word “form” above; “thought” is false thought. The bodies of all sentient beings are nothing but a provisional union of the five aggregates. Hence it says: “form mixed with false thought, the thought-mark becomes the body”—meaning that the marks of form of the four great elements are mixed and joined with the false thoughts of feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness to form this illusory body. This passage plainly teaches that empty space, the world, and the physical body are all transformed and manifested from sentient beings’ dizzy, turbid false thoughts. False thoughts are themselves unreal and cease and arise in an instant. How could the body and world they manifest be real?

Everyone knows that a bubble in water is extremely frail and thinnest, most easily destroyed. They do not realize that the world is the same. Let no one say that rivers and mountains endure through the ages. Though the whole world may not be destroyed all at once, yet hills sink into valleys and valleys rise into hills, mulberry fields become the sea and the sea becomes mulberry fields, and changes arise from time to time. This is enough to prove that it is at every moment within formation and destruction. This is a matter that those of somewhat greater years have constantly experienced; it is no mere speculative talk.

Moreover the Śūraṅgama Sutra says: “Space is born within the great enlightenment, like a single bubble rising in the sea. The outflows’ countries of fine dust all depend on space and are born. When the bubble bursts, space is originally nothing—how much less the three existences.” “Outflows” makes clear that they must perish; “fine dust” makes clear that they are exceedingly minute. “The three existences” means the three realms. This passage says that the murky void is within the great sea of perfect enlightenment like a single bubble on the sea—bubble meaning foam. And the countries of fine dust are still more things clinging to the bubble of the sea. When the bubble bursts, there is not even the murky void, much less the three realms. All students should constantly contemplate this principle. The void that one acknowledges is still a murky, dizzy, turbid appearance, and is itself as tiny as a bubble. How much less the world, how much less this body—what are they worth counting? How can one cast aside the true, perfect, and bright sea of nature, which contains the void and encompasses the three realms, and acknowledge instead a tiny, frail, impermanent floating bubble?

As for a shadow: looked at from afar it seems to exist; examined in fact, it is nothing. This body is the same: it falsely appears to exist, but examined in fact it is nothing. For example, a person’s reflection in a mirror appears when it is reflected; fat or thin, long or short, not the least bit is off. This body is the same: because the mind creates karma, it appears following karma; long life or early death, beauty or ugliness, cause and effect are hard to escape. Great Master Si of Nanyue said: the pure mind is like a mirror, ordinary and sage are like the images. This makes clear that the body is visible because the pure mind inherently possesses the nature of seeing, just as an image is visible because a bright mirror inherently possesses the nature of reflecting. How can one, because it is visible, mistakenly take it as truly existent? Moreover, within the seeing-nature of the pure mind there is originally no such body; it is merely a shadow manifested by the seeing-nature. It is also like the reflecting nature of a bright mirror, within which there is originally no such image; it is merely a shadow manifested by the reflecting nature. All that has been said above still takes the illusory body as viewed from the pure mind, making clear that it is a shadow manifested by the pure mind. If one speaks in terms of the illusory body in its very substance, it is likewise like a shadow. Why? Because apart from the five aggregates it is utterly unattainable. And moreover the form among the five aggregates is precisely the four great elements; since the four great elements are like a floating bubble, the remaining four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formation, and consciousness—are likewise nothing but false. (They are called false thoughts, hence false.) Thus the five aggregates themselves are already utterly unattainable; how much less the illusory body, provisionally joined of the five aggregates—its seeming existence and actual nonexistence can be known. “Utterly unattainable” means that its existence is no existence. It is exactly like a shadow, which merely dazzles and deceives the eye; in truth it is originally empty.

What all ordinary beings most cling to as truly existent are the consciousness-mind, the world, and their own bodies. Now each is refuted in turn: the consciousness-mind is like an illusion (it was said earlier that the world is a theater and all beings are the roles in the theater, all nothing but the transformation of consciousness-mind and karmic conditions—hence “like an illusion”), the world is like a bubble, and this body is like a shadow. If body, mind, and world are still false and unreal, then all other conditioned marks of dharmas may be known likewise. Yet beings on the deluded path, though they know that body, mind, and world are unreal, may still drift along in negligence and fail to diligently practice the contemplation of dream, illusion, bubble, and shadow. Therefore they are again roused and spurred: like dew, like lightning. Dew dries at sunrise and does not remain long; lightning arises and ceases in a flash, passing in an instant. It is as is said, life lies within a breath. One should press on with one’s practice as though putting out a fire on one’s head. Taken together with the five similes of illusion and the rest, this is to contemplate that all things are like a dream, existing yet not existing. Hence it is said: the five contemplations of illusion and the rest are particular; the contemplation of dream is general.

Contemplating these six similes is, it is true, contemplating the empty mark of all dharmas — which is precisely contemplating the nature of suchness, because nature and mark are from the first interfused. So by contemplating dependent arising one may enter the unmoving suchness. Hence the nature of the unconditioned Dharma is approached by contemplating the marks of conditioned dharmas as dream and illusion: thus one clings to neither extreme, and so accords with the middle way. This meaning has been discussed in full above.

Let us now explain it again by the three natures and the three non-natures. In the six similes, whichever one simile you take up, the principle of the three natures and three non-natures can be made clear. Here we shall take the general simile of the dream; the rest can be known by the same pattern.

The three natures and the three non-natures are found in the Laṅkāvatāra Sutra and in the various sutras and treatises of the Dharma-characteristics school. They are the essential doctrine of that school. The Buddha set forth dharma-marks precisely in order to make this clear. If one does not know to give it weight, but only dissects minute details — though one may analyze every dharma-mark most exhaustively, one is still counting sand in the ocean and has lost the point of what one follows. You should know that students of the nature school, too, ought to be thoroughly familiar with the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures, for this meaning runs through both nature and marks. If you know it, you can understand dependent arising and the emptiness of nature more thoroughly, and your cultivation of contemplation will be more effective. What was said above about the contemplation of dream is still only a general contemplation of the main point; if one contemplates according to the principle of the three natures and three non-natures, one enters deeper and subtler ground.

What are the three natures? First, the nature of pervasive imagining; second, the nature of dependence on others; third, the nature of perfect accomplishment. Pervasive imagining means universal calculation and clinging. It is what the nature school regularly calls discrimination, clinging, grasping at conditions, ignorance, the deluded mind, deluded thought, and so on. The nature school also calls it the nature of discrimination. This is deluded thought; why call it a nature? The point is to make clear that although it is ignorance and deluded thought, it is nonetheless a transformation of the true mind and does not exist apart from the nature of reality. The Dharma-characteristics school names it the nature of pervasive imagining, speaking only with respect to the stage of ordinary beings; the nature school names it the nature of discrimination, which covers both ordinary and noble. The nature of discrimination at the noble stage means that the noble ones manifest responsively according to conditions and teach according to capacity with not the slightest error; it appears to involve discrimination because it is viewed from the side of living beings, but it does not mean that those at the noble stage still give rise to conceptual discrimination. This should be understood.

The nature of dependence on others is what the nature school calls dependent arising, arising from conditions, and arising from nature. It is precisely the marks and functions that the essential nature brings forth in accord with conditions. Marks and functions are never apart from the nature-essence; without the nature-essence there would be no marks and functions. Hence it is called the nature of dependence on others. To depend on means to follow; others refers to conditions.

As for the nature of perfect accomplishment: perfect means complete, and accomplished means inherently possessed. The words perfect and accomplished are spoken with respect to the essence, making clear that from the first it is complete and fully endowed and is not something manufactured. They also refer to marks and functions, meaning that marks and functions are inherently possessed by the essence, their pure virtues complete. Real means true. This is what the nature school regularly calls the Dharma-realm, suchness, tathatā, the true mind, the mark of reality, perfect enlightenment, the mind of intrinsic purity, and so on — its names are numberless. The nature school also calls it the nature of reality.

What are the three non-natures? First, the mark of no-mark; second, the non-nature of birth; third, the non-nature of the supreme meaning. The word no is very supple: it carries the sense of not, and the sense of emptying, that is, that one must not cling.

As for the mark of no-mark: living beings, in regard to all things, falsely reckon that there is a self and there are dharmas, and cling to them — this is what is called pervasive imagining. They do not realize that the marks of self and the marks of dharmas clung to by pervasive imagining arise entirely from mistaken recognition, as when one takes a rope for a snake. Not only is the snake's mark unreal; the rope's mark too — was it ever truly real? Hence it is called the mark of no-mark: illusory marks are not the nature of reality. One should realize that within the nature there are from the first no marks, and so one should not cling to marks but be without them; that is the nature.

As for the non-nature of birth: birth means birth from conditions. All dharmas merely, by the coming together of causes and conditions, falsely appear as marks of arising — this is what is called dependence on others. Since they are thus born of conditions, it is clear that all dharmas have from the first no substantial reality; their essence is only pure nature. It is just as the arising of a rope also comes about through the gathering of causes and conditions: the rope is not a substantial reality; its substance is hemp. Hence it is called the non-nature of birth: dharmas born of conditions are from the first not the true nature. One should realize that although dharmas born of conditions take the nature as their essence, within the nature-essence there is no such birth from conditions, and so one should not cling to birth from conditions but be without it; that is the nature.

As for the non-nature of the supreme meaning: the nature of suchness is the essence of all dharmas; it is called the foremost meaning, also called the supreme meaning. This nature is real, inherently possessed by living beings, from the first complete — what is called perfect accomplishment. Yet the supreme meaning is also a name, just as hemp is also a provisional name. Hence it is called the non-nature of the supreme meaning: the supreme meaning too is a name and is not the nature. One should realize that within the nature of reality there is from the first no name of supreme meaning, and so one should not cling even to the supreme meaning but be without it; that is the nature of reality.

The nature school sets up its names somewhat differently. It calls the mark of no-mark the nature of no-mark, meaning that only when one does not cling to marks is it the true nature. It calls the non-nature of birth the nature of no-birth, meaning that only when one does not cling to birth from conditions is it the true nature. It calls the non-nature of the supreme meaning the nature of no-nature, meaning that only when one does not cling even to the nature is it the true nature. This meaning precisely shows that marks, being apart from the nature, have no substance, and the nature does not exist apart from marks either. In meaning it is all the more complete.

Therefore the nature of no-nature is also called the non-nature of truth, meaning that only when even the view of reality is absent is it the nature of reality. It is also called the non-nature of no-nature; the second no means empty, nothing — meaning that only when one does not cling to emptiness and nothingness is it the nature of reality.
The names and meanings have now been briefly explained. We should next take the simile of the dream to make clear the principle of the three natures and three non-natures.

The Buddha taught the three natures and three non-natures in order to reveal the interfusion of nature and marks. Those with wisdom should surely understand the principle of the three natures and three non-natures so as to penetrate both nature and marks; then they can be unattached to emptiness and existence alike and accord with the middle way.

And this sutra has us contemplate all conditioned dharmas as a dream because, by forming such a contemplation, one can penetrate the principle of the three natures and three non-natures. In other words: only one who understands the three natures and three non-natures can thoroughly comprehend that all conditioned dharmas are like a dream.

So now let us expound the meaning of being like a dream together with the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures, in the hope that both meanings may be thoroughly understood. As for the other five similes — illusion and the rest — they were originally spoken to prove the meaning of being like a dream. So although we speak here only of the dream, the meaning is already complete.

You should know that in the pure mind there are from the first no marks — this is called the nature of reality, just as when the mind is pure there are no dream-marks. But because the true nature follows conditions, it brings forth marks of body and mind (this means the deluded mind, that is, consciousness) and of the world. This is called the nature of dependence on others — no different from the marks of dream-realms that appear in accord with conditions when one falls asleep. Then ordinary people, not understanding that all conditioned dharmas are illusory marks born of conditions and that their birth is from the first no-birth, fall to reckoning and clinging, taking the unreal as real; this is called the nature of pervasive imagining. It is just as foolish folk, not knowing that the dream is an illusory mark born of conditions, existing yet not existing, cling to the dream-realm as real.
Therefore, if you know that the marks of dream-realms are all transformations of the one mind and that existing they do not exist, you should know that the nature of no-mark is likewise.

Now all dharmas are nothing but mind-made; hence they are called conditioned. Since conditioned dharmas are all mind-made, it is clear that the mind-nature is the true essence. All conditioned dharmas are merely marks that arise in accord with conditions by relying on the mind and leaning on events. That is why whatever has marks is illusory. How could one cling to them as real? To cling to them is to be deluded about marks and blind to the nature. Why? Because the nature is from the first without marks.

If you know that the mind has from the first no dream and that dreams arise only from the perfuming of deluded thought, and that deluded thought is itself unreal, so that the dreams it perfumes into being exist yet do not exist, then you should know that the nature of no-birth is likewise. Now all conditioned dharmas are marks of birth that falsely appear through the meeting of conditions; it is clear that within the nature-essence there is from the first no birth. Therefore all conditioned dharmas must not be clung to as real, and even their illusory marks born of conditions must not remain in the mind. If they remain, one is still blind to the nature. Why? Because the nature is not born of conditions.

If you know that the mind in dreaming and the mind awake are not two minds, but that because of sleep it is named the dream-mind, and that in truth apart from the dream-mind there is no separate waking mind, then you should know that the nature of no-nature is likewise. The deluded mind and the true mind are from the first non-dual; only because of ignorance and non-awakening is it named the deluded mind. If ignorance becomes clear and non-awakening becomes awakening, the deluded mind is the true mind — just as, if one does not fall asleep, the mind in dreaming is originally the waking mind. Therefore a cultivator must not, apart from the deluded mind, cling to a separate true mind. In other words, one should not annihilate form in order to reveal emptiness, nor annihilate marks in order to see the nature. To do so is still to be blind to the nature. Why? Because only in not clinging to the nature is there the nature of reality. And why is that? If there is any grasping, it becomes the mark of self and the view of self, and is no longer the mind of intrinsic purity.

What has been said above uses the meaning of being like a dream to explain the three natures and three non-natures; thus the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures is thoroughly illumined. And again it uses the meaning of the three natures and three non-natures to explain being like a dream; thus the meaning of being like a dream can also be thoroughly illumined. Reviewing what has been said about the three natures and three non-natures, one may know that the essential work lies only in not giving rise to pervasive imagining; then dependence on others is itself perfect accomplishment. Why? Because when one reckons and clings to neither nature nor marks, though marks blaze forth, the mind is from the first without marks; though one manifests entering birth and death, the nature is from the first without birth. Reckoning is discrimination, which is the sixth consciousness; clinging is the seventh consciousness. This is ignorance and non-awakening; this is the view of self.

Therefore the single main purport of this sutra lies in non-abiding, which is to break the self. Reviewing what has been said about being like a dream, one may know that the contemplation of dream goes through to the very end: from coarse to fine, from shallow to deep, from first cultivation to the ultimate. Every gate of practice is nothing but this contemplation. For the word dream is spoken to illustrate ignorance and non-awakening; and then the word like illustrates that ignorance and non-awakening seems to exist but is truly not, that the nature is from the first not existent. How exquisitely apt, how exactly true. Nor is that all: like a dream means seeming to dream. Seeming to dream precisely shows that all conditioned dharmas exist yet do not exist, and also shows that all conditioned dharmas do not exist yet do exist. Seeing that they exist yet do not exist, one must not cling to existence; seeing that they do not exist yet do exist, one must not cling to emptiness. So the words like a dream do not merely have us contemplate existence as a dream; they have us contemplate emptiness and existence alike as a dream. If one can truly see all conditioned dharmas as existing yet not existing, what hinders one from seeing all conditioned dharmas as not existing yet existing? This is called doing the Buddha's work in a dream on a grand scale. When a student first sets hand to the task and forms this perfect and sudden wondrous contemplation, then he clings neither to the real nor to the unreal, nor even to nothingness. This is what this sutra calls having no mark of self, no mark of dharmas, and no mark of non-dharmas — empty through and through. Then though he moves among existence, he does not abide in existence; though he practices emptiness, he does not abide in emptiness. Thus he can enter, in the middle of the middle, the true mark that is neither mark nor non-mark, and so be unmoving in suchness.

This is non-abiding while moving among existence and practicing emptiness, which is precisely the contemplation that is itself calm abiding. And moving among existence and emptiness while non-abiding is precisely the calm abiding that is itself contemplation. So to form such a contemplation is to practice calm abiding and contemplation together, and so to make concentration and wisdom equal. Attaining realization in this way, one can reach the still and ever-illumining, the illumining and ever-still — stillness and illumination at one and the same time. Hence it is said that all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.

In sum: the whole of the Diamond Prajñā, its wondrous purport of non-abiding, rests entirely on not grasping at marks, on being unmoving in suchness. And the way to reach not grasping at marks and being unmoving in suchness rests entirely on this: all conditioned dharmas are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, and like lightning — thus should they be contemplated. Every student should enter by following this contemplation. This contemplation is precisely the Diamond sword of wisdom, which nothing hard can resist and no ignorance or affliction can escape. Therefore one should expound it thus and uphold it thus, forever circulating this unsurpassed great Dharma that perpetuates the Buddha-seed.
(C) Next, the formal conclusion on circulating the sutra.

[When the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra, the Elder Subhūti, together with the monks, the nuns, the laymen, and the laywomen, and all the worlds of gods, humans, asuras, and the rest, having heard what the Buddha said, were all greatly delighted, and they believed, accepted, honored, and practiced it.]

The words when the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra mean that this profoundly deep sutra had been spoken to the very end, with no meaning left unmanifest. The word finished answers precisely to the rejoicing and practicing that follow, showing that the capacities and the teaching met each other and that the great assembly was able to hear and to put it into practice. It also shows that believing, upholding, and transmitting it will go on forever without end: though it is called finished, in truth it was never finished.

The Elder is the one whose capacity the teaching met, and so he is listed first. Next are listed the four assemblies, all of them disciples of the Buddha's gate. The monks (which means mendicants, destroyers of evil, dreaded by Māra, and so on) and the nuns are the two orders of renunciates. The novices (a novice means one who rests in kindness, ceasing evil and practicing kindness, and is also called one diligent in the precepts) who have not yet received full ordination, and the novice nuns, are included as well. Laymen and laywomen are here rendered as pure-faith men and pure-faith women, also called male and female lay followers, meaning those who purify the three karmas and believe in and honor the path, and are fit to draw near the Three Jewels and to serve and make offerings to them. These are the two lay assemblies. A lay person who wishes to enter the Buddha's gate must first request a monk to confer the three refuges. If there is no monk, he may request a nun. This is formally entering the gate of the Three Jewels, and one may be called a disciple of the Buddha, also a disciple of the Three Jewels. When he then receives the five precepts he is called a layman or laywoman; without the five precepts he does not deserve the name. Going further, he may receive the bodhisattva precepts. Of the bodhisattva precepts, some are spoken universally for renunciates and lay people alike, such as the ten major and forty-eight minor precepts set out in the Brahmā Net Sutra; some are spoken specifically for the two lay assemblies, such as the six major and twenty-eight minor precepts set out in the Upāsaka Precepts Sutra. A lay person who examines himself and finds he can keep them one by one as a renunciate does may receive them together with renunciates; otherwise he had better receive the six major and twenty-eight minor. For once the precepts are received they must be upheld; if one receives them and does not uphold them, the offense is not small. One must weigh the matter carefully before receiving them. After receiving the bodhisattva precepts, one is called a bodhisattva-precept layman or laywoman. If one has not yet taken the three refuges formally, one is called only a faithful man or faithful woman, not a disciple of the Buddha, nor a layman or laywoman. Laymen and laywomen may all expound sutras and teach the Dharma and be Dharma masters; only they may not be masters of refuge and precepts, because they have not themselves received full ordination. The three refuges are themselves precepts. Nowadays there are those who seek refuge from a lay spiritual friend — this is a mistake. You should know that to seek refuge is to seek the transmission of the three refuges as precepts; this may be sought only from a renunciate spiritual friend. If one seeks from a lay spiritual friend instruction in sutras and Dharma, becoming his student and taking him as teacher, there is certainly no objection; and if that person's vow is sincere and he is fit to teach, the spiritual friend likewise should not simply refuse him harshly. Whether in a gathering place or on the road, the two lay assemblies should respectfully yield and let renunciates go first. Though renunciates and lay people are alike children of the Buddha, in terms of order the monk is like the eldest son, and after him come the nun, the novice, the novice nun, the layman, and the laywoman — the order must not be confused.

You should know that renunciates have cut off affection, left the dust of the world behind, and already stand among those who uphold the Three Jewels; how could the two lay assemblies, mired in the five desires and trailing mud and water, compare with them? Therefore they should be respected. Even a monk who breaks the precepts must not be slighted. Why? You should know that the precepts of renunciation are numerous, dense, and grave: a monk's full ordination has two hundred and fifty rules; a nun's full ordination has more than three hundred and seventy. With a moment's heedlessness one has already transgressed. The word upholding is easily said, but how hard it is. Even novices and novice nuns receive ten precepts, twice as many as lay people. How can one lightly ridicule them? If one truly knows that their words and conduct contradict each other, or that they fail to keep the pure rules, one may respect them from afar — this follows the Buddha's institution, what is called silent censure. Silent means not proclaiming their faults; censure means keeping one's distance. The same applies to lay people whose words and conduct contradict each other. This is the duty a cultivator should keep, and it must not be neglected.

In sum, if the Buddha-Dharma is to flourish, there must be, among both renunciates and lay people, those of lofty practice and weighty virtue whom the many accept, to serve as leaders; and the government must be clear and bright, with the principal men in it also able to believe in the Three Jewels, so that protecting and ordering one another, it may at last succeed. By the Buddha's institution, if a renunciate transgresses the Buddha-Dharma, the matter goes to the leading elders of the Saṅgha, who judge it by the Buddha's Vinaya. If he also breaks the laws of the state, then with the consent of those leading elders he must first be unfrocked, and only afterwards may he be judged by worldly law. And above all, at the time of tonsure and ordination the qualifications must be strictly chosen: this is the way to rectify the root and purify the source.

The Sahā world is one great trichiliocosm. Within it there are a billion four-continent worlds, a billion heavens of the six desires, and so on. Moreover, when the Buddha spoke the Dharma, bodhisattvas, gods, dragons, and others from countless worlds in the ten directions came to the assembly — very many indeed. Hence it says all the worlds. To speak of gods and asuras is to include the eight classes. The word humans here refers generally to those beyond the four assemblies. That bodhisattvas are not mentioned has two meanings. First, this sutra was spoken at the ninth assembly of the great prajñā gathering, and bodhisattvas were already listed in full at the earlier assemblies, so they are omitted here. Second, this sutra is spoken for those who have resolved upon the Mahāyāna, who have resolved upon the supreme vehicle; one may see that all present in the assembly were bodhisattvas-mahāsattvas who had resolved upon the unsurpassed bodhi mind, and so they are not listed separately.

That they were all greatly delighted means that hearing this great Dharma their minds opened and their understanding was released — this is delight. And knowing that to believe, accept, honor, and practice it is to shoulder the Tathāgata's burden, that they would attain bodhi and have hope of Buddhahood, which is no small matter — therefore they were greatly delighted. Every one of the assembly was like this, and so all were greatly delighted.

Faith means the faith whose mind does not oppose; acceptance means understanding, the understanding that deeply comprehends the purport. Because they had the faith that does not oppose and the acceptance that deeply comprehends, they therefore honored and practiced it. To honor means to revere and follow, that is, to follow the purport set out in the sutra. The word practice covers both benefiting oneself and benefiting others: having honored and practiced it oneself, one further spreads this sutra abroad and expounds it for others, causing all living beings to be without exception greatly delighted. Thus to believe and accept, thus to honor and practice — one must let the water of wisdom flow on forever and the lineage of Dharma be forever unobstructed, transmitted through dust-calendar aeons without stagnation, reaching all kinds of beings without omission. Then throughout the Dharma-realm and to the end of time, wherever this sutra is, there is where the Buddha speaks the Dharma. The earlier phrase when the Buddha had finished speaking this sutra is spoken only with respect to the circumstances of one time. The compilers' intent was that the whole great assembly would practice according to the teaching and the Buddha-seed would never be cut off; and so our World-Honored One's speaking of this sutra in truth has no time of finishing at all. Not only did those who compiled this sutra possess this vast vow: we today who speak it, who hear it, who initiate this Dharma assembly and who sustain it, are likewise all greatly delighted, believing, accepting, honoring, and practicing it, and share this same vow. To possess this vow is truly to believe and accept, truly to honor and practice, truly to rejoice. Herein precisely do we repay the Buddha's kindness. I, unwise, am ashamed that in this deep sutra I have not fulfilled the measure of its exposition; I have but spoken one drop of the great ocean. Yet even this one drop already holds the taste of the whole sea. I only pray that all spiritual friends may enter from true faith into pure faith, and from the conditioned realize the unconditioned, adorning the Buddha-lands with these practices and vows and converting living beings; then one may become a Buddha in this very body — how much more than merely being assured of birth in the West.

blocks.text: 1. Collation Notes on the Diamond Sutra

inline.s: This edition follows throughout the Tang dynasty manuscript from the Dunhuang stone chamber, and the text written by Liu Gongquan is one of the scriptures hidden in that chamber. Photographic reprints have long circulated in the world and can be checked against it. Therefore in the collation notes Liu's text is listed first, and the various texts consulted for comparison follow. I shall now set out in full, before the collation notes, the name of each edition relied upon and whether a separate edition of it circulates, so that checking may be easy.

The colophon after Liu's text reads: On the sixth day of the fourth month of the fourth year of Changqing, the court gentleman Liu Gongquan wrote it out for the monk-registrar Zhun of the Right Street. As to Liu's text: during the Xuantong reign of the Qing, the Youzheng Book Company of Shanghai gathered more than ten items from the stone chamber's holdings and reproduced them in collotype under the title Secret Treasures of the Stone Chamber. Liu's text is one of those treasures. Changqing is the reign title of Emperor Muzong of Tang.

Weng's text: the fifty-seventh year of the Qianlong reign, cyclical year renzi. Written out by Weng Fanggang. His colophon reads: followed the stone text of Dharma Master Daoyong of the Southern Tang. As Weng's text follows a Five Dynasties stone engraving of the Southern Tang, it is listed before the Song canon. A lithographic gift edition presently exists.

The Song canon: printed at the Qisha Yansheng Monastery of Pingjiang Prefecture in the Shaoding reign of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song — the so-called Qisha canon. This canon was begun in the fourth year of Shaoding and completed in the second year of Zhida of Emperor Wuzong of Yuan, eighty years from first to last before the work was finished. It was originally kept at the Wolong and Kaiyuan monasteries in Xi'an, and later moved to the Shaanxi Provincial Library. The Shanghai Society for the Photographic Reproduction of the Song Edition of the Canon is at present reproducing it.

Zhang's text: the second year of Baoyou of Emperor Lizong of the Southern Song, cyclical year jiayin. Written out by Zhang Chuliao, that is, Zhang Jizhi. His own colophon reads: followed the edition collated by the Tiantai teaching monk Zongyin. In the fourth year of Kangxi of the Qing, cyclical year yisi, Da Chongguang and others traced and engraved it on stone for the Shibi Hut at Mount Jiao. Note that the second year of Baoyou is more than twenty years after Shaoding. Its sentences differ slightly from the Qisha canon. Rubbings exist. There is also a lithographic gift edition written out by Wang Daxie in the seventeenth year of the Republic, following Zhang's text.

The Diamond Sutra with Commentary and Subcommentary, annotated by the monk Huijing of Jiguo Monastery of the Tang. Before the commentary stands a preface by Chu Liang of Henan, erudite of the Changtai Hall of the Tang, a contemporary of Master Hui. After it comes a colophon by the Japanese Sanyin of Danyang, which says in brief: this commentary did not circulate in China, nor was it seen in Japan. Recently Master Yikong obtained the true text and published it for lasting transmission. A treasure long hidden has in one morning shone forth its radiance — one may say it has met its time. Early autumn of the second year of Xiangbao, cyclical year dingyou. Note that the Japanese Xiangbao dingyou is the fifty-sixth year of Kangxi of our Qing. When the sutra text was incorporated is unclear. Collated against Liu's text, the words and sentences largely agree, and it lacks one passage of the Wei translation; it must precede the other combined editions, and so it is listed first.

The Diamond Sutra with Commentary, annotated by the monk Sengzhao of the Later Qin. It has a preface by the Japanese monk Jingxiong, which says: long ago it was brought back from China by the Great Master Cijue, and was kept secret in famous mountains for nine hundred years. Recently the Chan man Zufang brought it out to show me. I sighed and said: among commentaries on this sutra, Master Zhao's comes first; among commentaries that came to the East, this one also came first; and that it has appeared after all the other commentaries were already in circulation — is this not a matter of time and conditions? The Great Master of Tiantai once lectured on this sutra relying solely on Master Zhao, just as in expounding the Contemplation Sutra he relied solely on Jingying. If it is cut and circulated, how great will its benefit be? Summer of the twelfth year of Baoli, cyclical year renwu. Note that the Japanese Baoli renwu is the twenty-seventh year of Qianlong of our Qing, one hundred and seventy-two years ago. Going back nine hundred years from that puts it about the beginning of the Xiantong reign of Emperor Yizong, late in our Tang. When the sutra text was incorporated is likewise unknown. It differs here and there from the Southern Tang stone engraving and the Changshui Record of Definitive Editing. It has also added the sixty-two characters of the Wei translation, with a note beneath them saying: these sixty-two characters are absent from Zhao's text, and the Tiantai subcommentary has no sectioning either; but since all other texts have this passage, it is retained here. So one may know that it must be later than the combined edition of Hui's commentary. The two books above are both found in the Continuation of the Canon reproduced by the Commercial Press, and have no separate editions. (Gu Nong notes: the copy in the Continuation of the Canon was once engraved at the Ganzhou Sutra-Engraving Office in the ninth year of the Republic by Ding Weisen and others, following the edition collated by Li Duanfu.)
Master Zhiyi's Subcommentary on the Diamond Sutra, spoken by Zhiyi of Tiantai of the Sui; engraved at Jinling in the thirty-third year of Guangxu of the Qing.
The Meaning Subcommentary on the Diamond Sutra, composed by Jizang of Jiaxiang of the Sui; engraved at Jinling in the sixth year of the Republic.
The Praising Exposition of the Diamond Sutra, composed by Kuiji of the Great Ci'en Monastery of the Tang; engraved at Jinling in the sixth year of the Republic.

The Essential Compilation of Subcommentaries and Treatises on the Diamond Sutra, set forth by Zongmi of the Great Xingfu Monastery of the Tang; engraved at Beiping in the eleventh year of the Republic. Note that the four books above were all obtained from Japan. The Meaning Subcommentary originally had no sutra text; the text was incorporated when it was engraved at Jinling, and so it agrees with the presently circulating edition. The sutra text incorporated into the other three books either follows their old form or does not follow it in full, and so they agree with the circulating edition in some places and differ in others. The separate editions can be collated against the Continuation of the Canon.

The Combined Subcommentary and Record on the Diamond Sutra, engraved at Beiping in the nineteenth year of the Republic. The subcommentary is the Essential Compilation of Subcommentaries and Treatises; the record is the Record of Definitive Editing composed by the monk Zixuan of Changshui in the Song. Note that the Continuation of the Canon contains the sectional combination of subcommentary and record by the Ming monk Dabing, recut in the forty-seventh year of Qianlong of the Qing after an old Yunqi edition; by it one may examine how the sutra text of Ming times differed from the present edition.
Collation Notes
How should one abide?

(Identical in Liu's text, Weng's text, the Song canon, Zhang's text, the Ming engraving, and Hui's, Zhao's, and the Essential Compilation and three combined editions. The presently circulating edition and the early Qing edition read: how should one abide, agreeing with the wording of the Later Zhou. Note that the Praising Exposition, in quoting the sutra, also reads how should one abide.)
If not having thought, and not without thought.

(Identical in Liu's text and down to the Ming engraving, and in Hui's commentary, Zhao's commentary, Zhi's subcommentary, the Praising Exposition, the Essential Compilation, the five combined editions, and the present circulating edition. In early Qing engraved editions some add the character if before not without thought, noting: the ancient texts do not have it. Note that since the ancient texts do not have it, how could it be added indiscriminately? Collating all the editions I have seen, it appears that from late Tang onward the sutra text was successively enlarged and altered by people, and that the most additions and alterations were made between the Ming and Qing.)
If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of a being, or the mark of a life, then he is not a bodhisattva.
(In Zhao's combined edition the two characters bodhisattva are absent after if; all other editions have them.)
Then one sees the Tathāgata.

(Identical in Liu's text, Weng's text, the Song canon, Zhang's text, and Hui's, Zhao's, and Zhi's subcommentary and the three combined editions. The circulating edition reads then as that is. So do all Ming and Qing engravings.)
On these chapter phrases.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only Zhao's combined edition reads: these on the chapter phrases.)
Then one clings to self, person, being, and life.
(All editions ancient and modern agree. Only the early Qing engraving reads that is for then.)
Why? If one grasps the mark of non-Dharma.
